items.title: Tech Gifts That Won’t Rot Their Brains
items.description: Binge-watching. Doomscrolling. Rabbit-holing. Brain-rotting. These, it seems, are the behaviors encouraged by our computers and digital devices—intoxicating masterworks of engineering that we stumble away from, glassy-eyed. It’s a sad state of affairs, especia
items.author: Joshua Rothman
paragraphs: Binge-watching. Doomscrolling. Rabbit-holing. Brain-rotting. These, it seems, are the behaviors encouraged by our computers and digital devices—intoxicating masterworks of engineering that we stumble away from, glassy-eyed. It’s a sad state of affairs, especially if, like me, you grew up in the nineteen-eighties and nineties, when digital technology was exciting and liberatory. Back then, Steve Jobs called the computer a “bicycle for the mind”; parents bought PCs hoping that their kids would become “computer whizzes.” The idea was that circuits and software could unleash our potential.

Today, of course, we associate screens with mindlessness, and computers with distraction and drudgery. But it doesn’t have to be that way. Gadgets are still great, and computers remain delightful. In fact, it’s easy to turn your personal tech dystopia into a utopia: all you have to do is shift from being a consumer to becoming a creator. We live in a golden age of digital creativity. Forget A.I.: you, yourself, can record an album from your sofa, or curate a photo-essay on the train. In that spirit, here are some of my favorite creative digital tools.

Perhaps you’ve seen, on YouTube, videos of “infinite sketchbooks”—digital drawings that can be zoomed into seemingly forever, revealing worlds within worlds. It turns out that tablets aren’t just for Netflix: even a small model, like the iPad Mini ($699), can open up onto endless vistas when it’s equipped with a digital pencil ($124) and an app like Endless Paper (free). Tablets are always getting slimmer and lighter, making them better for watching than for drawing. But turning a tablet into an ergonomic drawing surface is simple: just get a drawing board ($45)—one of those slanted wooden surfaces that illustrators use. Add a book stand and a copy of “Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain” ($24).

If a tablet is too distracting, there are other ways to make digital art. For years, I’ve been doing a lot of my writing and sketching using e-ink tablets made by reMarkable, a Norwegian company. The deluxe version, the Paper Pro ($629), has a big screen and can be expanded with a keyboard. But the Paper Pro Move ($449) is the size of a pocket notebook and lets you sketch in color. There’s no e-mail, web browsing, or social media on these—only a Kindle-esque e-ink display that feels paperlike beneath your stylus. (When my eight-year-old son and I are bored, I sometimes make sketches so that he can color them in and add to them.) I also find that writing in longhand on an e-ink device can loosen up one’s brain, and I’ve written many articles—including this one—on my reMarkable, eventually using the device’s handwriting-recognition feature to transform my scrawls into editable text. For those who like writing but want to get away from their work computer, this sort of freestanding writing device can be a godsend. The BYOK ($199) is a little portable screen that’s made entirely for writing; as its name suggests, you should bring your own keyboard, and a tiny, pleasantly clicky model like the Keychron K2 ($60) would be a good choice. The Freewrite Alpha ($349) is like a digital typewriter, and includes its own keyboard.

I was in college when the iPod appeared. In the two decades since, dedicated music players have almost completely disappeared. And yet, beneath the radar, music-making devices have proliferated. Today, there are zillions of cool little synthesizers and “grooveboxes” on the market, and they’re not at all difficult to use.

You can make beats with a Teenage Engineering Pocket Operator ($59), which is about the size of a deck of cards. You can compose lovely melodies and soundscapes with the Roland P-6 ($229), a sampler the size of a paperback book, with rechargeable batteries so that you can use it on the go. (The P-6 can be hooked up to its siblings, which include a synth, for $230, and a drum machine, also for $230, to form a synth-pop band.) Bigger units let you build whole tracks, with different parts playing in parallel. The Elektron Model:Cycles ($349) offers modern sounds and medical-device chic; the Sonicware Deconstruct ($399) lets you pretend your living room is Berghain. The most elegant grooveboxes are probably the Teenage Engineering OP-1 Field ($1,999) and OP-XY ($2,299), which are like scaled-down music studios with Apple-calibre designs and batteries that last all day; the Field is better for keyboard players, while the XY works best for purely electronic music.

A computer or a tablet can, itself, become a musical gadget, with the addition of the right piano-style keyboard. The Arturia MiniLab 3 ($119) is a compact model that connects to your computer and lets you play, compose, and record in apps like GarageBand, which contain hundreds of free synthesized instruments. You can listen through the lightweight, comfortable Koss PortaPro headphones ($50), which weigh nothing but sound gorgeous, and record your songs with a phone app like Tape It, for listening on the go. If you know a lapsed musician, any of these tools could help get them back up and running—especially in combination with a lesson or two from an online instructor. I’m hoping to learn more about my synthesizers from Jeremy, at Red Means Recording, this winter.
Photography and Filmmaking

Everyone has a smartphone, and every smartphone has a camera; this means that everyone is just a step away from becoming a hobby photographer. Doing so is partly a matter of self-perception—you have to look at your pictures with a critical, artistic eye—but it also has to do with equipment. The Canon Selphy Printer ($159), which allows you to effortlessly print four-by-six photographs at home, can help bridge the gap between taking pictures and making photographs to keep. The Aura Carver Frame ($149), which can rotate through pictures you select, creates a place for your best digital pictures to live.

Giving someone a dedicated camera is like giving them a new form of self-expression. There are all sorts of cameras, and they suit different kinds of photographers—but don’t overthink it, since people can grow into the tools they happen to have. The Insta360 Go Retro Bundle ($299) contains an action camera (great for filming daredevilry and dynamic exploits) that can also be used as a pocketable point-and-shoot. The Polaroid Now ($120) is a stylish instant camera perfect for social butterflies. The Lomography MC-A ($549) is a 35-mm. film camera with autofocus. And the Panasonic Lumix L10 ($1,498) is a discreet but powerful model with a built-in zoom lens and options for “color-grading”—that is, giving photos or footage a professional, cinematic look.

Writing, drawing, music-making—an art form that combines them all is game design. Earlier this year, I bought our family a Playdate ($229), a handheld video-game console with its own easy-to-use game-creation tool, which runs in a web browser. My son and I had fun making a little game; we even moved beyond the browser-based editor, writing our own code directly (with a little help from Claude). And we also played Big Walk ($20), an unforgettable adventure from a game studio called House House. In Big Walk, you play together but on separate screens—I used a Nintendo Switch, he used his computer—solving puzzles while communicating almost entirely through systems of symbol and gesture that you improvise. It’s a video game that brings out new aspects of your own creativity and ingenuity—a perfect example of how humanizing technology can be. ♦
This article is periodically updated to reflect price changes and availability. Some items may have sold out.

items.title: I Am a 2026 National Book Award Finalist. The U.S. Denied My Visa
items.description: When the U.S. consular officer grinned and offered her hearty congratulations on my award nomination, I almost believed my visa interview might turn out differently than I’d anticipated.
items.author: Abdelrahman ElGendy
paragraphs: When the U.S. consular officer grinned and offered her hearty congratulations on my award nomination, I almost believed my visa interview might turn out differently than I’d anticipated.
“Such a huge accomplishment!” she said, beaming.

I’d been preparing for the interview for weeks, rehearsing my answers to every question I could imagine. My hand rested on a stack of transparent dossiers, each color-coded for quick access. One, marked with a yellow label, held my statement of purpose, explaining that my memoir, “Huna,” was a finalist for the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction and that I was expected to attend the finalist reading and award ceremony in New York in mid-November. Behind it, another dossier with an orange label contained my publisher’s invitation letter, my confirmed itinerary, and a sheet of contact information for the publisher and the National Book Foundation.

If I was asked about my history of political incarceration, I would reach for blue: the prison folder. It contained court documents, a case file from a Geneva-based human-rights organization, and a 2023 New York Times article about my six years as a political prisoner in post-revolution Egypt, the subject of my memoir. I was prepared to explain how I had been jailed as a teen-ager for protesting the 2013 military coup, given a fifteen-year sentence, and released in 2020, after one of my family’s many appeals was arbitrarily reviewed, exposing that I had been wrongfully tried as an adult instead of as a minor.

To answer questions about my ties outside the U.S., I would reach for green. That dossier held my current European residence permit, a one-year apartment lease, and confirmed U.K. and European book-tour events for the year ahead—evidence that I would leave the U.S. once my brief visit was over. I had a few more thematic dossiers, plus a final, unlabelled one for miscellaneous documents, just in case. Through it all, one anxious thought swirled in my head: Please don’t ask me about politics. Please don’t ask me why I left the U.S.

When my turn came, I stepped up to the window and deployed a persona that I’d refined over countless visa interviews and “chats” with border-control officers: open posture, steady eye contact, an easy smile with just the right amount of earnestness. I had to be prepared enough to show I had a legitimate reason to visit and enough funds, but not so prepared, so eager, that I came across as someone with something to hide. Desperate people, after all, are the ones who overstay their visas or, God forbid, immigrate. The trick was to exude the nonchalance of having nothing to prove while making absolutely sure that I proved everything.

The interview began more smoothly than I’d expected. One by one, the suspicions attached to my passport seemed to fall away. The consular officer nodded at the Penguin Random House letterhead, the printout of the National Book Foundation web page; appeared reassured that my flights and accommodation were fully covered; squinted and nodded at my European residence permit. Even my political incarceration took up less space in the conversation than I’d feared. The tension in her eyes seemed to ease as she saw the Times logo and profile.
She typed a few words into her computer, then scrolled down her screen. Her expression tightened.
“Unfortunately, I can’t decide on this application now. We have to consult Washington first, then get back to you.”

My stomach dropped. She told me that I’d be placed in administrative processing and that the decision would be e-mailed once she heard back from Washington. I thanked her and went home. The next morning, I woke to a formal visa denial in my inbox. They wouldn’t put in writing what the system had flagged or the reason that Washington provided overnight, only that I was found ineligible for a visitor visa under the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Years ago, in my prison cell in Egypt, I used to fantasize about writing a memoir. I would slip under a bright red duvet my mother had bribed the guards to let through, and imagine that everything happening to me would end up in a book. That a guard’s baton was battering not my ribs but those of the book’s protagonist. That a slap was landing on the protagonist’s face, not mine. I was the author, concerned only with how I would render the torture my body was undergoing on the page.

For six years and three months, I wrote steadily, smuggling the pages out one visit at a time. I started reading contraband books with an eye for craft, trying to reverse engineer the lines that lingered and emulate their moves. The scribbles on a smuggled page became a potential essay, the essay a potential published article, the article a book. I would imagine it winning an award. Hours passed as I delivered fictional acceptance speeches under Mama’s duvet, revising and honing them, fleetingly unincarcerated. Prison was my horizon, but this fantasy, despite the unhealthy dissociation from my body it entailed, helped. And in prison, if something helps, you keep doing it.

After my release, I kept writing, publishing essays and political commentary about my experience and that of politically incarcerated friends, many of whom are still behind bars. Before long, well-connected relatives warned me that my name was circulating as a potential target for rearrest. I fled Egypt that same year and began working on my book while moving constantly between countries in search of the next visa, for a semblance of home. Then, in 2022, I received a full ride to pursue an M.F.A. in nonfiction writing at the University of Pittsburgh.

The three years I spent at Pitt were crucial to the creation of my book. I made a home, found my people, and built a warm, tender literary community, one I lean on to this day. The M.F.A. also offered more tangible assistance: access to legal status, funds, mobility, access. I applied for swaths of research and travel grants, attended every literary conference I could, spoke on every stage, and put myself and my developing book in every room. I was building a life, but I was also stocking the color-coded dossiers I carried everywhere, assembling evidence that I was extraordinary enough to be allowed to keep that life.

In 2023, I found a literary agent and worked more intensely toward a full manuscript. I was disheartened to learn that only U.S. citizens could submit to major literary awards such as the Pulitzer and the National Book Awards. But, following years of advocacy by the organization Undocupoets and by writers such as the Salvadoran poet Javier Zamora, the Pulitzer Prize Board announced, in 2023, that it would expand the eligibility criteria for some categories, opening the award to authors with permanent residence, or whose primary, long-term home was in the United States. The National Book Foundation followed suit in 2024. The fantasy that had sustained me under my mother’s prison duvet for years was suddenly within reach.

Meanwhile, I worried about what would happen once my student visa expired. When the offer for “Huna” from Hogarth, an imprint of Penguin Random House, landed in my inbox in 2024, my agent called. Her first words were a thrilled “Congratulations”; my first words, breathless: “Can they write me a letter for an O-1 extraordinary-ability visa?”

After Trump returned to power in 2025, ICE was unleashed against immigrant communities and pro-Palestine international students. In the aftermath of October 7th, I had attended rallies on campus and written political commentary for outlets such as Foreign Policy and the Washington Post. I had criticized the relationship between Egypt and the U.S., and argued that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza—a position I believe should never have needed to be defended—and that this must fundamentally alter our understanding of international law. I knew that my activism put me at risk of being arrested.

My sense of risk escalated as I watched Rümeysa Öztürk, a Turkish national and Tufts Ph.D. student, get snatched off the street by ICE agents near her home, for co-authoring an op-ed relating to Gaza. I consulted lawyers who warned me that, given my public profile, my arrest was likely a matter of time. Concerned as I was about ICE detention, deportation to Egypt carried an even more terrifying prospect: imprisonment for the rest of my life.

I spent the month of April, 2025, revising my book behind the locked door of my apartment. I deactivated some of my social-media accounts and made others private. I cancelled readings and speaking engagements. My friends Kira, Miles, and laura scanned the street around my apartment every day, trying to make sure it was clear of undercover ICE agents before sneaking me into their cars like contraband. One day, I caught myself wondering what I wanted to be wearing when ICE came to my door. At that moment, I recognized the logic of the system that I had fled to the U.S. to escape—one in which speaking and writing openly made you a target and the possibility of imprisonment reorganized the smallest routines of daily life.

I knew then that I had to uproot my life again. I left the U.S. in late April and resettled in Europe, entering what I hoped would be a temporary exile within my exile. I attended my M.F.A. graduation remotely, and lost the chance to tour the country for my book, to celebrate with the people who had become my people.

When I learned that “Huna” had been long-listed for the National Book Award, and, weeks later, received a call from a 212 number telling me I was a finalist for the award, my joy was tempered by the fact that I could not share the experience with the friends who had witnessed the book’s journey. This visitor-visa application was my last stab at a homecoming—if only for a few days.

Visas, awards, travel: these are the problems of an unincarcerated person. As a seventeen-year-old boy shrinking in the corner of a cell, I fantasized about a day when these would be my problems. Back then, a life beyond prison, where my dreams could be crushed in this way, was itself the dream. This is why I write about those I left behind: Ayman, whose brown eyes creased as he joked torture away in our cell; Tooha, whose gap-toothed smile shone as he held me in Wadi Al-Natroun prison after our appeal was rejected; Adel, whose laugh buoyed me as we shouted through the peepholes in our cell doors, keeping each other company through the night. I dream that they, too, might be afforded a life in which stacking their color-coded dossiers is their most pressing concern. Still, there is a particular cruelty to being forced to outrun the fruits of one’s labor, to watch one’s work bloom from afar. My book has made it into rooms that I never will. I don’t know what to do with that, and so I write. ♦

items.title: The Impish Faxes Between Janet Malcolm and Philip Roth
items.description: In the course of the nineteen-eighties, the number of fax machines in the United States increased twentyfold, from two hundred and fifty thousand to five million. Suddenly, you could draft a quick missive that could be sent—and received—almost instantly. The f
items.author: Eve Sneider
paragraphs: In the course of the nineteen-eighties, the number of fax machines in the United States increased twentyfold, from two hundred and fifty thousand to five million. Suddenly, you could draft a quick missive that could be sent—and received—almost instantly. The formality of corresponding by mail was replaced, at least partially, by something chattier and less polished. And as with every other advance in communications technology before and since, not everyone was happy with the change. “My conservation project has taken me back to the pre-fax period of our friendship and I have made a painful discovery,” Janet Malcolm observed in a fax to Philip Roth in 1994. “We both wrote better letters when we mailed them.”

Little has been written about the friendship between Roth and Malcolm, but the record of their relationship is laid out, in rich detail, in their archives. The two literary greats each preserved notes from between roughly 1987 and 1995, a joint account of their intimate, active, and high-octane fax correspondence. Some of their messages to each other were voluble, others comprised just a single sentence. Roth called Malcolm a “faxoholic,” then joked that he himself was “attending FaxAnon meetings daily.” The dispatches are noteworthy not just for what they say but for how they say it.

The correspondence began formally, the old-fashioned way: on March 12, 1986, Malcolm typed a letter out to Roth on deep-blue paper stamped with her personal letterhead. The previous night, the two writers had crossed paths, maybe at a party or at the home of a mutual friend. Now Malcolm was kicking herself for having missed the opportunity to share her admiration for Roth’s work, and sent him a stilted note to express her remorse. Perhaps, if he had time to spare, he could stop by her apartment for tea and “more awkward praise”?

Though Malcolm and Roth were both in their fifties by this time, their literary trajectories hadn’t quite followed the same course. Roth won the National Book Award for his first book when he was not yet thirty, and was more or less off to the races from there. By contrast, Malcolm had only risen to prominence in the prior decade, first with a photography column in this magazine and then with a series of deeply reported stories on the world of psychoanalysis. Her star would rise meteorically over the next ten years, but she would also develop a reputation for provocation and controversy, all while her friend was battling demons of his own.

Despite their obvious differences, the two also had certain fixations in common. Each was obsessed, in their own way, with the mechanics of narrative, the fuzzy boundaries between truth and fiction, and the idea that, as Roth wrote in “The Counterlife,” “We are all each other’s authors.” After Malcolm read that book in early 1987, Roth asked for her opinion, and she wrote that he was “a very inspiring writer, in that you’re always writing about writing as well as doing it.” In the years to come, this would become a conspicuous theme in Malcolm’s work, and she would solicit Roth’s feedback, once telling him that “I feel extremely lucky to have gotten into your class.” Roth was a frank reader—he found a draft of Malcolm’s book on Sylvia Plath “seriously marred,” full of “unsatisfactory” metaphors that “fill the hole where intelligent commentary should be”—but also a supportive one. “The more playful, the more astute—law of kindergarten, law of life,” he wrote to Malcolm, about her Profile of the artist David Salle. “I enjoyed the piece enormously.”

It was only natural that the pair’s interest in the mechanics of writing would carry over to the writing they did for each other—especially because they were using a relatively new device to do it. As she grew closer to Roth, Malcolm wrote with delight that he was the first to receive a note from her new fax machine, and that, going forward, “faxes with no identification are apt to be from me.” Roth, too, seemed to enjoy the immediacy this technology afforded them. He had a running joke about them being addicted to faxing and reminded Malcolm that “there is a Power higher than your machine.” Their preambles and paragraph breaks went out the window, replaced with short, rapid-fire missives. In one, Malcolm reflected ruefully that her previous message to Roth included an “ungainly” error that she “would never have let go by in regular missionary position writing.” But they couldn’t help themselves.

Those of us who are accustomed to days punctuated by countless text messages and e-mails can appreciate how intense the dopamine hit of the fax must have been. Sometimes, perhaps when the work of writing was going slowly or poorly, Malcolm and Roth would volley silly faxes back and forth in the space of a few hours. When Roth’s machine broke and he was unable to receive messages, he wrote to Malcolm plaintively that his predicament was “a living hell . . . like living in Uganda.” Elsewhere, she joked about his treating his fax machine as though he were its indulgent Jewish mother.

There is a specifically Jewish humor woven through these exchanges. Remarks about circumcision and “Charlotte’s Veb” were very much in Roth’s wheelhouse, but the tone is more surprising coming from Malcolm. She was born Jana Wienerová in 1934, in Prague, and her family narrowly escaped the Nazis in 1939. She and her sister had no knowledge of their Jewishness until one of them used an antisemitic slur at home and their parents decided to set the record straight. “We had internalized the anti-Semitism in the culture and were shocked and mortified to learn that we were not on the ‘good’ side of the equation,” Malcolm wrote many years later. Though she had many Jewish friends and correspondents, there were precious few with whom she addressed her own Jewishness, at least in her papers.

Roth was one of them. When writing to him, New Yorker parties were “nebbish.” Malcolm appreciated a favorable review of Roth’s work specifically because it suggested one of his books was “good for the Jews.” Most remarkably, as their notes to each other became shorter and chummier, she started signing off with “Jana,” a name she used infrequently, and typically with other émigrés or Jews. Sometimes in her faxes to Roth, it was preceded with the casual Czech greeting “Ahoj!” It’s a telling detail, an indication that Roth was someone with whom Malcolm felt she could be a very specific version of herself, a self who otherwise made appearances only rarely. Such was the intimacy facilitated by this newfangled machine.

The ease of this correspondence is all the more striking because it coincided so exactly with the most trying years of Malcolm’s career. Shortly after she and Roth began writing to each other, she started work on what would become “The Journalist and the Murderer,” a two-part article published in this magazine in 1989, in which she famously deemed journalism “morally indefensible.” Almost immediately upon its release, the story unleashed a feeding frenzy among members of Malcolm’s profession, who were irate that she had not only excoriated their line of work but that she had also, in their view, neglected to implicate herself in her critique. Malcolm’s piece, about a journalist who was sued by a former subject, made no mention of the fact that she herself was facing a lawsuit from someone she had written about, though the circumstances of each suit differed markedly and Malcolm had reason to believe, when starting work on the article, that her own legal battle was mostly behind her. In fact, that was hardly the case: the suit would last for years, encompassing two trials and a Supreme Court ruling, before Malcolm finally emerged victorious, in 1994.

The lawsuit and the accompanying public critiques were scarring for Malcolm, spurring her to retreat as much as possible from the public eye. “I more and more feel that I am living in one of your books,” she griped to Roth as the case was winding its way through the court system. As the situation escalated, he proved to be an important part of her support system, offering comments on the afterword she appended, in her own defense, to the 1990 book version of “The Journalist and the Murderer,” and even staging a mock trial on her behalf to help her prepare to take the stand.

And Malcolm found ample opportunity to support Roth, too, who was facing his own challenges. Concurrent with their friendship, Roth experienced bouts of serious depression, the death of his father, and, most dramatically, the dissolution of his marriage to the actress Claire Bloom. When the couple separated in 1993, Malcolm, who was friends with both of them, quickly ended up in the unfortunate position of serving as their intermediary. In one fax in Malcolm’s papers, Bloom told Roth that not speaking to each other directly “makes this all so much more painful and difficult,” and that she felt badly about using Malcolm as a proxy. In another, to Bloom, Roth attempted to parse some of the particulars of the divorce: how much he felt she owed him for all the taxis and hotel rooms and meals out they had shared in their seventeen years together. “You don’t owe me anything for my attendance time after time at your plays and recitals,” he conceded. “That’s on me.” At one point, Malcolm enlisted her husband, Gardner Botsford, to intervene on her behalf. “My client has asked me to tell you that she would seriously prefer not to get into these arrangements,” Botsford faxed Roth, before extending an invitation for dinner the following night.

The function of an archive—Malcolm’s papers are at Yale, Roth’s at the Library of Congress—is that it keeps fleeting moments like these from being consigned to oblivion. The two writers seem to have mostly fallen out of touch by the two-thousands, and Malcolm, for her part, left little question for researchers that this choice was intentional. To one of her sweeter faxes to Roth, seemingly from around the time of his separation, she appended a handwritten note, dated December, 2012: “What a ridiculous letter!” Malcolm wrote. “The man gives nothing. (Yes, except to literature). He is completely selfish and manipulative. How taken in I was.”

Even the correspondence itself risks being lost. Roth and Malcolm appear to have both had thermal-paper machines for much of the time they were faxing, meaning that the notes that weren’t photocopied were doomed to melt away over time. (Some are already hard to make out.) In 1994, Malcolm tried to copy the fading notes she had received from Roth, and told him what she was up to. She felt that his letters ought to be preserved for his eventual biographers, and wasn’t sure that he would bother to save any himself. He did, fortunately: Malcolm’s fax about saving faxes is immortalized in Roth’s archive, a photocopy made at a point when the original was on the precipice of decomposition. And it turns out that Malcolm, like the rest of us, felt the joy of rereading their correspondence, old memories exchanged between two friends who loved to laugh. “My faxes are often almost as funny as yours,” she wrote to Roth, “sometimes as funny, and here and there funnier.” ♦

items.title: The Labyrinthine Betrayals of “Minotaur”
items.description: You can tell a lot about a filmmaker from the way they dispose of a corpse. In “The Unfaithful Wife” (1969), a coolly unsettling drama of adultery and murder, Claude Chabrol tidied a crime scene with the kind of brisk elegance that earned him the sobriquet the
items.author: Justin Chang
paragraphs: You can tell a lot about a filmmaker from the way they dispose of a corpse. In “The Unfaithful Wife” (1969), a coolly unsettling drama of adultery and murder, Claude Chabrol tidied a crime scene with the kind of brisk elegance that earned him the sobriquet the French Hitchcock. The room was clean within moments, and the body itself was swiftly wrapped up, driven away, and, after some pulse-quickening car trouble, dumped in a pond. Contrast this with an equivalent sequence in “Minotaur,” a mesmerizing new retelling of Chabrol’s story from the Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev, who is not one to hurry things along. As the culprit scrubs at a bloodstain that seems to grow smearier with every wipe, the camera looks on for what feels like an eternity, with a silent but unmistakable disdain. Have we taken on the perspective of the victim’s ghost? Or is Zvyagintsev merely reminding us that messes are harder to mop up than the movies usually suggest? (At one point, I almost blurted out to the killer, “You missed a spot!”)

“The Unfaithful Wife” has already inspired a steamy Hollywood remake, “Unfaithful” (2002), by the British director Adrian Lyne. It’s best remembered for Diane Lane’s sensational performance as the inaptly named Constance, a housewife who is flung, by a freakish gust of wind, into the path of her future lover. Desire really is a force of nature. The weather in “Minotaur,” by contrast, is gloomy but unobtrusive; Zvyagintsev’s storms are of a more interior kind. Certainly Galina (Iris Lebedeva), the Constance in this story, is not a woman to be knocked off her feet. She has a sleek, sharply planed beauty that matches that of her home, a lakeside house on the outskirts of a fictional Russian city called Krasnoborsk, where she lives with her husband, Gleb (Dmitry Mazurov), and their teen-age son, Seryozha (Boris Kudrin). The house is a gleaming mid-century-modern affair, spartan in its good taste, with tall windows that peer out invitingly onto gold-flecked woods. Yet it’s the view from outside, looking in, that compels Zvyagintsev’s attention; he makes the unexpected case for himself here as the Russian Hitchcock, alert to the voyeuristic byplay of seeing and being seen. Early on, Gleb spies Galina through the glass as she stands in the darkness of their kitchen, smiling down at her text messages. He can see, by the glow of her phone screen, that their marriage is in trouble.

He has likely known for some time. An air of frosty detachment, deeper than the autumn chill, seems to follow Galina from room to room. A dinner with two other couples—a sad attempt by Gleb to bring back happier times—backfires spectacularly; the bitterness of other people’s relationships will do nothing to sweeten theirs. During a heated bedroom argument, Galina unloads on her husband for his past infidelities, what she calls his “little girlfriends”—a novel twist, not to be found in the Chabrol or the Lyne, and one that makes it difficult to begrudge Galina her mode of retaliation. For some time now, she has been sleeping with Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk), a divorced photographer, who has an impressive build, a studio apartment in the city, and a wall decked with sexy snapshots of his new paramour. Gleb, a man whose doughy good looks hide a steely resolve, finds all this out in due course. He is the C.E.O. of a logistics company, and he tasks his head of security (Mihails Samodahovs) with spying on Galina and confirming his worst suspicions. That detail, too, is a canny departure from “The Unfaithful Wife” and “Unfaithful,” in which the husbands enlisted the outside help of private investigators. Gleb has enormous resources at his disposal, and the puppet-master authority that he wields both at work and at home is, you sense, precisely what Galina is rebelling against.

“Minotaur,” then, is the most corrosive version of this material imaginable, less the tale of a good marriage gone awry than that of a rotten one getting worse, plus something more: an icy study in the mechanics, and the erotics, of corruption and power. As ever with Zvyagintsev, who wrote the script with Simon Lyashenko, the pessimism isn’t limited to the domestic sphere. It’s the fall of 2022, and the grim consequences of Russia’s months-long assault on Ukraine are everywhere. On phones and computers, we see residential buildings being bombed and Russian cars fleeing toward the traffic-choked Georgian border. On the streets, billboards glorify the military’s efforts, even as some local graffiti (“FUCK YOUR WAR”) testifies to pervasive, if largely hidden, discontent. Gleb’s company is about to suffer the effects of the conflict in a particularly pernicious way. Krasnoborsk’s mayor (Vladimir Friedman) has ordered the city’s major employers to submit lists of male workers—the more physically fit the better—to be drafted into what Russia, avoiding the W-word, is calling its “special military operation.”

Gleb must provide fourteen men, a number that brings the film’s title, with its reference to Greek mythology, into crystalline focus. The Minotaur demanded that fourteen young noblemen and noblewomen be delivered to his labyrinthine lair, and Zvyagintsev’s film duly traps Gleb within his own moral maze. Faced with parallel dilemmas, one personal and one professional, he can address them, finally, only with the same banal disregard for human life. He may be a lesser monster than Putin, glimpsed here in a framed photograph on the mayor’s wall, but unquestioning complicity has made a monster of him nonetheless—one who profits from the blood of human sacrifice and perpetuates the most callous of the story’s innumerable betrayals.

Zvyagintsev, at sixty-two, has become a master at seeding the conventions of domestic melodrama with portents of sociopolitical catastrophe. It wasn’t always thus. His early features, including “The Return” (2003) and “The Banishment” (made in 2007 but not released here until 2018), were troubled-family sagas of a more spiritual than political bent, composed with a rapturous visual sublimity that earned lofty comparisons to the work of Andrei Tarkovsky. But Zvyagintsev’s pursuit of an uncompromising art-film purity could not, in the end, keep out an equal fascination with the malaise of modern life. In 2014, he directed “Leviathan,” about a husband and wife locked in a real-estate war with a small-town mayor, who, in his brutish overreach, clearly stood in for his country’s authoritarian leaders of the past, present, and future. (A photograph of Putin hung on that mayor’s wall, too.) Next came “Loveless” (2017), a bruisingly sad drama about the disappearance of a child, neglected and unmourned by his soon-to-be-divorced parents—a couple so bitterly at odds as to make Gleb and Galina look like honeymooners. “Loveless,” perhaps the most nakedly metaphorical of Zvyagintsev’s works, built to a blunt, summative image of a woman, in a conspicuously Russia-branded tracksuit, running on a treadmill—fierce, enraged, and going nowhere fast.

All of which is to say that Zvyagintsev has been here before, even though his sense of “here” has shifted. In 2022, while recovering from complications of a COVID infection that nearly killed him, the director moved with his family from Moscow to Paris, where he lives in self-imposed exile. France, long a haven for dissident artists and intellectuals, proved specifically instrumental in the making of “Minotaur”—and not merely because of its Chabrol-supplied source material. The film, which was shot entirely in Latvia, was mostly financed by French companies; it will represent France in the upcoming Oscar race for Best International Feature. (Another Gallic feather in the film’s cap: “Minotaur” won the Grand Prix, or second place, at this year’s Cannes Film Festival.)

Nine years, many of them fraught and full of upheaval, have elapsed between this film and its predecessor, and yet the sense of continuity between them is remarkable. In “Loveless,” the vanished child was an emblem of a lost Russian generation, cruelly abandoned by its elders. In “Minotaur,” and specifically in Seryozha—an ordinary, somewhat moody, clearly well-loved teen-ager—Zvyagintsev allows us a more hopeful vision of the future. There’s a moment when Gleb, learning of a potential bully at school, advises the kid to “never strike the first blow,” advice that he himself will swiftly disregard. His son, it becomes clear, already has a better head on his shoulders. In the film’s final moments, the emphasis shifts away from the fragile wreckage of Gleb and Galina’s marriage and toward Seryozha—seated with his parents yet slightly apart from them, happily lost in the clouds. You want the best for him, and hope that the only messes he’ll have to clean up are his own. ♦

items.title: Earth Was a Fixer-Upper
items.description: Every complex organism alive today—this includes not only you and me but also the mites that hang out in our hair follicles and the protozoa that lurk in our large intestines—is the product of an unlikely union. Roughly two billion years ago, a bacterium took
items.author: Elizabeth Kolbert
paragraphs: Every complex organism alive today—this includes not only you and me but also the mites that hang out in our hair follicles and the protozoa that lurk in our large intestines—is the product of an unlikely union. Roughly two billion years ago, a bacterium took up with a bacterium-like creature that belonged to a whole different domain, the archaea. From this microbiological meet-cute, a new kind of cell was born, one equipped with mitochondria, and, along with it, a new kind of organism: a eukaryote. (The term is pronounced “you-carry-oat.”) The particular eukaryote from which we and our mites descend is formally known as the “last eukaryotic common ancestor,” or, more affectionately, LECA.

By the time LECA entered the picture, archaea and bacteria had been grooving along, occasionally exchanging genes, for eons. But they, too, have a backstory. They are descended from a single organism, which, by the logic of phylogeny, also represents humanity’s unimaginably distant ancestor. This unicellular Eve goes by the acronym LUCA, for “last universal common ancestor.” A few years ago, a team of European researchers attempted to re-create LUCA—on paper, that is—by looking at genes that are shared among existing species of archaea and bacteria. LUCA seems to have liked it hot—probably more than a hundred and twenty degrees. The team decided that she was capable of synthesizing some twenty-six hundred proteins and made do on a diet of dissolved hydrogen and carbon dioxide. According to the researchers’ calculations, LUCA lived some 4.2 billion years ago.

For a one-celled creature, LUCA was pretty sophisticated. Her genome comprised some three million base pairs, and she possessed a rudimentary immune system, which implies that she already had to contend with pathogens, eager to attack her. By the time she emerged, then, life had been kicking around for a while. At some point even further back, a first universal common ancestor—FUCA—must have come into being. The weird thing is, there isn’t much further back to go.

Earth was created some 4.5 billion years ago, when a cloud of interstellar dust contracted to form our solar system. In its early days (and days were much shorter then, because the globe was spinning faster), the planet was a horrifyingly inhospitable place. There was no free oxygen and no protection from ultraviolet radiation. Asteroid impacts were frequent—some of these may have generated enough heat to boil the oceans—as were intense volcanic eruptions.

How did FUCA get by? Perhaps the explanation is simply that life is adaptable. Today, living things occupy steaming vents on the floor of the Pacific, frozen peaks in the Himalayas, and just about every space in between, so, clearly, they are flexible. As the movies teach us, life finds a way.

But perhaps that still doesn’t give life enough credit. This is the argument of two recent books, “The Co-Creation: How Earth Made Life and Life Made Earth,” by Olivia Judson (Penguin Press), and “Earth and Life: A Four Billion Year Conversation,” by Andrew H. Knoll (Princeton).

Judson is a science journalist who earned a doctorate in biological sciences from Oxford. Her previous book, “Dr. Tatiana’s Sex Advice to All Creation,” which was written as a series of advice columns to species like fig wasps and seaweed flies, explored the evolutionary dynamics of sex in a breezy, comic key. In “The Co-Creation,” Judson attempts something more ambitious: a work of popular science organized around not hanky-panky but the interplay of geology and biology, or, as the subject has become known, geobiology.

The book opens with a meditation on sand dunes. Though obviously not alive, dunes possess many of the attributes of life. They can move. They can grow. They can even, in a certain sense, reproduce; sometimes a large sand dune will spin off a smaller one. What dunes and life have in common, according to Judson, is that they “arise from, and are maintained by, an ongoing flow of energy and matter.” Life differs from dunes in that it actively seeks energy and, occasionally, reinvents itself to gain access to more of it. Judson ignores the conventional geological timescale, with its eons and eras and periods, in favor of a scheme of her own devising. The planet’s history, she writes, can be divided into five “epochas,” each defined by the emergence of a creature that could “intercept a new source of energy.” Living things, in Judson’s scheme, become “energons,” while inanimate objects—including corpses—are “statigons.”

The first epocha, the rock epocha, began when the earliest organisms learned how to extract energy from the chemical soup in which they floated. Judson believes that this skill was acquired in the sea, in places where a mineral called olivine was coming into contact with water and releasing hydrogen. “If you follow the thread of your forebears all the way back across the eons, you will find that your original ancestor was a fracturing wet, iron-rich rock,” she writes.

Judson’s second epocha commenced some 3.4 billion years ago, with the invention of photosynthesis. This was obviously a big deal, and it enabled life to greatly extend its reach. In the third epocha, a subset of photosynthesizing bacteria—cyanobacteria—developed the capacity to split water and liberate oxygen.

Next up in Judson’s scheme is an era she calls the flesh epocha. This started when groups of energons evolved the ability to dine on other energons. The fifth and final epocha is the age of fire, which began when some enterprising hominin figured out how to cook over an open flame.

Judson’s epochas and energons can be difficult to keep up with. (Her epochas have beginnings but no ends, so the energons keep piling up.) To help the reader out, she periodically interrupts her narrative to visit the office of a fictional “planetary accountant,” a harried, Nutty Professor type whose job it is to track the world’s growing complexity. Judson’s overarching argument, though, is fairly straightforward. Since FUCA first emerged, life has had to adapt to conditions on planet Earth. But life has also had a hand in determining those conditions. Life, in other words, can give as good as it gets.

Consider, once again, photosynthetic cyanobacteria. (These are sometimes referred to as blue-green algae, although they are not, in fact, algae.) Oxygen is a waste product of the process they use to harness energy from the sun. But free oxygen is highly reactive, and its appearance thoroughly transformed the planet. It brought into being many minerals that hadn’t previously existed. It caused vast quantities of iron that had been dissolved in the oceans to precipitate out and accumulate in what are called banded-iron formations. (These formations constitute the world’s major deposits of iron ore.) Eventually, it produced the ozone layer, which shields the planet from UV radiation. The ozone layer, for its part, changed the tint of the sky. Before the ozone layer appeared, the sky probably turned an eerie yellow at dusk. “In altering the composition and mass of the air, lifeforms have reached out and painted the heavens above” is how Judson puts it.

Meanwhile, the addition of oxygen to the oceans and the atmosphere made possible aerobic respiration, which, in turn, made possible the evolution of animals. When animals developed habits like burrowing, they allowed oxygen to penetrate the seafloor. This, it’s believed, helped create conditions favorable for the accumulation of gypsum, vast amounts of which were deposited around five hundred million years ago. Nowadays, gypsum is used in drywall; thus, anyone who’s renovated a kitchen or put in a new bathroom has ancient wormlike creatures to thank. “Truly, the advent of burrowing would change the world,” Judson observes.

Or consider the advent of predation. By consuming and then excreting their victims, predatory creatures invented a new kind of recycling. This allowed more nutrients to circulate through the system, thereby enabling more (and more various) creatures to find nourishment. Predators also spurred their potential victims to develop novel defenses, like shells or, in the case of one-celled creatures called coccolithophores, minuscule calcite plates. Calcite plates piling up on the floor of the ocean eventually became a new kind of rock: chalk. “The white cliffs of Dover in England, of the German island of Rügen, of the Normandy coast of France, of the Smoky Hill River of Kansas in the United States—these are all built of chalk,” Judson points out. Under high pressure, chalk can be converted into marble, which can be quarried and sculpted—a case of life initiating art.

As for man’s mastery of fire, it, too, has proved world transforming. From burning sticks, we’ve moved on to fossil fuels, which power our cities, our factories, our smelters, our fishing fleets, our industrial-scale farms, and, increasingly, our farmland-gobbling data centers. “Humans are, without doubt, causing more changes to the life-Earth system—in more ways and faster—than any lifeform ever has before,” Judson writes.

At the end of “The Co-Creation,” Judson offers a catalogue of researchers to whom she owes “intellectual debts.” Near the top of her list is Knoll, the author of “Earth and Life.” Knoll, a professor at Harvard, was more or less present at the creation of geobiology, and he played a key role in the discipline’s development. As a working scientist, he’s a lot more interested than Judson is in the nitty-gritty of how geobiologists piece together the history of Earth (and life) from fragmentary clues—isotopes of sulfur, say, or traces of compounds called sterols. (Conversely, he’s a lot less interested in promulgating neologisms.)

The “conversation” of Knoll’s subtitle is his organizing metaphor. Chapter by chapter, he recounts what geology and biology have had to say to each other over the eons. Sometimes the dialogue has been balanced, at other moments lopsided.

Initially, life was quite reticent. It was, Knoll reports, probably “a local phenomenon,” confined to watery spots where hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and “the minerals to catalyze their interaction were available.” Then, around 2.4 billion years ago, it started to speak up. This was the beginning of what’s become known as the Great Oxygenation Event, or, as it’s referred to in the scientific literature, the G.O.E.

Exactly what happened during the G.O.E. remains something of a paleontological puzzle, and Knoll devotes a number of chapters to exploring its mysteries. (He calls this section of his book “The Story of O,” in a nod to the rather racier French bondage novel.) Among the mysteries is the timing. Various lines of evidence suggest that oxygen-producing cyanobacteria showed up several hundred million years before oxygen levels began to climb. So what caused the delay? One possible explanation is that a shortage of phosphorus in the oceans limited the bacteria’s numbers. Phosphorus began to wash off the land when the earliest large continents appeared, so cyanobacteria may have got their big chance owing to plate tectonics. If this is the case, the G.O.E. would be the consummate example of geology influencing biology and biology influencing geology. In any event, once oxygen started to build up there was no going back. “The stage was set for environmental revolution,” Knoll writes.

On occasion, geology has come close to shouting down life altogether. About two hundred and fifty million years ago, in what’s known as the end-Permian extinction, huge volcanic eruptions in what’s now Siberia released huge amounts of carbon dioxide; this led temperatures to spike and the oceans to become both anoxic and acidified. Something like ninety per cent of marine animal species died out. A similar, if somewhat less devastating, die-off occurred about two hundred million years ago, probably owing to another burst of volcanism, this time from what’s been dubbed the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province. Sixty-six million years ago, a Manhattan-size asteroid plowed into the Yucatán Peninsula; roughly seventy-five per cent of species went extinct, including our distant relatives the non-avian dinosaurs. Catastrophe, Knoll writes, appears to be “sewn into the fabric of our planet.”

In recent centuries, the conversation has taken a strange turn. For the first time, an organism is not only changing the world but also looking on with dread as it does so. Fossil-fuel combustion is adding carbon to the air at a rate that exceeds the pace of the release during the end-Permian extinction. Now as then, temperatures are rising, and the oceans are acidifying. Meanwhile, people are rerouting rivers, messing with the global nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, and churning out so much stuff—concrete, plastic, asphalt, iPhones—that, measured by dry weight, human-produced materials now outweigh all living organisms combined. “Humans have become a dominant voice in the conversation between Earth and life,” as Knoll puts it. The result, he says, is “a distinct time in our planet’s history”—a new epoch, if not a new epocha.

If life on Earth has been partly, or even largely, responsible for rendering Earth habitable, what does this say about the possibilities on other planets? Knoll, who served on the science team for NASA’s Mars Exploration Rover mission, devotes the last part of his book to the prospects of what he calls “other conversations.”

Knoll is pretty confident that life is out there somewhere. The universe, after all, is ginormous. Our particular galaxy, which is just one among billions, is estimated to contain more than a hundred billion stars, most of which probably have planets orbiting them. “If only one planet (or moon) in a billion sustains life, the universe must be a lively place,” Knoll observes. But that doesn’t mean we’re going to encounter it. So far, at least, no signs of life have been detected emanating from any other planet (or moon) in our solar system, and other solar systems are awfully far away. After the sun, the star closest to Earth is Proxima Centauri. It would take a probe like NASA’s Voyager 1—the first craft to journey into interstellar space—about seventy-five thousand years to reach it.

And, even if life has emerged elsewhere, it hasn’t necessarily had time to generate creatures capable of sending out interstellar probes or messages. If not for plate tectonics, which has kept life’s key ingredients recirculating, evolution on this planet probably would have hit a wall billions of years ago. “It may be that what makes Earth unusual is not so much that life began here—that may happen widely in the universe—but that it has persisted so long,” Knoll notes.

Judson, too, ends her book contemplating the cosmos. Like Knoll, she believes that in the vastness of space there are many other planets where life could have emerged. And yet, also like Knoll, she thinks there’s no place like home.

In the final pages of “The Co-Creation,” Judson describes a fascinating experiment in applied evolution which has been running since 1988. That year, a biologist named Richard Lenski, then at U.C. Irvine, placed virtually identical populations of E. coli into twelve identical flasks. (This was a nonpathogenic strain of the bacteria, rather than the kind that causes recalls.) E. coli reproduce by splitting themselves in two, and, in Lenski’s flasks, the bacteria were free to keep doubling until they exhausted their supply of glucose. Every twenty-four hours, Lenski—or, more likely, his assistants—would remove a small number of the bacteria from each flask, provide them a new supply of food, and let the process repeat itself.

In addition to glucose, the growth medium contained a compound called sodium citrate. At first, the twelve tribes of E. coli ignored the citrate. But then, around the thirty-thousandth generation, something interesting happened: bacteria in one of the flasks developed the ability to consume it. That population gained a powerful advantage—the citrate-eaters had found their way to a new energy source.

By now, Lenski’s E. coli have gone through another fifty thousand generations. But the populations in the other eleven flasks still can’t consume citrate. The necessary mutations just haven’t been repeated. The lesson, according to Judson, is clear: major evolutionary innovations are fluky. This, she argues, should be kept in mind whenever talk turns to aliens. Even on Earth, the “conversation” between biology and geology could have played out very differently. There was no guarantee that it would have included LUCA, LECA, or oxygen-producing cyanobacteria. And, without all of these, it certainly wouldn’t have included us.

That we are in a position to study the history of life and wonder at its contingency is itself a contingency. It’s one that we (and our mites) ought to be grateful for, and also one that, Judson argues, ought to make us think carefully about how we treat our planet. “If humans really are the only technological species now, and perhaps ever, in the cosmos—what then?” she asks. “What responsibility might that bestow on us, should we choose to accept it?” ♦

items.title: Politicians Really Suck at GTA Memes

items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: You may have noticed that the long-awaited video game Grand Theft Auto VI is having a cultural megamoment this week. It seems like everyone is talking about it. The reviews are astounding. The sales are booming. The clips are all over social media, and the resulting discourse is tearing across the internet like a boosted monster truck. The New York Times Magazine has published a piece entitled “Grand Theft Auto Used to Satirize American Life. Now We’ve Caught Up With It.” Leftist streamer Hasan Piker briefly gave up chatting about politics to play it. And, yes, Fox News and the denizens of the manosphere have found reasons to complain about it. The game is arguably the most with-it thing that happened this week, and that also means it was inevitable that politicians would try to join — and thus ruin — the fun.
First, the White House social team could not resist trying to piggyback onto the hype and posted this on Wednesday night:
Then the similarly unpopular House Republicans, or at least the ones still coming to work, decided they, too, wanted in on the action:
And then the group Majority Democrats just could not let that stand:
But poor J.D. Vance apparently felt left out, so he posted his own AI-slop version (which includes a prominent image of him next to Trump):
And then whoever is still left at the Lincoln Project was like, “Au contraire!”
Finally, Mike Huckabee — the same Mike Huckabee who has been a critic of these kinds of video games since the 1990s — somehow decided this might be cool:
