Their falsetto-leaning vocals blend with their crisp, sleek production, and both expanded from more traditional R&B into increasingly maximalist, synthpop-adjacent work over time, while also foraying into film, TV, and other multimedia-centric projects throughout their careers (Tesfaye in Uncut Gems; Jackson in The Wiz and Moonwalker).
George Michael & Troye Sivan

The definitive and self-proclaimed “Father Figure,” George Michael (his artistry, songwriting and overall career) is integral to why and how artists like Troye Sivan exist today — and can exist so unequivocally out.

Sivan’s music mirrors the emotional depth that’s at the core of so many of Michael’s songs (especially post-AIDS crisis, post-being outed.) Tracks like “How To Stay With You” and “One of Your Girls” hide vulnerability in funkier club beats. The former, specifically, hit a certain part of the 2020s pop sphere as I imagine “Careless Whisper” did for the ‘80s mainstream.
Dijon has unintentionally filled a Frank Ocean void in the 2020s, and I didn’t realize how many people feel the same way until I dug deeper into their paths.

Both of them deal with heartbreak and anguish with poeticism; their music is centered on love but is emotionally expansive, diving into the more specific emotions that lie beneath. Both of their music feels like dream states, warm and fuzzy like you could wrap yourself in a sweater of their sounds. Faraway vocals and slowed, molasses-type ambiance mix with endless reverb and bleeding instrumentation. Their catalogs and collaborations show a genreless approach to songwriting, Dijon leaning into guitar-based, rootsy Americana (across Absolutely and in his production work with Bon Iver), while Ocean toyed with rap and hip-hop with Odd Future in his early years and A$AP Rocky later on.

If any of these father-son pairs are evil renditions, The Dare is categorically Evil Gen Z Mark Ronson. These two producer-forward, DJ-adjacent, NYC lore-fests have made their own impact on pop with their solo discographies, but more importantly, with their production work. While Ronson has worked with Dua Lipa, Lady Gaga and Amy Winehouse, The Dare’s hyperpop flirtations with Charli XCX, PinkPantheress and ADÉLA have made him left-of-center pop’s favorite collaborator. I’m not sure if we’ll see Harrison on the next Barbie soundtrack, but maybe he’ll be on Jordan Firstman’s nonexistent-but-probably-already-in-the-works Club Kid follow-up.

Bruno Mars, son of Elvis, is also, almost unavoidably, a father to many. But no son is more legitimate than Benson Boone. Boone is spiritually Bruno Mars, even if people conflate him with Harry Styles. It’s in the way I'm force-fed their music in grocery stores and airports everywhere. The way they both have undeniably strong voices (Boone covering Adele really did something to me.) But their songs just couldn’t fall flatter, couldn’t feel more like staring into a commercialized pop void.
Tell me you can’t picture Boone doing endless Vegas residencies in 15 years, backflipping into oblivion.

Prince built an entire career around refusing categorization, never staying in one place sonically long enough for everyone else to catch up to him. Chaz Bear takes this sensibility into Toro y Moi, blending and morphing between funk, rap, indie rock and psych pop (Bear has noted that Prince’s drums had a specific impact on his drum programming.) Born in the ‘80s, Bear takes to the time’s synth emphasis and hyper-electric, wah-heavy guitar tones. Mood and momentum drive each of their sounds, both artists maintaining a kind of ubiquitous presence where you broadly know what you’re gonna get, even if it could realistically sound like anything.

I actually don’t care if Shawn Mendes is two years younger than ROLE MODEL. I literally could not care less. You just can’t tell me Tucker Pilsbury isn’t the 2020’s version of “Lost in Japan”-era Shawn Mendes. It’s in their white boy of the month-ness, the way I can barely tell their songs apart, the way they permeated into cultural consciousness almost without a trace. And most importantly, the way their relationships are constantly superseding their musical output.

items.title: Sotheby’s Sold the World’s Most Expensive Van Gogh for $190 Million
items.description: This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.
items.author: Nate Freeman
paragraphs: This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors, from New York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

One thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in New York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

Speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.
We’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this issue: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian

Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

Honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

So who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of New York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is currently on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

The $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

— As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

The 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

— Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

— The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred said the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”

— For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

— Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. The evening raised $1.5 million for Ballroom Marfa.

— After the auction on Wednesday, the gallery Entrance, a space opened by dealer Louis Shannon on Ludlow Street nearly a decade ago, hosted an opening for the painter Victoire Bourgois. Lots of artists were there to support her—Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin—and the event was followed by a dinner at the ultimate Dimes Square redoubt. That’s right: Dimes itself. Can you believe Dimes has been open for—checks age—more than 13 years? And guess what? After all the Dimes Square discourse, the actual restaurant itself still slaps.

— The annual Baby2Baby Gala went down in LA last weekend. I wasn’t able to make it out West, but luckily for Vanity Fair, Tallulah Willis was on the scene and wrote a fabulous party report that you can read here. I also want to note that the live auction of artworks, curated, as always, by Darrow Contemporary founder Meredith Darrow, included an Annie Morris sculpture that achieved $410,000.
THE ENCOUNTER: MICHAEL CHOW

On a Friday in November, I walk into Gagosian on Madison Avenue for a meeting with Michael Chow, the artist, collector, filmmaker, designer, actor, and founder of the restaurant Mr. Chow. There’s a portrait of Chow by Jean-Michel Basquiat, a portrait by Julian Schnabel, a portrait by Andy Warhol. There’s a drawing of Chow by David Hockney, made soon after Mr. Chow opened in London in 1968.

Michael Chow: So I opened that restaurant. You’ve got Hockney, you’ve got fashion, you’ve got every single thing. It’s almost like a Dada movement on the First World War thing. This one is in London—all happening.

He starts talking about duopolys: Christie’s versus Sotheby’s, Coke versus Pepsi. There was an Italian restaurant in London’s Soho, so he opened a Chinese restaurant in Soho with Italian waiters. He has a theory about name-dropping.
Chow: I hate people who drop names, and Lady Gaga agrees with me.
True Colors: That’s a good one.
Why is name-dropping important? Because the minute I say “Napoleon,” you will go there immediately. So it saves a lot of time. Okay, so why am I saying that? Do you know who Robert Fraser is?
The art dealer from the ’60s. Groovy Bob.

I was looking forward to meeting him, blah, blah, blah. He was sitting there. Name-dropping. Sitting in front is Jim Dine. Name-dropping again. I say, “I would like to borrow some paintings.” I said, “Just like”—do you know the Kronenhalle restaurant?
We walk over to the Hockney portrait of Michael Chow sitting in his restaurant.
Chow: The first person I went to is David. He drew one and I said, “Boy.” You know what he did? Tore it all up.

Simultaneously, I went to Peter Blake. I say, “Give me a painting that’s the antithesis of racism,” which he did. At that time he’s into the circus, he’s into all that shit. All right? So I asked him, “Why did you do that?” He did a portrait. So now Peter Blake is fucking crazy. He loves the circus, he loves wrestling and all that shit.

Larry Gagosian walks in and gives Chow a fist bump. Gagosian takes a long look at the Schnabel and then flips through a book of drawings made by artists for 57th Street’s Mr. Chow when it was the art world’s clubhouse. We walk up to the Basquiat.
True Colors: To have it as this sort of landscape, you have the horizon line here, but it’s almost like a Western. It’s almost cinematic.
Chow: Name me three classic Westerns.
Shane. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. High Noon.
I’m going to act out the first scene of each. Okay, High Noon.
He uses his hand to pull a finger gun on me, then gets distracted by the Ed Ruscha and the Warhol double portrait.
Chow: Andy said, “Oh, what do you want?” I said, “Hold the color and add lots of diamonds.”
Gagosian brings up Anselm Kiefer, and then Richard Serra.

Chow: If you look at the year 2000, Charlie Rose and Richard Serra, their conversation on the culture of China, and Richard Serra identifies very clearly what is fine art: poetry, music, sculpture, and painting.
The works in the show are for sale. I ask Chow if he’s emotional about parting with them. He seems very calm.
Chow: I’m only a temporary steward of the works.
“Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow” is up at Gagosian’s 980 Madison space until December 22.
Have a tip? Drop me a line at nate_freeman@condenast.com. And make sure you subscribe to True Colors to receive Nate Freeman’s art-world dispatch in your inbox every week.

items.title: This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur
items.description: Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unp
items.author: Nate Freeman
paragraphs: Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unpredictable; when I went there this summer for lunch with a movie producer, we spotted a powerful name-brand media executive, an architectural bigwig who designs the homes of billionaires, and a two-time Academy Award–winning actor. A few nights later, I sat near Walter Isaacson, who’s a regular. And don’t just take it from Elon Musk’s biographer. Matthew Schneier, the chief restaurant critic at New York magazine, recently named Borgo the city’s best all-around restaurant.

On one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades. He met Ross Bleckner there, and David Salle. He used to have a massive loft studio in Williamsburg, but as rents went up, he moved deeper into Brooklyn, to Fort Greene, where he built a studio in his basement.

The twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art. That’s because he was Andrew Tarlow—the painter and restaurateur who kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic with his restaurant Diner and, yes, also owns Borgo.

After launching that instant hit in an old, reclaimed diner, Tarlow opened five more era-defining Brooklyn spots before finally venturing into Manhattan with Borgo. All along, he’s still been the artist who got a job at The Odeon so that he could meet his heroes. He’s still painting away in his brownstone, doodling on notepads during concept meetings. He’s had shows recently at galleries such as Tiwa Select; he’s loosely associated with the Galerie Sardine extended universe; and he’s someone whose work I’ve been told about for years by those in the know.
As they put it, Tarlow is an emerging artist who happens to own the best all-around restaurant in Manhattan, as well as a bunch of other successful spots in Brooklyn.

“I realized, opening Borgo, that I really loved working in restaurants—and not that I had forgotten, but I hadn’t actually worked services in a while until I opened,” Tarlow told me during a studio visit. “And then, in a similar way, I think—I love making paintings. I actually will paint forever, no matter what happens.”

The studio had dozens of unstretched canvases heaped on the ground, some still rolled up, and others hanging via a pin on the studio wall. They showed figures grappling with pain in fierce color-blocked fields, automatic-painting abstractions, faces fading into other faces. One painting was a portrait of the artist Joe Bradley, a friend.

The studio is in the basement of the Fort Greene brownstone where Tarlow has lived for two decades with his wife, Kate Huling, raising four kids in a kind of neo-boho paradise. There were no studio assistants, no art handlers, no frames, no boxes, no packaging—just the artist and the work.

“It was kind of just as chaotic as everything else there, but in the most perfect warm embrace of a way. I saw the pure energy that he put into his paintings and the stories that they told,” says Alex Tieghi-Walker, the founder of Tiwa Select, calling from London. “So many artists could be quite—rightfully so, but quite precious with their works. And I love that Andrew was just like, ‘Oh, pull out the ones you’re taking and just take them in an Uber home.’”
Tarlow grabbed at a canvas bare-handed, one with a bit of a conceptual bent, and put it up on an easel.

“I’ve had this up on the wall for a while now, and I just continued to look at it because I’m happy with it. I’m also a little unsettled—I mean, I’m showing you the inside of my drawers. I’m also a little unsettled by how far it’s gone abstract-wise.”
He told me he couldn’t really do his other job, the restaurant job, without painting at odd hours. They’re totally separate, but complementary in a cosmic way.

“What are the processes? Like you said, for some people, it’s nine to five. Then you listen to the news, smoke a cigarette, drink coffee. It’s either working or it’s not. The door either opens or it’s not,” Tarlow said, gesturing around to his studio. “But I’m going to go here every day, and I’m going to push some paint on canvas.”

Diner opened in 1999, a few years after Tarlow moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg—where the crumbling street dead-ends into the East River. While looking for a cheap studio space, he found a 6,000-square-foot loft across the street from an abandoned diner from the 1920s. The loft’s landlord bought the diner, and in 1999, Tarlow opened Diner with then partner Mark Firth—and watched as it was patronized by only the artists across the street.
“You could stand outside the restaurant in those days and not see a single person walk by,” he told Bon Appetit in 2010.

Tarlow kept expanding. He opened Marlow & Sons, and then the butcher shop and specialty food store Marlow & Daughters. He founded a bakery, She Wolf, and a literary magazine, Diner Journal. He operated the restaurant at the Wythe Hotel, but only for a few years. Instead of doing the easy thing, Vegas-ifying Diner in some new development on the Williamsburg waterfront, he got even weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far-out corner of Greenpoint.

A dealer with a gallery in Tribeca was the first, but far from the last, to tell me I had to check out Tarlow’s paintings. After an introduction was brokered, Tarlow invited me to lunch at Borgo this past summer. The restaurant has many fantastic pork-laden dishes, but we ate almost entirely vegetables, as well as one very elegant, simple piece of fish. A summer lunch. We fell into an easy patter, talking about exhibitions, other artists—but mostly his painting practice. He’d been working on Long Island, not on the East End but in the middle. He’d had a few shows. There was discussion of representation. He spoke about all this with an unpracticed earnestness and complete confidence. He sounded like a very prominent emerging artist, which, at 56, he is.

“I don’t know if it’s just age or time, or I was too much of a young person, or a young mind, but I’ve been more secure with my ability to hold all these things in the same time,” he told me back in the studio. “I can go work tonight in the restaurant and feel perfectly confident in that work, and I can show you this work and feel perfectly confident in this work. Whereas, I think, as a young person, I felt like, Am I fake?”

Sometimes it’s not the enfant terrible who breaks out—it’s the working parent, the person with a desk job, the successful entrepreneur who back-ends into revolutionary art making. Think William Carlos Williams writing “The Red Wheelbarrow” while working as a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey. Or Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children in San Francisco. Or Jeff Koons working on Wall Street in order to earn money to make his sculptures. Having a demanding job actually granted them the freedom to be artists. Tarlow started drawing during restaurant concept meetings.

Sometimes Tarlow hangs his own paintings upstairs in his brownstone’s salon room, or at his house on Long Island, to see what they look like in the wild. The paintings have a confident thrust to them, with the colors bold-blocked in a way that reminds me of Albert Oehlen, drawing from Roman and Greek mythology in Twombly-esque riffs: visages multiplying and fading like a Kippenberger-ian pomo ride into the ether. Sure, any painter who’s spent time in Europe since the 1990s has wanted to be Martin Kippenberger. But Tarlow has an actual connection to him: Like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a lover of Italian food and good wine, and he made art to hang in restaurants. And like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a restaurant owner, balancing his studio practice with running Capri, a Venice, California, spot in which he invested after moving to Los Angeles in 1989. According to those present at the time, Kippenberger became a part-owner of the place because, as the artist put it, “You can’t get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles.”

As a bartender at The Odeon, Tarlow maintained a working painting studio but found it hard to produce art. After opening Diner, he skipped painting sessions in favor of opening businesses and starting a family. Once that duality settled, he started drawing on the move, carrying sketchbooks and working through potential paintings. Eventually, once the kids got old enough, he built out a studio in a nook of his 19th-century basement.

“I really started painting back downstairs. Let’s just say, after dinner, it was 8 p.m. and they were watching Nemo. No one actually needs me, they’re totally happy. My wife’s up there, everyone’s laughing, giggling with little fish,” he said. “And I can just walk down here and do my thing. Having it in my house for sure is the only way I could do this amount of work, and for sure even get to this place. Because I do think you have to do a certain amount of work to get to this place unless you’re just a born prodigy. But when you think about the genius of Picasso or whomever, he made a million fucking paintings.”
Tarlow didn’t really show anyone his work for a long time.

“I met Andrew socially. I knew his restaurants way before I knew Andrew. And one day he was like, ‘Come and see my studio,’” Tieghi-Walker tells me. “It did not surprise me at all that he had an art studio in his basement and that these were the types of works he was creating.”

The show at Tiwa Select was on view right as Tarlow was getting ready to open Borgo. There was a certain amount of unconscious transference, Tarlow told me. For the Tiwa dinner, instead of creating name placards, the artist hand-sketched an artwork of each guest’s name on the paper tablecloth. Now, when a regular makes a reservation at Borgo, Tarlow will elegantly sketch out their name on the paper tablecloth.

The showcasing of his art at Borgo marks the first time Tarlow has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant. Tarlow doesn’t exactly promote this. When I asked about it, he told me that only one of his own works was up at the moment, then changed the subject. Alex Levy, the media strategist and theater producer, has been a regular at Borgo since it opened. “Borgo is the grown-up Platonic ideal of what a restaurant can be,” he said. After several visits, Levy, who also collects a bit of contemporary art, noticed what was on the walls.

“I complimented one of the paintings, and Andrew said, ‘It’s by my daughter.’ And then he pointed to another one and said, ‘That’s by me,’” Levy says. “I had no idea that there’s this whole other part of him.”

Like Tarlow, Levy balances two seemingly divergent but strangely complementary careers—as a speechwriter on one hand, a Tony Award winner on the other—and Tarlow invited him to see his studio on Long Island. Levy bought a painting immediately. Seeing the studio, Levy says, helped him realize, to some extent, what the special sauce is behind a place like Borgo. It’s for incredibly confident, hyperproductive creative types, run by an artist who has complete faith in his ability to work.
And for Tarlow, the focus and passion in one arena lead right into the passion for the other.

“I’m also being very present for your needs in the same way as I’m trying to be very present with these paintings,” he said. “They’re not separate boats. When the restaurant’s working, I feel creative inside of it.”
Have a tip? Drop me a line at nate_freeman@condenast.com. And make sure you subscribe to True Colors to receive Nate Freeman’s art-world dispatch in your inbox every week.

items.title: Are the Royals More Relatable Now Than Ever?
items.description: Prince William and Kate Middleton’s visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony marked their first joint overseas tour in four years, and the couple used it as an opportunity to demonstrate their star power. Through their action-packed itinerary, which too
items.author: Katie Nicholl
paragraphs: Prince William and Kate Middleton’s visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony marked their first joint overseas tour in four years, and the couple used it as an opportunity to demonstrate their star power. Through their action-packed itinerary, which took them from Mumbai to New Delhi, the Prince and Princess of Wales have paved the way for a new style of royal tour.

From Kate unexpectedly presenting an award and delivering a speech at the star-studded Earthshot Prize event to her and William playing cricket and traveling around Mumbai in an electric rickshaw, there have been plenty of photo opportunities and headlines around the world about the environmental initiative William is so passionate about.

According to royals author Russell Myers, who followed the couple on tour, the speech Kate gave at the awards was kept top secret. “None of us knew she was presenting an award on the night, or that she was going to speak. The auditorium was packed. There were about 5,000 people there. It’s been the biggest Earthshot yet, and you could see Catherine was nervous, but she delivered an absolutely brilliant speech. I’d say her best yet.

“It’s been wonderful for her to be here, supporting William, and you can see they’ve really had fun. Because of ongoing terror threats, there have been less walkabouts, but it’s been a very successful and varied tour, and I think, being shorter than most tours, it sets a new blueprint when it comes to royal tours for the couple in the future.”
There are seemingly already plans for another royal tour, says Myers.

“William let slip that Australia is on the cards next, and if that’s the case, I imagine they will go as a family. They don’t want to be away from their children for too long, and what a way it would be to win support for the monarchy Down Under,” Myers says.

According to royals insiders, there had been some nervousness around the trip after the couple’s disastrous tour of the Caribbean in March 2022, when their visit was overshadowed by calls for the UK to apologize for slavery. Then some of their photo calls, including one that involved the couple riding in an open-top Land Rover, led to accusations of the royals appearing colonial and out of touch.

“I think there has been a slight nervousness about how this tour would be received, but the reception has been really good,” Myers says. “The fact that William and Catherine have included a visit to New Delhi to see Prime Minister Modi is a clever move. While this is a private trip to promote Earthshot, the Foreign Office was keen for William to meet with the Indian prime minister, so they have packed that into the itinerary too.”

The visit to India has come at a time when the royals are on something of a charm offensive following a difficult year for the royal family, from Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest to what one palace insider calls “the ongoing soap opera” with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has not been charged and has denied all allegations of wrongdoing.)

William and Kate are keen to carve out their own initiatives and projects focusing on their major priorities, including the environment, children’s early years, and mental health. With the challenge of having Harry and Meghan carrying out their own engagements, the Prince and Princess of Wales have been careful to establish clear parameters that set them apart as working royals. In one telling moment while on an engagement in Mumbai, Kate was asked for an autograph. She politely declined, so as not to breach protocol, a clear contrast to the Duchess of Sussex, who has signed autographs in the past.

“Catherine was asked to sign an autograph, but she was right not to. It wasn’t a snub; it was just adhering to protocol. An autograph could be sold for money,” notes Dickie Arbiter, former press secretary to Queen Elizabeth II.

According to author Tom Bower, the royals are more relatable now than they were during the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, who famously never gave a press interview. In recent weeks, Prince William has appeared as a guest on The Graham Norton Show (to promote Earthshot), and he’s revealed how he drinks his cider and his love of wild swimming as part of his guest-editing stint for a recent issue of Country Life magazine.

“The royals are more relatable, perhaps, than they ever have been, but they are not celebrities. There’s a danger of being too relatable, too much ‘one of the people,’ which means they can lose some of their mystery,” Bower says.

“William will have been advised to do TV appearances and take on media opportunities to bolster his public image. Of course, it’s charming to hear these nuggets and see this side of the prince, but I do think there’s a need to see and hear more from William about his broader plans. Over the years, Charles has made huge efforts to appeal to all cultural aspects of society. I’m not sure William has done that. He’s got to find a way of connecting with everyone, not just the younger generation,” Bower adds.
The Earthshot Prize awards have been a powerful way of demonstrating that William doesn’t just talk the talk; he is insisting on action.

“The Earthshot is a master class in what needs to be done,” concludes Arbiter. “He’s pushing for environmental issues and climate change, and he’s getting people to do something about it. The fact that he is so well supported, and by so many high-profile people, shows his pulling power and influence.”

items.title: Lesley Manville, Pierce Brosnan, and More Celebrate Violinist Joshua Bell at the Langham London
items.description: At the age of four, Joshua Bell was given his first violin, and he hasn’t put it down since. “I don’t remember falling in love with music,” says Bell. “Music has just been my life. I used to string rubber bands on my dresser drawers and make pitches by pulling
items.author: Bridget Arsenault
paragraphs: At the age of four, Joshua Bell was given his first violin, and he hasn’t put it down since. “I don’t remember falling in love with music,” says Bell. “Music has just been my life. I used to string rubber bands on my dresser drawers and make pitches by pulling the drawers out. I was fascinated with strings. It’s the closest instrument to the human voice. And I find it the most expressive instrument.”

Today, the Grammy Award–winning musician is one of the most celebrated classical violinists of his era. By 14, Bell was performing with the Philadelphia Orchestra, and would soon be touring the world. “I live in hotels 250 days a year,” says Bell of the nonstop schedule he has maintained since his teens. Specifically, Bell has been “staying at the Langham for decades now,” he says, referring to the regal central London hotel that first opened in 1865. “I chose it on my own because it was near one of my favorite halls in London, which is the Wigmore Hall. And now I stay with them whenever I’m traveling.”

That kinship was solidified over coupes of Champagne and hand-dived Orkney scallops, with the hotel celebrating Bell, a “Langham Luminary,” in its London ballroom packed with writers, artists, designers, and musicians.

Attendees included actor Simon Callow, House of Dragon actor Emily Carey, former British culture minister Ed Vaizey, Saturday Night Live UK cast producer Susie Hall, stage and television actor Indira Varma, and Verity actor Ismael Cruz Córdova.

Held in partnership with Vanity Fair, the evening marked the latest iteration of the Langham’s Luminaries in Residence program. The event series is continuation of the hotel’s legacy that brings together a diverse, influential community—an evocative reminder of prominent guests from its storied past, including Charles Dickens, Winston Churchill, George Orwell, Oscar Wilde, and Mark Twain.

“I’m not going to put my name in the same sentence as Toscanini or Mark Twain—who has stayed here, or Churchill, who has stayed here. But it’s cool to be part of the history,” says Bell. “So maybe someday, in a hundred years, there will be a violinist who might say that—that I stayed here. I don’t know, maybe that would mean something.”

It certainly does mean something. Pierce Brosnan and his wife, Keely Shaye Brosnan, “have been huge fans of Joshua for many, many years,” Brosnan tells me. “Keely went to go see him…I don’t know how many years back. Unfortunately, due to the LA traffic, she got there late, five minutes late, and they wouldn’t let her into the concert. So tonight is one of those nights.”
Bell, who performed mid-dinner with members of the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields—with a surprise appearance from his wife, soprano Larisa Martínez—brought about a collective catharsis.

Dazzling, fiery, and flamboyant, the experience of watching Bell up close is impossible to replicate. “I just think he’s incredibly soulful, and there’s something really elegant,” actor Russell Tovey tells me, before explaining how he actually discovered Bell via his Instagram algorithm.

For actor Lesley Manville, the event marked her introduction to Bell’s music. “I’m a bit embarrassed that he was not on my radar. But isn’t that nice to have a surprise like that?” says Manville. “Schubert’s String Quintet is one of my favorite pieces of music. It’s unbelievably beautiful. You think of a violin, you think of those strings. And it’s instant emotion. They just make you cry.”
There is a great power in being able to access the emotions of others, as Bell does.

“I think it is the ultimate gift to be able to make people happy,” says Brosnan. “My job is being an entertainer—to take the words of great writing and try to transform it into something that is meaningful and memorable.”

Speaking of entertaining, the week’s announcement that Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond was front of mind. “I wish him every joy and every success. He and I made a movie a number of years ago called Remember Me. I played his father. So I was very, very pleased and joyful for his nomination and now his success, and I believe he will be magnificent.”

And that creative full circle is exactly what the night was advocating. “Our own Luminaries in Residence program reflects our belief that meaningful hospitality creates genuine connection with extraordinary talents with one another, and with arts,” Bob van den Oord, CEO of Langham Hospitality Group, explained as he took the stage. “The Langham isn’t simply a place to stay, but a place to gather, exchange ideas, and indeed celebrate.”

items.title: THE BIRTH OF BOND | Vanity Fair
items.description: Half a century ago, at the dawn of the commercial-jet age, James Bond strode into movie history, to show audiences how stylish and thrilling life could be. But creating the cinematic Bond was fraught with peril, as best-selling author Ian Fleming discovered wh
items.author: David Kamp
paragraphs: Half a century ago, at the dawn of the commercial-jet age, James Bond strode into movie history, to show audiences how stylish and thrilling life could be. But creating the cinematic Bond was fraught with peril, as best-selling author Ian Fleming discovered when he first tried to take his hero to the screen. DAVID KAMP recalls the unlikely team—two small-time producers, a journeyman director, and a "rough diamond" of a star―behind 007's film debut, Dr. No,, the beginning of a $5 billion franchise
ORIGINALLY PUBLISHED IN OCTOBER 2012

nter Sean Connery, dark hair slicked with pomade, eyes locking hungrily upon a beautiful green-eyed girl. Her return glance leaves no doubt—the feeling is mutual. His slouch and casual banter exude languor and nonchalance, but there's an undercurrent of coiled menace to this man, as though he might, at any moment, spring into table-overturning, crockery-shattering action.

Except nothing of the sort happens. Instead, the other fellow in the scene cuts the tension by taking out his fiddle and favoring the room with a jaunty tune learned, he says in a stagy brogue, "in the old ruins on the top of Knocknasheega!"

This isn't a James Bond picture. It is 1959, and Connery is putting in time in a cornball live-action Disney feature called Darby O'Gill and the Little People. He's the second male lead, billed beneath not only Albert Sharpe, the elderly Irish character actor in the title role—a kindly farmhand who sees leprechauns—but also the greeneyed girl, the ingenue Janet Munro. Though verily pump-misting pheromonal musk into the air, to a degree unmatched before or since by any actor in a Disney family movie, Connery is still a jobbing scuffler, not a star. He has no idea of what lies in store for him.

The seventh of Ian Fleming's Bond novels, Goldfinger, has recently reached the shops. But there are no Bond pictures yet. In London, a Long Island-born film producer named Albert R. Broccoli, known as Cubby, is still lamenting that he blew his chance with Fleming. The previous year, Broccoli had set up a meeting with the English author and his representatives to talk about securing movie rights to the Bond series, only to miss the meeting to tend to his wife, who had recently been diagnosed with terminal cancer. In Broccoli's absence, his business partner, Irving Allen, let Fleming know that he didn't share his colleague's ardor. "In my opinion," Allen told Bond's creator, "these books are not even good enough for television."

This is an older, stiffer world, with Britain just five years removed from food rationing and America still in an era of Kramdens, Eisenhowers, and finned Caddies. It is a world unfamiliar with the catchphrases "Shaken, not stirred" and "Bond, James Bond," where no ears have ever heard Monty Norman's four-note Bond motif and no eyes have ever taken in Maurice Binder's amniotic credit sequences of lissome women undulating in silhouette to lavishly charted John Barry arrangements.

But it is also a world in transition. Transatlantic jet service is newly available to commercial passengers, thanks to the carriers B.O.A.C. and Pan American. G.D. Searle & Company, a pharmaceutical concern, is awaiting approval from the Food and Drug Administration to market one of its products, Enovid, as a birthcontrol pill for women. A scrubbed, fit group of U.S. military test pilots has just been introduced to the public as the Mercury Seven, America's first astronauts. And the undeclared Democratic frontrunner in the next presidential election is only 42 years old.

In March 1961, when he actually is the president, John F. Kennedy lists Fleming's fifth Bond novel, From Russia with Love, as one of his 10 current favorite reads in a Life magazine article. That same year, Broccoli, having parted ways with Allen and joined forces with another producer, a Canadian by the name of Harry Saltzman, finally gets the rights to turn Fleming's books into movies. After an arduous and seemingly fruitless search to find a lead actor mutually agreeable to the two producers and their studio benefactor, United Artists, Broccoli circles back to one of the lesser-knowns among the candidates: Sean Connery. To confirm his hunch that this tall, handsome Scotsman could be the guy, Broccoli, while in Hollywood, arranges for his new wife, Dana, to join him in a screening room at the Samuel Goldwyn Studio. There they watch the only Connery footage that Cubby has been able to rustle up: Darby OGill and the Little People. Dana Broccoli's response is instantaneous: "That's our Bond!"
And so on October 5,1962, at the London Pavilion theater, in Piccadilly Circus, Connery joins Fleming, Broccoli, and Saltzman on the red carpet for the world premiere of the first Bond film, Dr. No.

half-century later, even in an era inured to skin, gunplay, and wide-screen shots of tropical waterfalls, Dr. No remains exhilarating to watch. The azure brightness of Jamaica, with Connery striding purposefully through it; the seawater-salted flesh and ounces-light wardrobe of Ursula Andress; the modernist bachelor-pad fantasia that is the undersea lair of the titular doctor, played with cool reserve by Joseph Wiseman—it's all so fantastically stylish, racy, and forward-looking. So imagine what it must have been like for the people who actually saw the picture in a theater when it first came out.

Dr. No took just a few months in the U.K. to recoup its $1 million budget and ultimately made 20 times that amount in its initial release. Theater bookers in the U.S. hedged their bets at first, putting out the film "in the sticks," as a chagrined Broccoli noted, before allowing the sophisticates in New York and Los Angeles to see it. Nevertheless, the drumbeat had already begun, with North Carolina's Rocky Mount Telegram, for example, relishing how Connery "twists his supple body through a tiny aperture to potential freedom." The syndicated entertainment columnist Erskine Johnson suggested that "tawny 26-year-old Ursula Andress should have been billed not by her last name, but as 'Undress.' "

As it turned out, the coastal intelligentsia were pretty easily won over, too. "Oh, it was dazzling: Ursula coming out of the ocean, the brilliant art direction, straining your eyes to see the almost-nude women in the opening credits. They were cheap tricks, but good tricks," says Buck Henry, who, with Mel Brooks and the TV producer Daniel Melnick, was inspired in '65 to create the sitcom spoof Get Smart in homage. "It wasn't Brueghel," Henry says of the early Bond films, "but it was like the stuff that Lichtenstein and those other guys were doing—great Pop art carried into another medium."

Dr. No and its two follow-ups, From Russia with Love (1963) and Goldfinger (1964), are the cornerstones of Bond mania. Like the early Lennon-McCartney singles that spurred Beatlemania, they augured bigger, more elaborate things to come, but the sheer excitement they generated remains unsurpassable. Not only were these movies terrifically entertaining, they also delivered a sort of jet-age holodeck experience, granting regular folk an opportunity to glimpse the future awaiting them. As of 1960, fewer than 2 percent of all Americans had traveled internationally by air. So both Dr. No and From Russia with Love include what are essentially fetish shots of Pan Am jets landing on runways as air-traffic controllers announce their arrival. ("Hello, London, your flight PA1 just landed in Istanbul")

"It was a sense of 'Buy your ticket—we're going to take you places!' " says Guy Hamilton, the director of Goldfinger. He recalls the Broccoli-Saltzman attitude toward Bond transport as "Don't take a train when you can take a plane, and if you're going to take a plane, take the newest one around. And if you give Bond a car, don't show what's been seen—show what's not out yet." This is why, while Bond drives an Aston Martin DBIII in Goldfinger the novel, he drives a DB5 in Hamilton's movie, made five years later. It's also why, when Bond comes to after being knocked out with a tranquilizer gun in the same film, he is told, by no less than Honor Blackman's knockout aviatrix, Pussy Galore, that he is aboard "Mr. Goldfinger's Lockheed JetStar"—this at a time when the very concept of a private business jet was virtually unheard of. Even Bond's room-service breakfast order in From Russia with Love— "Green figs, yogurt, coffee, very black"—sounds ahead of its time.

Beyond the travelogue aspect, there was the sex aspect—another way, as it were, to hitch a ride with James Bond. "The actual film, to film, was sexy," says Shirley Eaton of her scenes with Connery in Goldfinger. Eaton is famous for being the blonde girl whose body is discovered nude, lifeless, and coated in gold paint—her death (by "skin suffocation," not a medical possibility in real life) a punishment by her boss, Auric Goldfinger, for switching to Bond's side.

But it's Eaton's first scene with Connery that packs the erotic wallop. Bond, poolside at Miami's Fontainebleau hotel, has worked out from which room Goldfinger's accomplice is spying on his opponent's cards, thereby allowing Goldfinger to cheat at his alfresco games of high-stakes gin rummy. Letting himself into the room, Bond discovers Eaton's Jill Masterson lying stomach-down in a black bikini on a balcony lounger, using binoculars and a radio set to convey the card info into Goldfinger's earpiece. Wearing a shorty jumpsuit of pale-blue terry cloth that only someone as masculine as Connery could pull off, Bond, grinning, simply lowers himself gently onto Jill, shrewdly opting for horizontal bodily contact rather than force to accomplish his mission.

Eaton, then 27, had been acting in movies since her teen years, "always playing the girl next door," she says, or a pretty thing to be ogled in one of Britain's low-budget Carry On comedies. "But this was entirely new," she says. "It was grown-up sexuality. Sean and I just fell into our natural sensuality without any rumpy-pumpy, and I think that's what made it so exciting."

Honor Blackman, likewise, had already established herself as the judo-chopping, leather-clad Dr. Cathy Gale on the British TV series The Avengers but found the Bond universe to have an altogether different dynamic. "Cathy Gale was a very proper lady, with collars up to the chin," she says, "whereas Pussy was supposed to match Bond's sexuality. She was a tough broad who also showed a fair amount of bosom." Johnny Carson, just a few years into hosting The Tonight Show, was so taken with the scene in which Pussy finally surrenders to Bond's charms (they trade martial-arts body flips in a hay-filled barn before falling into a love clutch) that "he badgered and badgered me—would I show him how it was done?" she says. Blackman feared injuring Carson, but she flew to New York to rehearse the bit with him, and when they performed it live "he passionately kissed me at the end, which wasn't planned. It was funny, but it also showed how much even someone like Johnny Carson wanted to be James Bond."

an Fleming had long been alert to the screen potential of his books, but realizing this potential proved to be something of a chore. Twice in the late '50s, Fleming worked with American networks to develop a TV series, first with NBC on a Bond-inspired spy show provisionally titled Commander Jamaica, and then with CBS on what would have been an explicitly Bond-based weekly drama. Neither show made it to the pilot phase. A little earlier, in 1954, CBS had aired an anemic one-off adaptation of Fleming's first Bond novel, Casino Royale, in which the character had been Americanized into "Jimmy Bond" and been played by a miscast, chipmunk-cheeked actor named Barry Nelson. Fleming then sold the book's movie rights to the actor Gregory Ratoff, who died before coming close to getting a movie produced. These rights, unbundled from rights to the other Bond books, eventually fell into the hands of Ratoff s agent, the Hollywood mcicher Charles Feldman, who, after Bond mania took off, produced the abominable meta-parodic version with David Niven, Peter Sellers, and Woody Allen that came out in 1967. (Only in the last decade was Casino Roy ale, the novel, reeled into the hands of the "official" Bond producers—Broccoli's heirs— the result being the 2006 franchise reboot starring Daniel Craig.)
"OH, DISASTER, DISASTER, DISASTER!" DIRECTOR TERENCE YOUNG SAID WHEN SEAN CONNERY WAS CAST.

Fleming had higher hopes for a treatment he worked on in 1959 for a film to be called James Bond, Secret Agent. It was not an adaptation but a new Bond story, and his collaborator was Kevin McClory, an up-and-coming Irish screenwriter. But this project, too, foundered. Fleming, unbowed, folded his ideas for the shelved movie into the next Bond novel. Not long before this book, Thunderball, came out, in 1961, McClory got hold of an advance copy and was angered by its resemblance to the story treatment he'd labored on with Fleming and another writer, Jack Whittingham. McClory filed suit, and, while the book's publication was allowed to go forward, the issue of its film rights would take another three years to resolve.

In the movie industry, Fleming had at last run into a thickety, double-dealing milieu that he, a suave operator his entire adult life, was ill-prepared to contend with. Before that, to all appearances, he had been Mr. Smooth. It has often been said that James Bond was Fleming's fantasy version of himself, while Fleming declared that Bond was "a compound of all the secret agents and commando types I met" during World War II, in which he served in Britain's Naval Intelligence Division. Whichever way it was, Fleming had certainly known Bondish people and lived through Bondish episodes of his own by the time he sat down in 1952 and created the character at his typewriter.

In his youth, Fleming, born in 1908, had been a rascally, athletic ne'er-do-well who attended but did not graduate from Eton and the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, distinguishing himself more as a trainee roue than an officer candidate. In the '30s, he finally found some measure of professional fulfillment, first as a journalist working for Reuters, the news agency, and then, as war broke out, as an aide to Rear Admiral John Henry Godfrey, Britain's director of naval intelligence.

Godfrey, brusque and imperious, became the model for 007's superior, M. He took to Fleming, inviting the younger man to accompany him to overseas meetings with J. Edgar Hoover, the F.B.I. chief, and William J. "Wild Bill" Donovan, the founder of the Office of Strategic Services, the Central Intelligence Agency's precursor. Godfrey also granted Fleming significant leeway to conjure imaginative schemes to trip up the Nazis. One of these, Operation Mincemeat, is among the more celebrated in the annals of British espionage. In 1943, British intelligence officers took possession of the corpse of Glyndwr Michael, a homeless Welshman who had recently died by his own hand. After dressing Michael's body in the uniform of a major in the Royal Marines, stuffing his pockets with phony identification materials, and chaining to his wrist a briefcase containing a letter labeled PERSONAL AND MOST SECRET, they dumped him off the coast of Spain, creating the impression of an officer who had died in a plane crash. Spain was infested with Nazi spies, and the hope was that one of them would inevitably get his hands on the letter and pass it up the chain of command. It worked. Hitler was fooled by the documents, which indicated that the Allies were about to invade Greece, and hastily moved a division of 90,000 troops there. The Allies, with considerably less resistance than they would have encountered otherwise, proceeded to take their true target, Sicily.

A fter the war, Fleming landed a job as foreign-news manager for Kemsley Newspapers, which owned, among other publications, The Sunday Times—a assignment that allowed him to spend every winter season in Jamaica, a place he'd first visited during his naval-intelligence years. In 1946 he built a home on the island's north shore that he called Goldeneye, after the code name of an Allied plan to defend Gibraltar against seizure by the Axis powers. From '52 onward, Fleming used Goldeneye as his writing roost, banging out one Bond novel a year. Nevertheless, by the beginning of 1961, he had still had no luck with Hollywood, which he described to a friend as "a hell of a jungle" and full of "specious promises."

It was at this time that, for $50,000, he granted Harry Saltzman a six-month option to put a film deal in place for the Bond books. A stout, hedgehoggish man born in 1915 to Jewish immigrants living in Quebec, Saltzman had hustled his way into the American movie industry, eventually venturing to England to take advantage of the tax breaks the U.K. afforded filmmakers. On the face of it, Saltzman was a peculiar deal partner for Fleming. While he had achieved modest success producing film adaptations of John Osborne's table-thumping social-realist plays Look Back in Anger and The Entertainer, he was decidedly small-time compared with previous suitors. Saltzman's children have long puzzled over how their father, who died in 1994, managed to secure the option. One of his daughters, Hilary Saltzman, stumbled upon some revelatory clues when, in 2003, she decided to relocate with her children from Los Angeles to Quebec. Having let her Canadian passport expire, she ran into a hitch while getting her citizenship papers in order: The Canadian government required documentation of her father's reasons for immigrating to the United States. The next surprise she encountered was that her request to pull her father's U.S. records, a process she expected to be routine, set off alarms at the State Department. When, after more than two years of petitioning, Hilary finally received the documents she needed to satisfy the Canadian government, she also received a bonus: reams of material revealing that her father, who she knew had served in the Royal Canadian Air Force in the early years of World War II, had subsequently worked for the U.S. Office of War Information, specifically its Psychological Warfare Division. The senior Saltzman had never been forthright with his children about how he spent his war.
"SEAN AND I JUST FELL INTO OUR NATURAL SENSUALITY WITHOUT ANY RUMPYPUMPY," SAYS SHIRLEY EATON.

"I'm reading these letters of Robert E. Sherwood, the O.W.I.'s director of overseas operations, about my father," Hilary says. "The countries he was to visit overseas: 'Confidential.' Nature of business: 'Confidential war mission for O.W.I.' I'm stunned. It just blew me away that, finally, I understood what my father had done in the war. Finally, I understood his fascination with the spy genre of films." (In the '60s, Saltzman also produced a trilogy of films starring Michael Caine as Len Deighton's spy Harry Palmer, based on the Deighton novels The Ipcress File, Funeral in Berlin, and Billion Dollar Brain) One of Sherwood's unredacted letters, from 1943, informs G. Howland Shaw, assistant secretary of state, that "Mr. Saltzman will be assigned to the North African theater of war to serve on the staff of Mr. C.D. Jackson." Jackson was a noted psychologicalwarfare expert and propaganda mastermind who was then working for the O.S.S. and later served as a Cold War adviser to President Dwight Eisenhower. His base, Algiers, to which Saltzman was sent, was also one of Fleming's wartime destinations.

Hilary Saltzman and her brother, Steven, have yet to turn up evidence that their father and Fleming met before 1961; it's possible, even probable, that they did not. But Hilary posits that "because they had a similar background during the war, which was in confidential missions, they had a mutual understanding. Even though they couldn't publicize it, I really think Ian felt that this series was safe in my father's hands."

Yet by mid-1961 the Bond option was about to slip through Saltzman's fingers: He was five months into his six-month option and hadn't put together any backing. By happenstance, Cubby Broccoli was working with a screenwriter, Wolf Mankowitz, who not only knew Saltzman but was aware that he held the Bond option. Broccoli wasn't pleased with the script for an Arabian Nights-thcmcd movie that Mankowitz had pressed upon him, and when Mankowitz asked Broccoli what he'd rather be producing, Broccoli brought up his long-held desire to make films of Fleming's books. Mankowitz agreed to introduce Broccoli to Saltzman. Though Broccoli, having just shed his old partner, Irving Allen, hoped to buy the option in its entirety, Saltzman insisted on maintaining his piece of the action—and, in fact, had already drawn up a document for Broccoli to sign, affirming that "you and I have mutually agreed that we shall equally share" the film rights to all the Bond books save Casino Royale. And so, in June 1961, was born what Guy Hamilton calls "a wonderful double act": Broccoli, affable and teddy-bearish, serving as a tempering counterpoint to the volatile and argumentative Saltzman. They named their venture Eon Productions.

Broccoli was born in 1909 to an Italian-immigrant family from Calabria. His father, Giovanni Broccoli, and great-uncle Pasquale de Cicco were Long Island truck farmers who sold their goods in New York City and were actually instrumental in popularizing the vegetable broccoli in the United States. Notwithstanding his humble family roots, Cubby was better connected than Saltzman. In the '30s, through his sharpie cousin Pat de Cicco, Pasquale's son, a Hollywood playboy and the first husband of Gloria Vanderbilt, he had gained a toehold in the film industry, landing an assistant job on a Howard Hawks picture and later becoming close to Alan Ladd, the matinee-idol star of Shane and The Great Gatsby.

Taking advantage of the same tax breaks that had lured Saltzman to England, Broccoli and Allen had founded a British company, Warwick Films, that made its mark in the '50s with such war and adventure pictures as Paratrooper, Hell Below Zero, and The Cockleshell Heroes, the first two starring Ladd. In 1961, Broccoli worked his connections to secure a meeting in New York with Arthur Krim, the head of United Artists. Krim agreed to a budget of just over a million dollars for a James Bond movie. At last, a deal had been done.

Broccoli and Saltzman were keen to begin with the latest Bond novel, Thunderbolt. But in light of Kevin McClory's pending lawsuit, they opted instead for Fleming's sixth book, Doctor No, from 1958, which offered both a cinematically picturesque Jamaican setting and a sinister Eurasian villain who, on his private Caribbean island, Crab Key, plotted to sabotage U.S. rocket launches from Cape Canaveral—a story line that presciently anticipated the Cuban missile crisis, which unfolded the very month that Dr. No (as the film version was titled) was released in Britain. To ensure that things would run smoothly, Broccoli brought in a pair of trusted veterans from his Warwick days, the British director Terence Young and the American screenwriter Richard Maibaum. Maibaum was paired with Wolf Mankowitz to come up with a script.

Young, like Fleming, was a tall, rakish character of privileged background: educated at Cambridge, a tank commander in the Irish Guards during World War II. Maibaum, a native of the Bronx and frequent collaborator with Ladd, served in the war as director of the U.S. Army's Combat Films Division, handling footage both for classified use and for dissemination to the public through newsreels. The first screenplay he wrote after the war was for Ladd's film O.S.S.: a 1946 dramatization of the wartime work of the Office of Strategic Services that featured such proto-Bond touches as a clever espionage gadget (a Minox mini-camera) and a comely lady spy (Geraldine Fitzgerald).

In Young, Maibaum, and Saltzman, the Bond-movie team had a group of World War II vets who, like Fleming, were well versed in matters of military intelligence and would bring a level of verite and nuance to what were otherwise playfully escapist entertainments. In Broccoli, who did his wartime bit as an ensign in the navy and a wrangler of Hollywood talent for morale-boosting shows for the troops, the Bond pictures had their great showman and salesman.

Fleming's books are at once grittier and more preposterous than the Bond movies. His Bond registers fear and panic and has hangovers. But he's also something of a bizarre, half-mad sociopath, at times evoking Patrick Bateman, the vain, self-assured brand-name dropper of Bret Easton Ellis's American Psycho, and Jean des Esseintes, the debauched hyper-aesthete of J.K. Huysmans's A Rebours. Here is how Fleming, through Bond's eyes, rather creepily describes Vesper Lynd, the first Bond girl (in print, anyway), in Casino Royale: "Her medium-length dress was of grey soie sauvage with a square-cut bodice, lasciviously tight across her fine breasts. The skirt was closely pleated and flowered down from a narrow, but not a thin, waist. She wore a three-inch, handstitched black belt." In Goldfinger the novel, Bond, while tracking the villain through France, stops in Orleans—a place he dislikes, "a priest and myth ridden town without gaiety"—and takes in "one of his favourite meals: two oeufs cocotte a la creme, a large sole meuniere (Orleans was close enough to the sea. The fish of the Loire are inclined to be muddy) and an adequate Camembert. He drank a well-iced pint of Rose d'Anjou and had a Hennessy's Three Star with his coffee."

Clearly, the filmmakers were going to have to tamp down the soiesauvage-noting and muddy-fish-despising aspects of the character to make him more sympathetic and relatable to audiences. At the same time, Cinema Bond would have to maintain the man-of-action toughness that warranted his Double-Oh status—his license, as granted by M.I.6, Britain's foreign-intelligence service, to kill. This is why the casting of Connery was a masterstroke. Alone among actors, "Sean was able to suggest that dichotomy," said Maibaum in an interview with the film historian Patrick McGilligan. "Fleming thought David Niven would have made a great James Bond," Maibaum said, "but David Niven wasn't all that physical. Originally, Roger Moore was considered for Bond, you know. Then Cubby saw something in Sean which he thought was what they wanted. They took a gamble with Sean; they would have been much safer with Roger."

There is a phrase used almost universally by those involved in the early Bond films to describe Connery circa 1962: a "rough diamond." He was born in 1930 in Edinburgh to a truckdriver and a charwoman. As a young man he worked a variety of menial jobs in Scotland, including driving a milk truck—a detail that seems to captivate biographers and associates ("He was a blasted milkman!" says Honor Blackman)—before traveling to London to compete in a bodybuilding contest, in which he finished third. When he was 22, he landed his first acting job, an ensemble part in a London production of South Pacific.

Connery's looks and muscular build led to a middling early film career that showcased how attractive he was but little else. Moore, three years his senior, had the better track record and was on the verge of television stardom as the noble thief Simon Templar in The Saint. But Broccoli found Moore, at the time, to be "a shade too pretty" for Bond, and even when Moore finally assumed the role, in 1973's Live and Let Die, his light touch and fundamental lack of menace required a recalibration of the Bond character.

Connery's rough-hewn background served Cinema Bond well; it made him a more plausible creation than Fleming's Bond. Whereas the latter is a roguish posh boy, steeped in the finer things in life, who just happens to be a cold-blooded assassin, the former is not unlike Don Draper as portrayed by Jon Hamm in Mad Men: a mysterious self-creation whose virile good looks opened doors in his young adulthood and who seized upon these openings to learn the ropes as a gentleman, connoisseur, and lover, transforming himself into a convincing but dangerous facsimile of all of the above.

Not that anyone, Broccoli included, had any certainty of how well Connery would come off. Fleming was known to have his doubts, and Young, who had worked with Connery on one of the actor's uninspiring '50s films, Action of the Tiger, made no bones about his feelings when Broccoli told him that Connery had been signed. "Oh, disaster, disaster, disaster!" he said.

But Young overcame his initial misgivings, becoming, in fact, the man most readily credited with shaping Connery's Bond persona. It's a disservice to Connery's acting skills to say that he was simply doing his best Terence Young impression, but "Terence taught Sean, who was very basic in those days, a lot of good manners, and Terence felt himself like a James Bond-like person," says Ken Adam, the production designer on nearly all of the Conneryera Bond movies. Young, who died in 1994, took Connery out to restaurants in Mayfair and introduced him to his bespoke tailor, Anthony Sinclair. While the oft-told tale that Connery acclimated to his new handmade suits by sleeping in them is possibly apocryphal, Sinclair took pride in how his clothes functioned like a second skin on the star. "Any well-made suit," he told an ABC News interviewer in the '60s, "you should be able to take it, roll it into a ball, crush it, stamp on it, sleep in it, and then"—smoothing the narrow, impeccably draped lapels of the Sinclair suit he himself was wearing—"there you are, you're back again, you see?"
r. No's gestation was not without its problems. Sometimes a sentiment prevailed, perhaps as a hedge against failure and ridicule, that the movie was just a bit of nonsense, a B picture. Adam, whose w

items.title: Los Javis and Penélope Cruz Agree the Kids Are Alright
items.description: Los Javis and Penélope Cruz Agree the Kids Are Alright
items.author: Penélope Cruz
paragraphs: Los Javis and Penélope Cruz Agree the Kids Are Alright

In Spain, they’re simply Los Javis. Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo started as actors, staged a small Madrid musical that became a film, then built a run of television hits that made them famous at home. Their latest, La Bola Negra, is on another scale entirely. Inspired by an unfinished Federico García Lorca play, the three-era queer drama about love and war won them Best Director at Cannes, set box office records in Spain, and has made them Oscar hopefuls. Few directors get a moment like this. Even fewer get Penélope Cruz, who appears in the film, to interview them about it.
FRIDAY 3:15 PM OCTOBER 9, 2026 LONDON
PENÉLOPE CRUZ: I have so many things I want to know, but we should start from the beginning because I’m a tiny bit older than you guys and I want context.
JAVIER AMBROSSI: Do you think so?
CRUZ: A tiny bit. You obviously have a shared obsession with cinema, but how did it start? At home on TV? Renting films? Going to the movies?

JAVIER CALVO: My father used to take me every weekend to the cinema, but also do you remember this DVD collection of Spanish films El País released? It included all the [Pedro] Almodóvar movies, it had—
CALVO: [Luis García]Berlanga, [José Juan]Bigas Luna, [Víctor] Erice. I was obsessed with that collection, and I would watch these films over and over in my room, on my little DVD player.

AMBROSSI: I started with an obsession for books and literature. From the time I was very young, I read every day, every kind of book. That stayed with me a long time before I switched to entertainment and television.

CRUZ: I watched everything. I wasn’t interested in going anywhere. I wanted to watch all the shows and all the movies. Whatever they were showing on television was fine with me. That was the happiest time of my life.
AMBROSSI: We are the same. I learned about entertainment from television before I discovered cinema.
CRUZ: And we all three have a shared crush on Almodóvar. Your experience of discovering him and his world was similar to mine, right?
AMBROSSI: Yes. As a kid, I saw the poster for Kika, the one that had the guy in a tank top. I was flushed, looking at that poster. So even the posters for Pedro’s films made a big impact.
CRUZ: I feel the same way.

CALVO: I went to the movies with my family, and I remember seeing you in Volver. It was shocking to see a reality similar to my own could be portrayed in the movies in such a beautiful, fun way. That was so inspiring for me—the way you talked, the way I recognized my culture and myself in there.

AMBROSSI: I went to a Catholic boys’ school and my mother knew I needed to see other things. Every week, she’d say, “Let’s go to the movies,” and everyone around was like, “Ah, but Spanish movies are not okay,” because I come from a very traditional family. But she was like—
AMBROSSI: “Let’s go, because I know it’s going to wake up something in you.”
CALVO: At a certain point, I discovered Gus Van Sant and other queer directors, but it was hard for me to find queer movies.
AMBROSSI: You had to go to a video store. It’s so funny when people say, “In Spanish cinema, there’s always gay people and civil war.” That’s not true.
CRUZ: And actually there are not so many films about the civil war.
AMBROSSI: No, it’s not true. I don’t know who said that, but some people think it’s a reality. This year, La Bola Negra is the only Spanish movie with a gay leading character.

CRUZ: That is incredible. Aren’t you looking forward to the day when a queer film is made and the first question in every interview is not, “How do you feel that this subject is being talked about?” It’s the same when you work with a female director and the first question is, “How is it different working with a female director?” It makes you realize how modern, important, and necessary the words of Federico García Lorca still are. I think that’s why everyone is connecting so much with your film, because you did something so brave without lecturing anybody.
CRUZ: You are reminding us what it is to be on the right side of things. It’s so heartbreaking to still hear that as almost the first question in every interview.
AMBROSSI: I understand why.
CRUZ: I also understand why they would ask, but in 2026, we are still like, “This is a big deal.”
AMBROSSI: I would love for it to be super normal to have leading gay characters, but it isn’t.
CRUZ: In the same way there are not so many female directors.

AMBROSSI: There are not. They can repeat it and repeat it and repeat it, but it’s not true. It’s a big thing now because our rights are being threatened. Fascism is growing. I think art comes when it’s needed, and it’s not a coincidence we’re seeing so many queer stories this year.

CRUZ: You’ve done something very huge. People are going like crazy to the theater to see this film, not only once, but two and three times. If you had done this from a place of, “I’m going to tell you what to think,” they would have rejected it, but what you did is so smart and so deep, and you did it from a point of view of no judgment. I don’t feel like we are giving enough credit to young people. Everyone is saying, “They’re so confused,” but they are seeing much more than we think. And you both knew that in the way you wrote this—you treated them as they deserve to be treated, as a smart generation, aware of the traps they are being served every day through social media. They are aware of the threats to democracy, the threats to freedom, the threats to respect. You are such old souls to have written something like this. You inspired teenagers to skip school on the day of the premiere because they wanted to be the first ones there. In the theater, you can see a 17-year-old and a 90-year-old man or woman hugging, strangers hugging. I don’t know if you realized how powerful it is.

AMBROSSI: I don’t realize yet, but when we did La Mesías, I was very surprised by young people because we were told specifically by everyone, “Young people are not going to watch this.” Everyone was worried because the first two episodes are so challenging, and everyone was like, “Guys, this time young audiences are not going to follow you,” but it ended up being the favorite show of a lot of young people.
CRUZ: That is my hope for the future, that these younger generations will say, “Wait, I also want to be part of this artisanal way of doing things, because the world wants to rob that from me.”
AMBROSSI: It’s happening. Young audiences know they want the real thing. They know better.
CRUZ: They also know so much about politics. We have to encourage them and make them feel seen and heard.

AMBROSSI: La Bola Negra is a movie specifically about Federico García Lorca, who was part of a free generation. He experimented a lot. He was a young, vibrant guy trying to understand what he wanted to do, mixing poetry with naturalism and family drama. Suddenly he wanted surreality, to experiment. Lorca represented young people very well because he was young, and that’s why people are connecting with his spirit.
CRUZ: There is hope for the world.
CALVO: There is hope. It’s beautiful to see young people from all over being interested in Lorca. Having a hit movie that talks about literature is amazing.
AMBROSSI: And about our Spanish literature.
CRUZ: This is like a revolution, and I’m so proud to be part of it because it’s huge and so necessary.
CRUZ: No. I’m very much aware how lucky I am to be part of this film.
AMBROSSI: But you being a part of this gave so much attention to the movie worldwide.
CRUZ: The movie would’ve gotten the attention anyway, because it’s a masterpiece.
AMBROSSI: Without you, it wouldn’t be La Bola Negra.
CRUZ: I know the two of you are very different, but it is amazing how life has put you together. This is not a coincidence.

CRUZ: You have been together so many years, and even now that you’re not a couple, you’re working together because you are best friends. The level of respect I see you have for each other is so inspiring.

CRUZ: It is beautiful to see people can continue to share things when a relationship is over. You told me a little bit about your writing process, the schedule. You wake up really early and exercise before you start writing?
CRUZ: I would like to spend a day with you both when you are writing. [Laughs]
CALVO: There’s a lot of silence, a lot of reading, a lot of thinking. There’s a lot of walking around the house, there’s a lot of music, and there’s a lot of talking.
AMBROSSI: At the beginning, it’s all about researching.
CRUZ: Together, or do you do that separately?
AMBROSSI: Together. I don’t know the words but it’s like “double body” or something. Hyperactive people work very well as couples.
CALVO: With someone next to you.
AMBROSSI: Is that the body double?
CRUZ: It’s because of ADHD?
AMBROSSI: Yeah. Body doubling.
CRUZ: I didn’t know it was called that.

AMBROSSI: It’s a strategy of productivity for people with ADHD that consists of realizing a task in the presence of another. I think both of us have that. If we are not in the presence of the other, we are not going to work.
