items.title: The Altruists Recap: Overdraft Protection
items.description: Who is giving the best performance on The Altruists? I suspect most viewers would agree on Julia Garner, who’s doing a good job anchoring Caroline Ellison in something concrete and real, no matter how much the writing lets her down. Aside from her and Anthony
items.author: Ben Rosenstock
paragraphs: Who is giving the best performance on The Altruists? I suspect most viewers would agree on Julia Garner, who’s doing a good job anchoring Caroline Ellison in something concrete and real, no matter how much the writing lets her down. Aside from her and Anthony Boyle, though, Alex Lawther deserves some kudos. Yes, his English accent slips through every once in a while, and sometimes he goes a little too big with the expressive monologuing and compulsive fidgeting. But in his screen time, Lawther has managed to create a vivid, real-feeling character — someone nerdy and socially unaware but often funny and charming in his own sparkly way.

So in some ways, I’m inclined to view “The Duck” as the best episode of the show thus far. It’s sort of the climax of the whole story, seemingly filling in all the remaining pre-2022 details and depicting the central act of fraud that wrecked everything Sam and Caroline had built. That clears the way for two more streamlined final episodes unpacking the fallout, which is a good thing; the series could certainly benefit from less timeline hopping. But it’s also a standout episode because it puts the spotlight on Sam Trabucco, one of the show’s strongest characters and performances. Lawther is just watchable.

That’s not to say this episode actually indicates some big jump in quality. After all, I’m still keeping this at three stars. Filtering the established narrative through Trabucco’s perspective lends the episode some focus, but it also raises even more confusion about culpability instead of putting the full blame where it should probably lie. I try not to pay too much attention to the fact-versus-fiction discrepancies on this show, but even without knowing exactly what went down, most of the specificities of Trabucco’s involvement are pretty difficult to believe.

His tale begins at Cambridge in 2011, where his friend Sam has recently earned a little rubber duck to symbolize his place at Epsilon Theta, a nerdy fraternity at MIT. Sam shows early klepto tendencies, stealing some liquid nitrogen from Trabucco’s lab so that Epsilon Theta can make instant ice cream — and so that Trabucco can earn the cred to get him his own duck. Trabucco doesn’t mind, though. He doesn’t realize that Sam will be replicating this little incident on a much larger scale a decade later.

Here’s where we start to see how much of a role Trabucco has actually played in the story we’ve been watching. He was the one who advised Sam to simply laugh at Todd’s jokes to get by at Jane Street; more importantly, he was the one who introduced Sam to the multipart arbitrage idea that made Alameda Research an early success. And it doesn’t take much convincing for him to abandon his stable finance job and move to Hong Kong, where he is the one to suggest the company mint its own FTT coin.

That last move is pretty important, because Alameda can now take out loans against FTT, whose value will rise if tied to trading on FTX. This creates a sort of infinite moneymaking loop, or a “hack” in Trabucco’s words — a trick they can use in times of emergency, though Sam immediately starts abusing it and even using the hack to buy out CZ. Trabucco, who pivots to becoming the cautious one around this point, tries to fix things by joining Caroline as co-CEO at Alameda, rather than joining Sam at FTX, but it’s impossible for him to convince her to look at Sam more critically. At this juncture, they’re too wrapped up in each other. We see that when Trabucco tries to warn them about the danger of making an exception for Alameda and disabling the safeguards: If the fund takes a big loss on a trade and goes negative, it will draw from customer money as overdraft protection.

It’s becoming clear how this fraud came together. As always, though, the scheme needs a romantic angle. In this case, Trabucco starts really dedicating himself to breaking up Sam and Caroline, sowing seeds of discord by pointing out their issues to each other and encouraging miscommunication. The pandemic and resulting Chinese crypto crackdown help: Sam ultimately decides to move FTX to the Bahamas while Caroline holds down the fort with Alameda here in Hong Kong, forcing the lovebirds into a long-distance relationship.

It’s pretty easy to guess what happens next: In 2022, Trabucco discovers the $8 billion shortfall while going through the master ledger, a massive error that went undetected due to a lack of an accounting department at the company. Sam and Caroline were both paying for everything out of Alameda’s account, including naming rights to the Miami Heat stadium and private jets, so each has a reason to blame the other.

Surprisingly, “The Duck” doesn’t actually depict the conversation that follows, when Sam and Caroline break up for good. But both react in predictable ways, with Sam pushing for more growth instead of shrinking the company down to fill the hole. His stubbornness leads to a huge, friendship-ending fight with Trabucco, during which each of them delivers some low blows. They’re pretty deserved, though, especially the ones aimed at Sam. Maybe Trabucco was a coward who benefited by letting his friend take the risks he didn’t feel comfortable taking himself, but Sam is a spoiled brat relying on the safety net of his parents and the assurance of a bailout.

Honestly, there’s enough established history between these two now that this conversation works pretty well. It’s a tad silly that Trabucco’s biggest betrayal is telling Caroline that Sam was a virgin, but most of the dialogue is stronger and more cutting than usual. The fight is a solid enough way of transitioning Trabucco out of the main story, and the frame narrative, with Trabucco describing all of this to a worried, pissed-off Lily, adequately sets up the biggest threat going into the next episode: CZ, who sees the leaked balance sheet and now knows he could send the company into free fall by off-loading the FTT used to buy him out.

It’s all fairly entertaining, as far as this show goes, and the script does a nice job filling in background details that influenced most of the major events throughout the show. But it’s still difficult not to think of how much of this material is fabricated for the series, including the sheer level of Trabucco’s involvement in Sam’s major ethical compromises. Why is The Altruists so keen on letting Sam partially off the hook when there’s every reason to believe he made most of these decisions with full awareness of the likely ramifications? Sam blaming Caroline is true to reality, but he didn’t need to be delicately manipulated by Trabucco to go that route.

Kevin T. Dugan’s own reporting for New York acknowledges the more likely reality: “[Bankman-Fried] told biographer Michael Lewis that he learned Alameda was borrowing from FTX customers only after it was too late to do anything about it, and he has chalked up the problem to an $8 billion or so accounting error. Throughout the trial, former FTX and Alameda executives have testified that the opposite was true: Bankman-Fried directed a fraudulent crypto empire in which his hedge fund was secretly and purposely able to take money from unwitting customers, and he got caught when it was too late to stop it from crashing.” This is the real story here, but The Altruists only occasionally seems interested in telling it.

• I actually kind of like the scenes of Trabucco and Caroline becoming close friends. I doubt they had this type of dynamic in real life, but it felt believable here, and it adds a little bit of stakes for what’s to come. That said, he remembers her as “the girl with the glasses” at a Math Olympiad final?

• Caroline creates a spreadsheet detailing her hopes for the relationship, many sexual in nature, and Trabucco suggests she forward it directly to her boyfriend. Not gonna lie, I’d be in shambles if I were Sam, too.

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: World’s Worst Proposal
items.description: Hello, it’s me, your recapper, just sitting over here completely disturbed by what goes down in “Another Man’s Shadow.” Listen, those of us who’ve been watching Outlander from the beginning have seen some shit. We should be used to how unapologetically dark th
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Hello, it’s me, your recapper, just sitting over here completely disturbed by what goes down in “Another Man’s Shadow.” Listen, those of us who’ve been watching Outlander from the beginning have seen some shit. We should be used to how unapologetically dark these shows can get. And yet, watching how Colum and Letitia handle the birth of their son with deformities on top of Grace getting assaulted — it’s too much, Blood of My Blood. Perhaps my tolerance is gone; perhaps it’s that we’re constantly bombarded with equally dark images from the real world, but whatever it is, this episode was hard to stomach.

Well, Letitia has her baby. Scholars of Outlander already knew something was going to go wrong here because, if you recall, one of the worst-kept secrets in the mothership series is that Colum can’t have children, and he eventually enlists Dougal to impregnate his wife. (We also meet the child Letitia and Dougal have, and he’s way too young to be born at the moment.) So when the baby is born, and Mrs. Fitz and Letitia look on in horror, it’s not completely shocking. The baby, a boy, has deformities in his legs and head, and it’s clear he won’t live very long. Instead of mourning that, when Colum walks into the room, Letitia tells her husband that this simply is not their child. The Fair Folk must have replaced their son with a changeling, and she wants Colum to go leave the baby — he’s referred to as “the creature” at one point, should you need your blood boiled any further — out in the forest overnight in hopes the faeries will switch them back.

And sure, you can argue that these are beliefs of a certain people from a certain time if you want. Mrs. Fitz does genuinely believe that her choice to open a window in the room during the birth is what brought this bad luck on. Letitia is so bereft that, of course, she’s reaching for any bit of hope that could turn this situation around. But like Claire Fraser when she comes across this practice of leaving sick children in the forest for the faeries in season one of Outlander, I’m going to refuse to accept any of this. Could someone just hold that poor baby while he dies? Moreover, if Outlander already tackled the “changeling” of it all, did we really need to retread this idea in Blood of My Blood? I don’t need to see it. We’re all suffering enough here. It’s also frustrating because this whole point of this story line could’ve been made without the changeling aspect. It’s about grief and denial, and it’s also very much about Colum adding yet another thing to that internal list he’s been running through his head of his failings as both a man and a laird. I’d argue you can still get to that without us needing to watch a child left out in the forest, but maybe I’m old-fashioned.

Colum has really been taking L’s all over the place this season, and realizing that he must have passed on his disease to his son, realizing that he can never give his clan an heir or his wife a child, brings him to his lowest low. Has he ever looked so defeated? The best scene of this episode is the emotional conversation shared between Colum and Dougal after the baby dies. Colum rails against himself and his failings — and opens up to Colum about how the problems with his legs are from more than a horse accident — while Dougal tries to lift his brother up. (Colum offering himself up to Redcoats instead of turning Dougal in has really turned the tide on their relationship, it seems. For now.) But Colum tearfully insists that the only reason he can do anything as laird is because of his brother, who has become his legs and his sword. His son wouldn’t have had anyone to do that. But even when Dougal promises that he would be his son’s shield, too, Colum won’t hear it. He is a failure, and that’s all there’s to be said about it — and so he makes a drastic, and rather dramatic, move. He walks into Letitia’s room and tells his wife that he’ll never have sex with her again, that they will never have a child together. Yikes, I get that Colum is in the throes of a shame spiral, but he couldn’t have waited, like, a week to drop this on this woman who is still actively trying to put her body back together after pushing a human out of it? It’s not all about you, my guy.

The fact that Colum is clearly unable to pick himself back up after this latest tragedy is going to affect Dougal a lot, too. Surprisingly, Dougal seems quite sympathetic toward his brother and loyal, too. It’s Maura who is pushing the other MacKenzie brother to use this moment to make a move and prove to the clan that he should’ve been laird all along. She praises him after he has a great showing in the Hall when he fills in for Colum attending to clan business. And sure, she feels bad for Letitia, but when she tells Dougal she’s pregnant, she frames it as “a way to mend what’s broken” — she and Dougal will provide the heirs for Clan MacKenzie. The romance between these two has never been hotter — Dougal really has it bad for his wife, what a thing to see! — but something tells me it’s about to get super awkward in Castle Leoch. Having these two brothers share leadership responsibilities was the only way to keep their family in power at the time, but I don’t know if anyone really thought about the long-term ramifications of this agreement.

You’d think nothing could be bleaker than current events at Leoch, but the shenanigans over at the Cameron house are giving them a run for their money. It’s no secret: John Cameron sucks the big one. He’s awful and abusive to Jocasta and mostly just mocks her when she expresses legitimate fear at being left alone with John’s cousin Hugh while John heads off to the West Indies. Then, he promptly strolls into Grace’s bedroom just as she’s supposed to be meeting with Murtagh in the barn and demands she get on the bed. (Again, this is something that’s been heavily enough implied; we did not need to see it. Think of our mental health, please.) Mercifully, Murtagh walks in and rips John off of Grace, but during their tussle, John falls, hits his head on a bedpost, and dies. The relief of this development is short-lived since Jocasta walks in and everyone has to figure out how they’re going to explain this.

I’m glad Blood of My Blood has decided to make Jocasta, much like her brothers, so morally gray. When she comes upon something so harrowing, she doesn’t have sympathy for Grace or even Murtagh; she doesn’t even have a real reaction to her husband being dead — she mostly looks angry and jealous that Murtagh would kill a man for Grace, that he would choose to love her lady’s maid over her. All of her next moves are motivated by this jealousy that the guy she likes doesn’t return those feelings.

She and Murtagh move John’s body to the bottom of the stairs so it looks like that head trauma was an accident, but when Hugh gets a look at the scene and sees how thick Jocasta is laying on the tears over the death of a man everyone knows she hated, he remains unconvinced. He susses out pretty quickly that this wasn’t an accident, but he doesn’t blame Grace (even though he knows what John was doing to her) or Murtagh; he thinks Jocasta killed John. He saw them fighting earlier in the day, and he knows the inner workings of their marriage. Jocasta tries to turn it around on him, reminding him how obvious it is that he wants John’s money, but Hugh is unbothered — he’s going to get a magistrate involved.

Meanwhile, Jocasta goes to Grace, hands her a bunch of money, and tells her that she needs to leave Scotland and never come back. Hugh suspects her; she lies, and if Murtagh were to be seen with Grace, he, too, would be implicated. They would both be hanged. The fact that Jocasta is using this situation to help her break up a couple is fucking diabolical. The MacKenzies are so unhinged; how did Ellen make it out of that family partially normal? The worst part is watching Grace stand there and thank Jocasta for her generosity and help. She also asks her former employer to tell Murtagh she loves him, but babe, there’s no way she’s doing that.

And she doesn’t. Well, okay, she does tell Murtagh that Grace loved him enough to leave so as not to implicate him, but when Murtagh, beside himself and wanting to go after her, asks if Grace left any message for him, Jocasta tells him no. Grace is gone, and it’s best for everyone if they just let this be. And is it just me, or when Murtagh grabs Jocasta’s hand OUT OF HEARTBREAK, does it look like she is waiting for him to kiss her? Jocasta, girl, go on a vacation and get a fucking grip.

All of Jocasta’s scheming does her no good with Hugh anyway. He decided not to get a magistrate involved at all — they are going to tell everyone that John got ill and died and keep everything else between the two of them. In return, Hugh demands Jocasta marry him so he can inherit all John’s money. Jocasta makes one last-ditch effort to blame this on Grace, but Hugh doesn’t bite. She will marry him, or he’ll turn her in, and they both know who people will believe. Jocasta’s stuck, and she knows it. “I hope John smites you from the grave and you fall down dead at the altar,” she tells him. Hugh’s response? “Best acceptance I’ve ever heard.” These people are freaks.

• I do love that amid all this bleakness, we get tossed a scene of Ellen giving Brian a bath in their new home as if that’s supposed to balance out everything else going on. It doesn’t work — these two don’t even look particularly happy. They seem lonely! At least they’ve decided to attend the Twelfth Night masquerade next week along with all of our other main characters. Drama is afoot, no doubt.

• I laughed so hard when, during that bath scene, Ellen started going on about the fear of having “too much good at once.” Sister, what show have you been watching? Too much good?! A man just poisoned you and killed your unborn child! Are these people out of their minds?

• Henry and Julia are mostly sidelined in this episode, but rest assured they will have a major part to play in next week’s finale: We get a scene at the Grant house in which Uncle Grant asks Henry to draw up a marriage contract for Lord Lovat and Margaret. Uncle Grant and Lovat play it off like this is all hypothetical, just in case this should happen in the future, but Henry knows this is bad news for Julia.

• There’s also bad news for the MacKenzies: Uncle Grant declares that he, Henry, and Arch Bug will be attending Twelfth Night so that he can finally get his vengeance for his nephew’s death. That masquerade is going to be popping off, it seems.

items.title: The Great British Baking Show Recap: Baba Black Sheep
items.description: I feel a little bit like Mo, who watched three hasty TikToks to figure out how to make all of his recipes for Patisserie Week. I’ve been to plenty of Parisian dessert shops, as Paul always likes to allude to during this week, but I’m still not sure exactly wha
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: I feel a little bit like Mo, who watched three hasty TikToks to figure out how to make all of his recipes for Patisserie Week. I’ve been to plenty of Parisian dessert shops, as Paul always likes to allude to during this week, but I’m still not sure exactly what they’re looking for. Are these just really ornate desserts? There seems to be little throughline in what these three challenges are looking for. Is that a problem with the challenges or a problem with the theme of the week? Like Mo and Moyin hearing about the Concorde, I have absolutely no idea.

What I do know is that I hate a baba, a booze-soaked dessert that I associate much more with summer in Italy than I do with pastry shops in France. Maybe it’s a south of France thing? Which I hear is a very Nice place. (Noel would love that joke.) I also feel like Mo because he says that it’s just like “soggy bread,” and I fear that he is right. Maybe it’s because neither Mo nor I drink alcohol, so we’re missing out on one of the key ingredients, or maybe it’s because Italians, while they have perfected other cuisine, are shit at desserts. Baba, tiramisu, and panna cotta are three of the most disgusting confections ever to come out of a forno. Sorry to a whole country, but stick to pasta.

Our four young men all do a mixed job on their babas. Maybe it has something to do with the extreme heat in the tent, where the bakers aren’t even using the shabby-looking proving boxes that have returned to their benches and instead just leaving their dough to rise on the countertops. That’s because it’s 34 degrees in the tent. That’s like 94 American degrees. (I’m sorry, the only thing worse than Italian desserts is Celsius — the scale, not the beverage.) Actually, that’s not true that they’re all mixed. Moyin gets high marks for his hibiscus and orange liqueur concoction that turns the dessert beet red. They think they’re maybe too boozy, which is a compliment. Nigella does have one quibble: that a baba “should squirt in your mouth when you eat it.” Luckily, she also leaves us with a “Boys behave!” as she walks away, making us aware that she knows what she just said.

The rest of the bakers don’t do so hot. Mo’s non-boozy lemon babas are overbaked and crunchy on the outside. Tom’s are underproofed and falling apart. Gabe’s look cute with little hazelnut shards on the top, but Nigella says they need more drenching and bigger holes. As those words left her mouth, both of Gabe’s boyfriends popped up from behind his bench and said, “Boys behave,” in a sing-song voice and then laughed to the tune of Kylie Minogue’s “Can’t Get You Out of My Head” until they got simultaneous Grindr notifications.

I’m beginning to think that it’s time to cancel the technical entirely. It never served much of a purpose in judging, but it was a nice time to see who had the baking skills and who didn’t. It was also fun for the audience to see our bakers not know how to do something, figure it out, and unexpectedly triumph. I don’t know if the caliber of bakers has changed or the challenges have changed, but this is no longer the case. So many times this season, they were given something, and everyone failed at it. This time it was to make a Gateau Concorde, which is the name of a Parisian drag queen who dresses like cabin crew and then makes you puke in an air sickness bag. The trick to making this meringue and chocolate mousse cake is something called a pâte à bombe, which is the name of a Parisian drag queen who dresses like duck liver and then explodes. No, it’s pouring a sugar syrup into whisked egg whites that makes a mousse set. The only one who knows how to do it is Moyin, but then he messes it up, takes too long trying to fix it, and comes in last in the technical. This whole challenge is basically testing one skill, and the one person who even knew what it was flubbed it, and Mo, who did not have TikTok to look up how to do this, came in first just out of dumb luck. Is that even technical, or is that just like [shrug emoji]?

The showstopper is the only thing that felt like patisserie to me. They have to make 12 highly decorated little cakes in an ornate, edible stand. These are the kinds of little cakes with polished exteriors or things made to look like other foods that Mo has watched on TikTok more times than he’s ever been excited about anything. (That means he’s seen three.) All of them decide to make more than one kind of cake, and they all look absolutely delicious even if some of them are a little wonky and two of them use the dreaded nougatine.

Three of them also make desserts that look like fruits. Mo had the brilliant idea of bringing back his mango mousse from episode five and made them look like mangos. What was weird is he also made raspberries and blueberries, which contained white chocolate mousse and mixed berry and blueberry compote, respectively. The mangoes are life-sized, but then the blueberries and raspberries are absolutely gigantic, like Willy Wonka hit them with some kind of super-sizing ray. The judges love all of them, and Paul says it’s a “resounding success.” We know that he’s going to be Star Baker and in the finals. It is so.

Next, with a drive-by fruiting is Moyin, who makes apples and oranges in a surprisingly delicious nougatine basket that Paul Hollywood ruins trying to pick it up with his sausage fingers, and Nigella shoots him a sideways look that says, “Sigh. Men.” Nigella says his orange is like a cloud, and they just love the cremeux and the baked element that Paul heavily hinted he should include. The apple, which was full of apple chunks, Paul isn’t sold on, and Nigella says it lacks a little bit of refinement.

Gabe says that his creation is going to be a little greenhouse like the one he had as a kid and that there are going to be tomatoes and radishes inside. However, the desserts, obviously, aren’t going to taste like tomatoes and radishes. As soon as I heard he was making fruits that tasted like other fruits, I knew he was in trouble. (The only time a fruit should taste like another fruit is if he was just making out with another fruit. That was a gay joke. I’m sorry.) In this case, the tomatoes are going to be strawberry and basil, and the radishes are apple and pink peppercorn.

Tom, once again, is going to pop culture for his inspiration, which, honestly, I love, even if his inspiration is Wicked, which seems a little two Oscar seasons ago. He’s making a biscuit yellow brick road, a nougatine Emerald City, and one dark green dessert that is pistachio sable and jaconde sponge, and one pink dessert that is white chocolate mousse and a cherry insert. While Tom’s ode to Judy Garland is pretty, Paul says that the desserts, particularly the pink one, were forgettable. Nigella says the white chocolate is a “blunt instrument” that takes over the whole thing. The green one has a biscuit base that is far too thick and, I don’t know, both of them look really gloopy on the fork.

I was worried that Tom was going to have rocked the whole competition and then lagged when it matters the most. Luckily, he just sneaks through to the final. That’s mostly because Gabe made foods that tasted like other foods. It’s too much of a mindfuck, like trying to part your hair on the other side of your head. While his greenhouse was more adorable than a kitten going out on a first date with a puppy, they didn’t like the biscuit and the cake in the tomato, and in the radish they couldn’t taste the peppercorn and, once again, the white chocolate took over everything. (White chocolate, the fart in the elevator of the baking world.) Gabe is the one who is sent home, and he gets a consolation handshake from Paul on the way out. Only one handshake? How is he supposed to share that with both of his boyfriends?

Next week is going to be a very interesting finale with three young men all vying for the crown. Tom was the early favorite but has been flagging in the final laps. Moyim has been on the rise for the past few weeks, boosted by his success and his love of Connie. Mo has been as erratic as his FYP feed throughout the competition, but is one day away from taking it all. Honestly, I’d be happy with any of the winners and can’t wait to see what wonderful things (and a stupid technical) they make them do next week.

items.title: Yellowjackets Season-Premiere Recap: Homeward Bound
items.description: “Hivemind” is available now on Paramount+; it will air on Showtime Sunday, November 22 at 9:00 p.m. ET.
items.author: Erin Qualey
paragraphs: “Hivemind” is available now on Paramount+; it will air on Showtime Sunday, November 22 at 9:00 p.m. ET.

As we head into the fourth and final season of Yellowjackets, is it weird that the person I’m most worried about is Jeff Sadecki? He’s (mostly) innocent. Sure, he helped cover up Adam’s murder, but that’s small potatoes compared to what the rest of the teen Yellowjackets have done and what the surviving adults are still capable of.

Fittingly, teen Jeff provides our entrance back into the world of Yellowjackets, effectively marking the beginning of the end by splitting the chronology into thirds. Now we are tracking the teen timeline both pre-rescue and post-rescue as well as the adults in the present. Everyone is scheming. Everyone is on tilt. No one is getting the mental-health care they need. (More on this later.)

When the season opens, teen Jeff is living what he believes to be his best life, working at the furniture store with his bestie, Randy, and getting high whenever he pleases. Jeff has certainly graduated from Wiskayok High by this point in time, and it looks like he’s chosen a life with a light lift. He was probably pretty shook after both his girlfriend (Jackie) and his situationship (Shauna) disappeared in the wilderness right before graduation but also maybe a little relieved? No shade to Jeff, but when he spots the news coverage announcing that the girls have been found, he seems to be experiencing more dread than excitement, especially as he doesn’t know who survived yet.

As we watch the talking heads reveal the news — hi, Kurt Loder! — Yellowjackets is successful in making the rescue feel like a seismic cultural event. In the late ’90s, social media wasn’t yet splitting our attention into tiny, fractured pieces, so big, human-interest stories were dissected incessantly for weeks, months, even years. The public would be hungry for all the details, which is why what happens when the girls actually return is so important.

We don’t spend a ton of time in the pre-rescue timeline here. We mostly see Natalie sprinting back to camp as fast as she can after her successful rescue call, and then she stumbles upon something quite shocking upon her return. The remains of the Mari feast, perhaps? We’ll surely find out next week.

The actual homecoming is a somber and muted affair. The first time we see the teens outside the wilderness, they’re roaming the halls of a hospital with Kurt Cobain warbling his rendition of “Where Did You Sleep Last Night” in the background. The music team on Yellowjackets remains on point; there’s so much to unpack in this song choice.

Cobain’s version of “Where Did You Sleep Last Night” was not released as a single until months after his death, quietly underscoring the fact that many Yellowjackets did not make it to this moment. In addition, the song is based on an old folk song, passed down through generations, with the core story shifting and changing slightly with every telling. The basic interpretation is that a girl (one way the song has been historically titled is “Black Girl”) flees into the woods to avoid persecution after her husband’s brutal death. The lyrics explore her potential complicity in the violence without ever coming to a definitive answer regarding her guilt. The ideas of complex guilt and what complicity and blame even look like in the wake of tragedy are very relevant to the survivors at this moment in time. Cobain’s haunted vocals beautifully punctuate the scene as the group stays relatively mum. They shower, they give each other knowing looks in the hallway, and Melissa checks and rechecks that she has the DAT tape.

At one point, the Wiskayok parents arrive, and we immediately get the sense that the Canadian infrastructure does not have the resources to deal with this rescue appropriately. Mari’s mother barges past the single man at the hospital entryway, through the hallways, and forces the first Yellowjacket she sees (poor Nat) to confirm that her daughter is dead. Damn, lady. I mean, I get it, but also this is the first instance in which the girls are retraumatized in fully preventable ways, and it won’t be the last.

Friends, as a therapist, I have always been curious about what type of help these teens were offered when they came home from their horrifying ordeal. And the answer is: basically none. Given what’s happened in the present timeline, I should have guessed, right? There’s a resident trauma counselor at the hospital — Dr. Brannack, a.k.a. Cynthia Stevenson from one of my favorite short-lived ’90s sitcoms, Hope & Gloria — but Stevenson’s kind face is doing a lot of heavy lifting. If Dr. Brannack is actually trying to do her job here, she’s doing a really fucking terrible job at her job. She lets Donald Kundla, the chief investigator for the Canadian Transportation Safety Board, sit in on their “therapy” sessions right away. Big mistake. Huge. Even though Kundla is ostensibly looking for evidence of the missing frog-research team, it’s wildly inappropriate to include him. This eliminates any possibility of building any trust or rapport with the girls before they’ve even begun to process their experience. These girls are in shock and traumatized in dozens of different ways, and the trauma counselor is going to bring in a literal cop at the very first meeting?! To quote Lottie, “No. No, no, no, no, no. NO.”

Why, oh why didn’t they bring in world-renowned trauma specialists to help these teens?! The moment kind of demanded it! I guess therapy wasn’t big in the ’90s? Mostly, I’m just mad that these girls didn’t get even a semblance of true trauma therapy before they were treated like criminals.

Yes, okay, yes, they are actually all criminals. And they probably would have all parroted their pre-rehearsed response even if Dr. Brannack had attempted to engage them in a true therapeutic relationship. It’s fun to watch the montage of all the girls repeating the same exact story — the exact speech that Shauna gave to Jessica Roberts in the series premiere, no less — in their interviews, and Kundla puzzling over what it could all mean. (Dude. They’re lying. Obviously.)

Lottie’s dad can’t stand watching his precious pumpkin suffer for even one minute, so he calls in a favor to the Canadian ambassador. Ambassador Bouchard has big entitled-white-guy-in-the-’90s energy and also the power of President Clinton behind him, so he’s able to whisk all the girls back to the United States without any further investigation or therapy.

It’s worth noting that Shauna does get taken aside at one point and asked if she’s ever given birth. Again, the team at this hospital is woefully awful because the doctor approaches Shauna while she’s reuniting with her mother, which, in and of itself, is a violation of privacy. Shauna denies ever giving birth, but it’s certain that the lingering trauma from her child’s death in the wilderness will fuel her choices once she returns to Wiskayok.

In the present, Shauna is still fully on tilt from reconnecting with her time as a queen in the wilderness. Without Jeff and Callie to care for, she has literally nothing to do with her days, and so she terrorizes the locals like a Karen on an acid trip. Melanie Lynskey is the best when it comes to the portrayal of weaponized suburban motherhood, but she’s added a sliver of true danger to the proceedings. Shauna is a cannibal of life, and she’ll consume anything and everything in her path until she gets what she wants.

When we first see her in the present-day timeline, she’s purchased a giant truck on Jeff’s company credit card, and she arrives at a gas station, seemingly solely to antagonize the poor teen at the register. It’s a great scene, especially when she lunges at the counter to intimidate the kid, and the behavior is repeated when she meets with Tai’s private investigator later in the episode. It’s worth noting that Shauna isn’t trying any of this nonsense with Tai, or even with Melissa at the end of the episode, but she is very ready for a fight. (See also: cutting holes in all of Jeff’s nice shirts.)

Shauna’s hubris is sure to cause her problems, though, as we see Tai and Misty forming an alliance on the side. These two have been in cahoots since the end of season three, and they’re conspiring to kill their former queen. Tai is playing both sides, while Shauna has conveniently forgotten about Misty. She never really thought about Misty much, but this time it’s certainly going to get her in trouble. For her part, Misty dutifully follows all of Tai’s directives. First, in the interest of tying up loose ends, she gets a death certificate for Van. Then, she works on finding Shauna’s journals and the DAT tape while considering the best way to kill her.

While Tai busies Shauna by meeting with the PI on Melissa’s tail, Misty breaks into Shauna’s house in order to find the incriminating evidence. (They’re not there, but Jeff does pop in to discover his Swiss-cheese shirts.) During this episode, we see that Misty has created a faux Shauna in her mind, much in the way that Shauna has a mental Jackie haunting her. While Shauna’s version of Jackie is all snarky put-downs and barbed insults, Misty’s version of Shauna is just exasperated and over it all, even super blasé about killing herself in various different ways. Misty’s Shauna is really delightful, especially because this is kind of how Shauna is — she’s forever rolling her eyes at everyone else — but also because we know that Shauna would never just roll over and die.

Near the end of the episode, Misty has settled on a domestic dispute as the cause of Shauna and Jeff’s deaths. I told you I was worried about him. Since this is the first episode of the season, this tableau likely (hopefully?) won’t come to pass, but Misty has a gun in Shauna’s name now, so the threat still feels imminent.

Melissa seems to think that the remaining Yellowjackets are enough of a threat that she’s concocted a whole plan to avoid their wrath. She’s right to think that they want to kill her, and her plan to flee with her family, only to move in next door to Shauna and call the press to alert them of her reemergence, is pretty clever. Even though Melissa tells her wife, Alex — remember, Alex is Hannah’s daughter (!) — the truth about who she is, she still does not disclose what she or anyone else did in the wilderness. If I were Alex, I probably would have run for the hills if my spouse wasn’t willing to be fully honest about why a gaggle of middle-aged women wanted to murder me and my family, but hey, growing up without a mom can do weird things to people.

From the ten Yellowjackets that were rescued, only four remain in the adult timeline. Who’s willing to bet that there will be only one (or none?) left when the credits roll? Has Yellowjackets been a modern-day version of And Then There Were None all along?
• Molly. Ringwald. That is all.

• By the end of the episode, Shauna is back to smoking weed in Callie’s room, which is a nice callback to the series premiere and also a sign that adult Shauna has not changed one iota since we first met her.

• While Shauna is terrorizing the gas-station kid, she says, “This isn’t Vietnam, Donny,” and he totally doesn’t get the reference. I believe this is a mashed-up line from The Big Lebowski, and now I’m heartbroken that kids these days might not know this movie. Also, the actual line is “This is not ’Nam, this is bowling, there are rules,” but Shauna doesn’t seem to be playing by the rules anymore.
• In the new opening-credit sequence, Misty considers a heart while dressed in scrubs. Will a third Yellowjacket consume a heart this season?

• Walter Watch: Tai and Misty chat a bit about Walter, and even though I know some viewers think his story line is dragging, I have to admit that I’m still pretty pumped to see how his story line plays out. When Misty tells Tai that things ended badly with Walter, Tai remarks, “A weirdo scorned.” True that. A weirdo scorned can literally do anything, so sign me up.

items.title: Cupertino Recap: Just Because You’re Paranoid …
items.description: In the real world, we just lived through a week where seemingly everything broke. Business software, air travel, online banking, air travel again … Day after day, the load-bearing systems that companies have been paid billions to build and maintain faltered on
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: In the real world, we just lived through a week where seemingly everything broke. Business software, air travel, online banking, air travel again … Day after day, the load-bearing systems that companies have been paid billions to build and maintain faltered one by one, disrupting daily life across the United States. And that’s not even taking into account the major scandal that dominated the headlines all week, in which the CEO of a company responsible for fueling many of those above-mentioned systems had to resign owing to sexual improprieties that could have compromised our national security. Meanwhile, in Cupertino world this week, everything goes haywire in a different (yet also similar) way.

Price, Siffre & Associates are working on what appears to be a simple case, representing reporter Judith Song (Ana Yi Puig), who is being sued by Chernata AI for coercing several of their employees into violating their NDAs. All PSA needs to do is persuade the court that Judith was investigating a crime — the murder of a Chernata whistleblower, Lionel Van Zijil (Matisse Ratron-Neal) — which would justify breaking an NDA under a “public service” exception. But after Michael and Olivia persuade the judge to side with Judith, she gets arrested for Lionel’s murder, and Michael is threatened with disbarment for misappropriation of the firm’s funds.

“Judith & Michael” is one of this season’s best episodes for a number of reasons. It has a white-knuckle intensity as one crisis stacks atop another, and it gets pretty zany in ways that only a Michelle and Robert King show can. But this episode’s primary virtue is that it speaks to the tech-exacerbated hopelessness that has overwhelmed so many of us lately. It’s that pervasive feeling that society and culture have begun regressing and that the people responsible for making everything worse are unreachable, huddled behind multiple impenetrable curtains. They won’t listen to us. They don’t have to.

For example, in this week’s Cupertino, it’s pretty obvious that Chernata is the villain, but because of the vagaries of the law and the intentional obfuscations of big business, Michael and Judith never get to face their accusers. They just talk to other lawyers — and to the law-enforcement officers who appear to be bought and paid for by this company but refuse to acknowledge it.

On the law-enforcement side, our antagonist this week is ADA Sabrina Egg (Mary Wiseman), a frustratingly upbeat character who asks to be called by the nickname “Sunnyside,” even as she’s telling Michael and Olivia that the best she can offer Judith is ten years in prison. PSA initially assumes the state is going after their client as a punishment for Michael humiliating a police detective on the witness stand. The cops had ruled Lionel’s death a suicide, ignoring multiple pieces of contradictory evidence. So when the ADA suddenly comes into possession of documents and video footage pointing to Judith as the culprit, PSA has to argue that maybe Lionel did kill himself.

But who really gains from either Judith being jailed or Lionel’s case being closed? That would be Chernata, who was concerned that Lionel would go public with how the company has secretly targeted swing voters with misinformation campaigns. As for the bar association’s investigation into Michael, it involves evidence that shows him playing at an off-the-books poker club and evidence that PSA has been paid in bitcoin. These two facts — unrelated but suspicious side by side — suggest Michael could be laundering money.

In both of these cases, the accusers — the ADA and the bar — have mysteriously acquired their damning evidence. The ADA has footage of Judith entering Lionel’s building before his death and an affidavit from a gun-shop owner who claims Judith asked him about the best firearms for faking a suicide. The bar has footage of Michael playing cards. All of this evidence is watermarked, bearing the stamp of Booker East, a data-miner that stockpiles information from random sources and then sells it to anyone who pays.

It’s here where this episode starts rocketing into crazy town. PSA invites a Booker East sales rep to drop by the office, where they sit through a slick, corny presentation in which the rep pitches Booker East’s services and explains that as long as they collect footage from public places, everything’s legal. (The rep also hands out T-shirts reading “I AM A DATA POINT.”) PSA follows that meeting by consulting with Felix Gromit (Greg Hildreth) from JPZ Data, who explains that he will find footage not from public places in exchange for PSA’s help with a lawsuit.

While all of this is going on, Christy is having her own strange adventure, as Bo — the rogue Colt AI agent who was supposed to have been permanently deleted — keeps finding ways to reach out to her on various low-tech devices. He talks to her via the display screen on a TGI Friday’s cash register, then via an arcade game, then via Alphabet Amigo, a child’s educational toy. The Kings have done this schtick before on both The Good Wife and Elsbeth, having ominous messages delivered via goofy-looking internet-connected gadgets. It’s funny every time.

But all of this silliness accompanies some real danger. The whole reason Bo returns is because, in his omnipresence, he has become aware of the intense scrutiny the PSA team is under. (He also came back because he was bored and missed his PSA friends.) He encourages Christy to call on Vik to help build an “air-gapped computer” — using two shopping carts, a gerbil cage, a lot of tinfoil, and the source code that Bo hid on a Hooters waitress’s cell phone — so that he can properly share what he’s found.

Felix, meanwhile, warns the team that Chernata has probably installed malware on their phones remotely, which is how they’ve been able to work up such a detailed dossier on every questionable move Michael and Judith have made lately. But JPZ is able to turn the company’s surveillance against them. By accessing the same material that Chernata has been covertly sending to the police and to the bar, PSA is able to prove that Judith actually has an alibi for the time of Lionel’s death and that one of the bar’s representatives took a $10,000 payoff from Chernata.

So the day is saved again. And yet long after this episode ended, I started thinking about how the PSA team weaponized data to get them off the hook in these two cases, but they’ll still be observed going forward — and without a whole lot of recourse to stop it. A condition of their continued existence may be submitting to being probed.

Then I thought about Lionel’s death. To free Judith, Olivia threatens Sunnyside into re-reclassifying the case as a suicide. But the question of who killed Lionel still lingers. Olivia and Michael seem to have convinced themselves that it probably was a suicide. But all the evidence Michael used in court to prove that the police closed the case too early is still relevant. The blood patterns, the lack of fingerprints, the fact that Lionel had just ordered takeout when he “killed himself” — none of this should be ignored, right?
And even if Lionel did kill himself, it was likely owing to Chernata’s pressure. Someone has to answer for this, yes? For once, won’t someone answer?
• Throughout the second half of this episode, a thunderstorm is rolling in, which allows for some dramatic lighting effects — especially when Bo is revived Frankenstein style.

• I hope we see ADA Sunnyside again. Wiseman (a favorite of mine since Star Trek: Discovery) gives a hilarious performance, overexaggerating her “ooh” and “ouch” facial expressions every time she describes the evidence they have against Judith.

• I’ve been keeping an eye on Olivia’s red flags vis-à-vis her drinking, but should we also be worried about Michael? He kind of hand-waves his gambling habit. He also accidentally calls Judith “Olivia” and by the end of this episode is pondering a fling with Natalia.

• For that matter, should we worry more about Natalia? Again this week, she swings between spending lavishly on the office and fretting over the firm’s shaky income. Also, according to my wife, she eats KitKat bars “the insane way,” biting straight through all four segments.

items.title: Robert Pattinson’s Bond Ascent: How Pricey Screen Tests and Amazon Execs Landed a Starry 007
items.description: What does an actor do in the quiet moments before the announcement that will change his life?
items.author: Matt Donnelly
paragraphs: What does an actor do in the quiet moments before the announcement that will change his life?

For Robert Pattinson, there were about 12 hours between the Sunday phone call confirming he’d landed the role of James Bond and Amazon MGM’s Monday-morning release of the first image of the actor rocking a tuxedo and pistol. He spent it, rather predictably, watching an arthouse horror film.

His longtime friend and collaborator Robert Eggers told Variety this week that Pattinson was screening the director’s forthcoming genre drama “Werwulf” when the Bond news broke. Nothing like a stark naked Aaron Taylor-Johnson terrorizing a quaint village to pass the time.

But after months (years, really) of toiling and speculation over who would replace Daniel Craig in the film adaptations of Ian Fleming’s spy novels, Pattinson took the crown. It buttons up a delicious, messy and very public guessing game over which lucky man would land the iconic role. When Amazon MGM bought out rights to James Bond from longtime custodians the Broccoli family in 2025, intentions were set for a young star who could shoulder the franchise for a decade or two. An A-list team of producers (Amy Pascal of “Spider-Man” and David Heyman of the “Harry Potter” movies) recruited Denis Villeneuve to direct. Together, with significant influence from Amazon execs Courtenay Valenti and Mike Hopkins (and yes, Jeff Bezos), they screen-tested a laundry list of virile performers — including Callum Turner, Tom Francis, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor — earlier this year.

For the curious, the batch of screen tests cost Amazon MGM between $300,000 and $500,000 to pull off, ostensibly in secret (everyone found out), sources familiar with the process say. But two wildcard actors who tested at the last minute — “Superman” star Nicholas Hoult and the DCU’s reining Batman, Pattinson — tipped the scales. Villeneuve’s voice became the most trusted in the room on the matter of Bond’s casting, two insiders tell Variety.

His shorthand with Pattinson from working on “Dune: Part Three” made the choice inevitable, according to industry insiders — especially after Turner, the early favorite, came under scrutiny against more established names like Hoult and Pattinson. Lowden, the heat-seeking star of “Slow Horses,” was even the subject of a suspected sabotage campaign when paparazzi footage circulated showed the actor bungling an on-set motorcycle stunt just two weeks before the Bond casting was confirmed.

A sect of the internet lost its mind when Variety reported earlier this month that Harry Styles and Theo James were both in talks for the role. It’s rare, even by tentpole movie standards, that such a long list of candidates would flow so freely through public channels. The studios hate it because it makes them seem indecisive, one exec says. Talent absolutely hates it because the also-rans will have to answer for almost being James Bond on talk show couches and podcasts for the next 10 years.
“Whatever, it’s really fun,” one top talent rep tells Variety of the audition merry-go-round.

While there will be detractors, it’s inarguable that the Bond gig now enshrines Pattinson in the upper echelons of movie stardom. He was already well on his way, with even civilian social media pundits having commented on the “generational run” Pattinson has been living out onscreen in films like “Primetime,” “The Odyssey,” “The Drama,” “Die My Love” and, obviously, “The Batman.” That’s to say nothing of the deeply indie era (“Good Time,” “The Lighthouse”) that followed major franchise moments like his star-making turn in the “Twilight Saga” movies and a prominent role in “Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.” The new job also represents a major win for Pattinson’s agent of more than 20 years, Stephanie Ritz of WME. Ritz and team have managed to populate massive IP with Pattinson’s face while still allowing the actor to take risks and brand himself a maverick for the cross-generational devotees of studios like A24.

Given the shocking November news that DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran had been jettisoned by the David Ellison regime, it’s doubtful Pattinson would linger long as Matt Reeves’ caped crusader — freeing him up to embody the sultry British charm and execute the bare-knuckle action audiences have come to expect from 007. Art-house horror movies may have to take a back seat.

items.title: ‘GTA 6’ Hits Massive $3.79 Billion in First-Day Sales
items.description: Crime pays: Rockstar Games’ “Grand Theft Auto 6″ preorder and first-day sales reached $3.79 billion, the game developer announced Friday.
items.author: Jennifer Maas
paragraphs: Crime pays: Rockstar Games’ “Grand Theft Auto 6″ preorder and first-day sales reached $3.79 billion, the game developer announced Friday.
Per Rockstar Games parent company Take-Two Interactive, that total sets “a new record for entertainment across any medium” and makes “GTA 6” “the biggest entertainment launch in history.”
A spokesperson for Take-Two Interactive declined to comment on the number of “GTA 6” copies sold.

For the sake of comparison, Sony Pictures’ “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” reaped $2.52 billion at the global box office in 2026, the No. 1 movie of the year to date. Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster “The Odyssey” has taken in just over $1.8 billion to date.

On its first day of release, “GTA 6” made roughly as much as James Cameron’s last two “Avatar” movies, “The Way of Water” and “Fire and Ash,” have grossed combined. With just Day 1 sales, “GTA 6” has already out-grossed the highest grossing movie of all time, “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion), in one day.
The game cost a reported $1.5 billion to produce over more than a decade of development.

“GTA 6” launched Thursday for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S and was also available on Xbox One via Xbox’s Cloud Gaming service. The game retails at $80 for the standard edition and $100 for the ultimate version. Preorders for “GTA 6” opened June 25.

With a reported total gameplay time of approximately 80 hours to complete its main storyline, “GTA 6” follows duo Jason and Lucia as they navigate their way through criminal life in the fictional Leonida.
“GTA 6” has reached a 99 Metacritic score (tying it for the highest-rated video game of all time) and received a nomination for Game of the Year at The Game Awards this December.

“It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI,’” Rockstar Games president and founder Sam Houser said. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.”

items.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Fact vs Fiction: Butkus the Dog, Bloody Knuckles and Stallone’s Fight to Get ‘Rocky’ Made
items.description: The beloved classic “Rocky” premiered half a century ago this week. Five decades later, “I Play Rocky,” in theaters now, tells the story of how unknown writer and actor Sylvester Stallone shoulders his way into not just writing the script but playing the iconi
items.author: Pat Saperstein
paragraphs: The beloved classic “Rocky” premiered half a century ago this week. Five decades later, “I Play Rocky,” in theaters now, tells the story of how unknown writer and actor Sylvester Stallone shoulders his way into not just writing the script but playing the iconic lead role of boxer Rocky Balboa, culminating in a best picture Oscar.

In the year 2026, is it really possible to go back in time and depict the making of “Rocky” with perfect accuracy? The unvarnished truth doesn’t always make for the best dramatic impact in a movie — and Stallone and the filmmaking team have told somewhat varying stories over the past 50 years.
“I Play Rocky” effectively toes the line between hitting most of the events of the production with some degree of accuracy and buffing up others for the sake of more effective storytelling.
Here are some of the scenes that happened just as “I Play Rocky” depicts them — according to most participants — and a few others that use a healthy amount of dramatic license.
Did Stallone really write “Rocky” in three days and then turn down hundreds of thousands so he could star?

“I Play Rocky” shows Anthony Ippolito as Stallone marching into Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler’s office and playing hardball with the big Hollywood producers, hearing offers of more and more money to give up his starring role until the producers finally agree. The need for a tidy narrative leaves out several details, though, and makes Stallone seem like even more of a total unknown than he was at the time.

The real story was a bit more complicated and left out the pivotal role that talent agents typically play in Hollywood deal negotiations. Chris Rumar, the son of one of Stallone’s early agents, Craig Rumar, said his dad and Rumar’s agent partner Larry Kubik were integral to getting “Rocky” off the ground.

“Since my dad died nine years ago, Mr. Stallone has been on sort of a tour about these inaccuracies about how ‘Rocky’ was put together,” Rumar tells Variety. “This time it was the triple whammy — we got the book, ‘The Steps,’ ‘I Play Rocky’ and the rerelease of ‘Rocky’ all within a month. He has been doing interviews with some of the biggest names in media and nobody challenges him.”

Kubik explained on the “Sexy Boomer” podcast that he and Rumar helped plant the seed for “Rocky” by introducing his friend, producer Gene Kirkwood, who had a deal with Chartoff and Winkler, to Stallone. Kirkwood and the agents first tried to set up Stallone’s script “Hell’s Kitchen” (which later became “Paradise Alley”), but Stallone had already sold it to another company and was trying to double-dip. So he went home and started work on another screenplay, influenced by a boxing match he had watched.

As seen in “I Play Rocky,” Stallone did work day and night for 72 hours to sketch out the basics of the script about an aspiring boxer, with his wife typing up his handwritten lines. But he didn’t write a fully-formed screenplay that fast — he sketched out the first third or so of the story, then made dozens of revisions before it was ready to shoot.

The neophyte actor insisted on starring in the movie he wrote — an idea which seemed preposterous to the studio, which would have preferred James Caan, Nick Nolte or Ryan O’Neal. “We negotiated a deal, and in the first deal he got paid for the script,” Kubik said. “I was told by United Artists that Mike Medavoy loved the script. But he loves it for Jimmy Caan. So I said, ‘That is not going to happen.’”

As seen in “I Play Rocky,” United Artists reportedly did offer up to $250,000 if Stallone would step aside, but “Stallone held his ground,” Variety reported. Did he ever deliver the titular line “I play Rocky” to the producers during the discussion of who should star? It’s not clear if anyone can remember.
Did Stallone really sell his bull mastiff Butkus for $40 when he was broke, and then buy him back?

In “I Play Rocky,” Stallone treasures the stray dog he found on the street during one of his lowest periods. After moving to Los Angeles, he’s still struggling to make ends meet, and sadly decides to sell Butkus to a stranger who compliments the dog for some $40. As Stallone often recounts and as seen in “I Play Rocky,” when it comes time to shoot “Rocky,” Stallone wants Butkus to be in the movie, so he tracks down the new owner, who says his kids love the dog, and ends up having to offer him thousands of dollars (the story varies from $1,500 to $15,000) to buy him back.

Stallone has told a version of the Butkus story many times over the years, naming a man called “Little Jimmy” as the one who bought the dog when he was broke. Stallone implies Little Jimmy was a stranger he met in front of a 7-11, before he sold the “Rocky” script.

But Jimmy Gambina, a diminutive boxing trainer who worked on “Rocky,” has a much different recollection of what happened. Gambina told “Going the Distance” author Mike Sielski that he dog-sat for Butkus during the movie’s production, and then Stallone gave Gambina the dog after his son Sage was born because he saw how close they had become.

When it was time to shoot “Rocky II,” Stallone wanted the dog back so he could appear in the movie. Gambina says he told Stallone, “You come over and explain it to my son. If my son says it’s OK, I’ll let you have the dog back. But we’ve had the dog going on three years now, and we love the dog.” Gambina says the two had a falling-out sometime after Stallone insisted on taking the dog back.
Did Stallone break his knuckles on a frozen meat carcass at a Philadelphia meat packing facility during filming?

Many people think “Rocky” was shot all in Philadelphia. But only the iconic steps, Rocky’s apartment and some other exteriors were captured in the City of Brotherly Love over a frenetic five-day period. “I Play Rocky” shows Stallone’s Rocky Balboa training with sides of beef at a Philly slaughterhouse, but the 1976 original was actually shot at Shamrock Meats in the L.A.-adjacent meat mecca of Vernon. The beef was frozen solid, though, and after Stallone pummeled the icy meat for eight hours straight, he ended up breaking a knuckle, so that part of the movie is accurate.

The ice skating rink where Rocky woos Adrian after hours was the Ice Capades Chalet in Santa Monica, Calif., which later became a Fred Segal store, while the climactic boxing match was filmed at the Olympic Auditorium and the L.A. Sports Arena.

“To help keep budget down, Kirkwood made arrangements for merchandising tie-ins to lure unpaid extras to the Sports Arena Monday. A foreign auto was to be raffled off, in exchange for a plug in the film, and other merchandise was to be given away at 15-minute intervals to keep the extras from leaving,” Variety reported during production. Extras were also given meals from Kentucky Fried Chicken, one background player recalled.
Adding to his injuries during filming, Stallone did break a rib during his final bout with Carl Weathers, while Weathers suffered a broken nose.
Did the studio really try to sabotage the production to get Stallone out as star?

Stallone pushed himself to run an estimated nine miles the first day of shooting and 11 the second, wearing Converse sneakers the whole time and giving himself a case of shin splints, according to the recent book “Going the Distance” about the making of “Rocky.” It’s not clear whether he was really told by doctors to stay off his feet for two weeks, as “I Play Rocky” shows.

But Kubik said that although the contract required a tight shooting schedule and budget, as well as giving producers the right to replace Stallone, it wouldn’t have made much sense to get rid of him. “I knew if they were going to shoot half the movie with him, there was no way they were going to shoot for five days and then say we don’t like him,” said Kubik.

Stallone had a similar memory of the contract when talking to Howard Stern in 2005: “We have a 14-day thing where we can fire you any time and, more importantly, we can reduce it down to 900 grand, all in, and if you can do the thing in 30 days, OK. If not, it’s over.”

So although United Artists did write the contract with strict requirements in order to come in under budget, it wouldn’t have been in anyone’s interest to try to get Stallone to quit after shooting had already started.

Variety reported that director John Avildsen used numerous tactics to save money and come in under budget, including saving $200 by having Stallone provide voice work for three or four disguised voices issuing from bars and TV sets.
Did Stallone call his dad, Frank Stallone Sr., and ask him to appear in “Rocky?”

Sylvester Stallone had a difficult relationship with both his absentee mother and his abusive dad Frank Sr., who could never seem to show his approval no matter what Sly had accomplished. “I Play Rocky” shows him extending an olive branch by calling his dad and asking if he can play a small part as the man who rings the bell at the end of the boxing match. Is that how it really happened?

Not so much, Stallone recounts in his book “The Steps: A Memoir.” As he tells it, when he showed up on set to shoot a scene, Frank Sr. was already there waiting for him and insisted on being given a part. There was just one problem, Stallone says in his memoir: The part had already been cast. “There was no reasoning with him, so with apologies, I let go of the timekeeper,” he recalled. When it came time to shoot, Frank Jr. repeatedly missed his cue and didn’t ring the bell, and the result was a “big Italian drama” of a fight, Stallone said.

items.title: Bowen Yang Apologizes for Calling Regina Spektor an Antisemitic Slur, Didn’t Know It Was ‘Popularized by Far-Right Movements’
items.description: Bowen Yang has apologized after he received backlash recently for calling singer Regina Spektor an antisemitic slur on a past episode of his podcast, “Las Culturistas.” A resurfaced clip from his Oct. 14 podcast came under fire when Yang referred to Spektor as
items.author: Jordan Moreau
paragraphs: Bowen Yang has apologized after he received backlash recently for calling singer Regina Spektor an antisemitic slur on a past episode of his podcast, “Las Culturistas.” A resurfaced clip from his Oct. 14 podcast came under fire when Yang referred to Spektor as “Zio.”

“I want to genuinely apologize for using a word on the podcast without knowing its antisemitic history, especially since we’ve repudiated antisemitism on the show as recently as the last two weeks,” Yang wrote on Instagram on Friday (his handle is @fayedunaway but has no connection to the actress). “Particularly upsetting to realize that I adopted language popularized by far-right movements whose rhetoric we should be wary of and act against.”
“Zio,” short for “Zionist,” has been used as a derogatory slur toward Jewish people and Israelis. Its origins trace back to Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke and white supremacists.

On the Oct. 14 episode of “Las Culturistas,” Yang, his co-host Matt Rogers and guest Edy Modica were discussing Spektor, her alma mater SUNY Purchase and her music when Modica added, “And now she’s out to lunch.” Rogers asked if Modica was “upset with Regina lately,” to which she responded, “she’s just like a little Israel hardcore.” Yang added, “yeah, she’s Zio.”

In recent days, social media users found the resurfaced clip of the podcast and called out Yang for using the slur. “Bowen Yang using antisemitic slang that was popularized and mainstreamed by KKK leader David Duke is really just chefs kiss for the guy who got Shane Gillis fired from ‘SNL’ for racism,” wrote Meghan McCain on X. “Well done buying this hate mongering podcast Disney.” “Las Culturistas” began streaming on Disney+ and Hulu on Wednesday.

“Bowen Yang, Matt Rogers & soooo many people LOVE preaching inclusion, compassion & protecting the dolls. UNTIL IT COMES TO JEWS,” Michael Rapaport posted. “They dismiss the GREAT Regina Spektor for supporting Israel. Funny how it’s ALWAYS Jewish Zionists they single out. Never Black, Christian, Muslim or LGBTQ Zionists. The self-appointed COOL KIDS CLUB is judgmental, mean & needs fixing Girl….Faye Dunaway would NEVER.”

items.title: ‘MobLand’ Season 3 Starts Shooting With Tom Hardy, Helen Mirren and Pierce Brosnan
items.description: Tom Hardy is officially back on set for “MobLand” Season 3, with cameras rolling this week.
items.author: K J Yossman
paragraphs: Tom Hardy is officially back on set for “MobLand” Season 3, with cameras rolling this week.

The actor, who plays fixer Harry da Souza in the Paramount+ crime drama, was rumored to have been booted from the show earlier this year after “creative differences” with producer David Glasser and writer Jez Butterworth amid claims he was late for set and had demanded script changes.

But as Variety reported at the time, reports of Hardy’s axing were premature, with Guy Ritchie and Paramount+ eager to hold on to the “Mad Max: Fury Road” star, and the trio managed to patch things up soon afterwards with filming for Season 3 due to start at the end of this year. That has now come to pass.
Hardy’s co-stars Helen Mirren and Pierce Brosnan also return as heads of the Harrigan crime family, playing Maeve and Conrad respectively.

The show also stars Paddy Considine, Joanne Froggatt, Lara Pulver, Anson Boon, Mandeep Dhillon, Jasmine Jobson, Teddie Allen, Emmett J. Scanlan, Johnny Flynn, Ophelia Lovibond, Janet McTeer and Toby Jones.
Exec producers are Glasser, Guy Ritchie, Jez Butterworth, Tom Hardy, Ivan Atkinson, Dean Baker, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari and Keith Cox.
Season 2, which Mirren called “madder and badder,” launched in Sept. with the tenth and final episode dropping today.
Hardy attended the Season 2 premiere in London alongside Glasser, Ritchie, Mirren and Brosnan where everyone made nice for the cameras.
Introducing the cast on stage inside the theater, Glasser called Hardy the “captain of our ship” saying he “stayed with it to the bitter end.”
