items.title: ‘Yellowjackets’ Creators on Closing Their Survival Story, Killing Characters and Thoughts on Spinoffs: “This Was Meant to Be the Final End”
items.description: [This story contains mild spoilers from the premiere of Yellowjackets season four.]
items.author: Jackie Strause
paragraphs: [This story contains mild spoilers from the premiere of Yellowjackets season four.]

The end is near for Yellowjackets. The fourth and final season of Showtime‘s hit survival story has begun, and the weekly drop of final episodes will send viewers on a wild ride as they ruminate on life, death — and the meanings behind those bizarre post-Yellowjackets dreams. If it’s any consolation, the creators have those dreams, too.

“Life just keeps getting wider, and the show has been part of that. It’s been an expression of that width and an agent in creating that width,” Bart Nickerson, chatting with his co-creator wife, Ashley Lyle, tells The Hollywood Reporter of the last near-decade making the hit Showtime series. The pair initially planned for five seasons, but when the Paramount renewed Yellowjackets for a fourth and final season, the creators pivoted.

“For us,” says Lyle, “it was about storytelling momentum and, with the uncertainty of the industry right now, let’s just finish a story if we can. We took a good, hard look at it. If we had felt like we couldn’t get it done, we probably wouldn’t have taken the chance. But it felt like we could.”

What they deliver is what viewers have been waiting for when the survivors of the Yellowjackets plane crash that began the series are rescued and returned home in the season four premiere. Following the teens as they reassimilate into life in New Jersey — while learning how to live with the murders and cannibalistic acts they harbor; the things they did to survive those months in the wilderness — delivers a fascinating watch and full-circle return to where this story began.

Below, Lyle and Nickerson dive into making the final season and what to expect, including the pain of killing off characters while always knowing who would survive in the end. They also explain why they aren’t interested in spinoffs — because they’re ending the story with a period, not an ellipses: “We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that’s important. I think that’s part of the contract with the audience — that you’re telling a complete story.”

We have been waiting for this rescue season. When we spoke with you two way back in the beginning of all of this, in your heads, you had envisioned Yellowjackets as a five-season show, and here you are ending with four seasons.
How big of a pivot was this to wrap up the show earlier than you planned?

LYLE Ultimately, as we were breaking this season, we realized that it was workable. It came down to: Do we potentially overstay our welcome? Of course, when you’re making television, there’s always a risk that you will not get another season. So we realized at a certain point that there was a much more high-octane version of this season that could accomplish all the things that we really hoped to accomplish when we first conceived of the show.

Coming off of the third season, we always knew we wanted to get the girls back home. Then we always knew in the adult timeline that we wanted things to start turning in on itself amongst these women in their relationships. And it did feel like we had hit that pivot point at the end of season three. So we just ended up going full steam ahead; burden the hand. The ability to tell a complete story, to finish it on our own terms, is something we’re incredibly grateful for. We hope everyone feels a sense of satisfaction with this final season.

Given the narrative of viewers dropping off after two seasons of a show, did you feel like season three was the hardest point to keep your audience, and did that affect what you wanted to do going into four?

BART NICKERSON To be honest, I didn’t know that was a thing — that audiences drop after two season. I think, in some respect, through the entire run of the show, there is, as it turns out, a gift in being, tremendously insecure and scared. (Laughs.) Every script we’ve ever written, even if we’re just going to our writers group, you have so much of your personal self-worth and the quality of that script, you kind of live and die on every piece of feedback. Although it sounds insane, the stakes of making a season of television are almost a little intellectual — you don’t ever stand in front of the audience and hear them reacting to your thing. Because the stakes are always so high, it wasn’t about: How do we keep this going? Or: People didn’t like this, how do we address that? At the end of the day, you just have to make the story you’re trying to make for better or for worse. And some may say for worse! (Laughs.)

LYLE I don’t really understand the metrics of how they’re counting viewership at this point. I’m not sure anybody does. I think they said season three was the most watched, but some of that, I’m sure, is people catching up on Netflix. For us, it was about storytelling momentum and, with the uncertainty of the industry right now, let’s just finish a story if we can. And we took a good, hard look at it. If we had felt like we couldn’t get it done, we probably would have taken the chance. But it felt like we could.
As the storytellers, you have a huge ensemble. So many stories to tell. What were some of the biggest challenges knowing that this was it? That you had a finite number of episodes left.

NICKERSON Yes, just that in and of itself [is the challenge]. We love television. We love telling television stories, and we love our characters and want them all to have a full, complete arc. Then there is the reality only having so many pages and so many minutes on screen. So it’s about how to be as efficient as possible, and that has always been a challenge. We’ve always wanted each episode, each season, each scene to have a beginning, middle and an end. So it’s about, how do you tell these stories with efficiency but also arc? That has always been an incredible challenge.
Did it leave more things on the cutting room floor? Anything you can share now that didn’t work or make the show?

LYLE Not necessarily in a macro sense for this season. Every episode, we’re always over time. We’ll sit with the editors and pull out 10 seconds at a time to get it under 60 minutes. You’re always cutting. That was the case in season one. That was the case in season two. Sometimes you go back and go, “Remember when that scene existed?” And the fact is that it was sort of telling you that it didn’t need to be there. So I think the process kind of works itself out as you go.
Does it leave more room for spinoffs?
LYLE That’s a question for Paramount Skydance!

NICKERSON Having one less season [I don’t think changes that], because we came to an end that was meant to be the final end. There are always ideas you haven’t had yet. So, never say never. But there isn’t something where it’s like, because we had one last season, we could come back and revisit that.
Do you two feel like you are closing the Yellowjackets book with this ending? No ideas for a tangent or a right turn in any way?

LYLE We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that’s important. I think that’s part of the contract with the audience — that you’re telling a complete story. I suppose in this day and age, there’s a never-say-never quality to this question, but at the same time, we wanted to tell a complete story. We wanted it to feel like the audience had been on the full ride. And hopefully, that there’s a lot of emotional satisfaction in the resolution that we find.

NICKERSON At the end of the day, there’s a level on which, if you’re telling a story about survival, you’re telling a story about death, and that means there has to be an end, because that’s what you’re confronting — the end-end. And, what does it mean when it’s over? I don’t think it would be possible to tell a satisfying ending if it didn’t feel like the ending … of everything … ever. (Laughs.)

You come out swinging with the season four premiere jumping right into the rescue timeline. You could have built your way up to it. Can you talk about why you wanted to lead with it, and fill in the gaps from the past as the season goes?

LYLE That is a storytelling paradigm we’ve always been drawn to: not necessarily the “what happens” but the “why.” That was a big part of season one with the question of whether or not they engage in cannibalism. There were people who said, did you ever consider teasing that out? And we’re like, “No.” We wanted to put it in the pilot, because to us, the most interesting thing wasn’t whether or not they’d do it. It was, why did they do it? How did they get there? What is the context for it?

Similarly, with this season, it was a clearing of the decks, a reset in a way that could set up this season as a standalone season. And again, it wasn’t if they get rescued, it’s how and why, and what happens in the aftermath?

We would talk in the writers room, now that we’ve got four timelines or (let’s just make things a little more complicated for ourselves!), in terms of post-rescue, pre-rescue and present day. And it felt like what happened in the interim between Natalie’s distress call and them getting rescued could serve much more effectively as a little bit of mystery. Because to us, the more important emotional heartbeat of this season was going to be the post-rescue: how they were coping with and the different ways they would personally strategize how they would handle the reintegration. That was a much more interesting question for us at this point.

So much has happened to these characters over the course of the series, but it’s also been almost a decade since you two started developing this show. Do you feel like you also have grown with the show, in terms of how you wanted to end it and what you want to say in the end?

NICKERSON Speaking for myself, yes, tremendously. It would be difficult for me to fully articulate what I mean, but so much of this story is a result of stuff that’s been churned up and has continued to churned up. I always say the best compliment that people will give us about the show is, “I just started watching Yellowjackets. My dreams have been so messed up!” This idea that there is a deepness to the show.
I’ve had some bizarre dreams while watching these screeners!

NICKERSON (Laughs.) That’s been our life for nine years! Just weird dreams. (Laughs.) I feel like life just keeps getting wider, and the show has been part of that. It’s been an expression of that width and an agent in creating that width.

This show is about surviving and about death. There have been so many big deaths along the way. We still feel Juliette Lewis’ exit and last season, you took so many of them away! Fans are always reacting. How much did you take the fans into account when you thought about who is going to survive this season?

LYLE We didn’t. I don’t think we can, because, ultimately, if we were trying to please some segment of the audience, we’re going to displease another. We have to write it for ourselves and use that as a guiding light and principle. It’s a fool’s errand to try to do fan service, especially when you’re planning how to end a show.

NICKERSON The first time we met with Julie Plec, who gave us our first job in television, it was a couple days after a big character death in Vampire Diaries. It was like, “Oh, my God. I can’t believe you killed this person!” She got very serious and was like, “It’s my job to service the story before I service what the fans think they want.”

Because, ultimately, when I’m rooting for a character, I have this relationship with them. I’m not really thinking about the story. I’m thinking about the character and my relationship to them. In order to give the fans something of value, you have to keep your eye on what you’re trying to build and not necessarily on how it’s going to be received.
Your characters are like your babies. Is there a death that still sits with you or any character you wish you still had around to play with?

LYLE I think that speaks to what Bart was saying. They’re all difficult. But one that always comes back around as being rough for everybody involved on set was when we killed Coach Scott last season. Steven [Krueger] knew very early on — we go way, way, way back. He was like, “It’s time. I’m surprised I lasted this long.” There are moments where, man, you miss the character, you miss having that actor on set. But at the same time, it had to happen.

NICKERSON And that’s one of the moments I am most proud of. Every time we watched, it was such an incredible performance by both of them [Krueger and Sophie Thatcher]. It was amazing. The whole thing to watch the Natalie character born in this ultimate sacrifice that she’s making for somebody else, but it’s also a grisly, violent act. I so miss that character. But, what are we doing if it’s not trying to create those moments?
I know those calls to your departing actors have been difficult along the way, but I imagine dying in the final season is different. You probably get some cheering. It’s like a badge of honor.
LYLE It’s easier the last season!
Did you always know who would be the final girl(s), or did it change along the way?
NICKERSON My only hesitation is that, on the path, you investigate different things. But, no, it was at the beginning. At the beginning, this was how we were going to do it.
LYLE We kicked the tires a lot. But we really ended up in the place we thought we would.
NICKERSON Yeah. Some of the particulars changed. Ultimately, the meaning of it has, for me at least, shifted. But yeah, we actually did end up where we thought we would.
I know you can’t talk spoilers. But is there anything you want to tease… will dead characters return? Will we ever see that lost episode? Any surprises in store?
NICKERSON We’re not allowed to say! We want to reveal everything. We just want you to see it!
You have always talked about having big beats you knew you wanted to hit throughout the show: Pit Girl, the scientists, rescue. Anything you can’t wait for us to see, in broad terms?
NICKERSON I don’t think it’s a spoiler to say that them coming back to New Jersey has always been a huge thing we wanted to do, and, in some sense, is the show.
LYLE There are a few things. There’s a scene in episode five that we’ve been talking about for many seasons.
NICKERSON Oh yeah, that is going to be really good! We’ve been talking about for a really long time.

There have been more than one scene that made your actors unwell — and even had them throwing up. For example, the Jackie feast … the Pit Girl reveal. Was there any filming experience in this final season that’s comparable to that?
LYLE I think they toughened up a little bit.
NICKERSON I mean, eating Jackie was rough. That was a tough day!
LYLE That was really, really rough. I don’t know that we could ever top that, in terms of torturing our actors.
NICKERSON Because that thing [Jackie’s edible body] looked good. I mean, not tasty, but, oh man. Just to have what they were going to eat like around is tough.

LYLE There was a moment on set this season when Melanie [Lynskey] brought her daughter to set and sort of regretted it immediately. Like, “Oh, just kidding! Go into the trailer.” I was like, “That’s not real. It’s okay!” She seemed fine. I mean, we don’t have to pay for her therapy! (Laughs.)
Yellowjackets is now streaming the first episode of season four on Paramount+ Premium.

items.title: “The Secrecy Was Insane:” The Making of ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,’ From Locked Safes to Original Cast’s Return
items.description: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.
items.author: Lexy Perez
paragraphs: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.
Before the odds could be in their favor, the creative team behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping had to survive a Games of their own, one played entirely in secret.
The rules were simple: one copy of the book, no internet and not a word to anyone.

When Hunger Games author Suzanne Collins called her trusted adapters, director Francis Lawrence, producer Nina Jacobson and original Hunger Games screenwriter Billy Ray, they were eager to read her new story. The catch: it wasn’t fully finished, and it hadn’t been announced to the public. That meant caution was essential.

Take Ray’s process for example. The screenwriter didn’t write his latest Hunger Games script on his own computer. Each day, he drove onto the Fox lot to Jacobson’s office and sat down in a small room with a safe that guarded Collins’ story. An assistant opened the safe, took out a laptop that had never been connected to the internet and set it in front of him. He wrote all day, said “Done,” and the laptop went back into the safe.
“That’s how the script got written, which of course I had never done before,” Ray tells The Hollywood Reporter.

It was an unusual way to adapt a novel that almost no one outside that small circle knew existed, yet maintaining strict confidentiality was imperative given the phenomenon Collins’ franchise has become. The original four films — The Hunger Games, Catching Fire and Mockingjay Part 1 and 2 — grossed roughly $2.98 billion worldwide. Debuting with its first book in 2008, the dystopian saga following teenagers forced into fatal combat has grown into one of the most successful young adult publishing franchises in history. Across its five installments, the series has sold more than 100 million copies globally.

In 2020, Collins released her first prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, which chronicled the rise of the tyrant Coriolanus Snow. The film was adapted for feature film starring Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler. Now with Sunrise on the Reaping, released on Nov. 20, Collins has returned to another familiar face: Haymitch Abernathy, the District 12 mentor Woody Harrelson played in the films.

The prequel revisits the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games, starting on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, when a younger Haymitch (portrayed by Joseph Zada) competes. Sunrise on the Reaping opens on Haymitch’s 16th birthday, which coincides with the second Quarter Quell, where the traditional choice of one male and one female from a district has been doubled to two of each.

Though initially not among the four selected tributes for District 12, Haymitch is automatically volunteered as punishment for trying to protect his girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) who reacts after one of the chosen boys tries to make a run for it and is shot by Capitol soldiers known as “Peacekeepers.”

The Haymitch origin story answers a question fans have had since the first film: how the hopeful, mischievous kid became the bitter, drunken mentor to Jennifer Lawrence‘s Katniss Everdeen and Josh Hutcherson‘s Peeta Mellark that Harrelson played.

Ahead of the film’s release, Ray, Jacobson and director Francis Lawrence spoke with THR about working under an NDA bubble, finding their new Haymitch and reuniting franchise alums Harrelson, Lawrence and Hutcherson.
Enlisting the Original Screenwriter

When The Hunger Games was first adapted for the screen, screenwriter Ray and director Gary Ross launched what would grow into a global success. Since both Ray and Ross parted ways with the franchise following the initial installment, Ray’s comeback to craft the backstory for a character he helped popularize represented a complete full-circle experience.
“Having launched that franchise, The Hunger Games has been such a blessing in my career,” Ray tells THR. “I can’t begin to enumerate all the ways it’s been great for me.”

“When the opportunity came to come back, I said yes before I read the book,” he says of his return. “It was something I wanted to do. I wanted to work with Francis, and I wanted to be back under the hood with Suzanne and with Nina.”

Ray has stayed close with Collins, who read an early draft of his debut novel, Burn the Water, which was released earlier this year. “It was as if we had spoken the day before,” he says of reteaming with Collins and others for Sunrise on the Reaping. “There was just no falloff at all.”
Reading an Early Draft in Secrecy

When Collins calls, producer Jacobson, director Lawrence and Ray answer, ready to find out what the author has created this time. But her first question is always the same: “Why don’t you guys take a look and let me know if you think it’s a movie?”
“This is always kind of hilarious… We read this one and said, ‘Yeah, it’s a movie, Suzanne,'” Lawrence says, laughing. Jacobson’s answer was just as immediate: “My first response was, ‘Hell yes.'”

Collins’ question is a sincere one, though, Lawrence explains. “She’s very serious when she says it’s OK to tell her it’s not a movie. When you create anything, you’re vulnerable, and when she hands something to us, it’s usually not completely finished. She feels vulnerable about it and wants some reassurance that it really is worthy of being on the screen.”

Getting that far took some doing. When the team read an early draft of The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, the world was in lockdown, so keeping it secret was easier, Lawrence says. Sunrise on the Reaping brought “a different kind of tension, because the book had not yet been published, so the secrecy and security around the project was pretty extreme,” Ray says.

“For us, the secrecy was insane,” Jacobson says. “We had one hard copy of the book. It had to be mailed or messengered from New York to L.A. in sections. First it lived at her [Collins’] agent’s house and then eventually we got a safe for my office and it moved into the safe. There was one copy, and people could make an appointment if they needed to read it.”

The secrecy extended to casting, too. “Even once we had our script, we couldn’t release sides, or even use a scene from the book instead of sides, because if we read an actor, people would know what scenes and characters were in the book besides Haymitch,” Jacobson says. “So we had the young actors do improvs, just so we could get acquainted with this generation of actors and start to collect knowledge about who they are.”
“Having to keep it locked down in this NDA bubble was exciting,” she adds. “It was sort of stressful, and I was incredibly relieved when we could finally talk about it!”
“Interpretation, Not Impersonation”: Finding a New Haymitch
“We knew Haymitch was going to be the trickiest person to cast, because we’re anchored with him,” Lawrence says.

Joseph Zada, who starred in Prime Video’s We Were Liars and had filmed Netflix’s East of Eden series, caught the attention of casting directors Debra Zane and Dylan Jury, who wanted Lawrence and Jacobson to meet him.
“He had sent in an improv tape. We had many, many people do improv tapes just to see who was out in the world, and his was pretty special,” Lawrence recalls.

From there, the audition process became its own Hunger Games. “We really put him through the wringer in the audition process,” the director admits. “We tested and tested to make sure he would be emotionally capable of going through everything he needed to go through, that he had the sense of mischief and irreverence Woody has, and that he could embody all those characteristics without feeling like he was doing an impression. That was the tricky thing. But he was definitely the guy.”

“We needed to know he had the range to experience all of the loss in the movie, and to do it in different ways: sometimes shame, guilt or anger, or just complete loss and grief,” Lawrence adds. “We needed somebody who could bring all of that.”

For Jacobson, the deciding quality was mischief. “You needed somebody who had mischief in them, and that’s a surprisingly hard thing to find,” she says. “There are some wonderful, likable actors who are very capable leading men, but who don’t necessarily have that mischief in them, that troublemaker vibe. And yet at his young age, it can’t be that dark, twisted kind of mischief-maker or trickster. It’s a boyish quality.”
Zada was someone who “had a hopeful, sunny disposition” and the mischief they wanted Haymitch to embody.

“When you first meet him in the original movies, you don’t understand why he’s so angry, drunken, broken and bitter. You assume, well, it can’t be easy being a mentor for the poorest, most disadvantaged district out there,” she continues. “What all of us wanted to see in this one, and what Joseph captured so beautifully, is that he was bright, funny, hopeful and very apolitical.”

Zada’s chemistry with Peak, cast as his love interest, Lenore Dove, sealed it. “You just felt it. You felt like this woman is the woman he loves. She’s his best friend. She’s the person who makes it all make sense for him,” Jacobson says of their chemistry reads together.

“There’s a quality about Woody, and we had to find someone who had that quality but wasn’t going to get burdened by it,” she says. “With all of our actors, we always said, ‘We don’t want impersonation. We want interpretation.'”
An A-List Cast Joins the Franchise

That philosophy extended well beyond Haymitch. From Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning to Glenn Close, Jesse Plemons and Ralph Fiennes, Sunrise wasn’t short on A-listers joining its younger, newer cast members that also included Mckenna Grace, Ben Wang, Molly McCann and Percy Daggs IV.

But joining an established franchise isn’t always an immediate yes, Jacobson says. “There are definitely some people who just don’t know the series that well, so it’s about educating them about it, and making sure they know we’re not looking for them to impersonate,” she explains. “We want their interpretation of the character. If they don’t know the series, oftentimes they have to go ask around a bit and talk to people in their lives.”

Culkin and Fanning, who play Caesar Flickerman and Effie Trinket, have been candid about finding their own interpretations while respecting the characters Stanley Tucci and Elizabeth Banks originated.

“What we tell people who are new to it, and I really do believe this quite earnestly, is that it’s one of the very few franchises where, for each of the renowned actors we cast, it is actually all about performance. It’s never about prosthetics or visual effects,” Jacobson says. (Well, almost never: “Of course we use those things sparingly here and there. Those are not Glenn’s teeth,” she notes.)

The appeal, she says, is the creative freedom that comes with everything being “rooted in performance.” “You’re going to be collaborating closely with Francis and the department heads on the creation, building and design of your character, and it’s going to come down to meaty character work. You’re very rarely against a green screen. You’re almost always in a practical location with, hopefully, some other amazing actors in the scenes with you. I think these movies give each actor a real showcase of their talents, in a way that isn’t always true in a lot of other franchises.”
Adapting the Story as Fans First

Jacobson recalls Sunrise on the Reaping being an “incredibly emotional” read. “I cried quite a few times, and then cried quite a lot at the end. I found it so fully moving and satisfying on so many levels.”
But how do you adapt a book fans haven’t been able to read yet? The creative team relied on being fans themselves.

“Nina and I consider ourselves fans, so there are a lot of things we fight to keep from the book, details we love ourselves,” Lawrence says. “And Suzanne is obviously going to fight for certain things: making sure her themes, ideas, the spirit of the characters and their emotional arcs are there. So there’s a good group of us there to protect what we think fans are going to love.”
“The funny thing is, it’s incredibly easy for me to know how fans will feel, because I’m the OG fan,” Jacobson says. “I’m as obsessed with the books as any diehard fan, and so is Francis.”
Still, some things had to go. “If I put everything that’s in the book into the movie, the movie would be six hours long. You can’t do that,” Ray says.

Sunrise doubles the number of tributes competing in the Games, and the team knew they couldn’t explore every one in depth. “Getting to know the tributes and understanding potential allies and enemies is one of the parts of these movies people really enjoy and are invested in. So figuring out how to balance the 48, and making sure we gave time and attention to the core characters whose stories are connected to Haymitch’s journey, was a definite challenge,” Jacobson says.

The book is also told entirely from Haymitch’s point of view, which posed its own challenge. “What we found even in the original movies with Katniss was that if she wasn’t in a scene, the scene still needed to be about her in some way,” Jacobson says. “But when you’re only ever with that one person, there’s important context and opportunities you might miss. So figuring out where to break with his point of view, when to show something he can’t see or know, was a big decision in the adaptation process.”
As for every other decision, the guiding principle was Collins.

“At the very beginning of the process, I asked Suzanne, ‘What is this book about for you?'” Ray recalls. “She talked about the philosophy of the book: the philosophy of propaganda and implicit submission, the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, David Hume and John Locke. And I said, ‘Suzanne, what’s the book about for you emotionally?’ She said, ‘It’s about love and loss.’ I said, ‘Great, that’s what I’m writing.’ So anything that didn’t stick to that had to go.”

The Haymitch audiences meet in Sunrise is a far cry from the broken alcoholic of the original films. In Sunrise, audiences encounter a teen initially easygoing and unconcerned with politics. But his life transforms when he is forced into the 50th Hunger Games. Refusing to simply comply, he attempts to disrupt the Capitol’s system and oppose President Snow, altering both his own destiny and the world around him.

Jacobson likens the young Haymitch to the “kind of guy who’s probably not very serious about school and is just waiting for the end of the day to run down to the beach with his surfboard and his girlfriend, hang out and catch some waves.” His attitude, as she sees it: “I can’t do anything about this broken world that I live in, but I’ve got a girl I love and a family I love, and that’s enough for me. Who am I? What difference would I make anyway?”

Jacobson sees Haymitch’s arc as similar to Katniss’, with a priority on family that grows to include their community and district. “Your circle of concern grows in each movie, and there’s a cost to expanding that circle, a price to pay… But it’s the things he hears and brings with him from Lenore Dove. He says the Capitol has all the power and always will, and she says that doesn’t mean they always have, and it doesn’t mean they always will. It’s this notion that it’s not a foregone conclusion that oppressive power structures can’t be disrupted and ultimately destroyed.”
The Haymitch of the film faces a dilemma: “What am I willing to give up for the people I care about? And what am I willing to give up to right these really profound wrongs and try to end the Games?”

“Seeing him get radicalized, and seeing him decide, even with all this loss, that the way to honor these people is to continue to fight: that was what was really important to me, and what I found really interesting and moving,” Lawrence says.

“You see Haymitch in the other movies, and Woody does an amazing job portraying him, but people laugh with him,” the director adds. “He’s a drunk, and you just don’t know the history. Now you follow this movie and see all that he went through, how long and hard he fought, all the years he had to escort tributes to the arena and watch them die. But he continued to fight and kept his promise to his girlfriend, his mother, his brother, to Maysilee (portrayed by Grace) and all of them.”

For Ray, filling in that history was the point. “In that first movie, obviously Haymitch is just broken, with a real serious drinking problem and a lot of pain. This was the movie that explained all that, and it was great to do that sort of history retroactively, to say, ‘This explains the behavior you’ve been seeing through all those movies,'” he says. “People know what happened, and the trick is saying, ‘Here’s the part you didn’t know.’ That’s what we were going for here.”
Telling an Emotional, Brutal Story That Parallels Present Reality

Collins doesn’t write unless she has something to say, and themes have been the foundation of each Hunger Games book. With the original trilogy, she explored the consequences of war for teens. With the prequels, she continues to examine the state of the world.

“Look at the themes she’s dealing with now and how relevant they are: there’s a bit of a call to action, this idea of implicit submission, and diving into the use of propaganda to get people to submit. So there are fresh ideas that feel very relevant. There’s meat on the bone,” Lawrence says. “Take this idea of implicit submission. You can look at any government, whether it’s authoritarian, fascist or one that calls itself democratic: as humans, we always agree to be ruled by the few. It’s a bit of a call to action: don’t be apathetic, stand up, voice your beliefs, and don’t expect instant gratification, because change may take time. I feel that’s very relevant now, but it’s also timeless, because people are constantly fighting for their rights. You see it in Hungary, with the ousting of a regime, and in Brazil, where people actually make change. That’s happening now, but it’s also something that’s been happening for thousands of years.”
Ray says he approached both the original film and Sunrise as if they were “true stories.”

“And they’re getting closer and closer to being that, which is the bad news for us as a culture, and the great news for Suzanne Collins, because she has her finger on the pulse of something, and it does feel like a true story. If you think of it that way, you can write it as a screenwriter from a place of complete outrage,” he says.

Haymitch’s journey matters now even more given it’s “a time when so many people feel like, ‘What’s the point of trying to make a difference?'” Jacobson says. “It’s a story that is so emotional about how hard it is to try to make a difference. It’s also about how what you set in motion today might not be realized for another generation, and how hard it is to continue to resist and to endure, knowing that the changes you hope for could take 25 years to accomplish.”
Toning Down the Story, Not the Darkness

Anyone who knows The Hunger Games knows the brutality of the story. “I think an audience that has bought into the concept that a government forces children to kill each other knows they’re coming to see something dark,” Ray says. “I don’t think anybody is going to come away saying, ‘Wow, I was expecting a musical. What the hell is this?'”
Even so, certain sequences in Sunrise had to be toned down to keep the film’s PG-13 rating.

“There’s a moment in the book where a character is holding the head of a child, and I thought, ‘We’re never going to be able to do that.’ There were probably three moments in the book where I went, ‘Come on, Suzanne, this is never going to happen.’ And she understands that when we get into the process,” Lawrence says.
The story’s emotional darkness stayed intact, and Lawrence says it was “toughest” on Zada, who had to ride that roller coaster on set.

“Whenever we led up to certain days, whether it was a Lenore Dove scene or a Maysilee scene, it was always a little scary for him, because he knew he’d have to sit in those feelings for 10 or 12 hours, basically all day,” he says.

The Games were filmed first, with the District 12 scenes shot later. “He was so happy to just be happy: going to work convinced he’d never get called in the reaping, having a nice scene in the meadow with Lenore Dove, being in the candy shop. He looked forward to those days,” Lawrence says.

But the darker turns were never far off. “We also had to do things like shoot his and Lenore Dove’s first scene one day and then, because we were in that location, jump to the end the very next day and do that whole scene (readers know the one.) That was tough on Joe. Even when he was happy to be happy, he knew what was coming tomorrow. That weighed on him more than it did on me,” the director says.
Bringing Back Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson Was Always the Plan

Though the book and film follow a younger Haymitch, the book’s epilogue, featuring Katniss, Peeta and an older Haymitch, was in the script from the start. “It was such a profound honor to get to write those characters again. It was just pure joy,” Ray says.
“I remember reading the epilogue in the manuscript and thinking, ‘Wow, this is fantastic.’ I found it really moving,” Lawrence says of the trio’s return in the book.

“The hope was always to bring them back,” the director says of Harrelson, Hutcherson and Jennifer Lawrence. But because of the secrecy surrounding the book and the adaptation, “We didn’t reach out to them until, I want to say, the day before the announcement. That’s when I called the three of them.”

While the team hoped for an immediate yes, they prepared in case scheduling conflicts or other circumstances kept the actors from returning. “We had already tasked ourselves with figuring out how to make the story as fulfilling as possible if it didn’t happen,” Lawrence says.

But there was no need to rethink the epilogue: the actors were “all very excited to return,” he says. “Then it was really just a scheduling question: when can we get the three of them together and out to Germany?” the director says.

Francis Lawrence has stayed in touch with the cast, but working together again in the world of The Hunger Games made for an especially meaningful reunion. “I think it was a Wednesday night when they arrived, and I got a text from Jen that she and Josh were having a beer in the hotel bar. I was coming back from set, so I joined, then Nina joined, and our cinematographer, the still photographer, the sound mixer… It’s the same group of people who have been making these movies for 16 years, so we had this great reunion of about 30 of us before costume fittings and all of that.”
No Conversations About More Stories … Yet
With two prequel novels and films now out, the question is always whether there are more stories to tell in Panem. The creative team admits they’re just as in the dark as everyone else.
“She only really writes when she has something to say, so I hope she has something she wants to write about in this world, because I would miss it a lot,” Jacobson says.

Fans have been quick to name the characters they’d love to follow in their early years, with Finnick (portrayed by Sam Claflin) and Johanna (Jena Malone) at the top of the list, along with the first Hunger Games. After Sunrise, Jacobson’s own fascination is Plutarch. “When I realized from this book that Plutarch has been playing a double agent for 25 years by the time you meet him in Catching Fire, that to me is pretty fascinating. How do you pull that off? How could you possibly live that close to such danger? And what compromises did you have to make? He is not a morally clean character at all, so I have a total fascination with him,” she says.

If the prequels have proved anything, it’s to never say never, a lesson Jacobson says the team learned early. “When we finished the original trilogy of books, we really thought we were done. We’ve never tried to make a movie without a book of hers. We only make her books. We never tried to develop anything that wasn’t based on something she had given us as a book she was going to publish. So when we first got Ballad, all of a sudden it was, ‘Oh my god, we’re coming back to this world.'”

“I was so wowed by the way she’s taken us on this journey, and by the amount of things that come together in this movie from all of the books and all of the movies. On the other hand, honestly, you could make this [Sunrise] the first book you’ve ever read, or the first movie you’ve seen. You could start here, make it your jumping-off point, and then go in any order you wanted. So there’s accessibility for everyone.”
As for future stories, Lawrence and Jacobson are hopeful but note only Collins will know the answer.

“I don’t know if ‘superstitious’ is the right word, but she really does not let on whether or not she’s writing,” Lawrence says of Collins. “If she gets an idea and works on it, she keeps quiet, then turns it in to her publisher, who she trusts immensely, and waits to hear that it’s a publishable book. Only then does she tell us she’s written something.”

“I have not heard anything. Would I love her to write another book? Yes, I sure would, because I still love the world so much, and I still find there’s so much to learn,” Jacobson says. “Because she digs so deep in terms of both history and philosophy, I hope she still has so much more to say, and I hope she’ll decide to say it in Panem. But I don’t know. We haven’t gotten any winks or nods yet. I hope I get a wink and a nod, but I have gotten no winks, no nods so far.”
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is now in theaters.

items.title: Archie Renaux on ‘War’s Resident — and Misunderstood — Bad Boy
items.description: [This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the War finale.]
items.author: Seija Rankin
paragraphs: [This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the War finale.]

Archie Renaux is hesitant to call his character in War a villain. Johnny, the ambitious (often to a fault) junior lawyer who plays a double-agent litigator in the slick divorce drama, is often the one called upon to do the dirty work: the double-crossing, the manipulating of both witnesses and plaintiffs, and then, of course, the whole business of being a mole. “He does awful things, but he’s a puppet more so than anything else,” says Renaux. “He’s been taken advantage of, really.”

The series, from George Kay (Lupin), follows two rival London firms — the white-shoe Cathcarts and the newer, scrappier Taylor & Byrne — as they represent a tech mogul (played by Dominic West) and an actress (Sienna Miller) at the tumultuous end of their marriage. Renaux’s Johnny ostensibly works for Taylor & Byrne, but has been promised an eventual job at Cathcarts in exchange for double-crossing information about the high-profile case. Throughout the season, we see him cheating on his girlfriend with Miller’s Carla and framing a fellow junior lawyer after he’s almost caught with compromising inside intel. The actor, who previously starred on Netflix’s Shadow and Bone, likens the behavior to what happens in the third act of The Drama.

“There’s that great bit where Robert Pattinson has a kiss with someone, and it comes out of nowhere,” he explains. “And it’s like, what are you doing mate? Why are you making these decisions? But he’s just manic, and I was watching it in the cinema going, oh, that’s what Johnny’s like. He’s manic.”

In the series finale, Johnny redeems himself — at least as far as his interference with the court case is concerned, but his personal life is seemingly left in shambles. Below, Renaux talks about his take on the episode, what he knows about the show’s pending second season, and what it was like to act alongside Sienna Miller.
What do you remember about the audition process for the show?

I was on another job and we were doing night shoots in Canada, and I got an email about the audition but it was so hectic that I didn’t feel like I could afford to give my attention to anything else. This happened on Shadow and Bone, too, where my agents really pushed me to audition because they said it was really good. They were like, you’ve got to read this. The audition scene was when Johnny’s getting interviewed by Cathcarts, so it was a lengthy paragraph of dialogue I had to learn. And I had an offer for another show at the time, and I couldn’t keep that project waiting too long if I wasn’t going to take it, so I got the offer for War very quickly.
How did you make the decision that you wanted to hold out for the role in War and not the other offer?

It was the character. Johnny’s the audience’s way in. You’re really rooting for him at the beginning, or at least I hope so, and then people are quite disappointed by what he does. But that’s great. It’s complex and divisive. When I was reading the script, I was going, oh God, why’s he done this and that?
Everyone on this show is badly behaved to a degree, but he’s often the person that you feel like could be making better choices…

The other people are smooth-talking, very well put-together, calculated villains. The typical sort. Johnny is not that. He’s done some mad things, the cheating, and he’s a mess. But he’s in a state of constant stress and people do weird stuff when they’re in shock.
Some of what he does feels calculated — but calculated incorrectly — but do you think his affair with Carla was planned or did he get swept up in her beauty and fame?

The way I saw it at the start was, OK, he’s playing the game. If he gets close to the client, and the client’s able to give him information, that’s great. Obviously he’s attracted to her, and he plays along and flirts, and then he enjoys the flirting. When it’s reciprocated, I think it takes him by surprise and he gets caught up in the moment.
Where do you think the desperation comes from?

I wonder if he would have done any of it had he not got fired. Or had Angus not provoked him at the restaurant at the beginning and made him feel insecure about his job. That ignites a sense of, I’m going to succeed by any means necessary. Being around people that have money and big careers is very humiliating, and I think that restaurant scene is something of a villain origin story. I know he does punch him, but I imagine everyone thinks, OK, that’s fair.

In the final episode, when he convinces Flora to come take the stand and to read the letter to Carla, is that him being sneaky again to try and win the case to get himself out of a jam? Or is he trying to redeem himself on a deeper level?

I think it was trying to fix the mess he’d made. I think he’s a good person. I know he is. He knows that’s the least he could have done. He lost everything trying to get what he wanted and going about it in the wrong way. He’s got some sneaky skills and this is him putting them to good use. I think he is a good lawyer, and you only get a glimpse of that. His real personality is when he’s working at the restaurant at the beginning of the season. When he’s interviewing at the law firms, it’s a performance he’s putting on and he’s overcompensating for his education and background.
What did they tell you about plans for future seasons of the show?

Well they’ve got plans for multiple seasons, and it’s sort of an anthology series following the two law firms over different cases. So I knew there was a possibility for doing more seasons. I don’t want to say much more right now. [Read THR’s interview with creator George Kay on the finale and season two plans here.]
All episodes of War are now streaming on HBO Max in the U.S. and Sky NOW in the U.K.

items.title: Matt Damon on the Oscars, Tarantino, and the Roles That Got Away
items.description: In the desert, as the song goes, you can remember your name. So it’s fitting that Matt Damon has come here—to a sweltering stretch of inland California near Lancaster—to reflect on his 30-odd-year career as one of the most familiar and bankable faces in Hollyw
items.author: Frazier Tharpe; Richard Burbridge
paragraphs: In the desert, as the song goes, you can remember your name. So it’s fitting that Matt Damon has come here—to a sweltering stretch of inland California near Lancaster—to reflect on his 30-odd-year career as one of the most familiar and bankable faces in Hollywood, and specifically on a year that will go down as one of that career’s most challenging and rewarding passages.

Damon set 2026 off with The Rip, a throwback pulp thriller that reteamed him with his lifetime BFF Ben Affleck. He then went on to dominate the summer to a degree most actors crossing the other side of 55 wouldn’t dream of, with Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey—a noisy, thrilling, engrossing feat of big-budget moviemaking that wouldn’t have worked without an Odysseus compelling enough to command audiences to take the 20-year journey with him. The role demanded everything in Damon’s toolbox, and then some, but the result was a cultural and commercial run that only Spider-Man himself could top.

This is rare air, and Damon knows it. Lightning struck once for him, with Good Will Hunting in 1997—he never thought he’d see that happen again, much less 29 years later. If exhaustion is the price of beating those odds, then so be it. Still readjusting to life on dry land, Damon sat down to unpack the most unlikely filmmaking experience of his career—and begin working out where he might want to go next.
This interview has been condensed and edited.
Matt Damon: That is amazing coming from him. Yes, I did hear about it.

Yeah, I think if you talk to any actor my age, any of the usual suspects, they’d probably say the same thing. I think the more you do it, if you’re working with really good people, you’re always improving, you’re getting better. And then you’re living more life and you have your family dynamics, all of your primary relationships kind of fill up your reservoir. I’ve talked to other actors my age about it, Ben included—I think there’s a tendency to push when you’re younger, a little bit, to try to work yourself up, and the older you get, the more available a lot of this stuff is. These very, very, very big emotions are kind of just sitting [near the surface]. And so you can really relax into the work, and it can be very full without being forced.
I think so, yeah. I mean, I’ve never been a part of a movie like The Odyssey that was…. Well, I guess Oppenheimer, to an extent, was somewhat of a phenomenon as well.

My workload was a lot heavier on this one, and everybody’s was, and that was kind of the joy of it. We knew we were the first ones to ever try to do a full film in IMAX [70 mm], and that comes with a whole host of challenges for every single department. We were all, I think, very patient with each other because we knew what was being asked of the other people. So in terms of the acting department—the IMAX load is two and a half minutes or three minutes. And so these big, heavy emotional scenes—you couldn’t play them all the way through. You’d have to cut them up. And the crew was just awesome, very patient with us. It felt like we were explorers, in a way. We got to be the first ones to do it, and that really bonded us.

I never would have expected it. And also, to play a role that’s so physical and, at my age, to even have a role that’s available on a scale like this. I’d always wanted to make a David Lean movie. To have it come at this point in my life, I felt incredibly lucky, not only to be able to do it, but also to be able to contextualize it. I don’t think I would’ve appreciated it as much 20 years ago.

No, I just don’t think I would’ve been able to understand and to hold as much gratitude as I am and as I did throughout the process. It’s all about how you look at things. And in retrospect, yeah, we were probably cold and wet. There was a lot of physical discomfort that was temporary. But because I felt so grateful to be there, I was just so excited. I was just so joyful the whole time that I didn’t really notice any of that.
[Laughs] There are no sure things, man. I think that’s where you get into trouble, being like, Well, this is a surefire hit. I’ve heard that before.

I felt it when I saw it. There is that thing that can happen where you make a movie, and you feel like it’s really good, and it just doesn’t connect, and there’s just nothing you can do about that. But as the audience reactions started to come in and the critical reactions were great as well, it was like, Okay….

Chris [Nolan], the most nervous he is in the entire process, from the very beginning to the very end, is the eve of the film coming out. He’s genuinely nervous. He talks openly about it, because that is the moment that you put it out into the world and you have to live with the reaction. Ultimately, the audience decides. Once it opened and the responses were what they were, I think I felt like, We’re going to be okay. It was a big bet in the sense that it was a big budget. I’m not used to playing in that arena. The numbers that movies have to get to just to break even at that level are just so beyond the movies that I’m known for.

A few of them. But The Martian, which I think is the biggest movie that I’ve ever headlined—I think The Odyssey made three times what that made. And that was a real hit for me. But there’s this other league of these kinds of movies that are in the billions that I’ve just never….
[Laughs] It’s just, like, What?

Well, the thing about a role like that is every single day I was paired with an unbelievable scene partner. One day I’d be working with Annie [Hathaway], and then the next day I’d be working with Himesh [Patel]. It’s following this character through all these different stages of his life and people who are close to him. So every day was a different, exciting little challenge, a little puzzle to figure out. I’ve always said that when you’re working with a great actor, they’re so good that they’re good enough for both of you. And it’s almost like this wave comes and you just stand up on your board and ride it. Then you have Samantha Morton, who literally just picks you up and shoulder-carries you.

It’s very hard to come in and do really intense things in a very short time frame. [Morton’s scenes]—that was under a week of shooting. Each day being incredibly intense. And that was what was so incredible about these actors who would come in. They’re under a lot of pressure. Nobody says that, but we all know the deal. These are critical scenes, and everybody just came in and killed it. It just got more and more exciting as we were going.

I agree. She’s incredible. She’s always been incredible. We had a near-miss working together in 2003—and I got to know her then—in a movie with Heath Ledger. I just think the world of her as an actress, and I was excited when we did the scene. I was like, This one’s going to really work. And I hope—it doesn’t always happen right away, but hopefully it’s lodged her back in the minds of people who are making those decisions, because she’s just extraordinary.

That’s the emotional spine of the movie. A lot of that monologue that I have at the end is in voiceover, but I wrote it all out and I had it on my phone and I would just carry it with me off set. I would just revisit it and run through it a few times, and I was doing that for months and months. Firstly, I thought it was just so beautifully written, but also because I knew that scene had to land. If that lands, then the movie works.

And that also means setting them up as a young couple before he leaves. There’s a lot of engineering that goes into getting to a scene like that and then you have to execute it. I spent an inordinate amount of time thinking about that one.

Well, at that point, the audience has been on the journey with you, and it’s been a hell of a journey, so you don’t have to tell them that. We were tired. That scene I shot with Samantha, oddly, we had come from Iceland, but we were shooting nights, and we came to Scotland, and I had it happen two or three times on this movie where I just didn’t sleep. I was tired and I went to bed, and I’m sure everyone’s had that feeling where you’ve got to get up the next day and you have something that you have to do and you can’t fall asleep and you’re kicking the blanket around and you’re staring at the ceiling. By the time I got to work to do the scene with Sam, I hadn’t slept in 24 hours, and by the end of the day it was 36 or whatever. I remember thinking the great thing about this character is he probably didn’t sleep last night. Don’t worry about it. So the weariness was very real for a lot of the movie.
It’s all in there because it’s what I’m actually feeling. As I was saying before, it’s very easy to relax into what’s real and available and to have access to it.

This was the biggest one that we’ve ever done, and we’ve always had a two-week rule. I think the first stretch [on The Odyssey], I was away for three and a half weeks. The first half of the movie was the hardest because the kids were still in school. And then once the summer hit, they could come to set and we could be together. But that first stretch—luckily they’re huge Chris Nolan fans and they knew that it was this incredible role, so they were really supportive, and it was a sacrifice for them, and they were awesome about it.

He’s turned down a lot of work. And in fact, he really wanted to take on the CEO role at [Damon and Affleck’s production company] Artists Equity because it would keep him home. So when he directs—for instance, Animals, that was all shot in LA. He said to me when we started the company—he’s got joint custody, which means he gets to be with the kids half the time. And he said, “If I go to Estonia and do a movie, it’s not like I get that time back.” So that for him means he’s got to stay in LA.
It’s all downhill from here.

I felt that way when I did Air with Ben. It was such a joyful experience, and we had so much fun, and we really loved the movie we made. We had this discussion about how I don’t want to do [a project] unless it’s joyful and unless it’s really right for my life. So much of being a young actor is you’re afraid it’s going to go away. You’re very much still in touch with that feeling of being unemployed. And so when Ben and I got famous, we both really worked. Buried ourselves in work. Partly because people are suddenly offering you things and you can’t imagine turning anything down, right? It just seems counter to everything you’ve been trying so hard to do for your entire life.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Absolutely.

The first time was before The Bourne Identity came out. I had done The Legend of Bagger Vance with Will [Smith] and Charlize [Theron], and that movie didn’t do well. And Will was, as he is now, the biggest star. And so it’s like, it’s not Will’s fault. [Laughs] And then I did All the Pretty Horses with Billy Bob [Thornton], and that was a whole fraught experience. There were different ideas between the studio and between Billy Bob about what the movie should be, and so it ended up getting cut in a way that wasn’t to Billy’s liking and it didn’t do well. And so I had had these misses. And so there was this stretch where the phone just didn’t ring. The silence was…. It was a real rose-colored lenses coming off.

Well, the other thing was that The Bourne Identity was delayed something like a year. And so the word was, That’s going to be a stinker. But in that time, I went right from [filming] Bourne to Ocean’s Eleven. Then there was this whole period of time where nobody was calling, except for Steven Soderbergh, who called and offered me the movie The Informant! And I was so confused. I asked him, “Are you asking me to write it?” Because I couldn’t imagine he was asking me to be in it, because nobody else was calling. He goes, “What? No, Scott Burns is writing it. I want you to be the lead.” And I’ve never forgotten that. He just paid no attention to what everyone else was saying. But anyway, leaving that aside, nobody else was calling. And then The Bourne Identity came out, and it was a big hit.

It’s not personal. It’s business. And people can’t really go out of their way to help you. It’s really a pretty cold calculus that determines whether or not you’re on the list or off the list. And you never know who’s on the list. And the list can be different for different studios, who they’ll greenlight a movie with.

No, no. There’s very, very frank conversations between agents and studio people going like, “I can’t greenlight the movie with X, but I can with Y.” And that list is always changing, and I know that sometimes I’m on it and sometimes I’m not. I just have to remember it’s not personal, but you can feel it if you’re on the list or not.

Yeah. And [the] quality of projects [you’re offered]. I’m sure I’ve worked my way off that list a number of times. I’ve had some movies that didn’t work, and then you got to pay attention. I remember 2012 to 2014-ish, maybe, Patrick [Whitesell], my agent for 35 years, said I was taking a lot of supporting roles—because again, I’m not strategizing at all. I’m just like, Oh, True Grit. I want to work with the Coen brothers. Great.

Yup, George [Clooney directing], great. So there was this string of movies like that. Patrick called me and he said, “You’ll become a supporting actor. We got to think about this next one.” And then what happened to come along was The Martian. But that’s about as much strategizing as we’ve ever done.

Interstellar was in there too. I’m so happy that I’m in that movie. I love the role, even though it’s a tiny part. When Chris offered me [the role], we hadn’t worked together, and [when] he offered me the part in Interstellar, he said, “Do you know that saying ‘There are no small parts, there are only small actors’ ? This is a small part.” But I think he undersold it, because it’s a really kind of pivotal role, and I had a ball doing it.

Yeah, I think I was on a Bourne movie or about to go do Green Zone with Paul Greengrass. That and Milk. I was supposed to play the Dan White part. And I was really excited about it. I’d spoken to Sean [Penn], and I’d started the research. I’d been watching the documentaries about him. Then Sean’s schedule changed and the movie had to push three months, which meant that it was going to conflict with the movie I was going to do with Paul. So I had to bow out, and I just loved that script so much. And I love Gus [Van Sant], obviously. And so that was a bummer. But having said that, they got Josh Brolin, and Josh is absolutely brilliant in the movie. That helped a lot, I think, with this feeling that I have, that I do believe that the right actor gets the part.

I never like to say that, because I don’t want to live with the regret, but I can tell you that I passed on Ted, and I’ve never had this experience where I laughed so hard reading a script. I literally took it to dinner and was reading parts of it out to my friends at dinner. And then I just got too clever by half. I don’t know what I was thinking. I was like, Well, maybe the teddy bear’s actually the best part.…

So I overthought it and I talked myself out of it. And because it shot in Boston, it would’ve been a chance for me to be home—my father’s passed away now, and I look back and I go, Man, that would’ve been six months back [home].
But, again, the right actor got the part. Mark [Wahlberg’s] great, and the movie’s great, and I wouldn’t have made it any better.

They’re really hard to do. And I don’t read a lot [of them]. I don’t think people think of me for comedies a lot. But I love them, and I love watching them, and I love doing them if I can get my hands on one. But they’re few and far between. I think because they don’t travel well. They’re harder to get made because you really have to get all your money back in America. Comedy is so cultural. So the margin for error, I think, is smaller, which is what’s so great when you see a great one.

Anthony [Minghella], I think, was the first, with Talented Mr. Ripley. And he talked openly about it. A lot of these directors do. They want to use whatever it is that you have to offer in a new way and in a fun way and in an unexpected way. Some of those roles are the best roles that I’ve ever had a chance to play. Really interesting, complex people, and I love that.

I shot a scene in a movie theater with [Jack Nicholson], and Jack was working with an earwig. It was just the three of us before the crew came in, and we were just rehearsing. Marty [Scorsese] goes, “Let’s run this and see how we think it’s going to go.” And Jack took the earpiece out and we rehearsed the scene a few times and Jack was letter-perfect with his dialogue. And so Marty went to get the crew, and as people were coming in I said, “Hey, man, what’s the deal with the earwig? You obviously know all your lines—you’re writing stuff.” And it was really interesting because, he goes, “The older you get, the harder it is to remember your lines.” And that feeling of going up on a line, that panic, that surge of adrenaline that you get—he goes, “It just makes me so uncomfortable.” It’s a fail-safe. And if he knows [the earpiece is] there, his body stays in that relaxed state. People might think it was laziness. It was the opposite. He was a grinder. He worked really, really hard. It was more about just protecting himself.

No, no, no, no, no. I think everybody was really focused on Marty. And I remember I was shooting second unit for The Bourne Ultimatum during that Oscars, so I didn’t go. I was living in Miami at the time, and I had an infant. [My wife] Lucy and I were laying in bed watching it and so nervous for Marty. And then when he won, I was jumping up and down in the bedroom and I remember being really excited. And then the next category was best picture, and The Departed won. And I realized in that moment I hadn’t even considered that that could happen. And I turned to Lucy and I was like, “Shit, we should be there!” And then the next few weeks, I got all these calls from all the cast and the studio, like, “Hey, where were you, man?” I totally blew it. And then the next time that that happened was on Oppenheimer, and we had this whole scary thing happen where my wife had a brain aneurysm.

She’s totally fine, thank God, but [she] had this brain surgery the week before the Oscars. But it was the first night she felt good enough to get up and had her energy back. And she surprised me and got a dress and we went out to the after-party, because she remembered that the last time it happened, I didn’t do it. And she was like, “This time we’re going out.” And it was pretty fucking heroic of her to do that and really meaningful.

It’s not something you can control. You got to just do the work, and that’s got to be the reward. Because it’s like, then if you don’t win, do you feel bad about something that was really positive? Don’t turn this into something bad. It’s a tricky one. I always think about old movies when I look at them and it says, “So-and-so won an Oscar, so-and-so didn’t.” You’re judging it in a totally different way. It’s not attached to that anymore. I think the real way they should do them, really, is 20 or 25 years later. You’ll have a really good idea of which movies really endured and really still matter to you. There can be hype in the moment, or it can be a zeitgeist thing, but it doesn’t hold up. The goal for me is to make as many of those movies that are around 20 years later. That’s a cool thing. People come up [to me] about Good Will Hunting and I realize they weren’t born when the movie came out. It’s just very cool for Ben and me to have a new generation of people actually see it.

I don’t know what that means. I live in Brooklyn. [Laughs] If the trail is in that area, yeah. I don’t know what that entails. I will say, the technical side of this movie—I think of someone like Willie Burton, our sound guy, who’s in his 80s and he is a legend in the business.

And I did not loop a line in this movie, which is incredible. And I did not loop a line in Oppenheimer, which is incredible. Willie and Doug [Shamburger], his boom operator, are so good. Every scene on the ship, Willie is down below in the hold mixing in storms. The fact that he salvages all of that dialogue is nothing short of amazing. The technical achievement of our heads of department and their teams were really special. And I just hope that people realize that, realize what it took to do what they did, because from a technical standpoint, I hope they all get their flowers.

I didn’t think I was going to work. And then the Daniels called me and they had this project that was so out there, and it was such a Daniels movie and it’s so different from anything I’ve ever been able to do that I couldn’t pass it up. They’re really good people, and this movie’s like a cosmic love bomb for the world. So it felt like the right place to put my energy, but we’re almost done shooting it, and yeah, I’m going to take a long time off.

I haven’t thought about it. There are a lot of great performances. Paul Newman had some great ones at the end. We have the studio now with Artists Equity, and I feel like we’re just going to do stuff we really want to do, because it’s a very time-consuming job, and if you’re not 100 percent in, it’s just not worth doing. You have to really let it take over your life. I think that was one of the joys of The Odyssey—it dominated our lives.

There was a funny thing that happened on The Odyssey. We were in Scotland. I was with my kids. They’d just come over and gotten out of school, and we were eating dinner in this tiny hotel in this tiny town. And so there was one little dining room, which had 10 little tables in it, and the crew had watched dailies and so they were shuffling in, and I was already eating with my kids—I had jeans and a flannel shirt and a baseball hat on. And Chris came in and he walked by the table and I said, “Hey, Chris.” And he turned and he goes, “Oh, hey, Matt. I didn’t recognize you with the beard.” Chris doesn’t say stupid things—it was definitely the stupidest thing he’s ever said, because we’d been next to each other for six months.

He had just walked out of dailies watching close-ups of me, I’m sure with this giant beard. And I looked at him and he immediately realized what he’d said and he just looked at his shoes and then he looked up, like, Can we just agree that this never happened? And he shuffled off, and my kids go, “Dad, does Chris Nolan not know who you are?” I was like, “No, guys, he’s just exhausted.” He was that tired. He hadn’t seen me out of wardrobe in a while, you know what I mean? We were so tired by the end of that movie.
Well, he should write us a movie. We would be very happy if he did that.

Who knows? I have no right to expect it, let’s put it that way. I don’t want to sound like a broken record, but I have such gratitude for the fact that this came along my path at this point. I have no right to expect anything like that to happen again. But in the meantime, I just want to make good stuff and definitely keep working with Ben, because we’re at that point in our life where we’re like, “Fuck it, why not?” This was our dream as kids, as boys. We got to honor those boys and keep working together if we can. ✦
Photography by Richard Burbridge
Hair by Johnnie Sapong using Leonor Greyl
Tailoring by Susanna Badalyan
