items.title: ‘If He Knew How Much Stuff I Was Buying, He’d See Me Differently’
items.description: It’s widely known that money is a leading cause of marital conflict. But what about online-shopping habits? “Stealth shopping” — when couples hide purchases from each other or hope the other won’t notice when a package shows up — has been on the rise for years
items.author: Charlotte Cowles
paragraphs: It’s widely known that money is a leading cause of marital conflict. But what about online-shopping habits? “Stealth shopping” — when couples hide purchases from each other or hope the other won’t notice when a package shows up — has been on the rise for years (along with problematic online shopping more generally). Sure, plenty of partners choose to keep their finances separate and spend their money how they see fit. But there’s a difference between independence and deception: When you’re squirreling away packages to keep your significant other from noticing, things can get weird. Below, three women share the online-shopping conflicts that have nearly upended their own relationships.
“It’s almost like porn for me. A private hobby that I keep to myself.” —a 45-year-old attorney in Washington, D.C.

My husband and I keep our money in three pots — his, mine, and ours — and we don’t ask each other about our separate expenses. I think it’s healthy, and it works for us for the most part. He can spend his money on golf or whatever, and I spend my money on Botox and things he doesn’t need to know about. But sometimes my online shopping feels a little furtive. I definitely don’t want him to know how much I spend on it.

I get packages delivered to me at work, partly because it’s easier. (I don’t have to worry about missing a package when it gets delivered to my apartment.) But if I’m being honest, it’s because I don’t want him to see them. It’s mostly clothing, shoes, occasionally stuff for the house. I return a lot of it. I’m not proud of this, but I just really love shopping. It feels like something that’s just for me, a guilty pleasure. This is gross to say, but it’s almost like porn for me. A private hobby that I keep to myself. It’s a vice.

If my husband knew how much stuff I was buying, I think he would see me differently. He definitely perceives me as having more self-control than he does, or maybe being more discerning and thoughtful. I’d like to believe this is true, but my shopping habits might indicate otherwise. I don’t know what he would think if he knew I spent a couple thousand dollars on shoes last year. I worry that he’d lose some respect for me.

I don’t feel great about my shopping habits. I definitely know I could save more money and be more on top of my finances. But I also really enjoy the stuff I buy. My husband definitely knows that I like to shop and kind of rolls his eyes when he sees me bringing something new home. Sometimes I stash it away so he doesn’t see, but sometimes I’ll ask him what he thinks of a new dress or shoes or whatever. Once he got upset that I’d returned a dress he really liked on me. So it’s not that he wants me to shop less — he wants me to be happy. I just don’t want him to know quite how much I shop.

If I came clean tomorrow about how much I spent on clothes, I doubt he’d be mad, exactly — it’s more that he’d have something on me. It gives away some power to show this weakness. That makes us sound like we have a terrible marriage, and we really don’t! But I want to show up as a certain person for him, and someone who shops a lot is not it. It makes me look and feel frivolous and materialistic, and I don’t want him to think that about me.
“He’ll be like, ‘Why is this thing in the house? Don’t you have two of those?’” —a 42-year-old journalist in New York

When my husband and I got married a few years ago, we bought a house together, and I told him we needed to buy a package box — a box that delivery people put packages in so they don’t get stolen off your stoop. I wanted to buy the big version of this box, and my husband was like, “Why would we ever need one that big?” I didn’t want to tell him that we were going to have 18 deliveries from Amazon every day.

Now, it’s become a thing where I’m trying to hide my purchases. I will move the Amazon delivery date to when I know my husband’s going into his office, so I can be home to get the packages before he sees them. I work from home, and he’s hybrid.

It really got out of hand when we had a baby. I quit Instagram for a while, but that made my online shopping worse; it was my alternative to scrolling on social media. I’ve tried deleting all the shopping apps on my phone, but then I’ll eventually crack and go on some weird shopping excursions, like buying stuff on eBay. During the newborn phase, there was also the era of buying so much baby stuff because you’re throwing spaghetti at the wall. You’re spending so much money at that point that it’s like, who cares about another $50? We need to buy five swaddles because we don’t know what’s going to work.

I think that when the structures of your daily life disappear, buying something is a way to make yourself feel like something’s happening. It’s a marker of time. You buy a new object, and then you wait for it, and then it arrives. You’ve made it happen, and it gives you a sense of accomplishment. I don’t know if it’s a shopping addiction or a phone and internet addiction. They’re definitely related.

Whenever I have a problem, my instinct is, “What can I buy to fix this?” I definitely get this from my parents. My mom ships a new cheap rice cooker to our house every time she visits. Once she shipped a nightlight to the house before she came, and when I asked her why, she was like, “I didn’t like your lighting.” And then she left it here.

My husband and I have only fought about my consumption a couple of times. It’s less that I’m afraid he’ll be mad; it’s that telling him the truth would make me feel ashamed and sort of trashy. He’s a more disciplined person, and he definitely has this distaste for cheap junk. I think that’s the root of our conflict around this: It’s less about the money and more about the residual shit. He doesn’t like to confront me about it, though. He doesn’t want to police what I’m buying. But occasionally he’ll be like, “Why is this thing in the house? Don’t you have two of those?” And I’m like, “No. Yes.” And he really hates that.
“When I ask him why he buys all this stuff, he gets really defensive.” —a 34-year-old nurse in Portland

My husband is a quasi-hoarder. I think he gets it from his parents; they’re the same way. The stuff he buys is specific. It’s almost all workout gear: stuff for his bike, heart monitors, stretchy resistance bands. He buys a lot of supplements and protein stuff, too. We have two different blenders for his protein shakes. It takes up a lot of space in our kitchen, and we can’t even park our car in the garage because of his bike stuff.

I think it would bother me less if he actually used it. But he doesn’t. He bikes occasionally, but it’s more that he wants to think of himself as a biker. He’s always talking about how he wishes he had more time to bike, but it seems he’d rather sit on the couch and buy bike stuff than actually do it. It’s like he’s trying to buy an identity, which is not sexy.

We’ve gotten in some big fights about it, actually. I think a lot of what he buys comes from Instagram ads. I know he’s on Instagram all the time because he’s constantly sending me posts. He gets a lot of it on eBay, too. When I ask him why he buys all this stuff, he gets really defensive. I think it feeds some kind of insecurity about his fitness or age, maybe. I know he hides stuff from me because I find broken-down boxes in the recycling all the time.

He once told me that after he bought my engagement ring, he then bought himself a new bike — like he wanted to get a gift for himself, too. I’m not really sure what that’s about. Whenever I’ve asked him if he plans to get rid of the stuff he’s not using, he makes a point of telling me it has a lot of resale value. Which is great, but he never resells it.

The financial element does bother me. He does well financially, so maybe shopping is his stress reliever. But sometimes I just think of how much money he’s spending and how it could be put to much better use. Like, why not spend half of that money on taking an actual biking vacation somewhere?
Email your money conundrums to mytwocents@nymag.com (and read our submission terms here.)

items.title: Can Shoptimism Save Us?
items.description: Sihaam Naik, 24, sees herself in Yoshitomo Nara’s wide-eyed little girls filled with rage. “I started collecting art books about Nara’s work because I resonate with the idea of kids feeling the brunt of war and terrible decisions made by people way, way above
items.author: Emma Childs
paragraphs: Sihaam Naik, 24, sees herself in Yoshitomo Nara’s wide-eyed little girls filled with rage. “I started collecting art books about Nara’s work because I resonate with the idea of kids feeling the brunt of war and terrible decisions made by people way, way above them,” says Naik, a London-based content creator and video essayist. “It’s that thin line between the hopefulness and the hopelessness you feel as a young person, between being optimistic and realistic.” She frequents her neighborhood charity shops and indie bookstores like Climax Books, Broadway Bookshop, and the Common Press in hopes of finding rare art books, about Nara or another artist she admires, to add to her personal library. For Naik, buying books is bigger than “little-treat culture“: It’s shoptimism. “I know that in this lifetime I’m probably not going to own a house,” she says. “In the grand scheme of things, buying two books a month isn’t going to interfere with financial goals I likely won’t achieve anyway.”

In recent years, as headlines have become increasingly surreal and, at times, apocalyptic, shopping mindfully and solely for pleasure has become a sort of salvation. You’re worried about fascism, and we’re in an almost-sort-of-maybe financial crisis, but the blue wave gave you hope, so you allow yourself a trinket from the Japanese market or the fancy peppermint tea your grandma used to make you as a kid. Isn’t this just classic consumerism: acquiring material possessions to put a Band-Aid on your student-loan-size problem? Not quite. Where consumerism chases convenience and a quick hit of adrenaline, this approach requires taste and time. You can’t find it on Amazon or TikTok Shop; it’s a mood boost sourced only from small businesses and secondhand marketplaces, where the action of shopping is the point. In the face of AI doomerism, this type of hyperspecific shopping, which can’t be optimized and is driven solely by emotional investment, is a reprieve.

Mackii Shaye, 34, sources “screen-accurate graphic tees” from aughts TV shows and movies: Rory Gilmore’s “Reading Is Sexy” T-shirt from Gilmore Girls, the Swarovski-crystal-bedazzled “Bling Bling” tee Karen Smith wears in Mean Girls, and most of Marissa Cooper’s outfits from The O.C. It’s a practice built from hours of watching TV, combing through old issues of Seventeen, and digging in vintage bins. “When you’re in a thrift store and come across a tee you recognize from Lizzie McGuire or something Britney Spears wore, you’re transported back to a mall from the 2000s, and there’s nothing sparklier than that.”

Cecilia Gardner-Davila started buying vintage theme-park memorabilia on eBay with a price cap of $50 — (she has to keep an eye on the cost-of-living-crisis, after all) —when she moved to New York five years ago and was “craving the fun and magic I felt when I was a kid.” Flipping through a 40-year-old booklet from the opening of Tokyo Disneyland, she escapes the reality of her East Village apartment and PR job. A Mickey Mouse matchbook from the ’70s, back when it was legal to smoke in the Magic Kingdom, makes her nostalgic for an era she never lived. “I would have loved to smoke a cigarette while walking around Disney World,” says the 26-year-old, born and raised in Gainesville, Florida. Plus the parks today have been thoroughly digitized, swapping paper maps for iPhone apps and integrating AI into interactive entertainment. “Theme-park collectibles remind me of a time in the past that feels a lot warmer, simpler than today,” she says. “There used to be a sense of integrity built into the parks that has vanished — vanished from life in general. We’re missing a human aspect to things.”

For Isabelle, a 28-year-old corporate lawyer using a pseudonym, buying tinned fish from the Spanish market in her Brooklyn neighborhood after a day in the office is the highlight of her workweek. (She declined to share the shop’s name; “I don’t want TikTokers swarming the place and selling everything out.”) Her current favorite are $20 Cantabrian anchovies. “They’re egregiously priced but, to me, worth it,” she says. “If I have to work 50 to 70 hours a week, I’m going to buy my fish in a can and no one will say anything to me.”

Naturally, this emotion-driven approach to shopping leads to human connection, as there are few things more impressive to our fellow man than someone sure of themselves and their interests. Kristen Bateman, a 34-year-old fashion writer, has been stopped countless times by strangers who compliment the antique statement jewelry she collects from “literally everywhere: antique malls, flea markets, jewelry stores, Instagram sellers, estate sales.” In particular, Bateman’s Victim of Fashion brooches by Elzac, a vintage costume-jewelry brand founded by Ruth Handler, who later went on to create Barbie, spark lots of conversation. “Most collectors don’t wear their jewelry, but a big part of my interest comes from styling them with modern pieces and wearing them out in the world,” says Bateman.

Brick-and-mortar businesses have been buoyed by shoptimism, too. Sammy Levin, 28, designed Zaidi’s, her store in Chinatown, selling vintage tobacciana-like lighters, cases, and ashtrays, to be as playful and community-oriented as possible. Levin collects and restores vintage lighters and, in 2022, opened the store in honor of her grandfather, “a crazy old Jewish man, like Kramer from Seinfeld, and lifelong pot smoker.” “I want Zaidi’s to feel like you’re in a small Rhode Island town shop that’s been here forever,” she says. “But it’s not just about curating the space; it’s explaining to my customers the history of each lighter and that if anything ever happens to it, I’ll always fix it.” Levin has tables, chairs, and board games out front for anyone, shoppers and passersby alike, to enjoy. “I want to provide a space where you don’t have to buy anything, so people know there’s still community in Manhattan. Come, sit outside, smoke a cigarette, and play Jenga for free,” she says. “The local skater boys now hang out with the weird West Village guys in their Patagonia vests, and they never would’ve been friends before.”

Like Levin, Shaye turned her collecting pastime into a business. A “born-and-raised Valley girl who never left,” she launched a Y2K-specific vintage shop, Little Oyster Club, in 2023. But most of her as-seen-on-TV and in-the-tabloids tees are too sacred to sell and stay in her personal collection. Shaye owns the actual “Team Jolie” and “Team Aniston” raglan tees Paris and Nicky Hilton wore in the peak of the Angelina Jolie, Brad Pitt, Jennifer Aniston love-triangle drama in ’05. “Coming across those shirts — one on Mercari, the other on Depop — were some of the most exciting moments of my life,” she says. “They’re a piece of pop-culture history, of herstory. A lot of people say they should be in a museum, and I agree — but I can’t give them away.” They’re too special, too sentimental, to part with. “I don’t know what I’m going to do with all this stuff when I pass away,” Shaye admits. “But I know I’m going to make someone very happy with an awesome estate sale one day.”

items.title: ‘My Career in Fashion Hid My Compulsive Shopping Disorder’
items.description: For more than 20 years, author Dara Fleischer’s life looked incredible. She had a thriving career in fashion (first in magazines, and later at retailers such as the RealReal), an incredible wardrobe, a devoted husband, and eventually young twins. But she had a
items.author: Charlotte Cowles
paragraphs: For more than 20 years, author Dara Fleischer’s life looked incredible. She had a thriving career in fashion (first in magazines, and later at retailers such as the RealReal), an incredible wardrobe, a devoted husband, and eventually young twins. But she had a secret: Her life was buckling under the weight of a runaway shopping addiction. She hid her debt, stashed designer clothes in garbage bags at the back of her closet, and told herself she’d rein in her habits — but then more packages would arrive, and the spiral continued.

Compulsive shopping or spending disorder, also known as oniomania (from the ancient Greek word meaning “to buy”), is defined as “an overpowering, uncontrollable, chronic, and repetitive urge to shop and spend.” Despite frequent appearances in pop culture, real-life shopaholics are not well understood by the mental-health community, and many of them struggle to stick with treatment programs (which usually include therapy, group support, and medication). “There’s so much shame, guilt, anxiety, and constant fear about paying bills,” Fleischer says. “I’m sure people will read this and think, Well, how stupid are you? Why couldn’t you just stop buying things? But that’s part of the disease and the compulsion.”

Two years ago, Fleischer came clean to her family, started therapy, liquidated her retirement savings to pay off her debt, and committed herself to recovery. She has since written a memoir about her experience, At My Limit, and started a podcast where she interviews other recovering compulsive shoppers. Below, she shares the moment she knew she had to stop, her advice to fellow problem shoppers, and why she’s still tempted by the retail marketing traps she helped build.
How did your shopping habits begin?

I hate saying that fashion is in my DNA, because my mother is also a shopaholic and I love her dearly, but it’s true. My parents worked hard, and they instilled good values, but my mom always spent too much, and I learned from her. I worked hard for my money, and I spent it all on clothes. Growing up, shopping was really our love language. I was a latchkey kid, so I was given things — it was my parents’ way of showing their love because they weren’t around. Later on, I worked in fashion, so it was normalized to shop all the time. When I hit rock bottom, I had $124 in my bank account and owed more than $50,000 on my credit cards and “buy now, pay later” platforms.
How did you get into the fashion industry?

I’m from Montreal, and I always knew that I wanted to live in New York. I moved there in 1994, as soon as I graduated from college in Toronto. I remember going to Bleecker Street and buying Converse high-tops, one pink, one purple. Fashion put me in a kind of trance.

I worked for a bunch of websites and publications. I also started my own blog, Fashion Junkie. I would go to Barneys, Bergdorf, Bloomingdale’s, and other stores and take pictures of myself in different outfits and then ask people what I should buy. Looking back, it was kind of a cry for help. But at the time, I didn’t realize I was a compulsive shopper. I just thought it was fun. Then, when I was about 33, I moved back to Toronto to help launch a shopping magazine called Lou Lou. I became the shopping editor, and it was my dream job. I literally traveled the world to write shopping guides and interview designers and store owners. I was exposed to so much fashion and I got industry discounts, which, of course, I graciously accepted. I had events to go to and meetings and whatnot — I used any excuse to buy new things.
When did you start to overspend and get into debt?

I was always overspending, but it didn’t get really out of control until I got my first credit card in my early 30s, in the early 2000s. Before I knew it, I owed $30,000 in credit card debt. Then I got engaged to my now-husband, who lived back in New York. He didn’t know I had the debt. So before I got married in 2005, I told myself that I would pay it all off. I took out a low-interest loan from a bank, and I paid it down before our wedding.
How did you hide your shopping from your husband?

The irony is that we are complete opposites when it comes to money. He was an investment banker. He’s frugal, he saves, he’s always dealing with money and spreadsheets. And I’m the irresponsible, selfish asshole gallivanting around the city, living paycheck to paycheck. When we got married, I moved back to New York from Toronto, and in 2009 we had twins. For the next ten years, I worked and consulted for a number of different fashion and beauty brands, like the RealReal and Sephora. I also worked at Ventes Privées, a flash-sale website. My job was business development, so I was constantly pitching luxury brands and retailers to get them to sell their excess clothing and accessories on our site.

At one point, the company hired a consultant and she told everyone, “You have to dress the part.” Of course, we weren’t given a clothing allowance. It was just good vibes and my own credit card. And I didn’t bat an eye. I would spend $1,300 at Bergdorf on leather pants and whatever leather jacket I saw. It felt normal. I was surrounded by people who had impeccable taste and a lot more money than me. And I always felt like I needed to keep up with the Joneses, to my detriment. I was making decent money, so I’d be able to pay down my debt for a while, and then it would creep up again. Pretty soon, it was another $40,000 on my credit card. And that’s when buy now, pay later came into the mix. So I owed tons of money on Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm … all of them.
When things got really bad, what did that look like?

Right before COVID, I was laid off from my job. Then the pandemic hit, and things just spiraled. I was so depressed and stressed that I kept buying more clothing. Every day, I’d have packages coming from Intermix or Neiman Marcus or Shopbop. I was hiding things from my husband. I would tell my doorman to turn off notifications for any incoming packages. I had so much shit everywhere. I had piles of clothing in garbage bags. I would stash things in filing cabinets and the laundry bin and my kids’ closets. We had to get extra closet units from Ikea. In a New York apartment, there’s only so much you can hide. It was so embarrassing. My husband did not like it. He’d be like, “We have to clean this up. We can’t live like this anymore.” He knew I had a shopping problem, but he didn’t quite understand how bad it was or how to help me. So he avoided it, just like I did.

Then, unfortunately, my husband lost his job too. At one point, we were both unemployed, and I still had packages coming. I was consigning stuff to the RealReal, but there was no way I could make enough to pay off my debt, especially since I was still shopping. Fortunately, my husband wasn’t unemployed for long. That’s when we decided to relocate to Austin, Texas. I was able to get a new job, too, but I was working remotely and just shopping all day online. Struggling with shopping addiction in the digital age, especially with frictionless payment — it just ruined me. I was stacking eight or ten payment plans at once. It was horrible.
When did you realize you had a problem and needed to stop?

Leaving New York was a really hard adjustment. I was lonely and anxious and sort of in shock. Now I know it was a really important part of my recovery, but at the time, my shopping got even more out of control. Finally, I just couldn’t do it anymore. I got laid off again, and there I was, $50,000 in debt with no job. I was totally fucked. And I was tired of the lies. It was affecting my relationship with my husband and kids. How could I be a role model for my teenage twins? My son would walk into my closet and say, “You have a college fund’s worth of Golden Goose shoes in here.” And I hadn’t realized he’d noticed. It really bothered him. It still does.

The only way I could stop the bleeding was to wipe out my retirement fund, my 401(k). Fortunately, it had about $54,000 in it because my husband helped me set it up and contribute to it. So I liquidated most of it and paid off my debt. After that, I told him the truth — the full extent of my addiction — because I was so sick of dealing with the shame, the anxiety, and guilt.

He was obviously very upset with me. But I told him that I wanted to get better, not just for myself, but for our family. I feel very lucky, but I also feel like such an asshole because my husband is such a hard worker. He didn’t divorce me, and I’m still amazed that he didn’t, because if I were in his shoes, I would’ve been kicked to the curb many moons ago. He’s a wonderful person. He obviously loves me a lot. He really wanted to help me, and he told me that I needed to go into therapy. In order to save the marriage, I had to stop shopping and get help. So I did.

I found a good therapist, and that really saved me. He pushed me to try Debtors Anonymous and put me on OCD medication. I don’t know if there’s one singular thing that really worked. I wish there were a magic pill that could get rid of addiction and overspending, but there isn’t. At the end of the day, you have to want to change. For me, it was being in so much debt, on the brink of divorce, and really upsetting my kids. Anytime I had a package at the door, my son didn’t want to talk to me. I wanted to stop.
What did recovery look like for you?

I had to take accountability. It’s the reason that I wrote this book. If I can help just one other person who’s struggling with this, then it will have been worth it. I had to cut up all but one of my credit cards. I had a Saks card, a Neiman Marcus card, a Bloomingdale’s card, a Bergdorf card. I used Venmo, PayPal, and then of course all the buy now, pay laters.

I’ve since stayed out of debt. I haven’t used buy now, pay later in two years, and I never will again. I closed every single account. It’s devastating to look back in my history and see what I spent. I still have urges. There are triggers, like Black Friday and hearing about a limited-edition drop of something I love. I’m working on that. I recently bought a pair of limited-edition cowboy boots and then was like, “What am I doing?” I returned them. It took me a while to stop chasing the dopamine hit, the high of the buy, but I’m not perfect. I still make mistakes. I’ll still shop, but it’s rare. Before, I was buying my fantasy self. I didn’t need anything. I had to ask myself, “Why do I continue to buy these things, many of which I’ve never worn? They’re sitting in my closet with tags attached.” And part of the problem with being so deep in a compulsive shopping addiction is you’re in the fog of vagueness. You don’t really realize what you’re doing. Your moral compass just flies out the window.
How did your parents react when you told them?

I think my parents always knew that I had a shopping problem, but not how out of control it was. Even my mother was pretty horrified. I mean, she’s a shopaholic herself, but not to the same degree as me. When my mother found out that I have 40 pairs of designer cowboy boots from the same brand, she was just mortified. That’s just horrible, selfish. My father sadly suffers from dementia, and that’s another reason why I had to change. What if, God forbid, I’m in the same situation as my mother one day, and I have to handle all our family’s bills and my shopping is still out of hand?
When you told your husband, were their ramifications in terms of your shared finances? How have you structured your accounts since you told him the truth?

He had to set up guardrails. He pays all the bills. We do share a joint Amex, and I only use it on essentials like groceries. He takes care of the savings accounts too, fortunately. I don’t have access to our kids’ college funds, which I understand. It’s going to take a while for him to trust me. Being honest has definitely improved our relationship, but it’s tough.

It’s still a daily struggle. It’s really hard and it does damage relationships. Thankfully, my recovery definitely healed my relationship with my husband. Things got much better. But it’s something that I work on every single day.

A big part of recovery was unsubscribing from every single email. You have to unsubscribe from texts and ask any sales associate that reaches out to take you off their list. I also use a Brick, to block apps and retailer sites and social media. Social media is kryptonite. I can’t spend any time on it. But if you don’t know something’s there, you’re not going to crave it.

Everyone laughs at shopping addictions. They shrug it off because they think it’s not harmful, like a substance addiction — “Oh, at least you’re not addicted to fentanyl.” But it does affect you physically and emotionally. It’s caused me a great deal of pain, because I did it to myself. I worked for the retail industry. I know all the tricks. We all know it’s bullshit. And yet I still felt prey to all the retail marketing traps.
Were there any specific parts of treatment that helped the most?

Two years ago, I joined a program called the Shopping Shift, founded by Hannah Blass in Vancouver. She was a former shopaholic herself, and she started this virtual private community to help other shoppers like me. What I like about it is that she incorporates your personal style into the program. You audit your closet, do no-buys, and try to retrain your brain. Fashion is still a big part of my identity, so that’s been good for me to incorporate it into my recovery. Through that program, I am now the no-buy lead, so I get to help other people, and that’s really therapeutic.

Debtors Anonymous wasn’t quite right for me, but I’m glad I tried it. It’s very spiritual, and I’m not a religious person. But I didn’t want to give up on it, so I attended Zooms and met lovely people I could relate to. It feels good to share with people who understand what you’re going through. And it doesn’t matter if they’re not in debt over luxury cowboy boots — some people focus on electronics or they shop too much on Amazon. It was helpful to hear other people’s stories in a nonjudgmental space.
Any other advice for someone who’s struggling with this?

You have to take it day by day. It’s corny, but it’s true. If you just say to yourself, “I’m not going to shop for 24 hours and I’ll be okay,” you can do it. I also think about how I want to be remembered. Do I want to be remembered for being in debt, for having a hundred pairs of Golden Goose shoes? Do I want my children to be stuck with this mess when I die? No.
Email your money conundrums to mytwocents@nymag.com (and read our submission terms here.)

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Hopes You Won’t Hate Her New Project
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Angelina Chapin
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Jennifer Lawrence has been here before. At this exact same sort of restaurant, the kind where celebrities discreetly mingle (this time, Gemma, the Italian trattoria attached to the Bowery Hotel), in a booth that gives her some privacy but not so much that her publicist and assistant can’t keep a watchful eye and ear from a table nearby. There’s always a stranger sitting across from her scribbling down notes on what she orders (a cappuccino and avocado toast with a soft-boiled egg) and what she’s wearing (an oversize bright-red sweater and a small beaded turquoise necklace). This is her cue to rehash talking points about her chemistry with a co-star or reverence for a director.

But when we meet for breakfast in early October, something about the familiar scene is different; she’s slightly outside her comfort zone. “I’m in this interesting transition,” she says. “For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can’t let doubt in. Now I’m experiencing doubt.” Lawrence, whose blonde hair is wavy from sleeping in loose braids last night, says any movie release comes with nerves, which she can normally soothe by bingeing the latest season of Real Housewives. This morning, though, she’s not here to talk about developing a Miss Piggy feature, working on a rom-com, or shooting a sci-fi thriller next spring. Instead, for the first time in her 20-year career, the 36-year-old is debuting a project you won’t find in theaters or on Netflix. And she’s still figuring out how to talk about it. “I have to pretend I’ve made the greatest thing on earth,” she says, her hands fiddling with the salt and pepper shakers. “Otherwise it gets too scary. It’s a form of forced manifestation.”

That thing arrives on October 27, when Lawrence will officially join the oversaturated world of celebrity brands by launching Mes, a “biodesigned haircare” company that is selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. She’s partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can. That sounds great and all, but “what if nobody gets it?” she asks. “What if everybody hates it?”

Lawrence might seem like the type of actor who would roll her eyes at the celebrity–to–beauty brand pipeline. She has an Oscar and a production company and just shot a Martin Scorsese movie alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Why spend time shilling a volume mist? Her answer doesn’t involve cracking jokes about girlbosses making #OOTD videos, the brand of self-deprecating humor she used as armor earlier in her career. Instead, she’s taking it very seriously, speaking about Mes as a natural extension of her art. “There is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product,” she says, twisting up her hair into a bun. “I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.” Lawrence has made peace with the humiliation inherent in being a creative person forced to talk about their work and doesn’t need to turn herself into the punch line. The baby-faced 22-year-old who laughed off tripping on the stairs at the Academy Awards is now more than a decade older and a mother of two. I watch her arrange her delicate features into a thoughtful expression while telling me how creatively satisfying it felt to develop a brand. I know she’s a good actor, one of the best, but I believed her.

Lawrence has always been a “hair girl.” “I feel like if my hair looks okay, then nobody’s gonna notice anything else about my face, clothes, or body,” she says. “I also can find myself using it to hide.” As a child, her thick curls would puff up in the Kentucky humidity, and she slept in braids to control the “floof.” In her teenage years, she ceded control to stylists, who did whatever they needed to get her camera-ready. “When you are a new and upcoming actress, you can’t be like, ‘Don’t put that on my hair,’’’ she says. “You sit in the chair and you say ‘Thank you’ and you shut your mouth.” Her strands would smoke and sizzle when the hair spray hit the straightening iron; her hair was dyed four different colors in one day for an X-Men screen test. After shooting the second Hunger Games film in 2013, her hair was so fried that she chopped it off into a pixie cut, a style she thought at the time “looked dope.”

Soon, Lawrence had bought every new product on the market in a desperate search for anything that would style her hair without hot tools. She even met with scientists about developing new products, but she struggled to find a like-minded collaborator. That is until 2023, when she watched a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a chemical biological engineer with a shiny brown bob and a beauty company who spoke about creating products that would fundamentally change the makeup of hair rather than just coating it in products — the industry’s current approach. Lawrence got goosebumps and emailed Aganovic to set up a meeting in the fall, just as the actors’ strike was ending. “It just seemed like a new way of going about things,” she said. “This is what I’ve been waiting for.”

Aganovic was initially less enthusiastic about the partnership. She had already founded a company, Arcaea, that uses DNA sequencing and skin microbiology to make, among other things, perfumes that reimagine extinct flowers or the smell of clouds. And while she wasn’t blind to the attention Lawrence could shine on her life’s work, she worried it could also be a distraction. “One of my biggest fears is having my work be misinterpreted,” she says. “Jen came across as credible and curious, but you never know how much she had actually looked into the company.” After a Zoom call, Lawrence set out to prove she wouldn’t be the kind of business partner with “25 assistants rescheduling something.” Within a few weeks, she flew to Aganovic’s Boston lab, showed up without an entourage, and smelled the smelliest bacteria in the fridge. Aganovic was impressed. “Jen literally said, ‘If you want to do this in five years, I’ll still be here,’” Aganovic remembers. “And I think that took the pressure off. I was like, Oh wow, she’s really serious.”

By fall 2024, Aganovic’s team of scientists was working on formulas that would make hair healthier while cutting down on styling time, damage, and shampooing. Lawrence had very specific ideas for the products, like a hair mask that would go on dry hair (and that could double as a “wet look”), a serum that got rid of her “floofs” without leaving residue, and a volumizing spray that wasn’t crunchy and improved her scalp. To execute her vision, Aganovic’s scientists had to become experts in lipids, proteins, and the scalp’s microbiome and experiment with different techniques, including developing a proprietary ingredient to promote a balanced, less oily scalp. “Hair masks are not usually applied to dry hair,” says Aganovic, “which is why it’s very expensive to produce them this way, without water.” (A 150-milliliter bottle costs $52.) Lawrence’s head became the guinea pig. She tried the products on her naturally curly hair, which she says makes her look like Isaac Newton. She tested the serum while doing promo for Die My Love and used the volumizing mist on the set of What Happens at Night, the Scorsese film she shot earlier this year. Her dedication was total, and she sent the serum back to the lab almost 150 times. At one point, she started to smell like fish after leaving on an unscented version of the mask for four days. “My husband was like, ‘If you don’t wash your hair, you have to get a hotel room,’” she said. Lawrence held firm.

When she wasn’t filming, she spent hours on weekly calls about the business and focused on developing the look of Mes’ logo and bottles. “I knew I couldn’t miss a Zoom and that I’d need to look over every single letter on the website,” she says. Sometimes it was hard to juggle everything. During one call, Lawrence tells me she was bouncing on a yoga ball at nine months pregnant when it occurred to her she was only in a bra. “I just turned my camera off and said, ‘I’m so sorry. I realized that I’m not wearing a shirt,’” she says, “And then everybody pretended like they hadn’t noticed.” But she wanted to stay in the weeds of the business. Lawrence took nose-training classes to help develop Mes’ scent; she sent product samples to everyone in her group chat and asked them for their feedback on fonts. She got so involved in the design that she had a colleague fly out to the New England beach town where she was vacationing so she could hold the 3-D-printed models in her hands. “I wanted them to be pretty,” she says of the bottles, which look like modernist mini-vases. “Bathroom products are always out, and it’s like, Why is this ugly?”

Lawrence trusts her eye, she assures me during our post-breakfast tour of the artist Robert Rauschenberg’s former Noho studio, a place she wanted to visit because it’s up for sale and could soon be turned into luxury condos. “I am good at telling when something’s going to be hot,” she says, now wearing a black baseball cap from her husband’s art business, American Pictures. After looking at a small exhibition of work by the mid-20th-century multimedia icon — “he’s kind of hot,” she says under her breath as she stands in front of a photo of Rauschenberg smoking — we sit in a room with sun pouring in through arched windows while Lawrence tells me about the vibe she’s trying to create. Mes, which is pronounced Mess (the latter was already trademarked), is meant to capture the kind of girl (gender neutral) who leaves the house with dewy skin and a rumpled-in-a-chic-way button-down shirt. “The moment something was fussy, it was like ‘no,’” she says. “Avoiding pretentious words and pretentious font is big. Our girl is not that. But she appreciates beauty.” Lawrence’s personal ethos is also looking good with minimal effort, despite the fact that she’s had a boob job and one day plans to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she says. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.”

But don’t expect to see GRWM videos in her bathroom before taking her toddler to school. She had resisted creating an Instagram account for her entire career — she did, however, make a Finsta to share memes with her friends — in hopes of keeping a few shreds of life private. But Lawrence knew Instagram was a necessity for any founder in 2026 and a few months ago met with a social-media expert, who explained that Lawrence’s strategy didn’t need to involve constantly pumping out content or filming her home life. Instead, since officially joining the platform in September, she’s only posted to the grid three times — “If anyone says anything negative, I will quit,” she deadpanned in her first video — and already has more than 8 million followers. She plans to do minimal promo for Mes, including product tutorials she might film in a “public or hotel bathroom” to keep her own sink offline.

It’s a tough time to jump on the celebrity-beauty-brand bandwagon. Fans tend to view these companies cynically, as cringe cash grabs rather than genuine passion projects. And the bar for success is high: The products have to be good on their own merits, and the celebrity selling them has to make sense. People want Kylie Jenner’s lips and Hailey Bieber’s skin, but on Reddit threads speculating about Mes, commenters are already questioning whether Lawrence’s hair is a standout feature. When I ask Lawrence if she feels pressure to have aspirational hair, she says, “That didn’t even occur to me,” with a look of panic. “Is that something people think about?” In her fortress of positivity, she hasn’t dwelled on the criticisms that could be coming her way and seems genuinely caught off guard when I bring them up. Is she concerned a highbrow beauty product is at odds with the every-woman persona fans love? “I think about how excited people will be to have something so sculptural and beautiful!” she says. “My little bubble is about to be popped.”

While beauty brands have turned rich celebrities like Rihanna and Selena Gomez into filthy rich business moguls, Lawrence scoffs at the idea that Mes was conceived as a source of financial stability amid Hollywood’s decline. “A smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise,” she says. “Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door.” And anyway, worrying about the bottom line is not her strong suit. When talking about the look and feel of Mes, she adopts the self-seriousness of any artist talking about their craft. But when it comes to the more technical sides of the business, Lawrence falls back on her familiar brand of self-mockery. “If you put a gun to my head and were like, ‘What are the numbers we would need to reach in order for Mes to be a success?’ I would have no clue,” she says. “Numbers don’t stick in here. I’m dumb but cute!” When I ask if the company has investors, she whispers “I don’t know” and redirects me to her co-founder. (Aganovic says her original company, Arcaea, which has raised $78 million, is funding Mes.)

But the shtick isn’t working so well this time — which is a good thing. It felt charmingly authentic when, in 2012, the Kentucky-born ingénue told David Letterman, “I hate myself. Don’t go see the movie. I’m a troll.” But Lawrence is in a much different phase of life. She’s a mother married to a prominent art dealer and serves as the face of Dior. In Hollywood, she calls the shots, green-lighting movies with her own production company and fielding requests from the most in-demand directors while slamming the industry’s pay gap. Even if she can’t balance a spreadsheet, it’s hard to believe she’s a buffoon in the boardroom. “It’s funny that she describes herself as the creative needing the business counterpart,” says Justine Ciarrocchi, who runs a production company with Lawrence and is her friend of almost 20 years. “I think she has an incredible business intuition, and she’s fearless when she is sure of something.” Molly Howard, the CEO of La Ligne — a brand whose coveted wide-legged pants are a staple of Lawrence’s “momboy” aesthetic — says her friend already has the most important quality in a successful founder: the willingness to pore over the most boring details of the business, from learning about EBITA to testing a bottle’s seal. “The ambition is that this becomes a Fenty Beauty of hair care,” Howard says. “I really think this could be a Rhode.” Lawrence actually has an even more audacious North Star in mind, one she’s too embarrassed to name. “If I told you, you would be like ‘Hahaha,’” she says. “It is so big and so huge that I’m aware Mes will never get there.” I beg her a few more times, but all she’ll say is that the aspirational brand is not beauty-related. “If I was Taylor Swift, the people on Twitter would figure it out.”

Towards the end of October, I visit Lawrence at her office in Tribeca, a Federal-style townhouse with exposed brick and barnwood panels. There’s incense burning on the long wooden coffee table, and as she curls up on a rust-colored couch, asking me at one point if I’m bothered by her bare feet, Lawrence claims to be feeling more calm than when we first met. “I’m back to being utterly and completely positive,” she says, wearing a sequined brown wool cardigan and a long black skirt. “I can always fall back on the product. It’s just kind of like, Well, these are obviously really good.” If she’s stressed about anything today, it’s a recent haircut that left her with uneven bangs, which she’s repeatedly tried to fix. “No matter what I do, it flicks out,” she says, pointing to a strand on the left side of her head. “And I went into a meeting today as a hair authority.” Come to think of it, maybe she is a little nervous, mostly about the idea that people won’t have enough patience to stick with the products. “If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” she says. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.” She’s already dealt with a few emergencies, like the mask leaking during the ship test or the cap on the restyling serum squeaking. (“This isn’t luxury,” she remembers saying. “It sounds like I’m stepping on mice.”)

Earlier that day, the Mes landing page went live, featuring a video of Lawrence’s blonde waves bouncing as she dances in a red cardigan. She immediately texted her group chat asking for compliments, which includes Howard of La Ligne, Tracy Dubb of Isla Beauty, and two women she won’t name because they are “very private.” On October 27, the full website will roll out, and if all goes well, Mes bottles will start filling people’s bathroom cabinets.

In a material sense, whether Mes is a hit or not won’t have a big effect on Lawrence’s life. She’s already rich, and Paul Thomas Anderson probably wouldn’t blacklist an actor whose hair mask doesn’t sell. For Lawrence, the stakes are more personal. She has the antsy intensity of someone who’s desperate for people to join in their obsession rather than mock it, like a friend who’s become a javaphile and wants you to adopt a new coffee-brewing technique. “Tell me about your experience because the products take time,” she says, fixing me with an intense stare. “I can answer questions.” She’s itching to nerd out about the eccentricities of her creations, excited for people to log on to the website and see the microscopic images of how these products affect the scalp. As she’d told me during breakfast, “I’m nervous about someone putting on the restyling serum and being like, Oh my God, this went on really oily, without knowing that in 15 minutes, it’ll all dry.”

Toward the end of our talk, she catches her foot bouncing and says, “I think the nerves are in my body. I work really hard to keep my brain disciplined.” At some point, Lawrence knows someone from the Mes team will call and let her know if the sales numbers are good or bad. But the real risk is a bruised ego, the idea that people won’t like — or simply don’t care — about a product she’s devoted years of her life to perfecting. “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension,” she says. “I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Is Very Proud of Her ‘New’ Boobs
items.description: Jennifer Lawrence has no qualms about sharing the details of her boob job. During an appearance on Watch What Happens Live on Thursday night, the actress highlighted her “new” implants to Andy Cohen. During the episode, Lawrence played a round of “Mystery or N
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Jennifer Lawrence has no qualms about sharing the details of her boob job. During an appearance on Watch What Happens Live on Thursday night, the actress highlighted her “new” implants to Andy Cohen. During the episode, Lawrence played a round of “Mystery or Not to Me,” which involved Cohen asking if it was a mystery to her “how a boob could break Hailey Glassman’s nose.” (The Real Housewives of New York star claims to have broken her nose while having sex with a woman with “big double-D tits.”)

“Yes, and I have implants,” Lawrence answered. When Cohen expressed his shock at Lawrence’s plastic surgery, she told him that they’re “new” and pushed her chest forward to show them off. Cohen told Lawrence that her new boobs are “beautiful,” and she gave credit to “Dr. Teitelbaum in Santa Monica.” I assume she means Dr. Steven Teitelbaum, who has a private practice in Santa Monica. His website boasts that he is “internationally recognized” for his breast surgery and that he delivers “beautifully natural results that honor each patient’s unique goals, anatomy, and lifestyle.”

Cohen, never one to shy away from a tacky question, asked Lawrence if her new breasts were B-cups. “No, it’s a full C, I think. It’s the same size that they were,” she said, referring to her body before having children. Cohen said he appreciated Lawrence’s “restraint.”

This is hardly the first time Lawrence has spoken about going under the knife. In an October 2025 New Yorker profile, she said that she was getting her boobs done that November, inspired by the changes in her body after having her two children. “Everything bounced back, pretty much, after the first one,” she said. “Second one, nothing bounced back.” She added that if she weren’t a famous actress, she would probably still be getting the surgery, but probably wouldn’t be “hustling to the appointment in the same way.”

In her Cut cover story last month, Lawrence confirmed that she had gotten a boob job and that one day she wants to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she said. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.” Shout-out to Teitelbaum for helping Lawrence achieve her goals.

items.title: Christopher Briney Is Happy To Be Here
items.description: Christopher Briney Is Happy To Be Here
items.author: Iva Dixit
paragraphs: Christopher Briney Is Happy To Be Here
The Summer I Turned Pretty star — who’s about to light up the holiday season with Clashing Through the Snow — copes with fame by remembering acting is just a job. He still can’t believe it’s his.

“Oh! Somebody watched this?” Years after it happened, Christopher Briney can still summon his incredulity from the first time a stranger asked to take a photo with him, his face screwed up in bewilderment as he starts telling me the story. It was June 2022, a time period that now feels near-Paleolithic, and that little show called The Summer I Turned Pretty had only been live for a day or two, tops. He and his girlfriend were on vacation in Boston, taking a walk through the city, when Briney had the oddest sensation that people were following him. He tried to shake himself loose of that feeling: “Why would they be?” Apart from his new project, he’d only been in one indie movie since graduating from his acting program. “What was extra weird about that for me was: I don’t live here. Like, I’m in Boston?”

But his hunch was, of course, correct. The next thing he knew, some friendly fans of the show had approached him for a picture (he obliged), which proved to be only the tip of the selfie-request iceberg about to come his way.

The Summer I Turned Pretty, the Amazon Prime Video adaptation of Jenny Han’s trilogy of YA novels, was a supernova that only got bigger and brighter over time, and as Conrad Fisher — the primary love interest of Lola Tung’s Isabel “Belly” Conklin, competing for her affections alongside his brother, Jeremiah (Gavin Casalegno) — Briney was at its white-hot center. Last year’s third and final season was the streamer’s most-watched season of television ever for women 18 to 34. The show dominated the cultural conversation to the point that even people who’ve never seen an episode probably have a credible opinion on “Team Conrad versus Team Jeremiah,” and it inspired an online fandom so passionate that the official Summer social media account issued a PSA reminding viewers that this is just a TV program and to please not bully and harass the cast and crew over it.

Briney imbued the elder Fisher brother with a kind of dignified suffering: the golden child of the family bucking under his burdens, including the devastating secret of his mother’s cancer diagnosis. Briney, with those searching blue-green eyes, could translate the storm brewing in Conrad’s head without uttering a single word. There are entire Reddit threads dedicated to screenshots of Briney staring off sullenly, which seem to crystalize something about Gen Z’s taste in heartthrobs. The way to this generation’s heart is through yearning. They want to watch their leading men suffer in thwarted longing. And nobody is yearning onscreen better than Briney.

Briney, 28, wears the mantle with good humor — the only approach when you’re subjected to breathless Leo comparisons — but not without a raised eyebrow at the ridiculousness of it all. His reaction to the idea of having fans hasn’t changed. “I never really expect anyone to like or watch or enjoy anything that I am in or do. I just don’t have that sort of expectation. Not even in, like, a self-deprecating way,” he tells me. But normie civilian activities are harder to pull off than they used to be. “There are definitely times when I’m like, ‘Ah, I wish I didn’t have to walk outside and worry about my privacy today.’” The only reason we’re even able to have our conversation in full public view uninterrupted is because we’re meeting after a photoshoot at 4 p.m. on a Thursday, and the Lower East Side restaurant where we’re talking is completely empty. Remembering that first fan encounter, “I look back and think: He had no idea what was coming.”

Because Briney does world-weary so well, you almost forget he can be a total goofball. Next week, Briney will star in Clashing Through the Snow, a Prime Video holiday rom-com in which he and Landman’s Michelle Randolph play rival employees at a downsizing publishing company who must race to secure the handwritten manuscript of a memoir from a pop star (Julia Fox) to avoid getting laid off. Full of the genre tropes that are somehow only more delightful the farther away you spot them coming — gasp! Enemies-to-lovers in forced proximity! — it arrives for the express purpose of being watched on a 56-inch television by families that are too full and overstimulated to talk to each other but nonetheless want more tryptophan-lulled togetherness. And for Briney, playing a jerky-eating, protein-obsessed wellness bro named Ryan was too much fun to pass up.

“When I met with the director and talked to some producers, they were ready to emphasize, and at least work to find, the comedy of it,” he says. “I don’t know if I would have done it if it were the other way around, where they were like, ‘Yeah, it’s kind of funny at times, but that’s not about you — your story is the romance.’” He recalls filming a scene with NBA stars Karl-Anthony Towns and OG Anunoby (cameoing as themselves), in which the athletes bluntly riffed about how annoying Briney’s character is, and how it sent him to actor-nerd heaven. “It made me really happy because I was like, ‘Yesss, you’re down to play!’” he says. “It’s all about making a fool of yourself.”
“I don’t really want someone to send me a tweet about me — unless it’s funny.”

For some actors in Briney’s cohort, you get the sense that they’d scrub the lighter fare of their early career off their IMDb in an instant if they could. That’s not the case with Briney. Those streaming projects fill the void of the midbudget romantic comedies that Hollywood studios used to make, which were essential training grounds in the leading-man ecosystem. You don’t get Matthew McConaughey in Dallas Buyers Club without Matthew McConaughey in How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days.

Briney’s only real concern coming out of a show like The Summer I Turned Pretty was being pigeonholed. And he indeed gets plenty of offers to play more overburdened young men transformed by love. “If you do something that does well, everybody wants you to do that again, and you get a lot of offers to do that again somewhere else,” he says. Clashing Through the Snow and its stupid-fun physical comedy is a way around typecasting. But he also seems to be having a wink at his floppy-haired sensitive-boy status, playing Aaron “your hair looks sexy pushed back” Samuels in the 2024 musical Mean Girls movie or a Harry Stylesian rock star on the final season of Hacks. With a French goatee and see-through shirt buttons undone to expose the bad chest tattoo covering one nipple, his character tried to woo Jean Smart’s Deborah Vance — only to have his heart bruised when she calls the paparazzi on their date for publicity, unable to look past his teen-idol star wattage to notice, you know, his actual feelings.

Not that he would put that fine a point on it. “I was like, ‘I’d do anything for Hacks.’ I mean, are you kidding me? Like, this show?” he says. Who wouldn’t want to soak up the brilliance of Jean Smart? “She was wonderful. We got to spend some time between scenes, just chatting — truly a lovely human. I’m grateful that she was willing to spend the time. She didn’t have to, you know? I mean, she owed me nothing.”
“There are definitely times when I’m like, ‘Ah, I wish I didn’t have to walk outside and worry about my privacy today.’”

If anything, Briney wonders sometimes if the success of The Summer I Turned Pretty lifted him to these kinds of opportunities a little too quickly. “I think it’s something that frustrates me with the industry as a whole, but it also benefits me greatly: If people see you in something that does well, they look at you longer, and they’re more willing to hear you out,” he says. “It’s a really rough industry, and the truth is, people making these decisions put so much merit in marketability, if you will. I would argue that the emphasis should be talent, but that’s not really how the world works, unfortunately.”

In September, Briney went to the Toronto International Film Festival to premiere The Julia Set, a coming-of-age drama about a promising mathlete starring Chase Infiniti and Briney as her tutor. “That’s one of the ones where I’m like, ‘I don’t know if I ever could have been in that if it weren’t for the things that came before,’” he says. (Sony Pictures Classics acquired the film, with a U.S. release reportedly planned for 2027.) “I think I could have delivered a performance in it, as any actor with an ego would say to you. But even for a movie that is closer to indie than it is anything else, it’s just hard to get in any room. I’d like to think in some other universe that could have been the first thing I ever did, but I just don’t know if that’s true.” He pauses to think some more. “I don’t know.”

You start to understand Briney’s bafflement at this level of notoriety when you hear him recount the time the universe seemed to slam the door in his face. Briney grew up in Danbury, Connecticut, where his former-actor parents had decamped after giving up the vocation to raise their two children. They were supportive of any and all of his interests: For a brief moment in his teens, Briney was basically living out the plot of High School Musical, as the junior varsity baseball player who was also auditioning for the school play. But after a summer theater intensive at Wesleyan University, he knew in his bones he was going to do this professionally. “I started applying to only the best theater programs in the country,” he recalls, “which was a stupid idea.”

Why? “Because I didn’t get in anywhere,” he grins. Twelve out of the 13 schools he’d applied to rejected him, including New York University, which he thought was a slam dunk because of the sheer number of acting programs it offered. “I was like, ‘Oh, I’m definitely going to be in one of them,’” he says. “Then I got rejected from NYU, and I remember crying in my car after school.”

He supposes now it was useful practice. “It was maybe a good thing because there’s a lot of rejection in this career, and a lot of people a lot better than me are dealing with more rejection than I have, but still, at any stage, it was a lot of nos,” Briney says. He ended up getting off the waitlist at Pace University, which he calls “one of the best things that’s ever happened for many, many reasons.” It’s where he met his girlfriend, actor Isabel Machado, and some of his closest friends and also got really into the work of director Paul Schrader. (At no point in our conversation is he more animated than discussing Schrader’s classic tome, Transcendental Style in Film: “I could talk about that for a while!”) The school’s emphasis on making a living in a fickle business also resonated with Briney.
“They waited for my heart rate to drop, because they were afraid I got COVID. I was like, ‘No, guys, I just got good news!’”

“The way they always pitched it to us was like, ‘We have nothing but respect for theater programs. We have nothing but respect for the ‘best’ schools’ — you know, like Juilliard and Carnegie and all these things. Like, they’re great programs. But ‘this is acting for acting that pays’ was sort of what our teacher said,” Briney recalls. Film and TV and theater, yes, but also voiceover work and commercials. “They were like, ‘This is what we found, and what we think will help you book jobs in the field.’ And it was never ignorant to training. It was never ignorant to the work that is needed as an actor, but it was practical in a way — as practical as pursuing an art can be.”

Briney graduated in 2020, not exactly a great time for anyone, actor or not, to enter the job market. At one point, two of his roommates caught COVID, so he and another friend partook in a New York City Department of Health program that put people up in hotel rooms if they’d been exposed to someone who had the virus. They thought they were getting something resembling a staycation. Far from it. “It was absolutely awful. They don’t let you out of your room. They bring you food like prison meals twice a day,” he recalls. “No hate to New York public workers. They’re doing God’s work, truly. But I was expecting Cancun resort. We brought a bunch of booze — they took it all. My friend brought his knitting needles — they took them. They took every sharp object.”

But this was where, in between the daily mandatory vital checks, Briney found out that he’d booked his first real job, as Salvador Dalí’s assistant in Dalíland, directed by American Psycho filmmaker Mary Harron. “I couldn’t get my heart rate under 100, so I had to sit on the floor for 30 minutes while they waited for my heart rate to drop, because they were afraid I got COVID,” Briney says. “I was like, ‘No, guys, I just got good news!’”

It got better: He’d be spending a few months filming in England and starring opposite Oscar winner Ben Kingsley. “I was like, ‘You’re flying me to Liverpool? Like, you’re paying for the plane for me to go there? And you’re paying for my housing while I’m there? And I’m working with an Academy Award winner? And all of these really acclaimed people?’ It just blew my mind.”

Occasionally, his gratitude gave way to self-doubt. Once, while standing next to Kingsley in between takes, Briney blurted out that he was nervous about a scene. “I was sort of apologetic for my presence, which I always am,” he says. But instead of coldly staring him down, Kingsley — about to perform a scene in which he delivers a speech in Catalan — replied that so was he. Even towering thespians like Kingsley could experience something as human as jitters in this job. “It was nice to know I wasn’t alone in that, because I felt like I was the green one — I’m the kid here who doesn’t know what he’s doing,” he says. “It was a moment of ‘Oh! None of us know what we’re doing. We’re all figuring it out.’ It settled me a little bit.”

While he was filming Dalíland, Briney booked The Summer I Turned Pretty, which he approached with the same psyched-to-be-employed energy as his last job. “At the time, I was just like, ‘Oh, what an interesting role! What an opportunity to do a TV show!’” He says he wasn’t fully aware of the fandom around Jenny Han projects like Netflix’s To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before (or their crush-minting powers). That Amazon had greenlit the show with a straight-to-series order and renewed it for a second season before the first one even dropped also went over his head. “That should have been a little note to me: Hey, people might actually watch this,” he says. “But I had no idea. I had no clue of the scope.”

Briney says the cast has mostly let each other process the mind-f*ck of its popularity on their own. “I don’t really want someone to send me a tweet about me — unless it’s funny,” he says. “We don’t have that many conversations. Honestly, now that I think about it, Sean [Kaufman, who plays Belly’s brother] — who’s a very close friend of mine — we’re just boys, you know? We just play video games and talk about them and get mad at baseball.”
“I never expect anyone to like or watch or enjoy anything that I am in or do. I just don’t have that expectation. Not even in a self-deprecating way.”

The story isn’t over yet: After the final season dropped, Prime Video announced an upcoming feature-length The Summer I Turned Pretty film, which filmed this year and will serve as the series’ true conclusion. (Briney is a vault on the topic: “I’d get in trouble,” he says. “I’m not really allowed to talk about it. The truth is, I don’t know a lot about it. Like, I don’t know when they want to put it out.”) But as his career has gotten bigger, Briney seems intent on keeping the rest of his life as close to himself as he can, holding onto it exactly as it was. “I’ve intentionally put more of an emphasis on my own privacy and knowing that there are things in my life that I like to keep to myself, and for myself,” he says. “I think I’ve just spent more time with the people in my life that mean a lot to me.”

Briney paints a picture of filming Season 1 in North Carolina, “before we took it for granted.” The housing complex where members of the cast were staying had swimming pools and billiards tables where they’d spend their down hours. “Sean and I played a lot of Wiffle ball, just in the park, and all these things that would require sort of extra carefulness [if we did them now],” he says. “It was like going to college again in a way. When you get there, you’re like, ‘What do you mean I can do whatever I want?’”
I start to ask if he ever thinks about that innocent, pre-fame version of himself, and he answers without hesitation: “Every day.”
