As it turned out, an awful lot of people had heard stories about seals that came to land as humans.

Nowadays, these shapeshifters are known as ‘selkies’. Selkie is a Scots term that came into widespread use via a Joan Baez cover, ‘Silkie’ (1961), of a traditional Scottish folk song. Yet the phenomenon it describes – of creatures who shapeshift between human and seal forms by shedding a skin – appears consistently in folklore spanning the Celtic world and beyond, even as far as Sweden. Before Baez insinuated the term into international parlance, selkies were identified in Irish and English by a constellation of descriptors. In Irish, the most common is mhaighdean mhara, or ‘sea maiden’, referring to selkies and mermaids. Even in English, many storytellers use ‘mermaid’ for both the phocine and the piscine. Sometimes the two are differentiated with context (fish tails, seal skins), but what matters more than phenotyping is that the mermaid or selkie is neither quite human nor animal. What defines the selkie is transformation.

Much of the folklore retains the quality of the best gossip, hyper-local and yet vague. Storytellers name names, offer precise locations for key scenes in the story. And several admit something startling: that they themselves are the descendants of human-seal pairings.

After the farmer spotted the woman on the beach, Ó Muircheartaigh said, he saw something else. A sealskin cloak lay beside her: her ticket to transformation and a return to the sea. Then he made a choice that would ricochet throughout the generations, and leave the selkie with no option but to follow him home. He stole the selkie’s cloak and secreted it away, thus securing her for a bride. These rough beginnings aside, the couple produced a brood of children and went about the gruelling lives of any impoverished Irish fishing family. The only thing disrupting the fantasy of a normal human wife, acquired in normal human ways, was the webbing between the children’s toes. That, and the fact that the woman never smiled, but kept looking out towards the sea.

What does it mean if your grandmother was a seal? The folklore attests that marriages between humans and selkies were common enough to generate a host of human-selkie lineages – Conneely, Gallagher, Dowd, O’Kane, O’Shea, MacDuffie, McPhee, Flaherty, Glavin – whose members were predisposed towards webbed digits and an ineffable longing for the sea. (‘My mother was one of them O’Sheas,’ the railway worker Séamas MacMathghamhna confided to a folklore collector in 1949, after explaining the selkie lineage of the O’Sheas.) The Celtic studies scholar Gregory Darwin has identified nearly 50 family groups whose members carry selkie blood.

Now is a good time to have a seal in the family tree. As our planet hurtles through climate catastrophe, everyone from environmental activists and TikTok influencers to academics and New Age pilgrims is turning towards animals-as-family rhetoric. Such gusto stems from a cultural exhaustion with extractionism and with narratives of domination and human exceptionalism that have dogged the culture and geopolitics of the Global North since the 19th century. Yet the naivety with which the zeitgeist tends to approach an expanded view of interspecies kinship presents its own problems. For one, it doesn’t quite ring true – and it is hard to fight for a worldview that you can’t see clearly. For another, if we reframe our relationship with the more-than-human around intimate familial connection, then we need ways of understanding what happens when that connection becomes fraught.

The selkie story is one of family dysfunction par excellence. After all, the gutting truth at the centre of selkie families is that one’s origins lie in theft, violence, rape and unimaginable loss. The children of human-selkie pairings face a mottled inheritance, at best. Writing for The New York Times in 2008, Bryan Patrick Miller recounted how his great-great-great-grandfather’s kidnapping of a mhaighdean mhara cursed the family, causing the couple’s half-human children to flee across the Atlantic. Some coastal communities saw seals as fallen angels or the souls of drowned fishermen: mating with them was dubious to say the least.

Mottled or not, a selkie genealogy had to be reckoned with. Having a selkie in the family forced an acknowledgement of a mixed inheritance that was dark and disturbing, and in which successive generations continued to be implicated. Only by considering these uncomfortable reverberations of what it means to be family do we move closer to reimagining our relationships with the more-than-human world.
A woman who is sexually unsatisfied in her marriage may cry into the sea and receive a selkie who is an absolute dynamo in bed

Among folklorists, the trope of the selkie is generally known as the Seal Wife – a designation that speaks more to the gendered hold that the selkie story has on our imagination than to the actual folklore topos. The selkie’s allure is such that men will risk curses and commit theft and kidnapping to possess her, regardless of the certain tragedy that forced marriage augurs. Yet the selkies of folklore are not necessarily wives, women or even seals (note the mermaids, above). Male selkies occasionally make cameos as the kidnapped selkie wife’s jilted husband, father of her aquatic children, keening for her release from outside the human husband’s house. At other times, they appear as her brother, or as characters in the quotidian interactions between humans and their environment: they are accidentally killed, kidnapped as pets, steal fish, issue prophesies, plead and bargain, proffer advice and opinions.

Male selkies also arrive as lovers. Sometimes their affair with a human woman is star-crossed – the paramours may meet only once every seven years, say – but generally sex with a male selkie is an occasion for straightforward joy. A woman who is sexually unsatisfied in her marriage or a maiden hoping for a youthful adventure may cry into the sea and receive a selkie who is, apparently, an absolute dynamo in bed.

What is fascinating about these stories is that they centre female pleasure in a way that the selkie wife stories never do (or male pleasure, for that matter). Instead, the selkie wife – despite the sensual appeal that incited her husband to theft – is noted for her competence in housekeeping and childrearing. But even the male selkie stories occasionally take dark turns. Sometimes, the human woman steals her lover’s skin to compel him into marriage; other times, the human woman is raped by the male selkie.

The hybrid relationships described in the folklore are multilayered and fraught, but they are also interwoven with the rhythms of rural Irish life. The Irish tendency to link themselves to the more-than-human world – including through creatures such as the merrow, or mermaid, the shapeshifting púca, and, of course, the aos sí, the supernatural, fairy analogue to humans – has been noted for hundreds of years. Even the Normans, frustrated with their new subjects’ disinterest in distinguishing themselves from animals, set about reforming the Irish Church and ‘civilising’ the population.

In their paper ‘Slipping Off the Sealskin’ (2015), the literary critic and research artist Clair Le Couteur points out that early selkie stories had far more gender parity than later ones: not only were male selkies better represented, but their female counterparts were more empowered. The change towards the comparably flat Seal Wife trope, they suggest, echoes mankind’s changing view of our ecological place. Male selkies have ‘been largely erased [and] replaced by a simplified Seal Wife story in which gender and species are cross-linked … the female, the animal (seals), and indeed the natural and supernatural realms are conflated into a simplified, exploitable identity formed in opposition to Man’s agency as protagonist.’

Yet if the Seal Wife stands for gendered and environmental exploitation, she does not submit without a fight. The would-be husbands who steal her skin are met with unhappiness, rebellion and sometimes violence. In one story, a mhaighdean mhara retrieves her skin by setting her kidnapper’s house on fire and following the smell of singed skin (in spite of the lore, as Le Couteur warns, that destroying a mhaighdean mhara’s skin may lead to her death).

One particularly difficult aspect of the selkie story is the repeated insistence that the marriage is a happy one. It’s a fair claim that this is patriarchal whitewashing: in one story, the teller describes the marriage as happy, only to admit two lines later that the woman laughed just three times during her spell on land – the last being at her departure. Yet the story raises a thorny truth: sometimes love is problematic. You can love someone who hurts you, and you can still leave.

The notion that humans and animals are kin falls into the broad bucket of relational ontologies known as animism, although the word occupies an uncertain place in Celtic studies. Edward Tylor, a British anthropologist and a towering figure in the nascent field, coined the term in his book Primitive Culture (1871). Here, he divided the world population into stages of evolution: ‘animism’ was reserved for savages so undeveloped they could grasp only the crudest expression of religion. It took more than a century for pioneering scholars like Nurit Bird-David to reclaim and refresh the term as ‘new animism’ and argue that animism did not describe a ‘failed epistemology’, but a relational one.

Initially, the Victorians were thrilled to equate so-called ‘backwards’ rural Europeans with those cultures abroad that they deemed uncivilised. Yet, as Natalia Schwien Scott, a herbalist, wildlife rehabilitation apprentice, and PhD candidate in religion at Harvard University told me, once colonialism became racialised, the language quickly changed: now animism as genealogical kinship between humans and animals was delegated to Black and brown cultures as a means of othering them. The Irish themselves, sick of British dehumanisation, wanted nothing to do with the term. Such leeriness is understandable – and, if history is anything to go by, completely warranted.

Beyond racial politics, the lived experience of animism – for all its zeitgeisty, Kumbaya reputation – is a complicated one. ‘Animism is easy to like when you’re not an animist,’ Guido Sprenger, an anthropologist at Heidelberg University in Germany, told me. In 2021, Sprenger published a paper cheekily titled ‘Can Animism Save the World?’ He’d written it after watching animism slip ‘from being an exciting analytical concept to a catch-all term for moral relations with the environment, without much regard for those who actually practise it and find themselves in all sorts of moral conundrums and dangers.’ He added: ‘Animism isn’t that pretty, peaceful, smoochy, nonhuman affair.’
If the bounds of human exceptionalism are dissolved, and every animal is a family member, then how do you eat?

Like many other anthropologists, Sprenger was initially put off by the term’s colonial origins and nebulous usage; yet, when animism started to gain traction in environmental anthropology, he reconsidered his stance. Now, he worries that the original sin of animism is returning to dilute the term, once again, past the point of usability, out of a desperation to find alternatives to late-stage capitalism and human exceptionalism. ‘Everything that’s not us, with our nature-culture divide, is somehow animist and therefore better,’ he says. ‘And this is a step back into that diffuse and theoretically thin use of animism.’ He worries that this sudden enthusiasm for animism means sidestepping some of its trickier realities.

The animists with whom Sprenger spends his time are the Rmeet people of the Laotian highlands. Some eco-philosophers argue for a closer connection with the nature spirits to address our ecological crisis but, for the Rmeet, ‘this would be the idea of a madman.’ Spirits are a fact of life for the Rmeet, but not a kind one. As Sprenger told me, from the Rmeets’ point of view: ‘Who wants to deal with spirits? Who wants to get close to them? The whole point is that you want to be on good terms with them because you want them not to interfere in your life. They are just entities that are there. They are not a normative category. They are just as normative as a tree – a tree can fall on your head, or it can give you shade. The spirits are just there.’

His words suggest that intimacy and safety are not the same. For example, one issue that besets animist cosmologies is cannibalism. If the bounds of human exceptionalism are dissolved, and every animal is a family member, then how do you eat? Some cultures resolve this dilemma by distinguishing between animals (leave the seal, take the salmon); others by using ritual acts – cooking, say – to metamorphose animals from person to meat. Still others fly straight into the conundrum. An animal family member might allow itself to be caught by hunters, an act of self-sacrifice that allows its kin to survive.

Love and violence are perpetually entangled in animist cosmologies, which makes me wonder: why does it matter to be descended from a seal? Why hold onto a family story so fundamentally sad and troubling? In ‘Violence, Mourning, Politics’ (2003), Judith Butler argues that it is our relations with others that put us at risk of violence – and yet to forfeit being in relation is to forfeit being human. ‘Loss and vulnerability,’ they write, ‘seem to follow from our being socially constituted bodies, attached to others, at risk of losing those attachments, exposed to others, at risk of violence by virtue of that exposure.’ In short, our attachments put us in jeopardy, while shedding them risks losing something fundamental to our place in the order of things.

Animism – or at least claiming a worldview in which we see ourselves as integrated into the more-than-human world rather than lording over it – does not offer safety. If anything, it does the opposite. To be in relationship with the more-than-human world, to take seriously our connections beyond the strictly human, is to become more exposed and also more attached. It puts us, as the selkie stories confirm, directly in the path of more violence. We kill a whale and kill our grandmother. We risk having our house set alight and our heart broken by an angry seal. But we do it because it is what makes us human – and if we lose that, we lose everything.

Whether we can learn from the fraught relationships of selkie kinship rests on an obvious question: did anyone believe they were part-seal? It’s difficult to say what rural seaside communities in Ireland thought about their world up until the 20th century, particularly when they had already undergone centuries of cultural and linguistic erasure. Yet, as Schwien Scott notes: ‘The material very clearly says: “Her mother was a selkie,” or “Her grandmother was a selkie.” Why would we assume that wasn’t actually believed?’

One Galwegian domestic worker, Máire Ní Shúilleabháin, told her daughter in 1938 that she knew islanders who were children of mhaighdean mhara. The mhaighdean mhara were a common-enough reality that her great-uncle had seen one; the year before, a sighting in Connemara led to a £4,000 bounty for the marine woman’s capture (she escaped). One school-age collector in Cork, Nora O’Sullivan, wrote in her notebook that her father told her a story of a man who married a mermaid whose daughter then married into the Sullivans – that is, her family. Her teacher wrote a small memo affirming the story. In 1882, one Ms Dolan claimed that she personally knew the three children of a Lough Owel man named Mahon and his lake-creature bride. ‘She was a very good housewife, as all those lake people are,’ Dolan noted approvingly. ‘She kept his house beautifully.’ In 1937, Micheál Mac Conagail recounted that he knew of a mhaighdean mhara whose son became a priest. Such testimonies abound.

What is more, many fishing communities had taboos on killing seals based on blood relations between humans and seals. The economic implications of this were significant. Not only were these fishermen unable to harvest seals, they also had to swallow the seals’ presence as fishing competition – a huge blow amid grinding rural poverty in Ireland. Given all this, it’s reasonable to adduce a widespread literal belief in selkies that has lasted through living memory. And this belief had real-world implications – none of which were easy.

Seán Ó Muircheartaigh recounted in his story that, when the oat harvest came, the farmer set about clearing out the loft of the house he lived in with his seal wife and their half-selkie children. In a moment of carelessness, he threw down his wife’s sealskin cloak. She grabbed it immediately and secreted it out of sight.

That night, she waited for her husband to step out for the evening, then she washed her children and brushed their hair, just as she had brushed her own the night she was kidnapped. And then she took her cloak and was gone.

One of the most devastating aspects of an already devastating story is that it is about a woman who abandons her children. Every so often, the selkie departs with a blessing, or a curse, but mostly she goes quickly and in silence. She almost never takes her children: and in the case of the O’Dowds, she turns her progeny into stone. She rarely says goodbye. In a small subset of selkie stories, the shapeshifting mother continues to visit her terrestrial family even after she has returned to the sea, in one, returning to comb her children’s hair. But most often she just disappears.

For the selkie herself, the loss is doubled. While her human husband appears incurious about his bride’s former life, storytellers offer occasional glimpses. Eibhlín Ní Chonchubhair tells of a selkie who pauses before her marine return to bid farewell to her human husband. Bewildered, he asks what the children will do without her. Her reply is acid: ‘I have children who are dearer to me than these.’ In this story, as in others, she is met in the water by her selkie husband, who embraces her with cries of joy. Behind the selkie’s flight back to sea is a terrible calculus, where a return to one family means the loss of the other. The situation is complicated by kidnapping and abuse, with children who are innocents and also byproducts of forced marriage.
The selkie story is a roadmap for navigating relationships that cannot be repaired

Family haunts us. In his paper ‘Of Mermaids and Marriages’ (1990), the folklorist Bo Almqvist notes that both he and the poet Seamus Heaney have considered the selkie story as a parallel for parental suicide – a choice that is often incomprehensible to those left behind: to wit, a woman brushes her children’s hair then walks into the sea and vanishes. The selkie story is in many ways a ghost story whose participants just happen to still be alive.

I’ve suggested, pace Judith Butler, that to be in relationship is to place ourselves at risk of loss. But the selkie story, in its peregrination through the undergrowth of complicated grief, takes things one step further: it explores what it is like to remain in relationship with a loved one who is gone and who has caused you immense pain. In some ways, the selkie story is a roadmap for navigating relationships that cannot be repaired, where there is no hope or desire for reconciliation. For one thing, selkie stories acknowledge that we don’t always get to choose who we’re in relationship with – and that, sometimes, the healthiest move within a relationship is to break it.

As we navigate the inevitable species loss attendant on the climate emergency, reckoning with those places on the globe where the greatest act of love may be to decide against human intrusion, the selkie story offers a model for processing meaningful relationships that are defined by absence. The losses and hauntings endure: many individuals and communities in Ireland continued to see themselves as entangled with seals even generations after an interspecies marriage. The selkie story acknowledges as real those relationships where one half of the duo has abruptly left the conversation, as well as the cruelty and love that led up to the loss. It affirms that you can love your children and leave them, or love your children and turn them into stone. These truths can rub shoulders with each other, clear their throats, look down uncomfortably at the floor. Love is messy and not always good.

The selkie narrative is powerful because it considers the aftermath of things going wrong and posits a world in which violence doesn’t mean an end to care. It deals in difficult truths. Yet it is also a story that allows people to look out to sea and see cousins and siblings, parents lost and family gained. It allows a human to look at a seal and feel kinship. To think: there she is. There goes my family.

items.title: A new answer to why there is something rather than nothing | Aeon Essays
items.description: Writing in 1714, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ Philosophers have long wondered why the Universe exists, but Leibniz is credited with framing the issue in precisely these terms. The question is head-spinning when
items.author: Andrew T Brenner
paragraphs: Writing in 1714, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ Philosophers have long wondered why the Universe exists, but Leibniz is credited with framing the issue in precisely these terms. The question is head-spinning when properly considered. This very obvious fact about the world – that things exist – can shift from seeming mundane and trivial to very surprising, even downright weird. Ludwig Wittgenstein expressed this astonishment when he wrote in his Tractatus (1921): ‘Not how the world is, is the mystical, but that it is.’ Arthur Schopenhauer in 1818 called the question ‘an unfathomable and always disquieting riddle’. And the Rigveda, one of the world’s oldest surviving religious texts, suggests that even the ‘overseer’ (adhyakṣaḥ) of the cosmos might not know the answer. Sheer existence is baffling.

Philosophers continue to discuss the question today, but there isn’t any consensus about the answer. Some have suggested that it’s the sort of question that couldn’t possibly have an answer. In 1973, the German philosopher Carl Hempel wrote:

But what kind of an answer would be appropriate? What seems to be wanted is an explanatory account which does not assume the existence of something or other. But such an account, I would submit, is a logical impossibility … No theory, no conceptual scheme, can explain the existence of anything without assuming the existence of something.

His idea is that if you were trying to explain why, for instance, any penguins at all exist, then you couldn’t appeal to a penguin in your explanation – after all, that penguin is one of the things you are trying to explain. Similarly, if we’re looking for an explanation for why anything at all exists, then our explanation cannot appeal to an existing thing, since that existing thing is one of the things we are trying to explain. But Hempel thinks that there couldn’t possibly be any other sort of explanation for why anything exists, since any explanation for why something exists has to appeal to some other existing thing.

One response to Hempel’s concern is to go ahead and do what he claimed can’t possibly be done: offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, an explanation that ‘does not assume the existence of something’. Many philosophers have attempted to do just that. But there is something wrong with these explanations.

Why might we expect there to be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing in the first place? Leibniz thought there must be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing because, as he put it, nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. It is this thought that lies behind much of the astonishment people have expressed at the fact that there is something rather than nothing.

A world in which nothing exists is how we should expect the world to be if it takes what would, by our usual criteria, be its most probable state. What I have in mind here is Ockham’s Razor. Simpler accounts of the world are more likely to be correct than complex ones. For example, consider all the traits shared among the species alive today. Whales and humans have similar bone structures, despite the fact that they live in very different environments. One of Charles Darwin’s key insights was that, while it might conceivably have been true that a creator just happened to want these various species to have similar traits, despite their different environments and lifestyles, it is so much simpler to suppose that they share those traits because those traits are derived from a common ancestor. And the simplicity itself of that explanation gives us an excellent reason to think that the common traits are derived from a common ancestor. We constantly rely on the assumption that the simplest account of the world compatible with our evidence is most likely to be correct. This is something we do in science as well as in everyday life.

Many of the proposed explanations for why there is something rather than nothing that have been offered in the past do not address the apparent fact that nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. The proposed explanations say that there is such-and-such a reason for why there is something rather than nothing, but they do nothing to address the thought that we should antecedently expect there to be nothing because, if there had been nothing, then reality would have been so much simpler.
There would have been a whole lot of non-ontological truths even if nothing had existed

What I’d like to do here is kill two birds with one stone: to offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, which simultaneously dissolves the suspicion that nothing would have been so much simpler than something. This also happens to be, as far as I can tell, a new explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, and new explanations are hard to come by given the antiquity of the question.

I would like to start with the important insight that there are truths that are not truths about existing things. Since they are not truths about existing things, we’ll call them ‘non-ontological’ truths. Contrast these with ‘ontological’ truths – truths that are about existing things, like the truth that Earth orbits the Sun, or that there are more trees in the world than there are dogs. The observation that there are non-ontological truths is an insight expressed by other philosophers puzzled by the question of why there is something rather than nothing. For example, in a number of publications, the philosopher John Leslie has argued that there is something rather than nothing simply because it is good for there to be something rather than nothing. Setting aside whether this is a successful explanation, note that it appeals to a non-ontological truth: even if there was nothing, then there would have still been the truth that reality was less good than it could have been. And that does seem plausible.
Once we notice that there are non-ontological truths, we can see on reflection that there would have been a whole lot of them even if nothing had existed. Here are a few examples:

- Negative existential truths, ie, truths regarding that which does not exist. A possible world in which nothing exists would have to have lots of these truths! This doesn’t exist, that doesn’t exist, and so on.
- Truths regarding what is possible and impossible. Even if nothing existed, it would still be possible for dogs to exist, and impossible for square circles to exist.

- Truths of logic. Even if nothing existed, we would still have what logicians call modus ponens, the logical rule that says that, if A is true, and it’s also true that if A is true then B is true, then B is true.

- Mathematical truths. Even if nothing existed, it would still be true that 2+3=5. Regardless of the existence of numbers or any other mathematical objects, it would still be true that if you’ve got two things, and you add to them three things, you’ll end up with five things.

- Moral truths. Even if nothing existed, all sorts of actions would still be morally better or worse than other actions. Even though Ewoks don’t exist, it’s still true that it would be wrong to pinch their fur. In fact, even if nothing existed, it would still be wrong to pinch Ewoks.

Again, these are just a few examples. I could list many others. Admittedly, it’s mysterious how we know about these non-ontological truths. Since they don’t concern existing things, it’s surprising that our cognitive faculties can ‘get a grip’ on them, in the way that they can get a grip on objects with which we can interact (eg, the dog in front of me that I can see with my eyes and pet with my hand).
There can conceivably be possible worlds – possible ways for reality to be – that are not merely ways things could be

An immediate objection is that if there were truly nothing then there would not be any non-ontological truths either. A truly empty world would have nothing at all, including truths of any sort. The philosopher Tyron Goldschmidt expresses this thought when he writes in The Puzzle of Existence (2013) that the question of why any beings at all exist is:

the broadest question of all … The question amounts to a question about why any world obtains. After all, worlds are ways things could be, and without any ways or things – beings broadly construed – there can be no world.

But I don’t think this is right. This view assumes that, in asking why anything at all exists, we are asking why there are any truths at all (in Goldschmidt’s terms, ‘why any world obtains’). That is not what we are asking. We are looking for an explanation for existence specifically. We are not asking why there are truths rather than no truths. That would, as Goldschmidt himself notes, be a confused question to ask, since there isn’t any alternative to there being truths, not even an impossible alternative. ‘A situation in which nothing is true’ doesn’t describe a situation, not even an impossible situation, since descriptions of a situation tell us what is or would be true were that situation to happen. With the concept of non-ontological truths, we can also see that there can conceivably be possible worlds – possible ways for reality to be – that are not merely ways things could be. In those empty worlds there would be truths, but no things.

Many non-ontological truths would still be true even if nothing existed because they are necessarily true, if true at all. For example, recall modus ponens. That logical rule couldn’t help but be true, whether or not anything exists. The same holds for many of the other non-ontological truths, such as truths regarding what is possible and impossible, mathematical truths, and moral truths.

Some of these non-ontological truths are more controversial than others. But you don’t have to buy into every non-ontological truth to see that a possible world in which nothing exists would be more complex than it seems at first glance. When we think of complexity we normally think of the complexity of things and their properties and behaviours. But there is this whole other sort of complexity that is more abstract: complexity with respect to non-ontological truths.

Even if a possible world in which nothing exists might be more complex than we initially thought, it doesn’t follow that Leibniz was wrong when he said that it is simpler for nothing to exist than for something to exist. After all, you might think that if something exists this would leave us with all those non-ontological truths cited above as well as ontological truths about the things that exist. But postulating something new can simplify our overall picture of reality if the new thing can explain a great deal that would otherwise remain unexplained.

A possible world in which something exists may very well simplify matters if one or more of the existing things could explain why the non-ontological truths are true. This is similar to how Darwin simplified our account of biological reality by postulating the existence of something we didn’t previously believe in: a common ancestor. So if something of the right sort exists, this might make reality simpler than if nothing at all exists, if the existing thing can explain why many of the non-ontological truths are true. The simpler that existing thing is, and the wider the range of non-ontological truths it can explain, the simpler our overall account of reality will be. But what sort of existing thing might do the trick? Three possibilities naturally suggest themselves, though I don’t claim that these three options are exhaustive.

First, God is a natural candidate. Here I have in mind the sort of God we find in the world’s major monotheistic religions, all-powerful, all-knowing and so on. The feature of theism most important for our purposes is the idea that God’s nature and decisions are supposed to ultimately explain many aspects of reality. It is God’s status as reality’s explanatory bedrock that makes God a natural candidate for explaining various non-ontological truths. For example, if there is a God, then God’s decisions would explain various negative existential truths. Mechagodzilla doesn’t exist because Mechagodzilla just isn’t one of the things God wanted to create, or allow to be created.

Divine command theorists such as William of Ockham (of Ockham’s Razor fame) explain moral truths in terms of God’s commands – an act is good or bad because God commands it to be. René Descartes notoriously claimed that God decrees which logical and mathematical truths are true. These truths could not be otherwise – they are necessary – but that too is only because God decided they can’t be otherwise. There is also a case to be made that God is a particularly simple being. If that’s right, then our overall account of reality might end up being simple if God explains why many non-ontological truths are true. There is the traditional doctrine of divine simplicity, endorsed by prominent Jewish thinkers such as Maimonides, Christian thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas, and Islamic thinkers such as Ibn Sina. According to this view, there are no distinctions at all within God, either between God’s attributes, or between God and God’s attributes. Over the past several decades, the philosopher Richard Swinburne has argued in detail for a more modest way of understanding the idea that God is a very simple being, and so theism is a very simple hypothesis. The basic idea, which I don’t have the space to discuss in detail, is that many of God’s attributes (omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness, etc) are ultimately derivable from one or two of God’s attributes, and those attributes fit together in a neat and tidy manner.

Here is a second option if the God explanation doesn’t appeal. Many of the non-ontological truths might be explained by a natural (that is, non-supernatural) object that explains why the Universe has many of the properties it has. Suppose that the Universe originated in a cosmic singularity, an object of infinite density. The state of the initial singularity would, given how the laws of nature dictate the Universe evolves over time, explain why various negative existential truths are true. This is because the Universe’s initial conditions plus the laws will result in the Universe’s history taking one course rather than another, one that either does or does not include the existence of various particular things in it. Even non-deterministic laws may dictate that the existence of certain things is very improbable, given the Universe’s initial conditions.
The actual world, though filled with existing things, may for all we know be the simplest possible world

Some philosophers think that truths regarding what is possible and impossible in the broadest sense are also explained by the properties had by an initial singularity. The idea is that what’s possible and impossible is grounded in which states of the Universe can result from the evolution of the initial singularity, given how the laws of nature say the Universe will evolve over time. If some state of the Universe can in principle result from the initial singularity and the laws, then it’s possible, but if it can’t result then it is strictly impossible, as impossible as a round square. In fact, on this view that’s what makes round squares impossible. But would an initial singularity give us a particularly simple explanation for various non-ontological truths? The philosopher Quentin Smith argued that an initial cosmic singularity is as simple as it gets, since an initial singularity would have had no spatial extension, no mass (at least on some models), and would not have been governed by any physical laws. So it’s certainly a candidate.

A third possibility is that we humans make many of the non-ontological truths true. And, with various degrees of plausibility, many of the non-ontological truths cited earlier have been attributed by some philosopher or other to our decisions, conventions, practices or whatever. For example, moral anti-realists such as Sharon Street think that there are moral truths, but that they are made true by our attitudes, conventions or practices (or the attitudes we would have in ideal conditions). Logical conventionalists such as Jared Warren contend that logical truths are a result of our linguistic practices. Mathematical intuitionists such as the mathematician L E J Brouwer think that mathematical truths are mentally constructed.

There are surely more possibilities than these three. But, confining our attention to these three options – God, singularity, human beings – is one of them clearly preferable to the others? It’s difficult to say. There are many non-ontological truths, and some non-ontological truths may be more plausibly explained by an existing thing than would other non-ontological truths. It is difficult to see how some of these explanations would work; I’ve never seen anyone claim that an initial singularity might explain which moral truths are true. And a full evaluation of the three options would require a detailed examination of the relative merits of the various explanations on offer. We would have to take a look at each of the versions of divine command theory and human-centred moral anti-realism on offer, and see if any of them seem plausible on closer inspection. That being said, the first two options (God, singularity) do seem to fare better than the third option with respect to simplicity. They propose to explain lots of non-ontological truths by appealing to one existing thing, an existing thing that might be very simple. By contrast, if we try to explain various non-ontological truths by appeal to human beings, we don’t seem to have a very simple explanation. Human beings are complex objects. There are also a lot of human beings. Are the non-ontological truths explained by some of them, or all of them? How would we reconcile conflicting human attitudes or practices that might result in contradictory non-ontological truths? It’s hard to see how we might come up with an elegant or simple way of accounting for how that’s all supposed to work.

We can leave further speculation regarding the details to another occasion. The main point is this: if we can posit some existing thing that is simple enough, and capable of explaining a wide-enough range of the non-ontological truths, we might very well end up with an account of reality in which one or more things exist, and yet which is simpler than an account of reality in which nothing exists. In fact, despite how counterintuitive it seems at first, the actual world, though filled with existing things, may for all we know be the simplest possible world, if it has a sufficiently simple explanatory foundation. In that case, Leibniz would have been incorrect when he said that nothing would have been ‘simpler and easier’ than something. If we found ourselves surprised that reality didn’t take its simplest and seemingly most probable state, one in which nothing exists, that sense of surprise should dissolve.

Suppose that if something of the right sort exists, then that would be simpler than if nothing at all existed. Would this fact explain why there is something rather than nothing? Presumably it would only if we think that reality is the way it is because of how simple it is. In other words, we would have to think that reality is somehow striving toward simplicity, so that, if the world is as simple as it can be, this is because it is as simple as it can be. You shouldn’t oppose this idea on the grounds that our world is very complex, since, as I’ve emphasised, that complexity might be accounted for in terms of a very simple explanatory starting point.

A more serious worry is that, even if our reason for thinking that something is true is because it is simpler (remember Ockham’s Razor), it doesn’t follow that the thing itself is true because it is simpler. The reason we think the various species have a common ancestor is because this hypothesis is the simplest explanation of the evidence. But that simplicity isn’t what makes it true that there is that common ancestor.

We should question this assumption that simplicity never explains why some state of affairs comes about. The idea that sometimes reality takes a simpler form because it is simpler is more defensible than it might first seem. It would have the benefit of explaining why simplicity is a guide to truth (that is, why we should accept principles such as Ockham’s Razor), a methodological practice followed in both science and everyday life, but which is notoriously hard to justify. What’s more, many of us follow Leibniz in being puzzled at the fact that reality didn’t take what seems at first to be its simplest form, wherein nothing exists. We tend to think that if nothing had existed, and if this would have in fact been the simplest way for reality to be, then nothing would have existed precisely because nothing was so much simpler than something.

My argument flips this line of reasoning on its head. We should expect reality to be simple, and for all we can tell that’s exactly what we find. There being something rather than nothing shouldn’t surprise us if that’s the simplest way for reality to be. That wouldn’t explain everything. Supposing that reality somehow strives for simplicity, for example, we might very well wonder why that’s the case. It won’t work to say that reality strives for simplicity because that’s the simplest way for reality to work, as that would be a circular explanation. So, even if my extremely speculative proposal is correct, we’d still be left with a lot of mystery. Out of the infinite number of ways for reality to be, why did it turn out this way? That’s still a baffling question, even if we conclude that one of reality’s features, that things exist, might turn out to be less baffling than it initially seems.

items.title: Why the dilettante is the anti-hero of our over-optimised age | Aeon Essays
items.description: Why, of all people, defend the dilettante? An amateur at best, a flighty rascal at worst: why take an interest in someone whose own interests are never more than a passing hobby? These are serious times – why take seriously someone for whom nothing is serious?
items.author: Jay Miller
paragraphs: Why, of all people, defend the dilettante? An amateur at best, a flighty rascal at worst: why take an interest in someone whose own interests are never more than a passing hobby? These are serious times – why take seriously someone for whom nothing is serious?

Merriam-Webster defines the dilettante as ‘a person having a superficial interest in an art or a branch of knowledge’. Encyclopedia.com calls the dilettante someone who cultivates an interest ‘without real commitment or knowledge’. Cambridge settles for someone whose understanding ‘is not very deep or serious’. Collins gives us someone who ‘seems interested in a subject … but does not really know very much about it’. None of it is flattering.

Clearly, the dilettante is no aspirational character. No university markets itself as training the next generation of dilettantes; no magazine runs a ‘dilettante of the year’ issue (except, perhaps, for the excellent Idler publication). He – for the dilettante is, historically and in popular imagination, so often a ‘he’ – is in essence an amateur, a role defined by wide interests and narrow expertise.

Such is the reputation of the dilettante, assigned and maintained by a culture that treats a single-minded devotion to one pursuit as the only route to a meaningful life. Pick something and stick with it, we are told. It’s not so much an explicit campaign against dilettantism I’m challenging, but rather the diffuse yet relentless pressure to narrow one’s interests, to specialise, to gain expertise, to forgo breadth for the sake of depth. We hear it in the barrage of imperatives to follow your dreams or find your passion uttered at graduation speeches, in self-help guides, and similarly corporate-sounding pep talks. Under this scheme, the specialist is the hero and the dilettante is but a cautionary tale: the person who never committed, never finished, never got good enough at any one thing.

But what if the scheme has it backwards? What if the dilettante’s perpetual movement from one thing to another is not a failure of nerve but a different and defensible way of being, one whose exploratory zeal turns out to be just what a hyper-specialised, over-optimised and all-too-serious world needs most? Then the dilettante would turn out to be not a capricious buffoon but a kind of modern anti-hero. That, I argue, is a dilettantism worth defending.

First, let’s consider how ‘dilettante’ relates to some of its conceptual cousins: the amateur, the dabbler, the jack-of-all-trades, etc. First, the dilettante is by nature an amateur, ie, a non-expert, a non-professional. But amateurism is a necessary though not sufficient condition of dilettantism. Anyone can be an amateur at any particular thing: woodworking, birdwatching, astronomy, etc. The dilettante’s amateurism is wide-ranging over several interests, and tends to orient around the production and/or appreciation of art and beauty. Like the jack-of-all-trades, the dilettante is a multi-dimensional amateur. But the dilettante’s amateurism is typically of the aesthetic variety.

Further, the dilettante is no dabbler. The dabbler scratches the surface of interests, whereas the dilettante, I argue, can and does go deep – without, however, anchoring a sense of self in any one interest. This also sets the dilettante apart from the flâneur, Charles Baudelaire’s urban wanderer strolling through the city’s offerings, sampling everything, invested in none of it. The dilettante is deeply engaged in interests, and more an active participant than a passive spectator.
The term originally referred to someone who pursues an interest, particularly an artistic one, for the sake of ‘delight’

In this respect, the concept is closest in spirit to the ‘Renaissance man’, minus the gender specification and historical context. The dilettante is one who is moved by enjoyment rather than necessity, professional obligation or the pursuit of credentials, and who purposefully cultivates a plurality of distinct, often aesthetic interests beyond mere surface familiarity.

One reason to defend the dilettante, then, is for lexicological justice. The term has been unfairly burdened with an overly negative connotation. It wasn’t always this way. From the Baroque-era Italian dilettante, the term originally referred to someone who pursues an interest, particularly an artistic one, for the sake of pleasure, or ‘delight’. Even as the term evolved, it stayed largely neutral, distinguishing enthusiasts from professionals in a given practice. The pejorative connotation familiar to us today is more recent, shaped by what I’ll call a ‘deficiency’ model, in which amateurism is viewed negatively as a lack of something: skill, seriousness, focus, expertise. This is the meaning ascribed by cultural gatekeepers like Theodor Adorno, who in 1929 dismissed the dilettante as one ‘unable to establish any standards’.

The more important aim, however, is to show dilettantism as a way of living that offers more than we might think. It is a life liberated from specialisation, instrumentalisation and meritocratic bean-counting, as well as from a Protestant work ethic that is suspicious of pleasure for pleasure’s sake. Arguments denigrating specialisation in education and vocation are well known, as are those championing well-roundedness and the virtues of the liberal arts. Though similar in spirit, this defence of dilettantism is less about the purpose or outcomes of academic or professional life and more about making the mental switch away from the socially conditioned pressure to find your thing and stick with it to an open and exploratory pursuit of pluralistic interests. Reclaiming this sense of joyful experimentalism is intended to show dilettantism as a mode of abundance rather than deficiency.

A good place to start is the essay ‘On Dilettantism’ (1799) by J W von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller. This fragmentary, never-completed project by the literary dream-team of Weimar-era Germany paints a deeply ambivalent portrait of dilettantism, praising the dilettante over here for ‘cultivat[ing] something serious in man’ and condemning him over there as a ‘plagiarist’ and a ‘bungler’. Viewed retrospectively, however, its almost scientific treatment of the ‘advantages’ (Nutzen) and ‘disadvantages’ or ‘harms’ (Schaden) of dilettantism helps give a clear-eyed view of the potential virtues and vices of dilettantism today.

Crucially, Goethe and Schiller’s analysis is squarely situated in the cultural context of Weimar classicism. This means that, first, the question of the dilettante arises (as it does in its original Italian usage) exclusively in relation to the arts. They treat the dilettante as a distinctly aesthetic figure, ‘a lover of the arts who wishes not only to contemplate and enjoy them, but also to participate in their production.’ This aesthetic dimension has (regrettably, I think) faded from the meaning of ‘dilettante’ over time. But nor does it need to be narrowly inscribed in 18th-century anxieties about who can and cannot properly be called an artist. Artistic engagement isn’t essential to dilettantism. But it is worth reasserting, maybe even foregrounding, the sense in which the ‘delight’ of dilettantism involves, to some extent, the experience of aesthetic pleasure, broadly understood. The dilettante, that is, pursues what Søren Kierkegaard calls an ‘aesthetic life’: the ongoing, everyday activity of observing, valuing, and participating in art and beauty.
The dilettante is comfortable in the garb of an amateur. For the dilettante, every night is karaoke night

Though rooted in classicist aestheticism, some of Goethe and Schiller’s criticism of the dilettante still resonates today. They worry, for example, that the dilettante ‘jumps over the steps’, gliding too glibly through the creative process and claiming victory too early. There’s something to this. Similar to Oscar Wilde’s concern about the ‘sentimentalist’ in his 1897 epistolary essay, De Profundis, who ‘desires to have the luxury of an emotion without paying for it’, the authors voice a reasonable objection to those willing to cut the line in chasing laurels. Progress is earned through practice, and those of us who have put in the work are right to protect it, as any trained therapist, frustrated with the quackery that passes for therapy on YouTube and TikTok, will gladly testify.

But due to their idealisation of the ‘true artist’ as a manifester of Truth and Beauty, Goethe and Schiller cannot help but view the dilettante as lacking in both aim and ability. To be fair, no practice is a total free-for-all, and some practices are less permissive of dilettantism than others (who wants to live in a house built by a dilettante architect?). But the notion that the dilettante tries and fails to follow the ‘true objective rules’ of art and beauty the way legit artists do rests on outdated and Eurocentric assumptions about what both artists and dilettantes are actually up to. In other words, take away the neo-classicist presumption, and suddenly the dilettante appears less like an imitator and more like a liberated creator. It’s not that the dilettante falls short in any given practice but, rather, has a different orientation toward it. Indeed, an overly goal-oriented attitude, especially in the realm of pastimes and pleasures, cuts against the very spirit of dilettantism. Part of its appeal is its ethos of open-endedness, its willingness to do something for the sake of delight rather than achievement. The dilettante is comfortable in the garb of an amateur. For the dilettante, every night is karaoke night.

From our Germans, we glean a sense of where the dilettante goes wrong. But they can also help us make the corrective mental switch from seeing the dilettante as a wannabe practitioner to someone who chooses a more experimental, exploratory orientation toward a given practice.

The key to perceiving dilettantism as abundance instead of deficiency is to appreciate the sense of freedom it affords. It is, in the first place, a negative freedom, a freedom from the constraints that otherwise bind professional practitioners. More precisely, it is a freedom of mobility within a practice.

First, the dilettante has greater freedom to engage in a given practice. For Goethe and Schiller, one of the most important ‘advantages’ of dilettantism is that it ‘stimulates a certain taste for art, and extends it to where the artist would not be able to reach’. Generalising a bit, the point holds well beyond art: the dilettante can act as a liaison between expert and layperson, closing the gap between high practice and everyday curiosity, introducing otherwise cloistered practitioners to wider audiences and extending an invitation to anyone who might otherwise feel shut out.

A personal example. A few years ago, I joined Mountain Haulers, a cycling group that meets on Tuesday evenings for a ride through Asheville, North Carolina. It is a ‘no drop’ ride: cyclists wait at points along the way for everyone to catch up, however slow or struggling, and the first ride of the month is always a chill ride along the river. This openness sets the group apart from a cycling culture of notorious cliques of devotees clamouring to outdo each other’s worship of the sport. Welcoming the less-experienced and the less-committed seems a more genuine way of loving the thing you claim to love. If biking is your thing, surely you want more butts on bike seats. The dilettante cyclists who show up for Tuesday-night rides make cycling better.
The modern admonition to ‘stay in your lane’ stems from assumptions about the commitment required to claim an interest as one’s own

The further sense of the dilettante’s freedom involves mobility between different practices – a freedom from the barriers dividing them. The dilettante maintains a certain detachment, or intentional separation, between who one is and what one does, to live the life of a cultural itinerant. Painting, gardening, MIG welding, beekeeping, language learning, comic-book collecting, dancing, swimming, printmaking, powerlifting, pickleballing, sourdough baking, accordion playing, brisket barbecuing – all exciting destinations to travel and explore without seeking citizenship or even permanent residence in any one. The dilettante is a wayfaring cosmopolitan whose sense of freedom is found in never being stuck in one place.

And yet, this mobility is also part of a positive freedom to satisfy the basic human need to explore and make one’s mark on the world. Goethe and Schiller credit the dilettante for activating this natural impulse toward curiosity and creativity, a drive they compare with children’s innate desire to playfully imitate their surroundings. Going further, I would say that dilettantism offers not only the satisfaction of scratching the Homo faber itch; making and exploring for the simple sake of joy and curiosity is a freedom that is every bit as valuable to self-discovery as any commitment or singular pursuit.

However, from the outside, mobility may look like mere lack of commitment. No doubt this drives some of the allegations of superficiality commonly lodged against the dilettante. Pulling up anchors and moving on from an interest gets flagged as surface-skimming. I’m speculating here, but such criticism seems rooted in a work ethic that tells us that investment in certain interests ought to yield dividends: authority, credibility, permission to enter culturally guarded spaces, etc. Just as the neo-classicist wants to set the ‘true artist’ apart from the poseurs, the modern admonition to ‘pick a lane’, or (more aggressive) ‘stay in your lane’, stems from assumptions about the level and length of commitment required to claim an interest as one’s own.

Dilettantism rejects this quasi-capitalist mindset. The petty territorialism common to social, academic and cultural spaces (think record stores, cocktail bars, art galleries, philosophy classes, etc) is unnecessary but, more importantly, at odds with a genuine interest in the thing itself. A crucial part of the switch from deficiency to abundance is learning to see the dilettante as an asset to a given practice rather than a threat to it. Even Adorno, snob par excellence, allows a version of this, arguing that the expert critic needs the dilettante around ‘in order to prove to himself that he isn’t one’.
More than simply escaping sickness, the dilettante’s movement is a headlong rush at vitality and vigour

Also crucial to making this mental switch is seeing the dilettante’s curiosity as equal in intensity to the expert’s, but different. Picture the dilettante as the love-child of two very different philosophical figures: Kierkegaard’s aesthete in Either/Or (1843) who finds and cultivates interests with an intensity that is abandoned before it hardens into obligation, and Friedrich Nietzsche’s ‘free spirit’, the fiercely curious, light-footed nomad whose restless pursuit of intellectual and artistic treasures provides a profound, if rootless, freedom. From Kierkegaard, the dilettante acquires an innate aversion to boredom (‘the root of all evil’) which is achieved by what he calls ‘rotation of crops’: perpetually changing ‘the method of cultivation and the kinds of crops’. From Nietzsche, the dilettante inherits a rejection of convention coupled with perpetual motion, a sense of permanent ‘homelessness’ that propels an unfettered perusal of interests. Passionate enough to go deep, detached enough to eventually leave, such a figure shows the possibility of being intensely invested in various ways of knowing, doing and making, but never content to let a sense of self form too firmly around them.

In a memorable scene from the Spike Jonze film Adaptation (2002), the journalist Susan Orlean (Meryl Streep), who is writing a book about the orchid thief John Laroche (Chris Cooper), is at once intrigued by his hunt for a rare hallucinogenic ‘ghost orchid’ and baffled to learn that it is only the latest in a lifetime of obsessions: turtles, prehistoric fossils, 19th-century Dutch mirrors, etc. How can he detach so abruptly from something in which he’s invested so much? He can only offer an anecdote. A profound and consuming love for tropical fish ended suddenly with the realisation that the passion had simply run its course. ‘Fuck fish,’ he tells her, disrupting her assumption that loving something means sticking with it forever.

The difference is that, unlike Kierkegaard’s aesthete, the dilettante doesn’t rotate crops out of despair. Dynamism, detachment and insatiable curiosity are constitutive of the dilettante’s free and full subjectivity, rather than a stage on the way to achieving selfhood. The dilettante chooses aesthetic life over the life of commitment that Kierkegaard’s ‘either/or’ dichotomy presents, and fully owns that choice. Nor is the dilettante simply recovering from existential illness, as Nietzsche’s free spirit seems to be. Rather than running the risk of relapse – or worse, the ‘cankerous vice’ of pessimism – dilettantism is a healthy embrace of this freedom; more than simply escaping sickness, the dilettante’s movement is a headlong rush at vitality and vigour.

In the dilettante’s genes is a compulsion to pursue passions, deeply coupled with a refusal to shape a life or identity permanently around any one of them. The dilettante possesses a unique capacity to dive deep into an interest, then surface and plunge into the depths of the next, each one an exploration, an adventure, but not a lifelong, life-defining project. It is precisely to hold open the possibility of the next reconnaissance mission that the dilettante rejects any dogmatic principle of stick-to-itiveness. Sometimes, the dilettante is a devout hobbyist parked on one interest for years at a stretch; sometimes, a juggler of several overlapping projects at once; and sometimes, a serial enthusiast on the hunt for the next novelty – what holds these modes together isn’t any fixed duration or rhythm of arrival and departure, but a disposition toward perpetual motion. The dilettante’s talent, energy and passion are constantly rechannelled through new outlets. Far from deficiency, dilettantism is a constant quest for abundance.

The life of the dilettante, so described, is not an especially easy one. It is a life of perpetual searching and fleeting satisfaction, in which accomplishment often arrives without accolades. Until breadth of interest is held in higher esteem, today’s dilettante will largely have to forgo public recognition and settle for a private life of pursuits and pleasures. Rarely is the dilettante widely celebrated as such. Consider someone like Susan Sontag, a novelist, critic and political activist whose wide-ranging work has earned both praise for its unconventional contributions to the intellectual life of 1960s New York and criticism for lacking rigour, for lacking substance. A ‘Win’ in the dilettante’s column, in other words, often comes with an asterisk – a conditional victory at best.

Further, the dilettante is also no pack animal; however much a part of a group one may feel, the dilettante will likely always be something of a tourist within it. The dilettante has to be comfortable travelling as a lone wolf at the margins of any community organised around a shared interest.

No, dilettantism is not for everyone. For anyone whom the universe has called to pursue a single passion – congratulations! Stay the course! But for those of us compelled by something closer to FOMO for the sheer variety and abundance the world has to offer, the dilettante’s path can lead to a genuine quality-of-life upgrade. If courage means overcoming the fear of new beginnings, without the reassurance of a title or a track record to show for it, then dilettantism may have much to offer. After all, not every crop is a monoculture, sowed and tilled to maximise output. Some of us need to cultivate our gardens through crop rotation. A defence of the dilettante is thus a call to follow the forked path of varying interests to a life made meaningful through abundance rather than acclaim.

items.title: We need a language to name the grief that comes without death | Aeon Essays
items.description: I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say
items.author: Derek van Zoonen
paragraphs: I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say goodnight, her cheeks covered in thick layers of night cream. Then, out of nowhere, the image would flip into the raging woman who was so entangled in her own suffering that she turned her frustration on us. Over the years, that second woman slowly swallowed the first, as she got pulled into my brother’s addiction. It’s hard to say where her own unhappiness ended and my brother’s suffering began, but together they drifted into a parallel reality, cut off from the world beyond their heads. There was no funeral for this. No condolence cards. No flowers. No phone calls. No leave of absence. What was I supposed to mourn?

And yet what I felt for them, what I still feel, has the unmistakable gravity of mourning. Can there be grief without death? I have come to think that we grieve much more often than we realise, and that death is grief’s most visible occasion rather than its essence. If that doesn’t match your experience, it may be because we rarely call these other losses by their name. Most of our losses arrive without a funeral. That is the human predicament: we are creatures built to attach, living in a world where nothing stays. Sooner or later, we lose the things we care about. And since we are complex beings with a body, a mind, a community and an environment – beings who love many different things – there is a great deal we can lose, from our physical health to our sense of who we are, from relationships to homelands to the natural world we share with other species. For creatures like us, there is no way around heartbreak: to live is to lose. Grief is what love does when its object is gone. It is love with nowhere to go.

Over the past few years I have accumulated many such losses. There is the psychological loss of my father as I knew and loved him: a brutal stroke rendered him incapable of walking and cycling, and cycling was the only thing that could ‘make his thoughts liquid’, as he used to say. There is the loss of old friendships. First you are no longer part of each other’s lives – you just update one another about your life – and then, one day, it becomes awkward to reach out at all. There is the gradual softening of an academic identity I’d spent the most vital years of my life constructing. It was a genuine vocation, a life of the mind that taught me to think slowly and carefully. But it was also, as I came to realise, a way of living safely at one remove from where actual life takes place. What is slipping away is a future in which being an academic philosopher would be the whole answer to the question of who I am.

There was the woman whose calmness, clarity and silence embodied the qualities I have come to like so much about the Nordics since moving to Norway. Like a magical stranger, she entered my life unexpectedly, but at the same time her arrival felt so natural, her presence so obvious, that it was as if she had always been there. After our first meeting, which lasted almost 24 hours, I wrote in my journal: Ze is gekomen om te blijven. ‘She had come to stay.’ And she did, for nine intense months. She tried to teach me to ski. We listened to the music of Nils Frahm, which reminded her of melting snow. And she made me see that the deepest form of intimacy happens in the space between the words.

But despite the depth of our bond, she left, abruptly, as if she had never been there. She had fallen in love with another man. I was left behind, dazed and disoriented, and although my heart was broken, this kind of loss did not have a name that matched how shattered I felt. It was ‘just a breakup’, and it didn’t even deserve that name: we had been dating, but it never technically became a relationship. It was also a romantic connection that ran alongside another one, a long partnership that was open by mutual agreement and conscious design. Much about it wasn’t legible to most people around me. I faced the grief largely by myself. No scripts, no rituals, no recognised form, no legitimacy, no shared language, no way to make sense of what had happened to me.

Part of what made the experience so disorienting was a narrow idea of what grief is. In psychology, in philosophy and in our Western culture at large, grief has been treated almost exclusively as a response to the death of someone we love. It’s a neat, tidy understanding. The most celebrated grief memoirs – think of The Year of Magical Thinking (2005) by Joan Didion and A Grief Observed (1961) by C S Lewis – are concerned with the loss of a life partner. And Michael Cholbi’s Grief: A Philosophical Guide (2021) – one of the most extensive philosophical treatments of the emotion – focuses mostly on the grief we experience at the death of someone we love or who otherwise matters to us.
Restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches

Death is visible and final: it has a body, a date, a medical certificate. The other losses are blurrier: they have no physical object, no clear beginning or end, no tangible proof they happened. We also have an infrastructure for death: funerals, condolence cards, flowers, casseroles, bereavement leave – a whole social script. Perhaps the infrastructure defines what counts: if there is no social and cultural scaffolding to digest the experience, it must not be real grief.

The prime reason for the single-minded focus on death loss, however, must be that bereavement is simply the most striking instance of a broader emotional phenomenon that comes in degrees. But restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches, anxiety to panic attacks, sadness to depression, or pleasure to ecstasy – it is taking the most extreme instantiation of something and making it the essence of that thing.

If grief isn’t just about death, what is it about? What do all these cases of grief share? A good way to answer this question starts from the observation that every emotion has a characteristic thing it is about. Fear is about danger or threat; anger is about offence or injustice; happiness and joy are about flourishing or harmony between self and world. What is grief about? If you say ‘death’, you are doing something weird: you are defining the emotion by the particular thing that sets it off, rather than by what that thing means to us. In technical philosophical jargon, you are making the mistake of conflating an emotion’s material object with its formal object. Fear of sharks, fear of public speaking and fear of heights aren’t three different emotions – shark-fear, public-speaking-fear and heights-fear. All three count as fear because they are about danger: their aim is to tell you something is threatening.

Grief clearly has something to do with loss. Although this gets us somewhere, it doesn’t get us far enough. Mere loss is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a pen or an old sweater, I am not experiencing any grief. If I have any emotional reaction at all, it will be a slight ripple of annoyance. Perhaps we should add that for there to be grief we must lose something we care about or love, but, again, this is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a book I really like or don’t get a dream job I applied for, what I experience is frustration or disappointment, sadness perhaps, but not grief.

What sets grief apart is how deeply the loss reaches into the fabric of your life: grief begins where your identity is disrupted. What is lost in the case of grief is not just some concrete, historical object, but a cluster of (future) possibilities that are tightly woven into your sense of identity, life structure or experiential world. When they go, you don’t just lose something: you lose a version of yourself, your life is turned upside down, and you come to inhabit, in a real sense, a different world. This is why death is grief’s most extreme instance, rather than its only one. When someone we love dies, every possibility – not only our own possibilities with them, but their possibilities too – is wiped out. As Matthew Ratcliffe and Louise Richardson, academic philosophers at the University of York, put it in their paper ‘Grief Over Non-Death Losses: A Phenomenological Perspective’ (2023):

Grief is thus distinctive insofar as it involves recognising and comprehending the implications of lost possibilities for the structure of one’s life or world, and – over time – coming to reorganise one’s life accordingly.

This reorganisation is not merely cognitive. It lives in many other places: in the body (the hand that still reaches for the phone to text someone who no longer answers your messages), in how you experience your surroundings (the café you used to visit together that now feels alien or even hostile), or in your autobiographical memories (the shared joke that simply doesn’t land with other people).
‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to’

My mother is still alive. No one has died: there is no concrete, historical object that has been pulled beyond my grasp. But a whole set of possibilities that had been woven into the structure of my life and world, all bound up with having a mother who was present, responsive, good enough – those are gone. It has become impossible to call her and poke that mind of hers, so unusually free and unusually deep.

The same goes for my father. Sure, he survived the stroke. But the man whose restless mind needed to cycle to make his thoughts liquid – the future I had with that man, the shared cycling trips in the south of France, the conversations that needed repetitive, cyclical movement to come alive – that future was negated. The same structure holds for the woman whose disappearance collapsed an experiential world that felt like a home I had only just found, and for the academic identity I had built over almost two decades. As other vocations began to call more insistently, a single, all-consuming way of being in the world – the thinker, the life of the mind, the person whose future would be organised around reading and writing – loosened its hold.

The case that makes this way of thinking about grief most compelling, though, is one where there is no concrete object of loss at all. Ratcliffe and Richardson’s central example is involuntary childlessness – grief for a child who never was, a future that was imagined, anticipated and deeply woven into one’s sense of self, but that never materialised. Here, no one died and no one left. There is nothing tangible to point to: no grave, no anniversary, no recorded name, no memorial service, no shared practices to give words or meaning to the loss. And yet, as one respondent in their study put it: ‘No one can understand what it’s like to carry this loss. In their minds, no baby meant no loss.’ Another respondent simply called their grief by its name: ‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to.’ And a third spoke, chillingly, of ‘the death of a future life’.
They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience

‘No baby meant no loss.’ Many forms of non-death loss are what the family therapist Pauline Boss calls ‘ambiguous loss’. These are losses without clear boundaries, without a definite beginning or end – cases where someone is physically present but psychologically gone, or physically gone but psychologically still there. Think of an Alzheimer’s patient whose self has been erased by the disease or of a soldier missing in action. Because many non-death losses are ambiguous, the grief that follows them is not openly acknowledged, socially validated or publicly mourned – what the grief scholar Kenneth Doka has called ‘disenfranchised grief’.

Those whose grief is disenfranchised because their losses are ambiguous don’t just lack scripts or rituals or traditions. They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience. When we lack the concepts to name what it is like to be us, what it is we are going through, we suffer what the philosopher Miranda Fricker calls a ‘hermeneutical injustice’ – an inability to make our own experience intelligible to ourselves and to others. This is not because we are confused, but because the shared language or conceptual apparatus – the frameworks we use to make sense of ourselves – hasn’t caught up. As two of Ratcliffe and Richardson’s respondents put it: ‘It took me a while to understand that what I was feeling was grief’; ‘I never realised this was grief until I found others in a similar situation.’

The same happened to me: when the magical stranger disappeared, my loss was ambiguous – she still existed, we were never officially together, I had another partner – and my grief went into hiding. In a culture where the end of a relationship is ‘just a breakup’ and monogamy is the unspoken rule, I lacked the rituals to digest the grief and the hermeneutical resources to conceptualise and communicate what had happened to me. For ‘self-interpreting animals’ like us, in the words of the philosopher Charles Taylor, the result is that we end up in the dark, as strangers to ourselves.

The narrowing of grief to bereavement is more than a conceptual mistake. It does real damage. What the writer and grief counsellor Stephen Levine called ‘unattended sorrow’ doesn’t dissolve but goes underground, hiding in the shadows, later resurfacing as unexpected symptoms. I have been there. A mechanical tightness in the chest and a hard belly, like wearing a harness to brace against life. Harrowing dreams. Attempts to numb what is too painful to feel alone. And, worst of all, cynicism and a slow erosion of trust. Not just in other people, but in your own feelings, your own intuitions about the depth, sustainability and future of any new connection. When no one around you recognises your grief, you begin to wonder whether you were wrong to feel it at all.

Sigmund Freud understood this, though he read it as pathology. In the essay ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ (1917), he contended that grief is healthy and normal, but only if it is intelligible and bounded. The job of mourning, he argued, is to detach you from the lost object and reinvest your emotional energy elsewhere. If you can’t complete that job, if the loss is unclear or unnamed or ambiguous, you are no longer mourning. Instead, you are suffering from an illness called melancholia. For Freud, grief that cannot do its work calcifies into something darker, something more elusive.
If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to themselves

But the damage runs deeper than that. When we cannot grieve a loss, we lose something else along with it: the chance to register what mattered to us. Grief is how we come to know what we loved in the presence of its absence. Or as the psychotherapist and grief worker Francis Weller puts it in The Wild Edge of Sorrow (2015):

Grief and love are sisters, woven together from the beginning. Their kinship reminds us that there is no love that does not contain loss and no loss that is not a reminder of the love we carry for what we once held close.
