Your grief tells you that you had the courage to love, that you allowed someone or something else to enter ‘the core of [your] being and find a home in [your] heart’. If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to what they loved and valued, which is to say that you deny them access to themselves. You don’t just rob them, then, of their love; you also rob them of self-knowledge.

The tradition I spent most of my life in – the lineage of Western thinkers who asked how a human being should live – was the first place I looked to understand what was happening to me. These thinkers had a lot to say about grief, but most of it was suspicious and sceptical. Plato believed a good man is the most self-sufficient of all, and least shaken by loss. In the Phaedo, Socrates’ wife Xanthippe is led away wailing before the philosophy can begin, and towards the end of the dialogue, Socrates rebukes his weeping friends for behaving like women. A similar sentiment can be found among the Stoics. Epictetus, in the Enchiridion, compares the loss of a wife or child to a jug breaking. And Marcus Aurelius, who lost many of his own children, reminds himself in his Meditations not to pray that he might keep his child, but to pray that he might not fear losing him.

Behind this way of thinking lies an expensive belief: that attachment is a liability, and that a wise person – someone who has figured out how to live the best possible life – does not need anything that can be taken away from him. If grief is love with nowhere to go, a tradition that treated such love as an error was never going to know what to do with it.

Christianity kept the verdict the ancients had arrived at. In his Confessions (397-400 CE), Saint Augustine looks back on his devastation after a friend’s death, and diagnoses it as a spiritual mistake: ‘Why had that grief penetrated me so easily and so deeply, if not because I had poured out my soul onto the sand, loving someone who would die as if he never would?’ Baruch Spinoza – not religious in any conventional sense of the word – reached the same conclusion. Sadness, he writes in his Ethics (1677), is the mind’s move to a lesser perfection, a loss of its power to act. This means it can never be a good in itself, and its typical source is too much love for things that are impermanent. The cure for grief – and this puts him squarely back into the ancient intellectualist tradition – is understanding: the moment it dawns on us that what we lost could never have been kept, our grief will relax.
The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder

Arthur Schopenhauer, unlike many before him, did not despise grief. In The World as Will and Representation (1818), he values sorrow for one reason only: great personal suffering breaks the will and leads to self-renunciation (Selbstverneinung). Grief is worth having, then, because it has the power to cure us of wanting the world at all, which means that, in the end, he is not so far from the thinkers who came before him. A good life, for all of them, is a matter of loosening our attachments to what is impermanent and fragile.

What began as a doctrine of philosophers leaked into the wider culture. In his landmark study Death, Grief, and Mourning in Contemporary Britain (1965), the anthropologist Geoffrey Gorer found that mourning was increasingly seen as ‘a weakness, a self-indulgence, a reprehensible bad habit instead of as a psychological necessity’. In the 1970s, the historian Philippe Ariès traced the same shift across the industrial West: death, once familiar, had become shameful, something to be hidden. Meanwhile, medicine had entered the debate. In 1961, the psychiatrist George Engel asked, half provocatively, whether grief was a disease. In 2000, the philosopher Stephen Wilkinson answered: yes. In one of academic philosophy’s leading journals, he argued that even normal, healthy grief qualifies as a mental disorder because it meets the standard definition of one. Like all mental disorders, it involves significant distress and interrupts normal functioning. In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders removed the clause that had excluded the recently bereaved from receiving a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Then, in 2022, the revised edition added prolonged grief disorder, whose possible symptoms include identity disruption, such as the feeling that part of oneself has died. The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder – though, tellingly, only when someone has actually died.

But the Western tradition had it backwards. Suppressing, eradicating, denying or pathologising grief doesn’t protect the good life; it sabotages human flourishing by cutting us off from the things we love. More than that, it cuts us off from each other. Grief named and disclosed is grief that can be met, grief that can be placed between you and another person, where the two of you can look at it and hold it together. That shared vulnerability lets one person recognise another in their common humanity. Grief, as Weller reminds us, was never meant to be carried alone; it was meant to be held and processed by a whole village. Strip it of its name and you strip people of the possibility of being seen in their loss, of discovering that the wound they thought was theirs alone is in fact shared by those around them.

Recently, while in the Netherlands, I visited the Kröller-Müller Museum with my father, the same father whose future was negated by a stroke. I looked at him from a distance, the man who once built his life around cycling – to France, to Rome, to Spain’s Santiago de Compostela – now hunched behind his rollator. We stood together in front of Vincent van Gogh’s painting At Eternity’s Gate (1890): an old man, face buried in his fists, clearly hurting. A sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man painted by a sorrowful man. Years before he painted it, when he first drew the same figure for a lithograph, Van Gogh wrote that there can be an ‘unutterably moving’ quality, ‘something precious, something noble’, in the expression of an old man like that.

I didn’t know my father loved Van Gogh as much as I do. We stood there for a long time – somehow in contact with the magic of grief – and something opened up between us that had no name but felt important, exquisitely alive. We didn’t talk about my mother, or how our family had unravelled, or what the stroke had taken from him. We didn’t have to. The painting said what neither of us could.

items.title: What cooperatives for an anticapitalist peace look like | Aeon Essays
items.description: When I was seven years old, my family was forced to flee escalating violence. We left Bakur – a Kurdish region in what is currently southeastern Turkey – for a city further west, where we worked in Turkish fields, living in a tent until we could save up to ren
items.author: Azize Aslan
paragraphs: When I was seven years old, my family was forced to flee escalating violence. We left Bakur – a Kurdish region in what is currently southeastern Turkey – for a city further west, where we worked in Turkish fields, living in a tent until we could save up to rent a house on the city margins, in a neighbourhood with no electricity or road access. Those are some of my earliest memories of everyday violence against people like me.

For centuries, my ancestors had lived in relative harmony with other communities. But, with the emergence of modern nation-states in the region, Kurdistan – the traditional homeland of the Kurds – was fractured into southeastern Turkey, northern Iraq, northwestern Iran, and northeastern Syria. A violent assimilation was imposed upon us. For more than a century, Kurdish people have been denied recognition as a nation, their language banned, erased from maps, stripped of citizenship rights, and dispossessed of their lands. For my generation, therefore, freedom was never an abstract political matter; armed struggle was often seen as a necessity to achieve it. Even so, national liberation movements always sought dialogue with the states they fought against. I grew up inside that insistence, carrying the hope of a dignified peace.

In 2013, after almost three decades of war, peace talks were held between the Turkish state and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), which first sought an independent Kurdish state and, later, autonomy and increased political and cultural rights for Kurds within Turkey. In 2015, these collapsed. War returned to Kurdistan and, with it, the persecution of everyone who had staked something on that possibility of peace. This included me. I was a doctoral student at the time, researching economic autonomy in Kurdistan, and it became clear that this work would no longer be tenable in the new political climate. I moved to Latin America, to complete my doctoral studies and study revolutionary movements in that part of the world, grappling all the while with a question that had become inseparable from my own existence: how could peace be built in Kurdistan?

The academic literature on peace told me I might find an answer in Guatemala. Between 1960 and 1996, civil war had ravaged the country, killing more than 200,000 people and displacing more than a million – more than a 10th of the total population. The conflict – which began as an uprising against extreme inequality, particularly in land ownership, and systemic discrimination against the Maya people – had turned the state into a counterinsurgency apparatus, powered by paramilitary death squads and a doctrine of the ‘internal enemy’ that erased the line between combatant and civilian. Against this backdrop, the Acuerdo de Paz Firme y Duradera (Agreement on a Firm and Lasting Peace) was both celebrated and touted as innovative when it was signed in 1996. The agreement broke ground by confronting the past directly: the Commission for Historical Clarification investigated the atrocities committed during the civil war, most of them attributable to the state, and, unusually, partly as a result of its findings, heads of state were later tried for war crimes.

But it was soon apparent that the peace accord had failed to address the problems that led to the conflict in the first place. The guerilla fighters who returned to their villages – or who had to reinvent themselves in cities where no one was waiting for them – found intact the system they had been unable to transform through armed struggle: poverty. Today, Guatemala remains one of the most unequal countries in Latin America vis-à-vis class, ethnicity and gender. The deepest wound of the war – land tenure – was never resolved: no equitable land redistribution took place after the 1996 accords. In fact, as the World Bank researchers Caroline Moser and Cathy McIlwaine have noted: ‘Guatemala has become a substantially more violent country since the end of the internal armed conflict.’

One ex-combatant had joined the insurgency as a 13-year-old and stayed in the mountains until the peace accord was signed. I met him in 2017, more than 20 years after the formal end to the war, at the community radio project he had built near Xela, in the western highlands of Guatemala. ‘Despite the deaths and the hardship of the war, I never cried,’ he told me. ‘But the day the war ended, I cried – because I didn’t know how to live in peace: I had no home, no job, no trade. And I asked myself: what now?’
Peace, as currently practised, doesn’t break the cycle of injustice that leads to war in the first place

I had come to Guatemala searching for an answer to my own political and existential preoccupations but it was the ex-combatant’s question – What now? – that stayed with me, an accusation directed at the very concept of peace he had been promised.

Guatemala is not an anomaly in this regard. Since the end of the Cold War, more than 30 comprehensive peace agreements have been signed around the world but few, if any, have succeeded in building a durable peace. Accords signed under the dominant peacebuilding paradigm focus almost exclusively on stopping direct violence through ceasefires, weapons handovers, disarmament, individual reintegration, all on the assumption that democratic institutions and free markets will naturally produce lasting peace. But peace, as currently practised, doesn’t break the cycle of injustice that leads to war in the first place.

The sociologist Johan Galtung, often described as the founder of peace and conflict studies, distinguished between ‘negative peace’ – the absence of direct violence – and ‘positive peace’, which requires dismantling the structures of injustice that fuel conflict. The typical approach to peace in post-conflict contexts is encapsulated in the United Nations’ classic disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration model, first implemented by its peacekeeping operations in El Salvador in 1989 and used in more than 30 countries since. Under this strategy, former combatants are required to surrender their weapons and disband their command structures, and are entitled to short-term stipends and training that will facilitate their reintegration into civilian economic life. This approach was also implemented in Guatemala.

But what neither Galtung nor other sophisticated theorists of a liberal framework for peace tend to question is whether capitalist relations of production can lead to peace when this is itself a structural source of violence. They propose reforms, redistribution, greater inclusion – but all within the same system that armed struggles in places like Guatemala sought to transform. As a sociologist interested in revolutionary social movements, what I have observed in my fieldwork in Guatemala, Colombia and northern Syria has led me to a more radical conclusion: real peace requires building economies that operate on an entirely different logic from that of capital – not just in postwar communities but more widely, because we all need more peace in our daily lives.

Cooperatives are one mechanism through which a different economic logic, one more conducive to a durable peace, can take root. In the language of the International Cooperative Alliance – an association established in 1895 when the concept, while as old as time itself, seemed to be gaining traction in Europe – cooperatives are collective entities established by people who come together to address common economic and social needs. They are founded on principles of democracy and autonomy, and built on voluntary participation and solidarity. From the Rochdale weavers of northern England in 1844 – often regarded as the forebears of modern cooperatives – to present-day credit unions, the cooperative movement has produced both genuinely emancipatory experiments and organisations that simply reproduce market logic under a different name. Cooperativism is also central to democratic confederalism, a political theory put forth by Abdullah Öcalan, one of the PKK’s founding members. It was through reading Öcalan that I became interested in the emancipatory potential of cooperatives.

A form of self-determination oriented towards the autonomy of all peoples, particularly women, democratic confederalism proposes a structure of governance organised from the bottom up. In Öcalan’s paradigm, cooperatives are the means through which an economy in service of these principles – communal, ecological, feminist – might be built. The cooperatives that interest me, therefore, have three defining characteristics: they are part of broader social movements and territorial struggles; they prioritise meeting collective needs over the accumulation of capital; and they challenge not just economic exploitation but also the patriarchy, racism, colonialism and statism entwined with capitalism. Such cooperatives are the building blocks of what I call an ‘anticapitalist peace’ – a peace not satisfied with the silencing of arms, nor with positive peace that doesn’t challenge capitalist logic, but one that transforms the economic relations at the root of violence. I have encountered two cases that demonstrate this concretely, in two different parts of the world.

In 2014, as Syria was disintegrating under the weight of a brutal civil war, something unusual happened in the country’s north and east. The Kurdish people – after a century of systemic oppression – declared de facto democratic autonomy in the territories they began to control. Instead of declaring a new nation-state, however, they set up a system of assemblies, communes, cantons and cooperatives that sought to reorganise social life from below, under principles of democratic confederalism. This project was formalised as the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria, better known as Rojava.
Everyone debated and made decisions about their neighbourhood, their communities, their families

By the time I arrived in early 2018, the project’s economic architecture – in service of a social economy that prioritised social, ecological and collective goals over profit maximisation – was already in place. I’d come to Rojava for doctoral research but also because it was the first time Kurds were putting democratic confederalism into practice and building cooperatives as part of a revolutionary movement. I wanted to witness that process myself, and to tell the world that an anticapitalist economy was possible. By then, half a million hectares of land had been communalised with collective-use rights, and cooperatives had sprung up in every town. Women’s economic committees are central to Öcalan’s argument that a communal economy should be guided by knowledge preserved by women over the course of capitalism’s development and spread, precisely because women think (or have typically had to think) about collective need and care. They were introducing the model to their communities with the slogan ‘one cooperative for every commune’.

Upon my arrival, what I found most immediately striking was not the scale of the project but the transformation of everyday time. In Rojava, people typically work until 2.30 pm, return home to eat and rest, then go out again at 5 pm – not to work more hours, but to take part in an assembly: of the cooperative, the commune, the women’s congress or the municipality, where everyone debated and made decisions about their neighbourhood, their communities, their families. Almost no one chose to stay at home. This organisation of time was a radical departure from the exhaustion that capitalism imposes seemingly everywhere else, where punishing schedules and precarity systematically prevent people from having any say over their own lives, leaving the state or the market as the only actor capable of making decisions about the collective.

Karl Marx called it alienated labour: work that doesn’t express human capacities but instead exhausts them, that turns both body and time into commodities. This form of violence produces no visible corpses, no headlines, but something essential is destroyed all the same: the possibility of deciding over one’s own life. What do I produce? For whom? How do I want to live? Under capitalism, such questions are answered not by people but by the market. In Rojava, people sought to answer these questions collectively – What do we produce? For whom do we produce? How do we produce? – in assemblies and other public fora, and established cooperatives accordingly.

In the commune assemblies that I attended, people deliberated these questions in relation to electricity, grain and bread. Answering ‘How many loaves will we produce?’ required knowing how many families ate bread and how much bread they typically consumed. But ‘How will we produce it?’ demanded something else entirely: the founding of a bread cooperative that reversed a belief – ‘We are a society that no longer knows how to make bread’ – born of what many considered the Syrian state’s colonial-era ‘prohibition’ on baking one’s own bread. Strictly speaking, no formal prohibition existed; rather, state subsidy programmes and a ration-card system for wheat and flour made people dependent on cheap, state-distributed bread, which undermined the practice of baking at home. To want to return to older methods was to have to relearn them, to recover knowledge that had often been taken away deliberately.

Then there was the question of milk, from a cooperative built to raise animals: should it go to the children first, to the neighbours, or should it become the basis of a yogurt factory? Answers to each had to be found. In other words, as communes debated how to produce to meet their needs, they were never simply weighing inputs against outputs; they were reaching for an economy grounded in anticolonial practice and in an ethical distribution of the surplus. Everyone who lived in the commune took part in these debates – the differences of political opinion, religious belief and ethnic identity that had been named as causes of Syria’s civil war were not, here, a source of conflict or division. They became, instead, the commune’s social wealth, raw material from which richer, more varied answers and solutions could be found.

Equally central to the project was its feminist dimension. Rojava’s social economy is based on a principle that mainstream economics – and most Left movements – have historically ignored: reproductive and care work, performed predominantly by women, is not a secondary complement to the economy, but its foundation. When that work remains invisible and confined to the domestic sphere, women cannot partake in political life and are unable to participate in the assemblies that build autonomy. Rojava’s social economy promoted the socialisation of such work through cooperatives where women could participate without commodifying their labour. Across Kurdistan, for instance, women have always prepared preserves for the turn of the seasons: cheeses, pickled vegetables, dried produce, ground spices. Done alone, for one’s own family, this work was never counted as economic activity, even though it catered to a large share of collective need. These preserves aren’t just food, either: they carry memory, culture, the rhythm of the land’s cycles. The cooperatives built around them safeguard that inherited knowledge and turn it into a shared capacity, allowing women to produce for their families and communities, and exchange or sell the surplus to meet other needs.

I found this to be deeply intuitive: if the organisation of the economy is itself the organisation of life, then transforming the economy ceases to be a distant or abstract struggle, instead becoming a concrete way of inhabiting the world daily. This socialisation is not incidental or complementary to peace; it is a structural condition of peace.
Political autonomy is destroyed by military force; cultural identity is granted as a gesture of tolerance

What I witnessed in Rojava was something I had rarely seen in post-conflict contexts: peace built not as the absence of war – because war continues in Rojava – but as a way of daily life. Historically, millions of people were living a process of true self-governance, with their identities reconstituted and their voices active in collective decision-making. To build anticapitalist peace, Rojava shows, negative peace is not indispensable. The form of social organisation is what matters.

Today, this social organisation is at an inflexion point. At the beginning of 2026, Syrian government forces, jihadist groups and Turkish-backed militias launched a large-scale offensive on Kurdish-administered territories, forcing the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) to withdraw from the Arab territories they had administered for years, falling back to the original Kurdish heartland of Rojava. A ceasefire agreement signed at the end of January required the SDF to formally cede key territories, renounce strategic oil fields, and integrate individually into the Syrian army, without recognition as an autonomous force. For many within the movement, this amounted to capitulation: the surrender of 14 years of revolutionary construction under threat of a war of extermination.

What the Damascus government offered in return was telling: recognition of Kurds as a cultural minority – the right to speak their language, to preserve certain identity expressions – but no autonomous Kurdish-language education system, no constitutional recognition of self-determination, no structure of self-governance whatsoever. Political autonomy is destroyed by military force; cultural identity is granted as a gesture of tolerance. This is the characteristic hypocrisy of state multiculturalism: erasing real power while preserving folklore.

This development does not invalidate what Rojava built – on the contrary, it makes it more urgent to understand. It shows that anticapitalist peace faces not only the direct violence of war, but also the structural violence of the state and the market, which seek to reclaim territories where people organised themselves differently. And it demonstrates that this form of organisation was real enough, threatening enough to the established order, to be deemed worthy of destruction.

Despite the current situation in Rojava, the sense of everyday peace that cooperativism fosters among and within communities that I observed over the course of my fieldwork has led me to reflect more specifically on the role of cooperatives in post-conflict and peacebuilding contexts. In fact, for the past two years, peace negotiations are once again underway between the PKK and the Turkish state; one of my aims in writing this essay is to make the case for cooperatives to be on the agenda for a potential peace agreement. It is in this context that I became interested in the role cooperatives have played in Colombia, following the peace agreement in 2016 between the Colombian government and the FARC-EP, the country’s largest rebel group.

The accord, signed after more than half a century of armed conflict, was described by the Kroc Institute for International Peace Studies at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana as the most comprehensive of the 34 agreements signed worldwide since the end of the Cold War. Among its notable innovations was a proposal for the collective reincorporation of ex-combatants through cooperatives and other associative forms of a social economy.
The project must sustain itself within the capitalist market even as it attempts to transcend it

During negotiations, the FARC-EP had challenged the UN’s classic disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration model. The FARC’s primary argument against this model was that it prioritised individual adaptation to the labour market and that this amounted to accepting the unjust order they had spent decades fighting. Instead, they proposed ‘reincorporation’ – a form of integration that recognised the political agency of signatories and their intention to continue the struggle for social transformation, now through civilian means.

This is how ECOMÚN (Economías Sociales del Común, or Social Economies of the Commons) came to be in 2017: a federation comprising approximately 6,200 peace-agreement signatories and 154 organisations across 26 of Colombia’s 33 administrative divisions. I attended its governing council assembly in 2024. What I found most significant about ECOMÚN was that none of its cooperatives – for coffee, cattle-ranching, fish-farming, textiles, rural tourism, to name a few – were composed exclusively of ex-combatants. Rather, they worked alongside peasant farmers, Indigenous peoples, Afro-Colombians – local communities who share histories of exclusion and dispossession. ‘We have fostered connections between people,’ Juan Camilo Londoño, ECOMÚN’s executive director, told me. ‘There are even organisations that are not signatories but have joined ECOMÚN.’ Internally, the movement describes this as a ‘pedagogy of peace’: the transformation of former war territories into spaces where people on opposing sides of the conflict build productive projects together and, in doing so, weave new social relations.

Yet, as its own leaders acknowledge with clear-eyed honesty, ECOMÚN operates under a fundamental contradiction: the accord did not guarantee the anticapitalist transformation that genuine peace would have required. The question of land tenure – the heart of the FARC’s struggle for decades – was negotiated but never translated into terms that guaranteed real agrarian reform. The project must sustain itself within the capitalist market even as it attempts to transcend it. Its viability depends on volatile political conditions and on international cooperation, which frequently imposes its own neoliberal logics. And because it emerged from the peace agreement, it operates within Colombia’s legal framework and under direct oversight from state agencies. ECOMÚN, in other words, cannot claim Rojava’s autonomy: it is woven into state institutions rather than built in parallel to – or against – them. What self-management it achieves is real, but limited.

What Rojava and ECOMÚN have in common is not their context – one is a revolution in the midst of war; the other is a post-conflict process within a capitalist state – but their wager: that peace is built from below, when people recover control over their time and territories, their cultures and economies.

Both cases also demonstrate that real peace is inseparable from anticolonial and antiracist struggles. For decades, the Kurdish people were denied recognition as an ethnicity, forbidden from speaking their language, and dispossessed of everything that belonged to them: their identity, but also their subsistence economies, their ways of organising themselves, their ways of inhabiting the land. In Rojava, therefore, cooperatives are spaces where the social fabric torn apart by decades of forced assimilation is reconstituted, and where power over one’s own life is recovered. Meanwhile, in Colombia, ECOMÚN’s cooperatives are organised in territories where peasants, Indigenous peoples and Afro-Colombian communities have been, over centuries, systematically dispossessed of their lands. The pedagogy of peace that emerges from these initiatives goes beyond reconciling former enemies – it reconstitutes collective identities that the nation-state and the market had reduced to subalternity, and undoes the manufactured hostility between groups set against each other through systemic poverty and violence.

But it would be a mistake to read these experiences only as responses to extreme situations – as solutions for those living in war zones or conditions of severe poverty. That reading reproduces, perhaps without intending to, the very logic it criticises: the idea that the problem lies over there, in places that have not yet reached capitalist ‘normality’, and that the solution lies in economic development that will better integrate them into the logic of the market.
Peace is not a state reached by signing a document but a way of living together each day

The rhythm of life I observed in Rojava – working until 2.30-3 pm, then going to the assemblies – is precisely what capitalism denies to most people in the world, not just those living in conflict zones. The urban worker who leaves home before dawn and returns at night, too exhausted to speak with their children; the woman whose care work is invisible to the economy and the state, who never rests because her work never ends; the debt-ridden professional who works to pay for what they need to keep working; the young person who sees no horizon in the future; the children who grow up without spaces to play. All of them experience forms of violence that have no name in peace debates but are deeply felt in daily life.

The Guatemalan ex-combatant’s question – What now? – is a question that might be asked not only by someone who survived war but also anyone who works without knowing why, who consumes without feeling satisfied, and who lives with the sense that something essential has been taken from them. Cooperatives are not the only possible answer to that question, but they do propose something that the dominant peacebuilding paradigm – and the economic system that sustains it – systematically refuses to admit: that peace is not a state reached by signing a document but a way of living together each day, of recovering self-determination over one’s own time, needs and relationships, of asking the question How do we want to live? and believing that it can be answered through collective deliberation, by people themselves, without bosses or owners.

This is what the Guatemalan ex-combatant did not find when he came down from the mountains, and what the cooperatives of Rojava and Colombia are trying to build – under very different conditions, with enormous contradictions, but with a clarity about the goal that peace agreements signed in conference rooms rarely possess. Galtung proposed that we dismantle the structures of violence and called what remained ‘positive peace’ – but an anticapitalist peace does not just settle for the absence of structural violence, it dares to ask what should take its place. And it answers with bread baked by hand, milk shared before it is sold, assembly meetings where people still have time and energy to decide. It rests on a form of togetherness in which life itself is harmonious and worth wanting, built each day, from below, through real practice.
This essay is supported by a grant from the Open Society Foundations.

items.title: AnOther Dish: Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba’s Oysters
items.description: The couple behind east London’s modern British restaurant, Waterhouse, share a hot and tart recipe for dressing creamy Lindisfarne oysters
items.author: Rose Dodd
paragraphs: The couple behind east London’s modern British restaurant, Waterhouse, share a hot and tart recipe for dressing creamy Lindisfarne oysters
The food we return to can say so much about us – AnOther Dish invites chefs and notable food lovers to share a recipe of personal significance

“Lindisfarne – sometimes called Holy Island – is a tiny island just off the northeast coast of Northumberland. We spent some time there when we first got together. As the tide comes in it completely covers the causeway you take to get there – sometimes you’ll see cars abandoned along the road, some swept out to sea. We once spent a night on Lindisfarne and drove right to the edge of the island to watch as the tide came in. You feel very remote, detached from the mainland, with no option of returning until the tide goes out again – it feels strangely natural, there’s a purity to life there.

“We visited a lovely little pub while we were there – that’s where we were first introduced to Lindisfarne oysters. Oysters are amazing – they filter and clean the sea. Every oyster has its own flavour profile, and these ones are spectacularly creamy. That’s why they balance so nicely with something sharp. The classic way to dress an oyster is with a mignonette or lemon juice, but it’s nice to play around with different ingredients to see how you can elevate the oyster while respecting and preserving its pure flavour – all without overwhelming it. You want the natural ingredients to speak for themselves.

“Oysters always feel special in a restaurant, don’t they? And even more so at home – served on a bed of ice, with an aperitif or a glass of something bubbly. We serve our Lindisfarne oysters with a cucumber, apple and sorrel granita, and finish them with a homemade green chilli oil. This dish has evolved over the years, but it’ll always remind us of the beginning of our relationship.” – Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba

Co-founded by husband and wife Gabriel Waterhouse and Trish Wakaimba, Waterhouse is a modern British restaurant and bar on east London’s Ezra Street. Just metres from Columbia Road, hidden behind its own gated garden in what was once a Victorian Warehouse, the space is reminiscent of a rural farmhouse. The restaurant seats 24 amid an open kitchen, minimalist steel surface tops, exposed timberwork, parquet flooring and mid-century oak furniture. Welcoming and cosy, dining at Waterhouse feels more akin to eating at someone’s home.

Seasonal ingredients are central to the 8- and 11-course tasting menus, sourced from across the UK and grown in the restaurant’s own garden, they draw on the culinary traditions of northeast England, Scotland and the northern coastline. Dishes include: Northumbrian rye bread, smoked haddock, and singing hinnies with Laphroaig cream. Seafood comes from the northern waters – hand-dived scallops, creel-caught lobster and said Lindisfarne oysters – and meat and game from the Lake District, Yorkshire and the Highlands. A larder approach makes preservation, fermentation, pickling and smoking key. “The restaurant has a big larder of misos, malt kojis and garums, made with things like wild garlic or seeds that we’ve foraged during the year,” says Waterhouse. On the drinks menu British grain spirits are infused with ingredients from the garden: a mugwort negroni, foraged from Hackney; a fig leaf martini; a homegrown rosemary vesper; and a sorrel margarita.

Waterhouse grew up in Northumberland and has been working as a chef for 15 years. In 2023, he earned his title as Champion for the Best Dressed Oyster at the London Oyster Championship. Wakaimba, an entrepreneur, also has a background in hospitality, coming from a family of restaurateur-hoteliers. The couple met on Waterhouse’s first weekend in London, having moved to the city the summer after university. “Set up by a friend, he came to my flat for dinner on a Saturday,” says Wakaimba. “He really didn’t have much time to look around.” Waterhouse was due to start working for Herbert Berger the following Monday. As is often the case in kitchens, so famously fast-paced, the working environment was intense. “Those crazy hours were never sustainable,” says Wakaimba. “I think Gabe knew all along he wanted to have something of his own.”

Their inaugural project together was a series of intimate supper clubs before the Covid-19 pandemic hit, when they started making delivery meal kits, with multiple courses, paired wines, even playlists. As normalcy resumed, so did their hospitality. In September this year Waterhouse, the restaurant, opened its doors, marking a new chapter. “Through all of that we built this lovely community and we’ve been able to see what works and what doesn’t – those years felt like learning, and it’s really informed where we are now.” “We shape our ideas together,” says Waterhouse. “Everything is passed back and forth between us, and that’s what the space feels like and reflects. It’s like a testament of our compatibility.”

For their chosen dish, Waterhouse and Wakaimba combine the pure, creaminess of a Lindisfarne oyster with the sharp acidity of pickled cucumber, served in the oyster’s shell with a tart sorrel and apple granita, and a chilli oil. Here, they share the recipe.
Lindisfarne Oysters, with Pickled Cucumber, Sorrel Granita and Green Chilli Oil
- 6 fresh Lindisfarne oysters
- 100ml white wine vinegar
Cucumber and Sorrel Granita
- 150ml fresh cucumber juice, extracted with the skin on
- 20–25g fresh sorrel leaves
- Fresh lemon juice, to taste

1. To make the pickled cucumber, combine the white wine vinegar, water, sugar and fennel seeds in a saucepan. Bring to a boil, then strain out the fennel seeds and leave the liquid to cool completely. Cut the cucumber into small, even dice, keeping the skin on. Place in a container and cover with the cooled pickling liquid. Refrigerate for a few hours, ideally 24, before using.

2. For the chilli oil, place the green chillies and pomace oil in a high-speed jug blender with a vented lid that allows heat and steam to escape. Do not use a completely sealed blender, such as a bullet-style blender, as pressure can build up as the mixture heats. Blend continuously for approximately 5–10 minutes, until the mixture reaches 70–80°C. The heat generated by the blender is important to the process. As the temperature rises, the oil will begin to separate from the liquid released by the chillies. Keep the lid secure and the vent unobstructed, following the manufacturer’s guidance for blending hot ingredients. Pass through fine muslin or a J-cloth to collect the green oil. Refrigerate until required. The green chilli paste can be reserved for another recipe.

3. To make the cucumber and sorrel granita, place the cucumber juice, apple juice and sorrel into a blender and mix together until completely smooth, then pass through a fine sieve. Season the strained mixture with salt and a little fresh lemon juice to taste. You want enough acidity to lift the cucumber and apple without overpowering their freshness. Pour into a shallow container and freeze. Once frozen, scrape with a fork to create fine crystals.

4. To prepare the oysters, scrub shells under cold running water to remove any grit or debris. I prefer to open oysters from the front, at the rounded lip of the shell, rather than from the hinge at the back. I find this much easier. Always use an oyster knife, which has a shorter and blunter blade. Hold each oyster firmly on a folded cloth, protecting the hand holding it, and carefully work the tip of the oyster knife between the two shells at the front. Gently twist to open, then slide the blade along the inside of the upper shell to release the muscle. Be gentle. The mistake lots of people make is that it requires a lot of force and it doesn’t. As each oyster is opened, pour its sea water into a clean bowl and reserve it. Remove the oyster from the shell and rinse the flesh carefully in cold water to ensure no small fragments of shell remain. Return the oyster immediately to its reserved liquor and keep chilled until ready to serve.

5. To serve: Remove the oysters from their liquor and cut each into three pieces. Place the three pieces of oyster at the bottom of each serving bowl and arrange a little pickled cucumber around them. Finish with a spoonful of cucumber and sorrel granita immediately before serving. I like to serve the green chilli oil separately in one half of the cleaned oyster shell, resting the shell on top of the bowl. This works particularly well with a small serving bowl. It allows each person to pour the oil over the granita themselves, finishing the dish at the table. You can also place a little yoghurt in the serving bowl for an added creamy tang.
Waterhouse is open at 7A Ezra Street, London, E2 7RH from Friday to Sunday for lunch and dinner. Book a table, here

items.title: Haruki Murakami’s Legendary 70s Tokyo Jazz Club Comes to London
items.description: From 1974 to 1981, and before global literary fame, Haruki Murakami ran a scrappy jazz club in Tokyo’s Sendagaya neighbourhood, resurrected this month at the Barbican
items.author: James Balmont
paragraphs: From 1974 to 1981, and before global literary fame, Haruki Murakami ran a scrappy jazz club in Tokyo’s Sendagaya neighbourhood, resurrected this month at the Barbican
I’m standing beside a flank of colourful vending machines next to a mini car-park near the Tokyo Metropolitan Gymnasium in Sendagaya, Tokyo, peering up at an Italian bistro during a busy lunch hour.

From the outside, there’s little to suggest that there’s more to this place (now known as Amphora) than the plates of spaghetti carbonara and imported wines being served to patrons at pokey wooden tables. But this address was once a source of passion and inspiration for one of the world’s greatest literary figures – and this month, its humble legacy is being celebrated some 6,000 miles away at London’s Barbican Hall.

Between 1977 and 1981, the premises was a jazz café known as Peter Cat – and it was run by the man who, in time, would become the most widely read Japanese novelist in the world. Years before penning classics like Norwegian Wood and Kafka on the Shore, Haruki Murakami spent his days stocking shelves, and his evenings mixing drinks to the sounds of his hundreds of vinyl records. Peter Cat was an expression of a musical passion harboured ever since he’d been “thunderstruck” by an Art Blakey concert in his childhood; it would prove a foundational influence on the entire literary career that followed.

Forty-five years since Murakami closed its doors, Peter Cat lives again this November via three immersive concerts organised with the EFG London Jazz Festival, titled Haruki Murakami’s Jazz at Peter Cat. And one performer from the cultured line-up of Japanese jazz greats is particularly fitting for the occasion: “As a rather irresponsible first-year university student in the spring of 1979, I started working at Peter Cat two or three days a week,” says saxophonist Sachi Hayasaka. “It makes me incredibly happy that such an extraordinary coincidence has brought me back, after all these years, to perform [in its honour] on such a prestigious stage.”

Hayasaka experienced Peter Cat during its twilight years. The original premises was established in a small basement club near Kokubunji Station in 1974, shortly after Murakami left college. There, young jazz musicians and students gathered as Murakami and his wife worked tirelessly in a windowless room, booking bands and washing dishes. It was a labour of love – the young couple reportedly went so deep into debt that, during the winter, they’d snuggle with their cat – the eponymous Peter – so that they wouldn’t have to pay for heating.

After upending to a second location in Sendagaya, though, Peter Cat came into its own. “I still remember the first time I visited the place,” Hayasaka tells AnOther. “One entire wall was made of glass, another was lined with records, and at one end of the wooden counter, there was a small carving of the Cheshire Cat from Alice in Wonderland, with its distinctive, mischievous grin.” Overlooking the neighbourhood’s striking greenery, the café’s big, sunlit windows – still intact today, at the bustling Amphora – ensured the space felt warm and bright. “The day I first visited, there was a live performance by [tenor saxophonist] Takao Uematsu,” Hayasaka continues. “I fell in love with the place immediately.”

Encouraged by a friend from her university’s music club, Hayasaka became a waitress, serving coffee and cheesecake by day to students and couples. By night, “the atmosphere changed”, she recalls, as jazz-heads and literary and publishing figures stopped by to enjoy drinks, music and conversation in the relaxed surroundings.

Murakami, at the time, was “generally a quiet person,” she continues. “He seemed to observe people carefully. But he was always kind to everyone, and had a wonderful sense of humour.” Between lessons on how to chop onions without crying (“you have to chop them quickly!”, he had said), Murakami was encouraging of Hayasaka’s ambitions, lending her albums off the shelves that he felt were conducive to her saxophone practice. “At the time, I was completely absorbed in the music of [John] Coltrane and Jimi Hendrix,” she says. “I thought jazz was supposed to be radical and intense, so I found Stan Getz – one of the artists he’d recommend the most often – a little too gentle for my taste.”

Ultimately, this divergence would foreshadow a greater rupture just six months after Hayasaka started working for Murakami. “My musical activities became increasingly busy, and the journey to Sendagaya began to feel like a burden,” Hayasaka wrote in a recent blog post. “I did something quite terrible. I simply stopped showing up for work without telling anyone.”

A month later, a note in neat, rounded handwriting arrived. “It read: ‘Here is the remainder of your wages’”, she says. “Even after I had treated him so badly, kind Haruki-san had remained considerate and sincere to the very end.”

In truth, Murakami was also being led astray. In 1978, the year prior to Hayasaka’s arrival at Peter Cat, the idea to write a novel had come to the café owner in the middle of a Yakult Swallows baseball match, just 15 minutes walk away from the café at the Meiji Jingu Stadium. “Running a service business … I [had] met all kinds of offbeat people and had some unusual encounters,” he wrote in his 2007 memoir What I Talk About When I Talk About Running. “I ran my jazz club – keeping accounts, scheduling staff, cooking and closing up in the wee hours of the morning – and only then writing at home at the kitchen table until I got sleepy … half an hour here, an hour there … ”

By autumn that year, Murakami had finished his first 200-page work, Hear the Wind Sing. It brought home the Gunzo Prize for New Writers. Hayasaka remembers it as a turning point: “One day, the café seemed unusually busy,” she says. “People who looked like editors kept coming in one after another … until then, I had only seen him quietly working at the counter. I had not even known he was a writer.”

A second novel, Pinball, 1973, followed in 1980, along with a few short stories. Soon after, Murakami opted to pack up shop: “I decided to close the business for a while and concentrate solely on writing,” he wrote, delivering his first full-length novel, A Wild Sheep Chase, in 1982.

By 1987, with the publication of Norwegian Wood, he had become a national sensation. Named after the 1965 Beatles song that marked the first appearance of a sitar in Western music, the book sold over 3.5 million copies in its first year alone.

Peter Cat may have ultimately been left in the wake of thousands of manuscript pages, but the music it played would remain at the core of Murakami’s craft – both guiding his writing practices and frequently appearing in his stories. “My style is as deeply influenced by Charlie Parker’s repeated freewheeling riffs as by F Scott Fitzgerald’s elegantly flowing prose,” he told the New York Times in 2007. “And I still take the quality of continual self-renewal in Miles Davis’s music as a literary model.”

Here in Japan, the café’s legacy can still be traced at Amphora. By the cashier desk, nestled between business cards and wine bottles atop rustic wooden furnishings, sits a Hello Kitty handbell, a framed illustration of the Cheshire Cat, and a box of tissues decorated with whiskery faces – subtle winks to the site’s feline heritage. There’s even a small, easily missed shrine to Murakami by the window, featuring books by, and photos of, the master author.

About an hour’s walk north of its former site in Sendagaya, meanwhile, the so-called ‘Haruki Murakami Library’ at Waseda University – where Murakami studied until 1975 – houses an archive of more than 3,000 books, photographs and artefacts donated by the author, including the piano and chairs from his beloved jazz café, and many of the vinyl records that once played there.

Back in London, documentarians like Philip Arneill – author of the Tokyo Jazz Joints book archive – have joined with production company Serious to ensure that our native celebration will feel as vivid as the original club did in the 1970s. In the absence of any extensive visual documentation of the original site (almost no photos exist today), Arneill’s photography of Japan’s jazz kissa culture has helped inspire the forthcoming Barbican production.

And as Japan-inspired listening bars crop up all across London – from Deptford’s Jazu Bar and Shoreditch’s Seed Library to the Barbican’s own, newly opened Spiritland bar – the influence of institutions like Peter Cat is only becoming more palpable. “Japanese jazz and the culture of jazz cafés is attracting attention all around the world,” Hayasaka agrees, as she packs her bags for the UK. And so the ghost of Peter Cat continues to linger: “I feel deeply grateful,” Hayasaka concludes. “Looking back now, I realise what an extraordinary luxury it was to be there.”
Haruki Murakami’s Jazz at Peter Cat is at the Barbican on 21 and 22 November, as part of EFG London Jazz Festival (13–22 November)

items.title: Death and Entrances
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Susannah Frankel
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
Among the earliest and most famous depictions of a female nude is the Venus of Willendorf.

There are many Venuses, a broad – and obviously retrospective – nomenclature for figurines originating from the Upper Palaeolithic period, dating back 10,000 to 40,000 years. The Venus of Willendorf is carved in oolitic limestone. Standing a mere 11.1 centimetres tall, she is reputedly 30,000 years old. She has swollen breasts and a protuberant belly, both suggestive of pregnancy. Many thousands of words have been written about her. Is she, in fact, pregnant? Is she an ancient fertility doll, designed to be held in the hand of prospective or birthing mothers? Is she not pregnant at all but a symbol of beauty as it was perceived at that time? Also conjecture: the perspective of this Venus and more than a few of her Venus sisters, the fact that she has no facial features, or indeed feet, has led some to surmise that her creator was female – she is a self-portrait. Of course, nothing is proven. The issues this little Venus’s provenance raises, though, seem pertinent now for Harley Weir, whose exploration of the female form – and just the female – including her own, has led to some of the most striking and evocative imagery of the past decade.

In the history of art, depictions of pregnant women are few and far between. They are predominantly seen through the eyes of male artists. Their bodies are either hidden – through the medieval and Renaissance periods it was the fashion for women to wear voluminous clothing – or idealised. The Madonna is the most prevalent of all pregnant females in art history – the mother of all art historical clichés? – and her baby’s conception was immaculate. In myriad portrayals, myriad Annunciations, that purity is signified by the presence of a white dove. Of that same era, for many years critics speculated that the female figure in Jan van Eyck’s The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) was pregnant. Emblems of fertility – a carving of Saint Margaret of Antioch on a chair by the bed, ripe oranges, a symbol of prosperity but also fecundity, on the windowsill – are present in the painting’s background. The fullness of her famous green dress has since been attributed to the extravagance of its fabrication, however. Three-dimensional laser scans of Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa (1503–17) captured some 20 years ago now are not so easily dismissed. A fine gauze veil – or guarnello – seen over her dress, until that point hidden by aged varnish on the painting’s surface, is typical of those worn by soon-to-be or new mothers of that time. Representation of pregnant nudes in classical painting, meanwhile, are likely negative. Titian’s masterpiece Diana and Callisto (1556–59), which hangs in the National Gallery in London, is the best known. Nymph Callisto’s shaming, the revelation of her naked, pregnant body and subsequent fall from chastity, is subject to the goddess Diana’s fierce disapproval. Raped by Jupiter, Callisto was later transformed into a bear by that god’s wife, Juno. Or so the story goes.

A few centuries on, and modern artists from Gustav Klimt to Pablo Picasso and Lucian Freud painted (and sculpted) pregnant women, but always – inevitably – from a distance. Klimt’s Hope paintings, dated 1903 and 1907–08, of his favourite model Herma were executed against her better judgment, and the earlier rendition, portraying her naked surrounded by mythical monsters, caused a scandal. Picasso’s 1950 sculpture La Femme Enceinte was inspired by his partner at the time, Françoise Gilot, who had recently given birth to their second child, Paloma; he used ceramic bowls and pitchers to create the figure’s rounded breasts and stomach. Freud’s portraits of pregnant women, some carrying his own children, were forensic in their attention to detail: the subject as specimen.

It wasn’t until the last century that female artists’ representations of pregnancy began to enter the gallery setting. Paula Modersohn-Becker’s nude self-portrait of an imaginary pregnancy in 1906, Alice Neel’s paintings of pregnant women, clothed and nude, in the Sixties and Seventies and Chantal Joffe’s pregnant self-portraits are impassioned in their bid for reclamation, showing not only pregnancy’s beauty and power but also its complexity. For the first time, there is a sense of women’s alienation from their own bodies antepartum, for their feelings of intense love alongside, and never unreasonably, fear.

Harley Weir is no stranger to the self-portrait. Her 2022 Beauty Papers monograph, dedicated to “all the dolls in the world”, is an unflinchingly visceral – at times grotesque – representation of the tropes of femininity and the preconceptions those raise. Four years on, and ten weeks pregnant, Weir began to regularly take pictures of herself naked or near-naked in the relative privacy of her bedroom. At 32 weeks a further, more studied series was taken, including portraits of Weir, now helped by John Kelleher, her husband and the father of the baby, and of a body double wearing a pregnancy belly and Harley Weir mask. With styling by her friend and longtime collaborator Georgia Pendlebury, these images serve as Weir’s visual response to her physical and emotional transition at a time that may be as challenging as it is joyful. And intimate, but: “The real private self isn’t this though,” she says. “It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait.”
SUSANNAH FRANKEL Do you know the Venus of Willendorf? She’s got no feet. People think a woman may have made her.

HARLEY WEIR Because she’s looking down at her body? I’ve been documenting my pregnancy from week ten and there are a lot of looking-down pictures and also looking up in the mirror. When you’re pregnant there are so many blind spots. My husband helped take many of the pictures for that reason. The series is called Death and Entrances because, from what I’ve read, it’s like an ego death. You’re giving birth but you’re also dying, you change. I felt, physically in this story, as if I was wearing a disguise.

That’s something I think connects back to the Venus of Willendorf, this idea of a woman looking down at a body that is powerful, but also unfamiliar. During pregnancy, your body becomes the most visible thing about you, but at the same time it can feel like it no longer belongs. Here, I don’t have my usual breasts, I don’t have my usual stomach. I felt almost free from the shame of being nude because the bump isn’t me or us.

SF The physical state of pregnancy is extreme. We are taught from an early age to control our bodies and our body image. When you’re pregnant, you surrender that control. Perhaps your body is preparing you for becoming a mother, because once that happens your life is not your own in the same way.

HW Yes, it feels like that. It feels good. I’ve always been self-conscious about my breasts because they were so small. Now they are engorged and full of stretchmarks, but I don’t care who sees them. They’ve become functional objects. And there’s a safety in that. I feel much more at ease. I love being this blob that will bring purpose to someone new and it in turn gives my body purpose, a reason for its irregular shapes that before felt like deformities.
SF Is there any fear involved?

HW There was a lot more at the beginning. But I’m still at the stage where you don’t really know what’s about to hit. I’m in the phase where I feel this is the baby, it’s this bump. But no, the baby is going to come out and rock my world.
SF Have you looked at the way pregnant women are represented in art?
HW I haven’t seen much pregnant art – especially from the past. There’s the Virgin Mary, but we rarely see her pregnant. She didn’t even have sex. The virgin and the mother.
SF There’s that – the Christian ideal – but also some quite violent portrayals.

HW I have to say I can’t think of one classical painting where you see a pregnant woman. Klimt maybe. My mother talks a lot about how, even when she was younger, you had to cover the bump up, you couldn’t show it freely. I feel now we’re having a renaissance for mothers. The mother is more celebrated. I didn’t feel secure enough to be having a kid until now. And I’m getting on. I’ll be 38 when it comes out.
SF People called me a geriatric mother. I was 37.
HW But they’ve changed it now.

HW I would have been, but they stopped using that term recently, which is great. I do think this is an amazing moment for mothers. On Instagram there are so many inspirational women sharing their motherhood stories. Once you get pregnant your algorithm knows and they’re everywhere. So many cool mothers online, which I feel is something you wouldn’t have seen in the early Noughties. Mothers were dismissed or hidden. There was the fear of overpopulation and that having children was bad for the environment,

I used to hear that a lot. Now in the west fewer people are having babies, pregnancy is a positive thing again. It goes in cycles, I suppose. I’ve just finished reading Born [The Untold History of Humanity by Lucy Inglis]. It’s fascinating how attitudes shift. During the Roman Empire, people would kill unwanted babies, by “exposure” – especially girls.
SF In China and Japan they are now rolling out financial incentives to persuade people to have babies.
HW Exactly. First China wasn’t allowing more than one baby. Now there aren’t enough. For now, it feels like we’re in a baby-positive cycle.
SF The death part of the equation is the old you saying goodbye to your old life.

HW And saying hello to the mystery of what is about to begin. I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed.

SF You’ve photographed yourself before. How much of that process is about showing yourself to the world and how much is it about introspection, working out what, in this case, your pregnancy means for you?
“I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed” – Harley Weir

HW My life is already very bump-forward. Wherever I go, it’s the focal point of conversation. It’s hard not to be obsessed by the pregnancy. At one point people argued that because the baby takes so much nutrition, the mother’s brain shrinks by 20 per cent. Now they are calling it rewiring. I’m rewiring. And my way of coping with things is photography – it’s like therapy. It’s a way for me to work out those ideas and also to detach from them. I was thinking how I’m kissing goodbye to this flat-chested girl and becoming a woman. The pregnancy at this stage is visual, the changes are reflected in the mirror. Every Wednesday I read my update that tells me how big the baby is.
SF How big is your baby now?
HW Honeydew melon. You know, it’s so silly. Apparently, there’s a dog one too.

SF How interested are you in the relationship between us as voyeurs and you as the subject? I looked at Beauty Papers. That’s overtly sexual, about fetishising women. This is almost more like you fetishising your own pregnant body.

HW I do think there’s something in the fact that I’m still a sexual being. In old tropes you become a mother and your sexiness was stripped from you. Almost as some kind gesture of respect that we never asked for. That’s what is interesting about fashion. It’s been a way to explore the female – that’s what I do. There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive. So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.

Styling: Georgia Pendlebury. Hair: Alex Brownsell at Streeters using KEUNE and BLEACH LONDON. Make-up: Leana Ardeleanu at Artlist using MAKE UP FOR EVER. Mask: Chaïm Vischel. Manicure: Lauren Michelle Pires using Le Vernis in Garconne and La Crème Main by CHANEL BEAUTY. Set design: Phoebe Shakespeare. Casting: Gabrielle Lawrence for People-File at MiniTitle. Model: Anna Ramfel. Talent: John Kelleher. Studio manager: Melissa Arras. Lighting director: Jordan Lee. Photographic assistants: Chiara Croserio and JJay Johnson. Styling assistants: Ethan Barbara, Michiel Heemskerk and Stoyan Chuchuranov. Hair assistant: Tommy Stayton. Make-up assistant: Gwen Ryan. Set-design assistants: Freya Purkhardt and Keelin Coyle. Production: Partner Films. Executive producer: Kimberly Arms. Producers: Star Santos Hannan and Valeria Rocca. Production assistant: Thea Levine. Special thanks to Ruben Riley Garrett

Charting fashion from the 19th century to the Nineties to now, the stylist Panos Yiapanis combines garments from his own personal archive with pieces from Pieter Mulier’s five-year tenure at Alaïa. The approach connects Yiapanis, Mulier and Azzedine Alaïa himself – all collectors of historical and contemporary fashion – via a shared passion for clothes of the past, present and future.
