items.title: Inside Amanvari, Aman’s extraordinary new Baja California hideaway
items.description: Amanvari means 'peace' and 'water' in Sanskrit. An ethos of seaside tranquility is woven into every aspect of the intimate, 18-key property. Unlike the sprawling resorts in nearby Cabo San Lucas, Aman’s exclusive new Baja California retreat is intentionally sm
items.author: Lindsay Cohn
paragraphs: Amanvari means 'peace' and 'water' in Sanskrit. An ethos of seaside tranquility is woven into every aspect of the intimate, 18-key property. Unlike the sprawling resorts in nearby Cabo San Lucas, Aman’s exclusive new Baja California retreat is intentionally small, with privacy, serenity and connection to nature of equal importance. The landscape drives the design, acting as both the inspiration and the backdrop for a place so at home in its surroundings it feels as though the land and sea might have given permission to build it.

Set within the exclusive Costa Palmas community on Baja California’s East Cape, Amanvari is positioned to escape it all. Aside from Four Seasons Resort Los Cabos at Costa Palmas, a 10-minute drive away, there’s not much around. And that’s exactly the point. The property is wrapped in nature, removed from tourist-trodden Cabo San Lucas, but accessible enough to venture to a buzzy restaurant or bar should the mood strike – though, speaking from personal experience, you’re not going to want to leave the premises, aside from, perhaps, a day trip snorkelling the ancient coral reefs of Cabo Pulmo National Marine Park or an off-road expedition into the Sierra de la Laguna.

The Baja California landscape – soft sand extending into the deep blue Sea of Cortez, swaying palms, towering cardón cacti, arid desert, an estuary and distant mountains – inspired Elastic Architects’ design. The award-winning firm, with initial contributions from Heah & Co., used local elements, embraced minimalism and spotlighted artistic expression – from contemporary Mexican art to ancestral crafts – to create an indoor-outdoor sanctuary with a deep sense of place.

At the heart of the resort is Casa Grande, an open-plan, atrium-like structure perfectly balanced by a restrained neutral palette with views of the ever-changing sky throughout the day and night. It’s also home to one of Amanvari’s most impressive commissions: an intricate, textured dome, inspired by the spiral chambers of an extinct marine microfossil, which took artists Abi and Luisa Calvete of Extra Neutro more than 1,000 hours to create.

To the left, the curved lounge bar is enveloped in earthy materials, still water and rounded edges, fostering a sense of softness and serenity that’s matched by sweeping Baja vistas. Descend the spiral staircase down to the lower level for the panoramic main pool crafted from Caledonia Black granite as well as three dining venues that follow the same nature-led principles.
Amanvari has 18 stilted casitas, which almost appear to float above the trees.

Contemporary rooms are anchored by white concrete, natural limestone and tropical hardwoods, complemented by bespoke furnishings, textiles in sandy hues and original works by Mexican artisans such as exclusive mixed-media pieces by Arozarena de la Fuente and sculptural ceramics by Tomás Díaz of Disciplina Studio.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
The alfresco living spaces are an extension of the interiors – generous terraces with seating areas for morning coffee, and below, heated pools and outdoor showers.

While all the accommodations are striking, the most soul-stirring views are found in those facing the estuary or situated directly on the sand. I stayed in Casita #4, a short stroll down the path from Casa Grande.

Entering through the large wooden door into the courtyard and through the floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors, the sightlines of the inlet extend, unobstructed to the generous, second-floor terrace, an extension of the white-and-wood interiors.

Below, the heated pool and outdoor shower served as a private holiday haven, an even quieter respite, devoid of other guests (not that I saw many during my stay), where the only sounds were the fish frolicking in the water and the birds chirping.

Back inside, clever choices such as thoughtfully positioned beds and a television that rises and hides at the touch of a button reinforce the idea that the best thing to watch is the outdoors. The bathrooms feature dual limestone vanities on either side, Vermont Beige marble floors and walls, a spacious shower and a soaking tub for the ultimate unwinding experience.
Staying for drinks and dinner?

The curved, open-air lounge bar, which faces the waves on one side and the Sierra de la Laguna mountains on the other, is the place for pre-dinner drinks (I recommend the Bartolo, a clarified concoction of raicilla, mango and habanero) with a soundtrack of soulful live saxophone and the gentle crash of the waves.

Sesui is a sleek Japanese concept, centred around a 10-seat wood counter, illuminated by loofah lanterns the shape of sea urchins. It’s here that Chef Masao Matsubara prepares his ever-changing omakase, spotlighting the culinary conversation between Japan and Baja California. When I dined, highlights included a stunning mix of raw oyster with uni and caviar, dashi broth with shrimp, tempura and nigiri.

Arva, the Italian restaurant, offers seating in the elegant dining room, complete with a full-wall temperature-controlled wine display, and on the fire-warmed terrace below the stars. The menu highlights seasonal produce in dishes such as heirloom tomato and burrata salad, yellowtail crisp with caviar and orange, linguine with clams and fresh catch of the day.
For something more casual, Luma, pairs coastal-influenced Mexican cuisine with an laid-back beachfront setting.

The entire resort. From the moment the car turns down the gravel drive, a sense of calm washes over. Of course, it’s not just the peaceful atmosphere that allows guests to switch off but the thoughtful amenities and services geared towards unwinding.

If you really want to relax, first head to the 600-square-meter Aman Spa, a sanctuary of wellness that leans into ancestral healing traditions from Mexico and across Asia (Aman originated in Phuket, Thailand). Facilities include a stunning white temazcal (sweat lodge) and hydrotherapy houses. Treatments range from purifying facials and body wraps to the signature Desert Damiana, a healing journey that combines reflexology, stretching and an aromatic oil massage that took the post-flight tension straight out of me.

There’s also a 24-hour fitness centre kitted out with the latest Technogym equipment, a movement studio and a yoga pavilion. Though, I would recommend joining the sunrise sessions by the gorgeous pool for a chance to flow with the soundtrack

The service goes above and beyond. Snacks, cold water and Starlink Wi-Fi in the car from the airport. An umbrella to block the midday sun when I emerged from the car. Fresh herb bouquets upon first touring the spa. Pre-breakfast coffee service available on your private terrace. Returning from paddle boarding to find a glass of ice-cold water alongside a tray of sun care essentials beside my beach lounger. Knowledge of my food allergies at every F&B outlet on the property without me having to say it. A personalised WhatsApp group for any additional requests.

Amanvari’s nature-led architecture and exceptional service make it a compelling destination for a restorative escape. If you’re looking for a true escape, a place that welcomes stillness but doesn’t demand solitude, a reset complete with spa treatments, delicious food and an unhurried pace, it’s worth every peso.
Amanvari, Eureka s/n esquina con Sta Maria la Ribera, La Ribera, 23570 Baja California Sur, Mexico

Lindsay Cohn is a freelance travel journalist with a decade of experience writing, editing and jet-setting, and bylines in Vogue, Travel + Leisure, W Mag, Bloomberg, Galerie, and more. In between trips to sunny islands, cobbled villages and bustling cities, you can find her in Los Angeles with her husband and two sons.

items.title: Ten cool new CD players provide the path to audiophile heaven at home
items.description: Maybe you never let your CD collection go, or perhaps you’ve started to rebuild a curated set of classic albums that streaming services just don’t seem to do justice to. Whatever your motivation for getting on board the CD revival train, one of these ten conte
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Maybe you never let your CD collection go, or perhaps you’ve started to rebuild a curated set of classic albums that streaming services just don’t seem to do justice to. Whatever your motivation for getting on board the CD revival train, one of these ten contemporary players will help you get back to the original digital source.

Arcam has a new flagship CD player, the CD25. Shown here partnered with the A50 Signature Class G Integrated Amplifier, the CD25 builds on the company’s four decades of experience building digital audio systems. The slender system has gently rounded edges, a black fascia containing the display, and dual-mono digital-to-analogue converters, one for each channel.

Quad’s 3CDT player is now available in a new satin black finish with a green illumination, a classic colourway for this 90-year-old British audio brand. Paired with the Quad 3 integrated amplifier, the 3CDT (a transport only, with no onboard amplification) follows the company’s purist approach. In addition to conventional CDs, the 3CDT is compatible with CD-R, CD-RW and data CDs, and a variety of audio file formats, including FLAC, WAV, WMA, and MP3.

The newest model in Musical Fidelity’s B-Line of high-end audio products, the B1xcd is a purist’s CD player that pairs well with the company’s B1xi integrated amplifier. You won’t find any extraneous features other than a straightforward front-loading CD player with an LCD display and analogue and digital outputs.
£549, details at MusicalFidelity.com. Stockists at henleyaudio.co.uk

Released as part of the venerable audio company’s Classic Series, the new C 569 from NAD joins the C 359S streaming amplifier to create a simple, no nonsense home system that follows a set of enduring design principles. That means push-button design, a modestly sized screen and stripped-back design.
Fitzwilliam Connect Amp + CD

If space is at a premium, consider the new Fitzwilliam Connect Amp + CD from Majority Audio. Although it the same form factor as a traditional stackable hi-fi component, the new model not only incorporates a 200W Texas Instruments amplifier but also has onboardDAB/DAB+ and FM radio and a USB slot, alongside a conventional CD drawer.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The new DP11 CD player from FiiO has a compact, desktop-sized footprint. Finished in retro silver, the DP11 can not only drive a pair of headphones but also includes a USB-C socket that lets you rip CDs straight to a thumb drive.
Eversolo DMP-A8 Master Gen 2

Another all-in-one solution, this time from Eversolo. The DMP-A8 is not only a network music player, high-resolution DAC and analogue preamplifier, but it also comes with a CD playback system with a top-loading mechanism. Thanks to the unit’s impressive connectivity, album information comes up on the large 8.6-inch touchscreen panel, while there’s support for Qobuz Connect, TIDAL Connect and Spotify Connect. An internal SSD can be added if you want to keep your ripped music all in one place.

Marantz’s latest CD player is the CD 70, launched alongside the Model 70 integrated amplifier. The CD 70 also comes with its own headphone amplifier, as the ability to play files back from USB. It’s available in classic black or a silver and gold finish.

The Shanling CD-S100 offers multiple features in addition to straightforward CD playback. The Chinese brand has created a full-size player that also serves as a DAC for phone and computer audio, thanks to the ability to receive and output music over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and USB.

Visually and physically hefty (over 25kg), the new Luxman D-100 Centennial is a CD player of exceptional robustness, stability and quality of componentry. Thick-gauge aluminium and steel give this model its gravitas, along with handmade circuitry and a high-resolution OLED display. Created to celebrate the centenary of the Japanese manufacturer, no expense has been spared.

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: The story behind R.E.M.'s album covers
items.description: Chris Bilheimer and Michael Stipe first met, 35 years ago, over a whirring photocopier and a mutual interest in visual art. It was the tentative start of professional relationship that would (literally) change the face of record sleeve artwork in the Peak CD e
items.author: Craig McLean
paragraphs: Chris Bilheimer and Michael Stipe first met, 35 years ago, over a whirring photocopier and a mutual interest in visual art. It was the tentative start of professional relationship that would (literally) change the face of record sleeve artwork in the Peak CD era. And, as it turned out, in the last hurrah for albums as a physical medium.

At the time Bilheimer was studying art at the University of Georgia in Athens, Georgia. A decade earlier, in 1980, Stipe had embarked on the same course, before dropping out to concentrate on the band he’d formed with fellow students Bill Berry, Peter Buck and Mike Mills: R.E.M.

Back then, recalls Bilheimer, 'Kinko's was the college town copy shop where students in bands would go to make their flyers. It was a creative epicentre for people who didn't have studios.' Ahead of the March 1991 release of R.E.M.’s seventh album Out of Time, Stipe 'had a bunch of disparate things that he wanted to make copies of to send to the record label. I ended up helping him collage those pieces together, because I happened to be at Kinko's when he was there.'

Then, 'a couple of years later, as computers started becoming more prevalent, I was at Kinko's working on [artwork] for a small band. Michael came in and wanted to do some reference material for [1992 album] Automatic for the People, and had me typeset what became the back cover of the album. I laid out the typography for the sign painter to hand paint that on glass.'

These 'little threads of connections to the artwork' were then braided together into a full-time position on 1994’s Monster, 'to assist Michael the way I had been assisting him at Kinko's. And it just grew from there.'

Having been forged in the 1990s, the decade when R.E.M. became one of the biggest bands in the world, the Bilheimer/Stipe visual partnership is still creating, three-and-a-half decades on. For the new, 25th anniversary release of 2001’s Reveal, the graphic designer and the former frontman have collaborated on a fresh iteration of the sleeve artwork for the band’s 12th album. It’s the latest in a run of quarter-century reissues – all beautifully pimped out with new imagery and unreleased and/or not-widely-available recordings – that began with a freshening up of R.E.M.’s 1983 debut, Murmur.

'It's been an interesting journey going through the reissues as a designer,' reflects Bilheimer, 55, from his home in Austin, Texas. 'When we started, it was Murmur, Reckoning, Fables of the Reconstruction – I was now re-designing albums that I grew up listening to. And I tried to keep them very faithful as a fan to how they felt when they came out.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

'But as this process has gone on, and we've gotten further along in the catalogue, Michael has wanted to fuck with it more. I have never asked him exactly what his feelings are, but there's been increasing desire in him to toy with the legacy. Or just have fun with it. More so than holding our breath and faithfully honouring the original.'

Bilheimer – once a fanboy, always a fanboy – admits to conflict about the legacy of a cherished group who split in 2011, 31 years young. 'There's part of me that wants to keep the [sleeves] as a timepiece. And there's a part of me that's like: “Oh, this is fun. We get to reinvent something we already did.” And Reveal is a really good example of that…'

The original, bleach-yellowed cover is a Polaroid that Stipe took on tour, with the shadow of the distinctively chrome-domed singer, camera in hand, in the bottom left corner. 'The first thing Michael said to me was: “What would that look like if it were infrared photography?” So, imagine what it would be like through different technology. Just fuck with the colours, give it a completely different vibe.' Hence the pinkified new look.

For his original work on Reveal, Bilheimer received the first of three Grammy nominations that would come his way, alongside Stipe, for his artwork for the band. Here he, yes, reveals the stories behind the other R.E.M. sleeves he worked on.
R.E.M.’s grunge-era album, dedicated to actor and friend River Phoenix, who died the previous year, with not-so-monstrous candy-coloured sleeve

'It’s funny you say candy-coloured because the starting point was fruit-flavoured cereal boxes from the early 1970s. Then it’s photography by either Michael or [frequent band collaborator] Jem Cohen – except the cover. That came from a weird balloon that Michael bought at a store. It was a full-body bear. But for some reason, its head and its body were separated on the balloon. So it's this very surreal-looking creature.

'We were photographing the bear, and the first picture I took was an accident, totally out-of-focus, and that's the one we ended up using on the cover. It’s copyright of The Tilly Balloon Company and we contacted them to see if they'd let us have rights to it. We were half-expecting them to see that this huge band wants to use their artwork and then have dollar signs in their eyes. They said: “Yeah, you can totally use it. But can you send us a couple copies of the album? Also, if you want to buy some balloons…” So we ended up buying a promotional amount of balloons from them.'
New Adventures in Hi-Fi (1996)
Trailed by suitably greyscale single ‘E-Bow the Letter’, a collaboration with Patti Smith, and with a black-and-white cover photograph, taken through a tour bus window, of a desert-scape

'That whole album was recorded during the Monster tour, and all of those photos were taken by Michael during that time period. Then we were in the studio in Seattle, and we had all these photographs spread out over the floor. And Peter Buck walked by and pointed at the one of the hill and goes, “That one should be the cover” and just kept walking. I think that was the one and only time Peter ever had an opinion about the artwork. So we're like: well, if Peter says it, then that's got to be the cover!
'I actually got to drive by that hill on the cover during the pandemic – someone texted me the GPS coordinates. It's in New Mexico or Arizona.'
Blocky colours and an R.E.M. logo hand-drawn by Bilheimer

'I found a bunch of reference images to show Michael of what I was really into in that era, and still am. There's a thing called spot colour – you mix a purple ink, and you mix a green ink, and you print each colour one at a time. You'll often print one colour on top of another colour accidentally, and you see through it, and you see the texture of the ink. It was very, very analogue.

'The “up” came from a book where someone had collected every version of the “up” arrow on cardboard shipping boxes. Originally, they wanted to call the album Up, Up, Up, Up, Up. But then somewhere along the line, it got shortened to just Up. Titling the records was always a thing, and it always came way late in the process. But it was different every time. Out of Time is called that because they ran out of time to come up with a title.'
Blurry aliens walk amongst us…

'Those are all overexposed photos of Michael taken on a sunny day. And he had this little plastic stencil that you could stick a pin in and make lettering. He just drew the alphabet, and gave me these photos, and said: “That's all I want for the album.” So it's really simple. That was an example where I just put the thing together. I didn't have any design input on it. Michael knew exactly what he wanted.'
A hellish metropolis on the front, David Carson-esque typography design on the inside…

'Michael sent me hundreds of photographs of buildings that he took while he was travelling. He said: “I want you to mash up these buildings into a dystopian landscape.” Every picture's taken from a different angle, nothing lines up. And it's very disorienting to try and create [a cityscape] out of buildings that are all at different angles.

'After Around the Sun, musically it was a rawer, more straightforward album. So I went with the punk rock flyer [aesthetic], back to Kinko's. Those were all full-colour photographs and I made them black and white on a Xerox machine, cut and pasted them together, and built a big diorama. And the R.E.M. logo was pen and ink.'
An R.E.M. album sleeve that – shocker – features the band on the cover, Stipe with his hand in the air. What could it possibly mean?

‘I did not know, when we were making that record, that it was going to be their last one. And it's really interesting, in retrospect, the things that Michael gave me as prompts. He gave me this photo, where he's waving goodbye. Then I poured on acetone, which is a solvent, to eat away the ink on the paper, so it was degrading and disappearing. The other element he gave me was that concept in illustration where things go off to a vanishing point in the horizon. That's why there's lots of lines going off into different directions.

'And it never occurred to me that him waving goodbye, us disappearing the band with chemicals and the vanishing point were all symbolic. R.E.M. are going off, away, into the distance. And I've never asked how intentional that was. I imagine it was probably pretty intentional.'
Reveal (25th Anniversary Edition) boxset is released on 20 November 2026

London-based Scot, the writer Craig McLean is consultant editor at The Face and contributes to The Daily Telegraph, Esquire, The Observer Magazine and the London Evening Standard, among other titles. He was ghostwriter for Phil Collins' bestselling memoir Not Dead Yet.

items.title: Meet the winners of Queer|Art's first Design Grant Awards
items.description: The New York-based non-profit arts organization Queer|Art has announced the winners of its inaugural Design Grant award as graphic designer and design director Luiza Dale and transdisciplinary architect Chong Gu. The winners will each receive a $10,000 reward,
items.author: Osman Can Yerebakan
paragraphs: The New York-based non-profit arts organization Queer|Art has announced the winners of its inaugural Design Grant award as graphic designer and design director Luiza Dale and transdisciplinary architect Chong Gu. The winners will each receive a $10,000 reward, which makes the recognition the highest cash grant given to LGBTQ+ designers working in architecture, graphics, landscape, fashion, and industrial design in the United States.

The winners were selected out of a pool of applications by a jury that included designer and New Affiliates studio co-founder Jaffer Kolb, Cristina Grajales, founder of the eponymous Tribeca design gallery, Salome Asega, who is the deputy director at New Museum’s creative think tank New Inc, fashion brand Chromat’s founder Bex McCharen, and Paul Soulellis, the founder of non-profit Queer.Archive.Work, which helps craftspeople have studio and tool access.

The initiative results from a partnership with UGG and aims to support focused projects with community-building in its core. While queer creativity has been a pillar for the advancement of design in all forms and expressions, the support that specifically targets queer makers has been drastically lacking, and the grant, as the organization’s executive director Río Sofia told Wallpaper*, aims to underline that 'our community has always taken care of itself, and in times of scarcity we keep having each other’s backs.' She also added that their main goal is to 'help preserve queer legacies and build queer futures – in design and in the culture at large.'

Out of two winners, Virginia-based Dale’s immediate plan is to work on building a summer school and a workshop geared towards graphic design in Los Angeles. She explained that the seeds of the project 'begin with a question of legibility: what gets understood, by whom, and on whose terms' and challenge the field’s standard forms of communication.

Gu, meanwhile, turns their attention to west Philadelphia, where they are setting up the nation’s first gallery dedicated to contemporary trans and queer spatial practices. The project’s name, Roberta, honours trans architect, activist and Philadelphia native Quaker Roberta Dickinson. Gu’s initial goal is to 'take archive off the wall and out of the boxes and shelves' and make documents of history an active nexus for new-generation designers and practitioners.

Kolb also underlined the initiative’s attention to 'draw from the past in order to project into the future' to build an intergenerational conversation on queer creativity, some of which has been erased or minimised through systematic oppression. 'Both projects decentre authorship in favour of producing relationships between knowledge and communities specifically through flexible and generous design systems,' he added.

Queer|Art, which was launched seventeen years ago, is known for its mentorship program and annual art prize, which was on a four-year hiatus due to support cuts following the backlash queer ally companies began receiving in the United States. The winners in both the inaugural design field and returning art categories will be celebrated in the organisation’s annual gala on 21 November at Performance Space.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Osman Can Yerebakan is a New York-based art and culture writer. Besides Wallpaper*, his writing has appeared in the Financial Times, GQ UK, The Guardian, Artforum, BOMB, Airmail and numerous other publications. He is in the curatorial committee of the upcoming edition of Future Fair. He was the art and style editor of Forbes 30 Under 30, 2024.

items.title: Home fragrance has a new look. Meet the jeweller exploring scent through material
items.description: For the recent evolution of her creative practice, jewellery designer Maria Sole Ferragamo of So-Le Studio started by considering a jewel as a whole object that both interacts with the body but also, as she explains, exists in an interior space. After launchin
items.author: Rosa Bertoli
paragraphs: For the recent evolution of her creative practice, jewellery designer Maria Sole Ferragamo of So-Le Studio started by considering a jewel as a whole object that both interacts with the body but also, as she explains, exists in an interior space. After launching a lamp with Bottega Ghianda earlier this year, her new project gives her sculptural work a fresh dimension. Exploring the world of scent, So-Le unveils Oracle, a scented object that combines leather, metal and fragrance.
Oracle by So-Le Studio: design meets scent

At the heart of the design is the flower, which, the designer explains, 'represents the most immediate image of scent'. Three ‘petals’ open to reveal a central pad, made from fragments of vegetable-tanned leather, that holds the scent.

Adding movement and performance to the ritual of fragrance, the 'flower' closes with a satisfying mechanism. 'Movement has always been a key principle for me because I work with leather, a living material, and I have always wanted my pieces to carry that energy, that dynamism, that life,' she notes. Once closed, it becomes a precious leather-clad object in three finishes, Gold, Silver and Gunmetal Foil, giving the illusion of metal while maintaining the lightness of leather, that also allows the object to function as a fragrance diffuser.

Ferragamo carefully crafted the object's forms; the way she describes her process is both technical and poetic: 'The leather is shaped on a hidden structure and holds a sphere that isn’t really there: you see it through its absence. Open, its outline is a flower, the most immediate image of scent. Closed, it becomes something else: an egg, a pomander, a vessel that keeps and protects.

'Without the body, the hand and the room become the reference, and the object needs a presence of its own. In this case, it also had to absorb and release a fragrance. So I was designing a form, but also time: how a material takes in a scent and gives it back.'

As a designer whose oeuvre largely hinges on craft processes, developing three fragrances that would encapsulate the studio's modus operandi took an unusual route. 'I started from our materials, not from perfumery,' Ferragamo explains. 'The mood board had more materials than images: leather offcuts, brass shavings, mineral surfaces, words, a few optical illusions.'

The scents includes Cuoio Reale, recalling her leather workshop in Tuscany; Optical Illusion, a 'clean and minimal' fragrance that nods to the lightness of reflective surfaces; and Grigio Minerale, the more botanical of the trio, closer to stone and brass. 'Together,’ says Ferragamo, ‘they say that So-Le Studio is [about] material research, and that this research can now be smelled as well as seen and touched.'
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Rosa Bertoli was born in Udine, Italy, and now lives in London. Since 2014, she has been the Design Editor of Wallpaper*, where she oversees design content for the print and online editions, as well as special editorial projects. Through her role at Wallpaper*, she has written extensively about all areas of design. Rosa has been speaker and moderator for various design talks and conferences including London Craft Week, Maison & Objet, The Italian Cultural Institute (London), Clippings, Zaha Hadid Design, Kartell and Frieze Art Fair. Rosa has been on judging panels for the Chart Architecture Award, the Dutch Design Awards and the DesignGuild Marks. She has written for numerous English and Italian language publications, and worked as a content and communication consultant for fashion and design brands.

Apartamento was founded in Barcelona in 2008. Its namesake magazine, published twice yearly and widely considered one of the most influential interiors publications of the past two decades, is rooted in how people actually live: the spaces they inhabit, the food they cook, the work they make, and the conviction with which they build their lives. Known for its unfiltered, human approach, each issue brings long-form conversations with artists, writers, designers, and thinkers across disciplines, accompanied by photography that unsettles conventional categories.

The values of the magazine extend beyond print. Through events, collaborations, exhibitions, design objects, and a growing body of short and documentary films, Apartamento builds community in real spaces around the world.

Since 2015, Apartamento has published books across a range of formats: monographs, cookbooks, photobooks, architecture series, artist books, and even a graphic novel. The publishing programme extends the editorial curiosity of the magazine into longer, more sustained forms, spanning art, design, architecture, food, and visual culture.

Members receive each issue of Apartamento magazine at a special 20% discount, plus unlimited access to our digital archive—including every interview, essay, and story ever published in our previous issues. In addition, members receive an automatic 10% discount in our Shop, as well as a free Apartamento Tote Bag and one 60-day trial for MUBI.

Current issues of Apartamento magazine tend to sell out quickly, and all earlier issues are sold out and can be hard to find. Our digital archive preserves each and every issue of the magazine on our website, a place where members can read every interview, essay, and story ever published!
The exact cost of shipping each issue express to your home is calculated at check out, according to the competive rates our courier partners offer us.

items.title: Apartamento Magazine Issue #38
items.description: In issue #38 of Apartamento magazine, isolation becomes grounds for imagination, encouraging the possibility of creating the worlds we want.
paragraphs: In issue #38 of Apartamento magazine, isolation becomes grounds for imagination, encouraging the possibility of creating the worlds we want.

On the cover, American artist Dozie Kanu, winner of the Hublot Design Prize, talks with writer Camille Okhio in the home and studio he has made in the Portuguese countryside of Azoia de Cima. Photographed by José Pedro Cortes, the story follows what took his practice from New York to Portugal, how ambition has emerged from his Nigerian heritage, and the existential pressures of Blackness. Dozie candidly recounts how his live/work space once caught fire just before a photoshoot with furniture company Knoll.

In Paris, Playboy author and provocateur to the French literati Constance Debré speaks with contributing editor Jina Khayyer about the contradictions of love and desire, and boredom as ‘a state where you develop the freedom to invent things’. Photographed by Osma Harvilahti, she shows us her minimalist apartment, which has no full bath, proving that showers don’t need to be in the privacy of the home.

Featuring: Dozie Kanu, Constance Debré, Anupama Kundoo, Julian Schnabel, Dave Baby, Peaches, Joey Arias, Martine Syms, Gerard Malanga, Rodney Mullen, Filip Pągowski, Go Hasegawa, Darina Allen, and Muller Van Severen.
Plus: Peter Hanley’s ‘The Culinary Academy of the Pyrenees’ with illustrations by Oscar Grønner, an ode to Inge Mahn by Anna Herms, and ‘Wei Xing Doesn’t Skate’, an essay by Jocko Weyland.
Members have unlimited access to the entire Apartamento magazine digital archive!

Shipping method: DHL/UPS courier service with tracking.

items.title: Peluquería, Ouka Leele
items.description: Peluquería is the first book dedicated to late Spanish photographer Ouka Leele’s formative years in Barcelona and her portraits of the city’s underground scene. Widely celebrated as a key figure of the Movida Madrileña, Leele settled in Barcelona one year befo
paragraphs: Peluquería is the first book dedicated to late Spanish photographer Ouka Leele’s formative years in Barcelona and her portraits of the city’s underground scene. Widely celebrated as a key figure of the Movida Madrileña, Leele settled in Barcelona one year before the country’s official turn to democracy. The improvised ‘hair salon’ referred to by the series’ title gathers legends of the counterculture movement at this moment of extraordinary freedom, marked by the playful, defiant objects on their heads. Peluquería’s electric colours, unique for the era, are achieved through Leele’s innovative use of watercolours, which she painted onto her black-and-white prints by hand. Original sketches that inspired the series, as well as previously unpublished writings by Leele are presented alongside contact sheets newly unveiled by the artist’s archive. Reflections by Javier Mariscal, one of the first artists photographed for Peluquería, and Rossy de Palma, an icon of Spanish cinema, honour Leele’s poetic vision, while essays by Pepe Ribas and Elisa Medde mine the radical landscape that informed Leele’s early work.

Ouka Leele (1957–2022), born Bárbara Allende Gil de Biedma, is a Spanish photographer and a fixture of the Movida Madrileña. She is renowned for the distinct visual language she pioneered with her work, beginning with the Peluquería series, in which she transformed black-and-white prints by painting them with vivid watercolours. She was awarded the 2004 Culture Prize by the Community of Madrid and the Spanish National Photography Prize in 2005.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: November 23, 2026
Shipping method: DHL/UPS courier service with tracking.

items.title: Written at Night, Ettore Sottsass
items.description: The third in our reading series, Written at Night is the fragmented autobiography of Ettore Sottsass, one of the most seminal figures of 20th-century radical design. Originally written in Italian and published posthumously in 2010 as Scritto di notte, it now a
paragraphs: The third in our reading series, Written at Night is the fragmented autobiography of Ettore Sottsass, one of the most seminal figures of 20th-century radical design. Originally written in Italian and published posthumously in 2010 as Scritto di notte, it now arrives in English for the first time, translated by one of the most distinguished translators of Italian literature into English, Alastair McEwen.

As he recounts his upbringing in Trento and Turin, his conscription in WWII, his Milan debut, his dance with poverty, and his travels—from Cuba with Hemingway to a snowy Italian night drive with Ginsberg to the fever of India—Written at Night begins as a slow tide into the mind of one of radical design’s greatest figures, only to sweep you up in its storm. Digging through the debris of memory, he finds the precious metals of people and places, so that what he’s writing in the dark is a sweeping blueprint of love, lust, and survival. In his attempts to start from childhood and climb forwards, Sottsass produces a piece of art in and of itself—self-interrupting, self-critical, self-affirming, self-annihilating.
Written at Night joins our growing reading book series, following Essential and The Unimportance of Form.

Ettore Sottsass (1917–2007) was an Austrian-born Italian postmodernist designer and architect, considered one of the most seminal figures in 20th design, and hailed for co-founding the design collective known as the Memphis Group. Considered a polymath by many, he moved freely between furniture, glass, lamps, jewellery, objects for the home and office, as well as the design of many buildings and interiors, magazines, and publications. Alongside a significant canon of published books, his contribution to design has earned him four Compassi d’Oro. His works are exhibited in the permanent collections of museums around the world, such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Centre Pompidou in Paris, and the Victoria & Albert Museum in London.

Alastair McEwen is considered to be one of the most distinguished translators of Italian literature into English. To date, he has published over 100 book-length translations, essays, articles, and poems, plus several feature film scripts and operatic librettos. He has translated some of the most important Italian writers of our time: Umberto Eco, Roberto Calasso, Antonio Tabucchi, Fleur Jaeggy, Alessandro Baricco, Aldo Busi, and many others.

items.title: The Selfies of Jonas Unger
items.description: The Selfies of Jonas Unger is German photographer Jonas Unger’s years-long investigation into how close a portrait can get to its subject. In this seductive photobook, Karl Lagerfeld, David Lynch, Rossy de Palma and dozens of others from the glittering corners
paragraphs: The Selfies of Jonas Unger is German photographer Jonas Unger’s years-long investigation into how close a portrait can get to its subject. In this seductive photobook, Karl Lagerfeld, David Lynch, Rossy de Palma and dozens of others from the glittering corners of fashion, film, and sport turn the lens on themselves, caught in ways you’ve never seen before. Handing his camera to his sitters and stepping out of the frame, Jonas tampers with the role of the photographer, surrendering the lens and some of its authority, while never wholly relinquishing his own.

Celebrity, honesty, and dramaturgy meet the defining photographic phenomenon of our time: the self-taken photograph. Moving through philosophical dives and detours, the photobook catches people shaped by the limelight at the moment control over their image briefly changes hands. Gathered over more than a decade, these self-portraits, known also as his ‘Autoportraits’, form a book about the puzzles of authorship and spectatorship. How close can a portrait get? And what are we really seeing when someone famous looks back at themselves?

The Selfies of Jonas Unger follows on from our growing photobook catalogue after Coincidence by American photographer Jeremy Liebman, shortlisted for the 2026 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards, and the quirky Birds of Paradise by Spanish photographer Ángela Suárez.

Jonas Unger is a German photographer living and working in Paris. He is known for portrait, fashion, and editorial photography with a direct, intimate approach. His editorial work has appeared in Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Vogue, W Magazine, Interview, and many more. Alongside his commissioned work, Jonas develops long-term personal projects. The best known is his series of celebrity self-portraits, begun around 2010, which was first shown as Autoportraits at Galerie Derouillon in Paris in 2014 and later included in Ego Update at the NRW-Forum Düsseldorf. His work has received the LeadAward and the Hansel Mieth Prize (2013).
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: November 4, 2026
Shipping method: DHL/UPS courier service with tracking
Delivery time: 2-4 days from the shipping confirmation

items.title: ADRIEN BRODY - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star
paragraphs: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star

Twenty-two years after he became the youngest ever winner of a best actor Oscar, for ‘The Pianist’, Adrien Brody has gone and done it again, this time taking home an Academy Award for his deeply moving performance as Hungarian architect László Toth in ‘The Brutalist’. What makes it all the more remarkable is that only a few years ago Adrien had all but given up acting. The awards are much deserved, of course. Adrien, 52, is an intense and uniquely gifted actor, which also makes him entertaining company. He doesn’t do things in half measures. He’s all in, all the time, and not afraid to speak his mind. In the following story Adrien engages in some energetic verbal ping-pong and gets dressed up in fashion by his friend Thom Browne. It captures some of the essence of what makes him such an incredible performer.
From Fantastic Man n° 40 – 2025
Photography by ILYA LIPKIN

The instant Adrien Brody sweeps into the room, he begins to express what I will soon come to think of as his resting affect: a kind of intense but fuzzy gratitude. “I just got back from London yesterday night,” he tells me. “Feeling very blessed with all the love that’s been coming my way. It’s a really special moment. It really is.” Maybe it’s just for now, in these hectic weeks promoting ‘The Brutalist’ ahead of the Academy Awards, but it’s with words like these that Brody seems at his most comfortable, and throughout our conversation he will periodically return to similar sentiments, restating and expanding upon them with evident sincerity.

With other kinds of words, though, it will often come to feel as though there are fault lines everywhere. Seconds after this initial declaration, I ask Brody – my question intended as little more than small talk to fill the empty space between us as we greet each other and take our seats – whether it feels like he’s being carried away in a whirlwind. He responds – not just in his words but in his body language too – as though he’s being somehow misunderstood or as though something wonderful is at risk of being spoiled.

“No, it’s not that at all,” he says, correcting me firmly. “No, my feet are on the ground. I’m ultra-present. I’m ultra-present and able to reciprocate the love. It’s different. Being older gives you a degree of perspective. It’s been a very long time since I’ve had an opportunity to do the work that I’m yearning to do. And the work is completed. So this is just something magical.”

Brody will prove to be engaging, fascinating company, and a man with plenty to say. In our conversation there will also be moments where he exudes a sense – verbally, but also through a repertoire of expressions that seem to hover between saddened and harried – that the world doesn’t quite get him.

What I then find myself wondering is whether such a sensibility might be a consequence of setbacks and reversals he has faced along his idiosyncratic chosen path, or whether it’s such a sensibility which sends you down that path in the first place. Conversely, I also find myself wondering whether it’s exactly this kind of off-kilter mindset which, when everything comes together in just the right way, somehow fuels Brody’s singular ability to inhabit and transmit a role like ‘The Brutalist’s’ László Toth with such compelling, all-consuming mastery.

It was back in 2019 when Adrien Brody was first given the script of ‘The Brutalist’, the expansive tale of a visionary Hungarian architect who escapes the Holocaust and makes his way to America, where he finds a new life – one of opportunity, but also one with horrors all of its own. Brody read it in the apartment he and his partner, fashion designer Georgina Chapman, then had in Manhattan. “I found myself very moved by the writing and the breadth of the storytelling, the complexity, the flaws of the character,” he remembers. “The opportunity for me to play someone that is experiencing so much and contending so much in life [was] wonderful. And I did consider parallels of László’s lived experience with my mother’s and my grandparents’ journey.” Brody’s mother, whose maternal grandparents were rounded up and taken to Auschwitz, survived the war in Budapest. She escaped in 1956, at the age of 13, buried under corn in a horse-drawn cart as she and her parents crossed the Austrian border. In New York, Brody grew up around his Hungarian grandparents. “So that, too, definitely is evident to me in reading it – saying: ‘Wow, I’m quite right to play this character.’”

After reading, Brody met with the director, Brady Corbet, who had written the script with his professional and personal partner, the filmmaker and actor Mona Fastvold, for brunch downtown. “A very long meeting – conversed a lot about lots of things,” Brody recalls. Nonetheless, he learned in due course that another actor had been chosen. “The message comes from your agent,” he says. “It’s either you get the message or they hope you’ve forgotten.” That’s the pattern. “I mourned the loss of this one,” he says. “I did not have expectations that it would be what it is today – I still mourned the creative loss of what I wanted to pour into it.”

Brody makes clear that over his career he has learned that this will happen, and maybe even why. “As an actor, you may be right for certain roles and you’re not necessarily eligible for them,” he says. “Even if you are quite a well-known actor and quite a successful actor. Because there are all these factors that are out of your control. You know, there are lists, and lists are based on a number of things that one might deem as an indication of success. Right? You know, consistent box office earnings are the primary reason you would be on the top of a list. But if you do make experimental choices and interesting choices in an artistic pursuit in a business, it’s not met with the same appreciation as, you know, your mother might have for your varied tastes.”

Brody points out that he’s balanced experimentation with “big blockbuster movies,” and that he enjoys those too. “But I like the range,” he says, and his suggestion seems to be that too much range has consequences. “I’m aware of how it has made certain things, such as this even, challenging,” he says. “Where I’m probably the most right performer for the role, but I wasn’t deemed valuable enough.”

This time, thankfully, everything eventually worked out. The film’s shoot was delayed several times, in part because of Covid, and by the time the project fell back in place the actor previously scheduled to play László Toth, Joel Edgerton, was no longer available. Brody heard from his agent that the role was back in play. Even then, it wasn’t as though Brody simply got a call saying the part was his. “No, not at all,” he says. “Not at all.” In the end, though, it was. Finally given the chance, he threw himself into it. “I knew we were making something special,” he says. “I wish I knew why things come when they do. This moment is because we’re very fortunate – all of us who have been involved in this project – that every collaborative creative element lifted up the other.”

It’s around now, a few minutes into our meeting, when another question seems to throw Brody, though this time the person asking is not me. It is the waiter, asking what Brody might like to eat or drink. From Brody’s reaction, you could easily think that he finds such an inquiry – at a pre-booked table by the window in a high-end New York hotel bar – somewhat perplexing. He talks aloud through this latest dilemma. “I’m not sure what I’m needing,” he says, then considers one kind of option. “I’m happy to have a drink,” he weighs, “but I’m also not needing it just yet.” He expands this thought. “I don’t really need anything.”
After vacillating further, he orders an oak milk decaf latte.
“Not too much milk,” he adds. “Just nice and strong.”

That ‘The Brutalist’ would allow Brody such a remarkable professional and creative renaissance is all the more marked given the place he has described finding himself in in recent years: sufficiently dejected by the opportunities coming his way that he had, unannounced, more or less turned his back on movies. As he recently put it, “I didn’t announce I was retiring, but I stepped back.” For a time, he concentrated on other artistic pursuits that he found more fulfilling, principally painting.

“I’ve been doing this so long, since I was a boy,” he says when I ask about that period. “There’s an ebb and flow in everything, in your own creative connections and personally, professionally in life, right? So I also was not under any illusion that it should just flow. But I found it oddly challenging to be up against things like this. I feel that I’ve proven my range. I’ve worked. The reason it seems inconsistent is I’ve been consistent in trying to break out of the box of subjective perception of what I am capable of doing, or what I represent for a character, or physically. Whatever it is. Too specific, often. And they find that…” He pauses, considering his words. “There’s a safer option, basically.”
“It wasn’t being reciprocated, for whatever reason,” he says. “It wasn’t. What I had to give was somehow not understood or not of value. I didn’t feel that I was of service and of value.”
How did that lack of reciprocation make him feel?

“I didn’t feel like I needed to prove that I was worth it. If I wasn’t, I’m going to go do something else that makes me feel good. I work primarily to feel connected and to feel immersed in something creative. And I handle my side of the bargain.”
I ask him whether he feels like he does all this for the same reasons as his peers do it.

“I mean, I would think so,” he says. “Like what? Like what reason?” Then he supplies his own answer. “I think anybody who cares about what they’re doing, which is such personal work – you have to embody the role. You have to ingest it and live it and feel it and be it. And you can only do that well if you feel it and believe in it.”
But, I put to him, my gut feeling is that a lot of actors, including some very talented people, may have a slightly more detached or casual relationship with their work.
“Yeah,” acknowledges Brody, and he laughs in a way that’s tricky to read. “I’m not detached enough. Or casual, I guess.”
I point out that, although I’ve only known him for 20 minutes, my sense is that he doesn’t want to be.
When I further echo this – suggesting out loud that he wants to be like he is – the notion seems to spark something in Brody, this time in a more helpful way.

“You know, it’s funny,” he says. “When I was young, there were a lot of tough kids in my neighbourhood, and I was always very sensitive. I was always amazed at how certain ones weren’t empathetic. You know, how they would torture ants and things when we would play, and how they got pleasure out of that. I was littler than them, and I didn’t really want to say all the time, like, ‘Why are you going to hurt…?’ because they’ll just pick on me. And I was always kind of aware that it was harder. It was harder to be more sensitive.”

From the age of four, Brody grew up in the New York suburb of Woodhaven, Queens, and he has occasionally alluded over the years to various rough aspects around the edges of this experience of growing up in a neighbourhood suffering from high levels of drug and gun crime. He compares it in general terms to his life these days: “Now, I have no one in my life that isn’t on the path that I feel we should all be on. But I think growing up in Queens I didn’t know anyone, really, who was on the path.”
And yet, I point out to him, it sounds as though while he’s grateful for what he didn’t end up doing, he still feels slightly romantic about that world.

“I am a little nostalgic for it,” he agrees. “It wasn’t terrible. It was also another time. Like, the whole world was different, let alone New York City. It was different. There were no [mobile] phones. I was on the street very young. I was taking the train. I was riding bikes with a bunch of kids around the neighbourhood. I was getting into trouble. I was kind of left on my own. I didn’t have a pager or a phone with a tracker on it. I wasn’t seeing what kids were doing on social media and living a better life, and ‘Why don’t I have these sneakers?’ I just lived. Lived.”

Following up on what he’d just said, I ask him what trouble he was getting into; this will be another of those moments where the mood shifts. “Here we go…” he says. But he nonetheless offers a response.
“I was around a lot of…yeah, a lot of stuff,” he says. “It was a lot of hardship…and there was a lot of… It was wild. It was just a wild time. You know, I was a good kid…but I was around a lot.”

There are a lot of long pauses in this answer, and as he speaks I feel like I can almost see all the things Brody is remembering but not saying flashing across his eyes and around the edges of his mouth. It’s quite a show. If I could transcribe everything he thought of between those sentences, I suggest to him, it would be quite a paragraph, wouldn’t it?

“It would be,” he confirms, and his laugh seems one of genuine shared amusement. “Yes. It sure would. And I’d love to share wonderful stories with you. Just somehow things always get taken out of context. I never would brag about doing things that…you know, whatever.”

We leave that there, but one of his mother’s books offers a fascinating snapshot into a different side of Brody’s childhood. His mother, Sylvia Plachy, is an acclaimed documentary photographer. ‘Unguided Tour’ was published in 1990, the year Brody turned 17. It’s far from a family album – it contains a dizzying variety of evocative photos, many taken around New York and quite a few in Eastern Europe, alongside occasional portraits of interesting notables (amongst them William S. Burroughs, Louise Bourgeois, Jorge Luis Borges, Claude Lanzmann, Hubert Selby Jr. and Tom Waits) – though there is one image of a joyous young Brody in a pool with his grandfather. But there are occasional pieces of text placed next to photographs, and several images are accompanied by words Brody apparently said to his mother when he was very young. (Brody is referred to throughout as Mishi, the name his mother used to call him.)

This, for instance, is from 1977, when he was four years old: “Mommy, I had a very sad dream. I was in a restaurant with a grown-up girl and I really liked her. She even bought me ice cream. But when we came out she just crossed the street and left me, and I’m not allowed to cross the street by myself. She just said good-bye and I don’t know why she left me. I loved her even more than I love you. I’m going to sing a song about it: ‘She left me and I don’t know why she left me, I really loved her.’”

And this is from the following year, when he was five: “Mommy, I had a bad dream; men made out of metal were after me with their metal ray guns. But then my nose started bleeding, I shouted ‘Time Out!’ and they all stopped.”
When I mention these to Brody, I comment that it sounds like he was a strange kid.
“I don’t think it was that strange,” he counters. “It was imaginative.”
What kind of four-year-old, I ask him, tells a fully realised story about a girl not being in love with him, or a five-year-old about men of metal coming at him?
“I don’t know,” he says. “This one.”
I reiterate: Not everyone, I promise you.

“But you think it’s strange?” he says. I point out that I like that he said those things. “Okay, good. It’s unusual – I don’t disagree. Yeah, it’s something.” After we talk a little more, he adds: “They sound like me. It sounds like something I would come up with.”
And that, I point out, is what I’m trying to understand.

“You can see that I’m an actor,” he reflects, “and that was her intuition.” He seems to be casting forward from age five to a famous pivot point in his life: when he was eleven, his mother was sent on assignment to the American Academy of Dramatic Arts, and when she saw their young people’s programme she thought it might suit her son. That’s how Brody started acting. He talks more about those qualities he had as a child. “I can see a lot of things, and I can see circumstances – imagine them fully,” he says. “Quite fully in emotion. I think those are qualities that are necessary to inhabit others. I am quite empathetic, and I think that’s been cultivated through that process.”
But it’s interesting, I say, that he was like this when he hadn’t yet had any training.

So where do you think it comes from? “No idea,” he says. “Just there.” But then he offers what seems like a suggestion. “My parents treated me with respect as a child. They didn’t treat me like a child.”

Brody has said that his parents saw acting as a way of keeping him out of the trouble that might have subsumed him in the neighbourhood. When I ask whether this was a big impulse, he says no at first but then offers up a surprising detail. “My dad considered me going to a military academy at one point. He knew what was around. Both of them understood that I needed some kind of creative outlet, that I was very creative. And that’s what’s evident in those things: that I had a very imaginative mind, a very curious mind. And hanging out on the block wouldn’t have given me a leg up in that space. It would suppress it, ultimately.”

Brody enjoyed some success right from the start. Aged 14, he was a lead in a TV movie, ‘Home at Last’, playing a New York orphan shipped out west. The following year, he was cast, if only for a day, by Francis Ford Coppola in his portion of ‘New York Stories’. A variety of roles followed before, at 23, he landed a wonderful, improbable opportunity. The director Terrence Malick was a legend, partly because 20 years earlier he had stopped making movies. The filmmaking world was abuzz with news that Malick was planning to return with an adaptation of James Jones’s World War II novel about combat in the Pacific, ‘The Thin Red Line’. It seemed as if the whole of Hollywood wanted to be in the movie. After Brody met with Malick – they talked for two hours in a hotel near where we are now, looking down at the skaters in Central Park – he was cast as one of the leads.

There’s a version of the script online, apparently close to the one Malick used when they all headed off to Australia to shoot for half a year. Brody’s character’s name, Corporal Fife, appears in the script 315 times. Fife speaks on 127 separate occasions. “We shot six months,” Brody recalls, “and we did many embellishments.”

In the lead-up to the release of a film Malick was yet to show to anybody, Brody did press interviews as the hot new young star he now was presumed to be. Malick did call him at one point and mentioned that his role had been “reduced,” but nothing even slightly prepared him for the truth. Just before the film’s release – still a grand secret – Brody was invited to what he was told was a private screening in New York. He took his parents. It wasn’t a private screening – selected press were there too – and as the film’s nearly three hours unspooled in front of everyone, Brody discovered that Malick had completely changed his movie in editing. Brody’s character appeared on screen for only a few minutes, and you could count the fleeting lines he spoke on one hand.

Brody has often talked about this as a formative experience and a key moment in his story, but today he seems less willing to reflect on it. “You want to get into all the past and the hardships. I don’t think about them. I don’t harp on them. You can reference them all you like, but I don’t harp on them,” he says.

I point out that the whole point of talking about any of this is to provide context to his role in ‘The Brutalist’ being such a triumph. And though it’s a little awkward to raise, I feel like he should know that I’ve spent much of the last eight years writing a book about events during the Holocaust in Lithuania and how one deals with the aftermath (the recently published ‘No Road Leading Back’), which, in a very different way, processes some of the same themes that lie at the heart of ‘The Brutalist’. We talk about that for a while. “It’s good to represent these stories,” he says respectfully.

Eventually I tell him that I should ask him some more annoying questions about his past. “It’s not annoying – it’s really not,” he says, and returns to the subject of ‘The Thin Red Line’. “It’s just, to then read it again – this moment, this terrible situation…” Even so, whether or not because of the break we have had, Brody addresses the situation with some thoughtfulness. “I do feel like you asked me why and how things happen,” he says. “And I don’t know, but that happened for a reason. You know what I mean? And that shaped me. It shaped my journey. It gave me a great understanding of loss as it pertains to my work. And had potential to be very detrimental to my future and the work that I’ve dedicated my whole life to. I gave everything to that project, too. Unquestioningly.”
It could have broken you, I point out.

“Yes,” he exclaims. “I was 23! But my dad always has a really great perspective of it.” (Brody’s father, Elliot, is a retired history teacher.) “He said: ‘That movie, as painful as it was for you, made a lot of people know about you in your business. Whether they saw your work or not, they knew about you.’ And he’s right. But I was concerned one could make the assumption that I must not have been good enough for the part. You have this iconic filmmaker who hasn’t made a movie in all these years, and then you have an actor who out of nowhere gets this thing – he must not have been good enough. And that’s what I felt. Like, I had no way to prove my side of this.”

Thankfully, at least through the lens of history, not too long a time passed between what could have been a debilitating humiliation and Brody’s first unequivocal triumph: playing the central figure in Roman Polanski’s ‘The Pianist’, based on the true story of a Polish-Jewish musician, Władysław Szpilman, and his desperate struggles to survive in the Warsaw ghetto during World War II. “It was profound – and also out of nowhere, you know,” Brody says. “It was only a few years from where I thought: ‘I may never work again.’”

To me, Brody seems like the kind of high-wire actor who, in a film that works less well, can sometimes appear stranded; you can almost viscerally feel the disconnect between the film he’s imagined and the film that is. But when everything works it’s the opposite: he entirely inhabits a character in a way which is mesmerising without being showy. So it is in ‘The Brutalist’; so it was in ‘The Pianist’. “It was nothing I had experienced,” he reminisces. “You know, I had such a responsibility throughout the making of it, saddled with the need to faithfully represent a survivor’s story and what it speaks to of the enormity of loss. And [as] a young man, I had to deeply immerse and understand that level of loss that was so profound that I didn’t have an understanding, really. I opened up a portal to a depravity and the horror and cruelty that exists. My association to darkness was very different prior to that. So that was a big shift. Darkness and light. And finding light through darkness…”

At this very moment, something remarkable happens. Presumably in response to the dwindling daylight outside, just as Brody says the phrase “light through darkness,” the lighting in the hotel bar suddenly surges to about twice its previous level of brightness.
“See!” he declares. “I have a way about me!” He looks delighted. “If we did that on the take,” he says, “that would be in the movie!”

For his role in ‘The Pianist’, Brody was nominated for an Oscar for the first time. The other four nominees – Jack Nicholson, Michael Caine, Daniel Day-Lewis and Nicolas Cage – had all previously won Oscars, and in the weeks beforehand, as the major precursor awards were announced, Brody won none of them.
But on the evening, it was his name that was read out. He became – and to this day remains – the youngest winner of the best actor trophy.

“Time did slow down,” he says. “I remember that. I remember that feeling where it literally warped down to something. It was enormous. It was enormous. And it was a real outpouring of love. That room lit up. And there I was, surrounded by so many people I admire, and all the influential people in my industry. And I just… I was plucked from obscurity. I had been working and toiling away as an actor for 17 years. And overnight” – he laughs – “I was now successful. In the world’s eyes.”

‘The Brutalist’ is now on the same awards circuit. So far, it is going well. A couple of weeks before we met, Brody gave an emotional speech after winning best actor at the Golden Globes. It is, of course, a strange quirk that the two roles towering above all others in his career, as different as they are in most respects other than the commitment and intensity he brings to them, are both connected to the Holocaust.

It’s also the kind of low-hanging fruit ready-made for awards show hosts, and in the first few minutes of the Golden Globes, during comedian Nikki Glaser’s opening monologue, she said, “Oh, look! It’s two-time Holocaust survivor Adrien Brody.” As the camera fixed on his face, Brody gamely grinned and blew Glaser a kiss.
As I watched, I tell him, I wondered whether he was wincing slightly inside.

“Of course,” he says. “Of course. You know the nature of her humour. Of course. I feel very privileged to have been able to speak to this horrific time in my work. Such great depths. And there’s been a lot of ancestral loss and struggles, and I don’t take it lightly, obviously.”
Not long before Brody leaves the bar, I ask him what he thinks his talent is. He takes some time before he starts to speak.

“I’ve managed to not lose the imaginative quality of my youth through my experiences in life,” he tells me. “And I can apply that similar curiosity and enthusiasm to my work, and my encounters with others. And it gives me a sense of freedom. And I can incorporate that into my work, and the process of doing my work. I can find, I can access, things that I find quite fulfilling and real, that shed light on lots of things in my work and in life. So that is what I’m most grateful for.”
I ask him when he’s happiest.
“When I’m working,” he says. “When I’m immersed in something creative. The most alive, yes. Definitely not on vacation or something. I don’t know. I’m more happy working.”

He says he doesn’t yet know what he will do next. “There are a few things that are interesting,” he says. (Naturally, those lists will be looking much better for him right now.) Even aside from ‘The Brutalist’, in recent times Brody’s world seems to have opened up a little. When he renewed his focus on acting after his unannounced break (he has credited Chapman with nudging him in that direction), he began to make distinctive contributions to TV shows, most notably ‘Peaky Blinders’, ‘Succession’ and ‘Poker Face’, and renewed his ongoing relationship with Wes Anderson, now five films deep. Brody also co-wrote, produced and starred in a dark revenge movie, ‘Clean’, and wrote its music. (He has been making beats for many years.) There’s another script he’s writing, inspired by a painting he saw in Madrid’s Prado museum. And, for that matter, he wants to get back to his own painting. “I have no time to do anything at the moment, unfortunately,” he says ruefully. “Like, literally no time. I would like a window to paint a little.”

Brody made a documentary, too, several years back: ‘Stone Barn Castle’, about the seven-year renovation of a building he owns in upstate New York. He showed the film once at the SXSW festival, but it hasn’t been seen since, and he tells me he wants to redo it sometime, change the structure and the storytelling. “I envision another iteration before it’s something to share publicly,” he explains. “But I have an enormous amount of footage.” And, like so many things, it may have already found its worth in another way.

“It’s fascinating,” he says of the documentary, “especially in context of me playing an architect, having spent a good seven years toiling away and trying to bring a building back to life and integrate all these architectural elements. And my aesthetic, which is quite unique, influenced from Eastern sources and modern things – that, too, probably informed some connection with my character.”

As he further explains the connection between the renovation and his most recent landmark character, I realise that Adrien Brody could just as much be talking about his life. And maybe that’s the point.
“The need to complete it,” he says. “And not letting it get the best of me. And all of the stuff you have to overcome to get there.”

Chris Heath, as mentioned in the preceding interview, is the author of the recently published book ‘No Road Leading Back: An Improbable Escape from the Nazis and the Tangled Way We Tell the Story of the Holocaust’. It was voted a 2024 book of the year by ‘The Washington Post’.

items.title: AI WEIWEI - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: The extraordinary artist makes monumental installations of a radical and provocative nature, telling the truth about China and putting his very life in danger
paragraphs: The extraordinary artist makes monumental installations of a radical and provocative nature, telling the truth about China and putting his very life in danger

The Turbine Hall at London’s Tate Modern is one of the world’s most coveted exhibition spaces, and the next artist to fill it is Ai Weiwei. Although a veteran of major art events such as Documenta 12 and the 48th Venice Biennale, in his home country of China Ai Weiwei is as much known for his activism as he is for his aesthetics. Based in Beijing, where he is under constant surveillance, the artist brazenly flouts the law to bring his view on modern day China to the rest of the world. He is an avid user of fashionable social networking sites, and on an average day he tweets approximately 107 times.
From Fantastic Man n° 12 — 2010
“Okay, let’s start,” says the artist Ai Weiwei, greeting me with a wide smile.

It’s 9am on a sunny Beijing morning – so much for creative types sleeping late – and Ai Weiwei has already been up and at it for several hours. Given his reputation, I assume he’s been irritating the Chinese government and tickling his legions of followers by way of his famously acerbic Twitter feeds. (Consider: “The system doesn’t follow the law. The people don’t believe in the law. So who’s out of luck?”)

I have made what’s been called the ‘ritual pilgrimage’ to the compound Ai designed and built for himself in the city’s northeast outskirts. It’s a journey previously taken by the likes of Gerhard Schröder, Diane von Furstenberg and countless others who fancy themselves sophisticated and international. From the centre of town, you go past unremarkable high rises and light industry zones, beneath highway overpasses and railroad tracks and, finally, along a quiet, gingko-lined road. A blue metal door marks the entrance to Ai’s fabled home and studio, which he shares with his wife, the artist Lu Qing, and which these days also happens to be under surveillance by Chinese authorities.

Inside, the word FUCK is mounted on a garden wall in big neon letters. Otherwise, the scene is quite tranquil. Ai is sitting next to a pleasant, grassy lawn framed by cypress trees, antique stone fragments and thickets of bamboo. He’s accompanied by a member of his 30-or-so-person studio – a young woman, Germanic, I’d say, possibly Scandinavian – and several of his unconfirmed number of cats and dogs. (“We don’t really know how many we have,” he admits.) Ai has close-cropped hair, an unruly beard and an ample belly that together define what you might call the Ai Weiwei look. Wearing a periwinkle T-shirt and shorts, he politely leads me across a patio and into his loft-like, grey-brick home.
“That’s Du Du,” he starts off, catching me glancing at another free-roaming canine as we sit down at a huge wooden table.
“Yeah. And there’s Danny,” he adds, pointing to a female cocker spaniel. “We also have two of her children here.”
Ignoring his pet-naming decisions, I ask how his day is going.

“Normally, I give two interviews in the morning, but today I only have yours,” he says, continuing the small talk. Ai is known to be accessible. “Don’t hesitate to ask me anything you’d like,” he offers.

Ever since 2006, when the architect Jacques Herzog first insisted that I try to meet him – they had collaborated on the design of Beijing’s Bird’s Nest stadium, a project Ai later disavowed as a “fake smile” serving Communist propaganda – the Chinese artist, architect and dangerously outspoken activist has been a distant yet recurring motif in my life.

There he was, popping up at the architecture biennale in Venice and at exhibition openings in Beijing – always with an entourage and rarely without an assistant videotaping his every move. Once, I briefly interviewed him over a bowl of beef noodles. Another time, I visited his studio on a day I was told he wouldn’t be there, only to find him typing away at his computer.

Ai has a knack for being somewhere even when he isn’t. He infiltrates things. As part of a massive, high-concept exercise, he took over Documenta 12 in Kassel, Germany, in 2007 with no less than 1,001 ordinary Chinese whom he’d flown in for the occasion. Earlier this year, he helped organise a protest march on a highly symbolic thoroughfare in central Beijing. The demonstration was totally unauthorised and quickly halted by police, but at least one Communist Party newspaper covered it – and guess whose name was on the photo credit?

Ai, 53, is a conceptual artist who’s become known for his activism and an activist whose provocations verge on art. He named his studio Fake Design, but it’s really his life that his art imitates, and the other way around. This October, Ai will become the latest artist to transform London’s Tate Modern as part of the museum’s blockbuster series of Turbine Hall installations. For many, he’s the godfather of contemporary Chinese art, the man – no, the concept – around which an intriguing image of China begins to emerge.

So who, or what, exactly is Ai Weiwei? A figure of controversy in his home country, for a start. “In China, the newspapers and magazines used to report on me a lot – but mostly fashion publications,” he tells me. (I kid you not: as I write this, a friend has stopped by my home, randomly wearing a Comme Des Garçons T-shirt emblazoned with a watermelon and the words THANKS TO AI WEIWEI.)

“People on the internet have seen me on CCTV” – the Chinese state television network – “and said, ‘Weiwei, what the fuck? You’re on CCTV,’” he says. “Maybe they’re using old programmes, but it’s a big joke because I’ve been censored by them. Officially, they cannot mention my name.” Programmes must sometimes slip through the cracks.
What about the Tate installation? What are you doing for that?
“I really can’t talk about it; they even asked me not to talk to you in particular about this.”
So now you’re being censored by the Tate?
“Partially,” he says with an ironic chuckle.

The proper way to address Ai Weiwei is, in fact, Ai. The Chinese place their surnames first; his is pronounced like ‘eye’. But mostly, Weiwei (‘way-way’), as many call him, is an enigmatic yet omnipresent abstraction, an iconoclastic artist and philosopher whose contours are hard to grasp. He works in a range of media, from sculpture, installations and photography to architecture, film and, for lack of a better word, “actions”, while at various times moonlighting as an antiques trader, gallerist and curator. Until recently, he was also the proprietor of Qu Nar (“Go Where?”), a restaurant specialising in the cuisine of Zhejiang province, at which he frequently held court before it was demolished to make way for a new development last year.

As for his art, Ai is unapologetically irreverent and sardonic. He can be seen flipping his finger at the White House and Eiffel Tower in his well-known Study of Perspective photographs, and he has painted the Coca-Cola logo on ancient pots. All the while, his work often relies on earlier wreckage, the kind of creative destruction that defines China’s contemporary crossroads. There’s Dropping a Han Dynasty Urn (1995), a photographic triptych in which he smashes a 2,000-year-old vase. And Map of China (2003), a hulking, geographically correct sculpture made of wood salvaged from demolished Qing dynasty temples. Ai hits a nerve shared by Chinese and non-Chinese alike. As the artist later puts it: “What does ‘China’ mean?”

Nowadays, however, the more pressing question may be just how far he can push the Chinese authorities. Ai has become a gigantic thorn for the powers that be, a vocal critic of the government – for its corruption, human rights shortcomings and other injustices – in a country where life has been known to get difficult for vocal government critics. He doesn’t go about it quietly and misses few opportunities to act or speak out. During our first interview, he tells me how one week earlier, he’d driven into the mountains to rescue an activist who he says was abandoned there after being beaten by secret police. “He announced it on Twitter, said he didn’t know where he was,” Ai says of the man, an advocate for migrant workers. “We had to go out and find him.”
Then, during our second meeting, he’s interrupted by a phone call. “That was the people from the earthquake area,” he says. “They’re still calling me.”
