items.title: A Brazilian Restaurant Showcases the Ingredients of the Amazon
items.description: Iara, a new Amazonian-Brazilian restaurant, is named for a river spirit from the folklore of the Tupi and Guarani peoples; half woman and half fish, she’s something like a vengeful mermaid, a freshwater siren who lures men down into the deep with her singing.
items.author: Helen Rosner
paragraphs: Iara, a new Amazonian-Brazilian restaurant, is named for a river spirit from the folklore of the Tupi and Guarani peoples; half woman and half fish, she’s something like a vengeful mermaid, a freshwater siren who lures men down into the deep with her singing. The first thing you see at her namesake establishment is a glass-fronted case of silvery tilefish, hung up to dry-age. Then the room gives way to a riot of wildly colorful walls, twirling and twining greenery, wood carvings and wall fixtures, wooden tables slashed with a stripe of rain-forest green, the clatter and whoosh of cooks in an open kitchen, and the heady aromas of smoke and spice. The restaurant’s chef-owner, Vitor Mendes, was most recently chef de cuisine at Theodora, in Fort Greene, which is known for its dry-aged seafood and excellent use of an open-flame grill. He’s brought both of those things with him—though the grill at Iara burns charcoal, rather than Theodora’s wood.

There are plenty of Amazonian ingredients to be found on the menu: cupuaçu, a relative of cacao; coumarou, also known as tonka bean, an analogue to vanilla; puxuri, a nutmeg-like spice that, at Iara, rims the glass of a lusty coconut-milk cocktail. But the most vivid through line in Mendes’s cooking is cassava, the world’s great polymathic tuber. It appears as a featherlight, tostada-ish rectangle under a layer of charred-pineapple relish and pearlescent slices of raw scallop. It comes in the form of tapioca—cassava’s starch, extracted—in a traditional pão de queijo, chewy little spheres that arrive with a trio of dips: pink guava; white requeijão, a mild and creamy cheese; and dark, smoky eggplant. Fermented cassava juice becomes tucupi, a tangy golden-brown liquid that’s used in the juicy hot-sauce set on every table; it also kisses a Martini punched up with soju and preserved-lemon brine; and deepens the vinaigrette on a hiramasa ceviche. It’s also the base for the broth in Iara’s tacacá, a soup from northern Brazil, where it is a popular street food in Amazonian cities such as Manaus and Belém. Mendes’s version is a composed take, with silky white beans and caramel-sweet morsels of roasted plantain, its surface dotted with green ribbons of oil infused with jambu, a mild herb that produces a sparky, tingly numbness on the lips and tongue, like an electrified Sichuan peppercorn.

New York is not short on Brazilian food, but it tends to arrive in predictable formats. At churrascarias, waiters circulate with hunks of meat on swords. At quick-service counters in the outer boroughs, tias sell coxinhas and pão de queijo by the dozen. And at home-style comida-caseira places the menus tend toward variations on rice, beans, and meat. A meal at Iara, with its specific and near-hagiographic focus on the indigenous ingredients of the Amazon, is almost nothing like any of these. If you haven’t had the good luck to dine widely in Brazil, much of the menu will feel thrillingly novel. Here in the U.S., I’ve previously encountered jambu as a novelty foodstuff, in its flower-bud form, under the frankly demeaning name “buzz buttons.” Mendes, who was born in Brazil, is an exuberant teacher. He immigrated to the U.S. as a child, and he was awakened to the vast fecundity of the Amazon Basin when he returned to Brazil as an adult, after his father’s death. His passion for these ingredients is palpable, and seems to have infected his staff. A server might linger for a moment to watch you take your first sip of a Romeo and Juliet Martini, a play on Brazil’s ubiquitous guava-and-cheese snack involving mezcal ingeniously washed with mild minas cheese. (The cocktail list was created by Calvin Czypinski, another Theodora alum, clearly having fun.) Another, dropping off a dish of picanha steak, might urge you to pay close attention to the creamy sauce au poivre upon which the meat is set, noting that it’s made not with run-of-the-mill peppercorns but with jiquitaia, a blend of dried hot peppers from the Baniwa people.

My favorite spot in Iara’s well-proportioned dining room is at a chef’s counter that rings the open kitchen. Sitting at a dining bar can sometimes feel tedious and penitent; here, it’s more like being pressed up against the stage at a rock show: the noise, the energy, the pyrotechnics! What a rush it is, watching a cook turn roseate pieces of tilefish over a roaring grill for a portion of the Bahian coconut-broth stew moqueca. Sure, Bahia isn’t an Amazonian state, but the dish fits right in: it comes slicked with red palm oil, in a clay pot sized for sharing, with individual sidecar bowls bearing toothsome white rice, farofa (seasoned, toasted cassava flour), and bright slashes of pepper relish. The battalion behind the counter whips and chops and sauces, looking up at the audience of diners only rarely while flying from one station to another with a forceful grace.

The restaurant is at its strongest when it’s most Brazilian, and weakest when it’s making concessions to what’s hot here in New York. A starter of raw tuna draped over fried puffs of tapioca is a clever enough riff on a ubiquitous crispy-rice sushi appetizer, but does the world really need more of that? A “palmito carpaccio” salad bore a few paper-thin rounds of fresh hearts of palm arrayed atop a nice but largely unexceptional chiffonade of chicories and other winter greens. It certainly can’t compete with an off-menu special of tambaqi, an Amazonian river fish, grilled until sizzling, butchered into hunks of collar and rib and fillet, served with a pile of tapioca fries and an açaí ketchup, piquant and sour and Tyrian purple. End your meal with pudim, a condensed-milk flan speckled with sesame seeds, or a couple of brigadeiros, Brazil’s famous chocolate bonbons. Or, if you still haven’t had your fill of cassava, try the bolo de mandioca, a sweet, coconutty cake whose density and tenderness come from the root, finely shredded into the batter. It’s crowned with a sphere of coconut-lime sorbet—a halo, a sun, a disco ball—a bit of sharpness to slice through the magnificent density of the Amazonian rain forest. ♦

items.title: Obama’s Book Club Is Actually Very Revealing
items.description: The midterms are over. The Democrats ran away with it. So we can be honest now: Barack Obama does not eat at the Cheesecake Factory. When the former president said, at a rally in Cleveland on October 24, that Trump’s remodeling blitz had “the White House looki
items.author: Sam Adler-Bell
paragraphs: The midterms are over. The Democrats ran away with it. So we can be honest now: Barack Obama does not eat at the Cheesecake Factory. When the former president said, at a rally in Cleveland on October 24, that Trump’s remodeling blitz had “the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory” — setting off a hollow and half-hearted Republican effort to turn the election around by provoking the wounded pride of Middle America — Obama was, indeed, being a bit elitist. Trump has bad taste. Garish, vulgar, low-class taste. The gilded, rococo style he loves, which reads to him as “fancy,” looks like shit. The décor at the Cheesecake Factory is similarly gauche. That’s the joke. (And also that Trump is like Saddam Hussein, which Republicans did not bother to be offended by.) People who share Trump’s unsophisticated tastes were not the butt of the joke, as conservatives insisted, but it’s fair to say they caught a stray or two. And the joke was probably most satisfying to people who — like Obama, like me — think the Cheesecake Factory is gaudy trash.

Obviously, it didn’t matter. Nobody cared. Ressentiment only gets you so far when gas is $5 a gallon. But this absurd, inconsequential episode did remind me that Obama and Trump, still the two towering political figures of our time, are deeply similar in one particular sense: They are both authentic cultural emissaries of their most dedicated constituents.

Yes, Trump is a soft-handed billionaire germophobe, but he genuinely enjoys the things that MAGA chuds enjoy: fast food, busty blondes, television. Likewise, Obama seems genuinely to share the tastes and hobbies of the archetypal urban liberal: dad rock, the NBA, well-reviewed literary fiction. By the criterion established by John Cusack’s character in High Fidelity — that what really matters in romance is “what you like, not what you are like” — the love relationship Trump and Obama have formed with their respective publics is sturdy and strong.

It’s not surprising, then, that Obama has made cultural curation — his seasonal lists of books, movies, and music — a core emphasis of his placid post-presidency. (Another beloved pastime of the coastal elite: making and arguing about “best of” lists.) “A Great Book with Barack Obama,” a six-part podcast series from Audible and Higher Ground (the Obamas’ media company), which premiered, somewhat unceremoniously, in September, is the latest expression of this curatorial impulse. In each episode, the former president invites a famous guest — all of whom he calls, per the podcaster’s privilege, “my friend,” even if they’re meeting for the first time — to discuss a book that “had a profound effect” on how he “sees the world.” The results are revealing, not only about Obama himself but also about the effete, morally anguished liberalism he so winsomely embodied, which, thanks to the Democratic rout, is poised to make a comeback in our public life.

Having listened to Obama’s previous foray into celebrity podcasting — a stultifying six-hour dialogue with Bruce Springsteen, during which neither eminence had the slightest inclination to disturb, much less penetrate, the thick layer of self-mythology surrounding the other — I was relieved to find these episodes lively and compelling. Our host proves a careful reader and generous conversationalist, deftly coaxing larger themes from his well-chosen texts. Marilynne Robinson’s novel Gilead prompts Obama and Tom Hanks to reflect on fatherhood, faith, and finitude. (Hanks: “There is a sense of tactile comfort that comes from, dare we call it, God’s world: light through a window, the dust that’s in the air, the smell of food, of warmth, of comfort.”) Robert Penn Warren’s All the King’s Men allows Obama and historian Jill Lepore to discourse on Huey Long and American populism. (Obama: “My first campaign for the state Senate, I had so many ten-point plans … it wasn’t until [later] I figured out — or was told — people are interested in hearing a story about you, them, their lives.”) Cormac McCarthy’s All the Pretty Horses occasions a struggle session over masculinity and male virtue with author Lauren Groff, the mother of two teenage boys. (Obama: “We didn’t figure out entirely what aspects of that old code were true and honorable and worth preserving.”) For many listeners — of the sort who don’t go to the Cheesecake Factory — the mere reminder that a president can be literate, humble, apparently endowed with an inner life, and capable of inhabiting the minds of others will be a balm.

Despite the diversity of material and guests — there’s also Ta-Nehisi Coates on James Baldwin’s The Fire Next Time and Percival Everett on Toni Morrison’s Song of Solomon — the conversations tend to circle around to Obama’s perennial concerns: about the challenge of maintaining one’s humanity amid large, amoral systems; about the smallness of men and their grasping reliance on the wisdom and tolerance of women; about the virtue of pragmatism and reforming institutions from the inside; about race, the responsibilities of power, and the redeemability of America’s foundational myths. These, after all, are the persistent leitmotifs of Obamaism. They are characterized, like liberalism itself, by a slightly discordant mix of optimism about the country — its providential role in the world — and Augustinian pessimism about man’s nature: our selfishness, hubris, and appetite for violence.

The task for the American patriot, Obama-style, is to temper one’s idealism with a sober assessment of man’s folly and thereby avoid becoming jaded. (The influence of theologian Reinhold Niebuhr on Obama’s formation is evident in this regard.) Between the corrupt-but-realistic beneficence of Willie Stark, the protagonist of All the King’s Men, and the unyielding idealism of Dr. Adam Stanton, Stark’s foil and eventual assassin, Obama sides firmly with Stark. “What you want is goodness,” Stark tells Stanton in the novel. “Yeah, just plain simple goodness. Well, you can’t inherit that from anybody. You’ve got to make it, Doc, if you want it. And you’ve got to make it out of badness. Badness… And you know why? Because there isn’t anything else to make it out of.” Quoting this passage to Lepore, Obama glosses it thus: “The only way anything gets done is just by men like him who are willing to act and get their hands dirty.”

The question of “dirty hands” also haunts Obama’s discussion of John le Carré’s Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy with Ben Rhodes, his former deputy national-security adviser. In the Biden years, Rhodes became an especially articulate critic of the Israel-oriented foreign policy Obama left largely intact. Together, they interpret Tinker Tailor — about a disgraced spymaster, George Smiley, smoking out a mole in the British secret service — as the story of one man’s thankless allegiance to an enfeebled empire, to the faithful execution of his vocation, to his colleagues and those who depend upon him, and to his beloved wife, whose very distance, her just-out-of-reach-ness, is the engine of his displaced passion. (Michelle Obama is consistently summoned in these conversations to play her husband’s superego, his unillusioned foil, the source of his humility and self-knowledge.)

Obama and his former aide seem a little dumbfounded, at once defensive and doleful, about their erstwhile roles administrating the national-security state. Their dialogue, thrilling at first, quickly devolves into banality. In their hands, le Carré’s novel becomes an argument for muddling through, for reveling in ambiguity without succumbing entirely to cynicism. The book becomes a testament to the fact — equal parts encouraging and ominous — that even the most impenetrable and instrumental systems (i.e., nation-states) are made up of fragile human people with passions large and small. “Even in bleak systems,” Obama says, “there’s humanity and kindness and courage.” In le Carré’s novels, Rhodes says, “You tend to be rooting for the better people, not the perfect people, but the people that want to help each other, that want to protect their networks, and make their institutions better. And, as you always said: Better is good.”
“That was an underrated motto,” Obama concurs. “Better is good.”

Obamaism is susceptible to cliché, in this way, because his answer to the thorniest moral questions is always the same: “It’s complicated.” For Obama, the worst thing you can be is certain. (That way lies fanaticism, which Smiley correctly identifies as his Soviet nemesis Karla’s greatest flaw.) Like many good liberals, he is ambivalent about many things but dogmatic about the value of ambivalence. “Life is ambiguous; reality is ambiguous,” he insists. Systems — philosophies, regimes — built on certitude will in the end “be brittle,” Obama cautions, “because this strange, chaotic, not-to-be-tamed thing called ‘life’ will undermine whatever absolute ideas you have.” No doubt there is wisdom in this counsel. But for Obama, it is also an alibi, an excuse to stop thinking, to shirk the harder work of judgment. It is tempting to assume Obama leans on cliché out of discretion or tact. But I don’t think that’s true. He believes these things. He has a genuine fealty to cliché, which is never stronger than when he talks about America. (Nationalism, after all, requires fealty to platitudes.) The belief that Obama possesses unrevealed depths — a more coherent and trenchant understanding that he judiciously conceals — is a solace to his devotees and the reason for the febrile irritation of his critics.

It is Coates who pushes Obama the hardest toward a squarer reckoning of his own legacy. Baldwin’s key point in The Fire Next Time, Coates argues, is that “Black people do not have the luxury of duplicating the morality of those who oppressed us … Somehow we will have to invent something new.” The impulse of the oppressed to get power and use it in the same barbaric ways it was once used against them — this, Coates says, “is the problem of our era.” And he sees it playing out today in Israel and Palestine, where a once-brutalized people, the Jews, have decided they are permitted to “do whatever it takes to ensure the security and the survival of [their] people… even it means replicating the systems that have been used” against them.

Obama, unsurprisingly, is reluctant to co-sign this position entirely. He acknowledges, circuitously, that “after what we saw in Gaza, it’s hard to not think … we didn’t learn the right lesson and we continue to learn the wrong lessons.” And he faithfully repeats the vague shibboleths of liberal Zionism: “the current administration” (meaning Benjamin Netanyahu) has “taken Israel down a very bad road”; the Palestinians “have been ill-served” by their own leadership; and “at the end of the day, it is incumbent on the stronger party … to arrive at a just solution.” He laments, rather lamely, that he “couldn’t do everything that I wanted to move the situation into a different position.”

But Coates, it turns out, is after something deeper. In The Fire Next Time, Baldwin asks, “Do I really want to be integrated into a burning house?” He had not quite fathomed the question that faced Barack Obama: What if I become the master of a burning house? And thus Coates’s challenge: What does it mean that a man with Obama’s particular biography — not merely a Black man in America, but the son of an African, born in Hawaii within living memory of its annexation, who spent some of his childhood in Indonesia in the shadow of a CIA-backed coup, who studied with Edward Said at Columbia and became enamored with Baldwin and the Black radical tradition — became the president of the United States? “I guess what I want to ask,” Coates says, “is how, carrying all that, do you walk into the White House?”

Obama responds with his usual clichés: “The essential question is, ‘All right, if we see a system that is in many ways immoral, how do we address that?’ Do we shun it? Do we leave it? Do we reform it? What compromises are we willing to make in that process?”

But Coates’s question, unresolved, haunts the rest of the conversation. Baldwin feared the achievement of inclusion for Black Americans would come at the cost of their moral witness, their capacity to puncture America’s self-flattering myth. “I cannot accept the proposition that the four-hundred-year travail of the American Negro should result merely in his attainment of the present level of the American civilization,” he wrote. Coates seems to fear this has come to pass — that Black internationalism and solidarity with the world’s poor diminished as Black inclusion advanced — and Obama, son of the Global South, was the apotheosis of this process. “If we’re only fighting for our place in the machine and the machine is going to be as it is,” Coates says, “if my name is going to be on bombs to uphold systems that my ancestors would oppose, then I don’t know what my connection to this struggle is … if that’s what the fight is.”

Toward the end of their talk, Coates asks Obama to imagine how Baldwin and other figures of the Black radical tradition would asses him. He responds, “I’m in an ongoing conversation with them. They’re my ancestors. They’re my ghosts. They talk to me all the time. I hear their voices. And they say, ‘Did you do enough? Did you really risk what you should have risked on behalf of this cause, this issue, these people? Did you speak as truthfully as you could in those circumstances? And are you doing as much as you could right now — when, you know, the sky’s aflame?’”
These are fine words. But everything Obama has said besides suggests his answer to each question is a qualified “Yes.”

At a certain point in their discussion, Obama offers Groff a distinction between the cynical and the tragic sensibility: Cynicism, he says, is when you think it’s “okay” that a terrible thing has happened. Tragedy, by contrast, is when you say, “Well, this is going to happen, and it breaks my heart. And I’m going to remember and know that what happened was wrong. But I’m also going to conclude that some things like this are going to happen.”

It’s clear that to the extent Obama can face his own failures, it is as a tragedian: a man buffeted by the winds of history, trying to do his best, failing — but humanly. He is remorseful about what could not have been otherwise; he is hopeful about what could be better soon. (This is why some of his greatest contributions as an orator were elegies.) “I found myself in the captain’s chair of this massive machine that inexorably moves forward,” he explains to Coates. Many times “I wrestled with deep ambiguities and moral questions involved in exercising power.” But “there wasn’t a time where I felt I was relinquishing my moral compass.” At the moments when his complicity is most acute, the heroic gesture is his personal vigilance, protecting his most precious moral competence — his ability to mourn.

items.title: The Day the Stuyvesant Test Glitched
items.description: Early on Saturday, November 14, eighth-graders from across the five boroughs made their way to the campuses of elite public high schools across the city — Brooklyn Tech, Hillcrest in Queens, Bronx High School of Science, Stuyvesant High School in downtown Manh
items.author: Anya Kamenetz
paragraphs: Early on Saturday, November 14, eighth-graders from across the five boroughs made their way to the campuses of elite public high schools across the city — Brooklyn Tech, Hillcrest in Queens, Bronx High School of Science, Stuyvesant High School in downtown Manhattan, and James Madison, in Midwood — to take the fearsome three-hour Specialized High School Admissions Test that determines whether they get to attend one of the city’s top public high schools, whose graduates include, among many notables, Talib Kweli, Thelonious Monk, Min Jin Lee, Lucy Liu, and, in the case of Bronx Science, nine Nobel laureates and Zohran Mamdani. But instead of the SHSAT (pronounced Shizat if you’re in the know), they encountered, per Reddit, a “shit show.” All 2,500 students who signed up for testing that day were unable to complete the test due to computer problems.

“They just told us to keep pressing reload on our tablets,” says Jackie, an eighth-grader who tried and was unable to take the test at Brooklyn Tech. “I pressed it like 20 times. For the first hour, I thought that it was gonna, like, load eventually, and then I just kind of wanted to leave.”

In the milieu of last week’s massive tech failures, the SHSAT meltdown received far less media attention than the nationwide FAA ground stop, the Microsoft outage, or the JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard cyberattack, but for 13-year-olds in New York City, this was a much more life-altering tech catastrophe. The SHSAT is offered only four days a year, and there is arguably no higher-stakes test in American education. It is the sole determinant in admission to some of the most prestigious high schools in America. It’s common to prepare for a full year or even longer (Jackie started working with a tutor in January of this year). Declaring “Stuy or die!,” students give up their summers, afternoons, and weekends, and their parents spend thousands with private coaches, test-prep companies like Kweller and Bespoke Education, or at storefront cram schools in Sunset Park. And then, once they’ve learned as much as they possibly can, they try to get a good night’s sleep and their nervous parents drop them off with a water bottle and a snack.

On Saturdays, after students signed in and started logging in to the test, the tablets started to crash one by one. Many students were never able to sign in at all. “We waited for, like, three hours,” says Jackie. “The person in my room was trying to call someone. People were annoyed because we didn’t have our personal devices, so we were just kind of sitting there.”

Charlotte, a mom in Park Slope, who declined to give her last name, received a call from her son, who was trying to take the test at Brooklyn Tech, around 11:30 a.m. He’d been there since 8 a.m. “I think he borrowed someone’s phone. It was a bit surreptitious, but he was just like, ‘We’re still here. We still haven’t started the test. It’s not going to happen today.’ There was all this anxiety and tension building, and they’re just having them wait and wait. And wait, and wait. And wait. And parents had no idea.”

Multiple sources told me students were told to sit at their desks doing nothing for two or three, or, in some cases, up to four hours. Proctors were “freaking out,” and in some places kids were “hysterical” and “crying,” says Frances Kweller, founder of Kweller Prep in Forest Hills. In all, 200 of Kweller’s students were affected.

What exactly went wrong? Dominique Ellison, associate press secretary for NYC Public Schools, emailed me to say: “We would defer to Pearson on this.” Pearson Education, an ed tech giant valued at $10.2 billion that runs the GED and Britain’s A levels, and a sizeable textbook and for-profit schools business, signed a $17 million contract with the Department of Education in 2024 to offer the test in an “adaptive” digital format for the first time this year. (The test only became computer-based, rather than paper and pencil, in 2025.) In an adaptive test, students are shown different questions based on their responses, so that if you’re doing well, the questions grow harder. This customization is supposed to make the test both more efficient and more accurate.

A Pearson spokesperson confirmed that the November 14 test administration was entirely canceled due to “an isolated software defect,” and added “Pearson takes responsibility for the issue, and we apologize to the students and families affected.” (Other administrations of this same SHSAT–on November 15 and November 18—have gone mostly fine, with occasional reported freezes of up to 30 minutes. The November 14 date was specifically intended for students who attend charter and private schools.

The SHSAT has been considered controversial for decades, and not just because of the pressure it places on students and Pearson’s past testing problems, like a notoriously nonsensical reading passage about a pineapple in 2012. The primary issue is that the schools the test gate-keeps end up with mostly white and Asian-American students in a mostly Black and Latino school system. Of the roughly 4,000 seats at these schools, only 3.5 percent went to Black students last year. Mayor Bill DeBlasio tried and failed to eliminate the test, even as his own son Dante graduated from Brooklyn Tech, a specialized high school. Currently, a coalition of elected officials and former NYC schools chancellor David Banks are pressuring Mamdani to reform the specialized high school admissions process.

Within this fraught context, Saturday’s computer crash sent rumors flying. City Councilmember Susan Zhuang represents mostly working-class and immigrant families in South Brooklyn. “I had a lot of families reach out to me and say their kids were not able to take the test. They fear that someone tried to sabotage the process, because a lot of people are speaking up against the SHSAT,” she said. “They feel targeted. They’re panicking.” She said these families value education above all else. Some have used all of their disposable income — eschewing vacations and even trips to the movies — to pay for SHSAT prep. They’re worried that this ordeal will spoil their kids’ careful preparation.

“The issue parents are raising, in the chat groups, in the feeds, is that there’s no actual named person at Pearson responsible for this,” says Kweller. “There’s no named person in the DOE responsible. There’s no one accountable.” Another potential issue: Some students completed part of the test, which could give them an unfair advantage on the retake, she adds.

Students who showed up for last week’s SHSAT have all been given makeup dates, some of which stretch into early December. The rescheduling has the potential to wreck Thanksgiving break as anxious students feel the need to keep on studying. December 4 is also the application deadline for all of the “screened” high schools, a separate and larger group of competitive public high schools whose applications require essays and portfolios. The rescheduling of the SHSAT thus creates a logjam. Charlotte’s son has been working with a tutor since January, and was supposed to be moving on to focus on his essays for other schools. Instead he has had to add extra SHSAT prep sessions to his calendar. Kweller is offering free additional tutoring sessions to all affected families.

“I just feel so bad for these kids,” says Audrey Korelstein, who has been coaching students for the SHSAT and other academic tests for 15 years. “They’re so fragile at this point because they’re prepping on so many multiple fronts. They’re prepping for the Consortium schools, they’re doing the Bard test, they’re on the Ravenna portal for private schools. These kids are just the most exhausted kids ever.”

items.title: Anthropic Got Rich With Record-Breaking IPO: As It Happened
items.description: The first big AI-generated IPO arrived, the money wasn’t hallucinated, and Claude wasn’t wrong if it told you it could be the biggest IPO in history. The AI company Anthropic finally made its market debut, and by the end of the first day of trading had become
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: The first big AI-generated IPO arrived, the money wasn’t hallucinated, and Claude wasn’t wrong if it told you it could be the biggest IPO in history. The AI company Anthropic finally made its market debut, and by the end of the first day of trading had become one of the world’s most valuable companies, turning its founders into billionaires and thousands of its employees into millionaires. Below is our running account of how it all played it out.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it won’t happen this year, but they may have to sooner than later:
What a time to be alive, continued
I’ve seen a lot of attempts to break down the Anthropic IPO “by the numbers” and some have been more useful than others. Not sure how I feel about this one, from the Associated Press:
How far a trillion U.S. dollar bills would stretch if laid end-to-end: 97 million miles (156 million kilometers)
That would surpass the roughly 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) between Earth and the sun.
The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. $1 trillion is a thousand times greater than $1 billion. And a million times more than $1 million.
There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the U.S. Census Bureau. If $1 trillion was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost $122.

So Anthropic’s end-of-trading market value of $1.77 trillion would be nearly $216 per person; if lined up in dollars, it would reach all the way to the sun and then nearly 85 percent of the way back to Earth.

Or, more realistically, you’d maybe get 60 percent of the way to the sun before the energy from the sun began to pyrolyze the dollars, leaving you with an enormous pile of unusable cash long before you even got close to the big yellow dwarf. Elon Musk will probably find a way to test this theory. He has the cash, loves space travel, and has developed an affinity for setting money on fire (though you would, of course, need oxygen to actually set paper money on fire in the cold vacuum of space).
In summary, it is indeed hard to comprehend $1 trillion, but too bad because it’s now something we have to do more and more.
An IPO the could be worth $156 billion for charities
TechCruch’s Tim Fernholz explains:

Anthropic’s employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes of their choice, and the company will match those donations 3-to-1 for longer tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. In its S-1 filing, the company said that it had reserved more than 550 million shares to fulfill pledges made before September 30.

Working backwards from that figure, and based on the disclosure that 84% of the shares were reserved for early employee matches, we can estimate that employees have pledged $23 billion of donations; the company’s match on those would be roughly $53 billion, depending on the stock price when those matches are delivered.

All told, it adds up to $156 billion — a huge amount of potential philanthropy. For context, Americans donated $617 billion to charity in 2025; if all of the pledged funds resulting from today’s transactions get to do-gooders, that will be equal to about a quarter of all U.S. donations made last year.
But a lot of the donations will probably go to effective altruism-aligned causes, as the Wall Street Journal’s Laura J. Nelson points out:

[E]xpectations are high that donors with links to the social movement known as effective altruism are preparing to give to charities and political organizations that reflect their values. The EA movement encourages people to “earn to give” and to try to maximize the amount of good they can do in the world with their time and money.

Philanthropic fundraisers expect a boom in contributions to donor-advised funds, which allow givers to make lump-sum contributions of cash or stock, receive a tax benefit in the year they contribute and disburse the money to charities at any point afterward. The funds don’t have annual distribution requirements, meaning if donors don’t have a giving plan, assets can pile up and not reach the causes they want to support.

Some Anthropic employees are considering creating private family foundations, which have a 5% annual minimum distribution rule. Political fundraisers and strategists expect money to flow into the movement for AI safety, which emerged as a major spender for Congressional candidates of both parties this year.
Exponential growth at one of today’s anti-AI protests
That’s the takeaway from Bloomberg’s Edward Ludlow:
All told, Anthropic will regard today as a success. (It’s not their job to resuscitate the AI trade, right?)
The money is in the bank. It has the accolade of the biggest IPO of all time — and, more importantly, it is the first frontier AI lab to make the leap into public markets.
But what struck me most from the Nasdaq floor, and from conversations with management and investors, was how deliberately Anthropic approached the day.

The message was consistent: They know how they want to run this company. They believe they are very good at what they do. And they are prepared to be brave when commercial pressure, investor expectations and their own principles come into conflict.
That tension is now public. Every earnings report, model launch, compute commitment — and decision not to pursue revenue for safety reasons — will be judged in real time.
Today was the easy part. Public-company life starts now.
ANT ends the day up 17 percent, but the rest of the market sank
Anthropic ended at $97.17, up from its $83 offering price. Here’s CNBC’s summary after the close:
Stocks tumbled on Thursday, falling to their lows of the session the very moment the widely anticipated artificial intelligence IPO Anthropic began trading.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to end at 23,879.20 after gaining as much as 2% earlier in the session. The S&P 500 shed 2.02% and closed at 7,175.83. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,101.11 points, or 2.19%, to close at 49,097.06. The last time the 30-stock index closed below 50,000 was in June. At one point, the blue-chip average was down 10% from its intraday high.
Anthropic, trading at the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, opened shortly before noon at $111.50 per share, a 34% pop. The stock ended the day about 13% off its first trading price and closed up 17%.

That means Anthropic’s market value after its first day (about 4 hours) of trading is now around $1.77 trillion. That’s bigger than Meta, but behind Space X. The Wall Street Journal’s Gunjan Banerji wonders where ANT will be months from now:
Will it last? SpaceX shares jumped 19% on the day of their stock-market debut but were recently trading around $138, a hair above its IPO price of $135.
Now Anthropic has the cash to go big
A smart point from New York Times Anthropic reporter Cory Weinberg:

One observation that investors have brought up with me today: Anthropic’s stock price might be the story today. But the roughly $120 billion of cash it raised yesterday — on top of the $132 billion it had at the end of September — will ripple across other publicly traded stocks for months and years to come. The company is at the early stages of developing its own chips (watch out, Nvidia), building its own data centers (watch out, Amazon), and selling a range of software applications that it hopes will displace a lot of tools workers use every day. Wishful thinking, perhaps. But Anthropic now has the cash to make a lot of CEOs scared.
That’s a lot of millionaires
Nearly every single Ant is now at least a millionaire, according to this analysis passed along by CNN:

For Anthropic, which has grown to 5,300 employees in under six years, today was payday. According to Hill.com, a platform for buying and selling shares in pre-IPO private companies, most “Ants,” as Anthropic staff are known inside the company, are now millionaires — some several times over.
Here’s the breakdown Hill shared with CNN:
• About 5,100 employees with equity worth over $1 million
• As many as 2,800 employees with equity worth over $10 million
• As many as 600 employees with equity worth over $100 million
The Anthropic founders are now worth $171 billion
Or at least that’s where their combined fortunes were as of 12:30 p.m., per Bloomberg:

The stock, which priced at $83 a share, was trading at $100.74 as of 12:30 p.m. in New York, valuing each founder’s fortune at about $24.5 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. The $107.3 billion public offering and concurrent private placement broke SpaceX’s record for the biggest-ever.

The group first became billionaires less than two years ago after the San Francisco-based company raised $3.5 billion at a $61.5 billion valuation. Another funding round that closed in May propelled all seven onto Bloomberg’s ranking of the world’s 500 richest people.
Also, for what that’s worth to causes:

All seven have pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal company equity to philanthropic causes. Anthropic’s prospectus specifies that these commitments aren’t legally binding and constitute voluntary, revocable pledges.
This is your moment too, random metal company
Pity anyone still looking to buy in the Bay Area housing market
CNN’s Samantha Delouya takes stock of the already insane prices:
In a city already grappling with a severe housing shortage, a fresh wave of newly wealthy buyers could push an increasingly expensive housing market further out of reach.

San Francisco home prices are already rising at their fastest pace in years. The typical home sold for $1.7 million in October, up nearly 19% from a year earlier, according to Redfin. By contrast, the national median home price was roughly flat over the same period, at $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.

It’s not uncommon for a luxury home in a desirable area of the city to receive offers more than $1 million above the original listing price, John DiDomenico, a San Francisco-based real estate agent, told CNN.

Rents in the city have grown even quicker. The median rent in San Francisco was $4,595 per month in October, up 30% from last year, according to Zumper, a digital rental marketplace. That means renters today are paying $1,058 more per month compared to last year.
New York Times real estate reporter Gregory Schmidt adds:

Anthropic’s market debut is expected to lead to “housing demand shock overnight,” said Jake Krimmel, a senior economist at Reatlor.com. “We’ve already seen down payments ramp up considerably during the A.I. buildout and anticipate a further surge in all-cash buyers,” he said. “The Bay Area already has the highest home prices in the country. That gap is only getting wider.”
Meanwhile here in New York:
This all makes Moskovitz nervous
One of the most important early backers of Anthropic, Facebook co-founder and AI safety advocate Dustin Moskovitz, told the New York Times the company needs to slow down:
In a statement to The New York Times, Mr. Moskovitz established some distance from the company, where he served as a board observer, or a nonvoting board member.

“Cari and I invested in Anthropic to promote safety, not racing,” he said, referring to his wife, Cari Tuna. “A.I. is moving too fast. Anthropic and everyone else on the frontier should slow down and stop racing.”

In an unusual move, the couple transferred their Anthropic stake — which would be worth billions of dollars today — into a nonprofit in early 2025 so that he and Ms. Tuna would not personally profit from selling the stock in the public market, a spokesman for the couple said. The spokesman, Mike Levine, declined to disclose the nonprofit.
Meanwhile in the rest of the market

Sam Bankman-Fried probably doesn’t have internet access, but if he did, he’d probably feel very left out today. As the Wall Street Journal points out, FTX’s ANT stake would have been worth $37 billion:

In April 2022, Anthropic announced a $580 million Series B round led by Bankman-Fried, who is now serving a 25-year prison sentence. Caroline Ellison, former CEO of FTX’s sister trading firm Alameda Research, and Nishad Singh, an FTX co-founder and its former director of engineering, also participated in the round, Anthropic said.

After the collapse of FTX in late 2022, the FTX bankruptcy estate sold its $500 million stake in Anthropic in 2024 for about $1.3 billion to help repay creditors. At Anthropic’s $83-a-share IPO price, that stake would be worth roughly $37 billion today.
A mental health break for anyone who didn’t invest in Anthropic and has nothing to gain today and/or for anybody watching the markets right now:
AI’s first official market rollercoaster is rolling:
ANT opens at $111.50 per share
That’s 34 percent over the initial offering price, and makes it a $2 trillion company.
Silicon Valley’s dancing plague?
At the San Francisco Standard, Theo Baker likens the mood in Silicon Valley to 1518’s biggest dance craze:

Are we barreling toward utopia or destruction or something in between? Prioritizing speed — because otherwise others get there first, because you need to justify your valuation day in and day out, or because, in the simplest sense, that’s where the technology is headed — seems like a way to guarantee the worst outcomes of the bunch.

In Strasbourg in the summer of 1518, a woman began to dance without music. Others soon joined in, mimicking her spasmodic, uncontrollable movements — and before long they were crying for help. They couldn’t stop. Dozens, even hundreds, joined this dancing plague, today understood by scientists as a form of mass psychosis, and could be released only by collapse or death, their bodies drenched in sweat and blood.
This is what it feels like to be living in Silicon Valley during what may amount to the most important week in its history. The music is getting faster, and no one thinks they can stop.
Sucks to be you, institutional investors without a prior relationship with Anthropic
CNBC says a bunch of big firms may be feeling FOMO today:

Anthropic prioritized allocating shares to institutional investors it had relationships with, according to people familiar with the details, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That meant roughly half of the firms that placed orders were left empty handed, they said.

It’s normal in most IPOs for some portion of institutional investors not to receive any allocation, but that happened to be a higher number than usual for this offering, one person said. Anthropic’s management team had experience working with institutional investors from raising capital through private rounds, so the company had a strong view of what would make up a good shareholder base construction, the person said.
The angst of the now-rich Ants
At the New York Times, Jasmine Sun sums up her many conversations with Anthropic employees ahead of the IPO

Juxtaposed with what they presume will be the imminent arrival of superintelligence, the upcoming payday seems parochial to many at Anthropic. Some employees describe the I.P.O. with a shrug, likening it to just another funding round.

This is a peculiar attitude for a crowd of young people who, in many cases, are about to become deca- and centimillionaires overnight. The Ants are not your average tech workers. They spend morning to night at rows of desks in the bare, high-security offices in San Francisco’s downtown, where the common books on display include Richard Rhodes’s “The Making of the Atomic Bomb” and paperback printouts of company writings, such as Mr. Amodei’s “Machines of Loving Grace” and the in-house philosopher Amanda Askell’s “Claude’s Constitution.”

No one is compelled to work the grueling “996” hours (9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week) that have become common in the tech industry, but a good number of Ants do so anyway out of their own feverish devotion. Many cram themselves into modest group apartments, host house parties where few, if any, drink and blank when I ask how they spend their lavish salaries, even with my prompts: “A wardrobe update, maybe?” “Ever considered flying business class?”
The money is secondary. The most common form of I.P.O. talk involves discussions of where to allocate the newly liquid stock in their charitable donation accounts.
And yes, of course, somebody brought up LOTR:

One former Ant referenced J.R.R. Tolkien’s parable in trying to explain Anthropic’s mind-set: Whomever builds superintelligence first will get Sauron’s ring. That person or company will possess the most dangerous cyberweapons in the world, the cures and recipes for every disease, and an army of tireless digital geniuses to do its bidding. The most load-bearing question, then, is the morality of the one who wields the ring. (Of course, in Middle Earth, the Ring was destroyed because even the purest soul couldn’t make it safe.)
And that, of course, started a whole thing on social:
The Wall Street Journal reports that it may be as high as $104 a share:
Shares in Anthropic are set to begin trading midday and could open at around $104 a share, roughly 25% above their IPO price of $83, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Pricing indications tend to shift before the opening and there is no guarantee the stock will open at that level.
Dude, where’s my billionaire car?
Did you know that Ashton Kutcher owns 0.5 percent of Anthropic? Now you do. Per Bloomberg:

Dario Amodei was arguably one of the least famous people in the Beverly Hills home he visited in 2023. The Anthropic PBC chief executive officer sat across from actor-turned-venture capitalist Ashton Kutcher, and Guy Oseary, the legendary music manager and industry broker who owned the house. Oseary’s framed art by rock legends like John Lennon and David Bowie hung on the wall behind them.

The group spent hours discussing AI safety, the global race to build better artificial intelligence models and the overall vision for Anthropic, then still an easily overlooked challenger to OpenAI. By the end of the meeting, Oseary, Kutcher and the team had decided to participate in the Claude maker’s first institutionally led funding round through their investment firm, Sound Ventures. …

The under-the-radar venture firm with Hollywood ties is now poised for a substantial windfall from Anthropic’s initial public offering, expected in the coming days. Sound Ventures owns roughly half a percent of the AI company, according to a person familiar with the matter. That stake would be worth approximately $7 billion at Anthropic’s current target IPO valuation of $1.4 trillion, according to Bloomberg estimates.
Inside the Anthropic office right now
Some investors plan to wait and see
Notes the team at Reuters:
Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, CEOs and political leaders split over its sustainability.

Much of the scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of the industry’s growth is being fueled by money circulating within the same ecosystem.
Anthropic’s breakneck growth has so far defied these concerns, but some investors have said they may wait for the initial euphoria to subside before buying.

“Anthropic is a one-trick pony. People compare it with Amazon because even Amazon lost money for several years, but Anthropic won’t have that luxury,” said Bill Gunderson, partner at GCG Advisory Partners.
“They’ve got to get to profitability soon.”
Will Anthropic still be Anthropic after this?
The Verge’s Hayden Field wonders:

Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power.

One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight.
What Amodei had to say before ANT hits the world
Here’s some of what the Anthropic CEO said at the Nasdaq this morning, per NBC News:
“I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.”
But Amodei says the technology has “very real risks,” too.
“These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or by nation states to economic disruption to losing control of AI systems.”
“We will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control.”
“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.”
The Nasdaq is already up nearly 2 percent
The Nasdaq Composite surged 1.9%, while the S&P 500 added 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 191 points, or 0.4%. …

Anthropic is set to pop 25% when it opens for trading, according to indications from the perpetual futures markets. Retail trader demand is expected to be even stronger than seen during SpaceX, according to Vanda Research.

The higher-than-expected pricing for the IPO gave the broader tech sector a boost. Chipmakers Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices were up 4% and 2.7%, respectively. Micron Technology gained 6%. Tech giants Microsoft and Meta Platforms also popped around 2%. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius advanced 8% and 6%, respectively.
Lets (let CNN) do the math
A helpful CNN explanation of Anthropic’s eye-popping $1.5 trillion valuation:

As for valuation: Companies create new shares to sell in an IPO, so the valuation involves the total number of shares that will exist after the IPO. This includes the shares created for IPO, plus those not part of the IPO offering — like unvested employee equity, non-voting shares held by investors and convertible debt.
These post-IPO shares are called “fully diluted” shares, and it’s why you might hear the term “fully diluted valuation.”
Offering price per share X total number of post-IPO shares = Fully diluted valuation
For Anthropic, that’s: $83 offering price per share X 18.14 billion total shares = $1.5 trillion fully diluted valuation
Let the ANT trading begin?
It’s 9:30 a.m. ET and things are probably about to get nuts. But the Anthropic trading won’t start right away, as the New York Times explains:

Delaying the start of trading in shares in a newly public company is part of an elaborate effort to ensure that the stock’s introduction into the market goes as smoothly as possible. A key part of that is deciding at what price Anthropic should begin trading.

Bankers will spend Thursday morning trying to assess from traders how much demand there is to sell and buy Anthropic shares at various prices. They are looking for an “equilibrium” price: the price at which there is generally the same amount of sellers as buyers.
The goal is to make sure that the company’s shares are relatively stable when they begin to trade.
The next Speaker of the House speaks Claude?

And he may not even realize it. The Washington Sun reports that “A member of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ staff operated a custom-designed artificial intelligence–powered program dubbed ‘Caucus Pulse’ to surveil various factions of the Democratic caucus and suggest messaging for Jeffries”:

The Caucus Pulse program, which was largely produced and fueled by Anthropic’s AI agent Claude, also generated a detailed report recommending steps Jeffries could take as minority leader to address concerns about the rapid development of Anthropic’s AI technology.
In a statement to The Sun, Jeffries’ office said the minority leader himself wasn’t aware of Caucus Pulse and didn’t use material generated by the AI-powered program.
Has your job ever made you an overnight centimillionaire?
CNBC on this massive rapid wealth-creation event:
The average Anthropic employee could be worth over $40 million after the company’s IPO today, with over 400 employees likely to be worth over $100 million, according to SEC filings and investors.

Anthropic was founded just five years ago and has only 5,300 employees. According to SEC filings, the artificial intelligence company has generated 1.77 billion options for employees, with a strike price of $2.91 a share. It has also paid out over 1 billion restricted stock units.

If the stock trades at $83 a share, the combined wealth of Anthropic employees will be around $232 billion, based on their share count in the filings. The total works out to an average of $44 million per employee.

Yet because many of the employees are later hires, earlier employees could have supersized gains since they’ve accumulated more stock. According to investors in the company, at least 400 early employees will be worth $100 million or more at a $83 share price. Several could become billionaires, they said.
The employee total doesn’t include the seven founders, who each own between 230 million and 240 million shares, which will each be worth around $20 billion based on a $83 share price.
Just in case you just got rich
Curbed has some suggestions on how the world’s new very rich effective altruists could invest in this fine city we all call home:

There is, of course, only so much that private philanthropy can solve — some issues, such as New York’s homelessness crisis and the increasingly bad signal system in the subways, are too vast and too bureaucracy heavy. But there are many areas of city life where a private donation of $100 million or less could make a dramatic difference.

A few months ago, we loosed reporters across the city to speak to insiders about what some of these projects could be. They probed experts and practitioners in different industries, policy wonks, local nonprofit directors, and lawmakers. They almost immediately happened on a trove of projects that were all but ready to go yet had lost funding — including ones with detailed renderings that had gone through the necessary approval processes and feasibility studies and were just awaiting a benefactor.

One example from the guide is how you could give the city a floating pool for the East River for only $60 Million. $75 million would teach 70,000 second grade New Yorkers how to swim. Or you could spend only $20 million to create a massive welding-apprentice workshop in the Bronx for our low-income neighbors. Read the rest here.
You know what’s cooler than a billion dollars?
Here comes ANT. Anthropic raised more than $107 billion yesterday, and their record-breaking IPO values the company at roughly 1.5 trillion. NPR reports:

Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share. The company’s seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic’s prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia. The total haul is more than $107 billion.
This post was continuously updated.

items.title: Trump Kept Embarrassing Himself at Summit With Xi and Putin
items.description: Donald Trump kicked off his meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin on Thursday by declaring, “We are really making history.” Technically, that’s true. It was the first time the leaders of China, Russia, and the United State
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Donald Trump kicked off his meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin on Thursday by declaring, “We are really making history.” Technically, that’s true. It was the first time the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States have had a formal three-way meeting.

However, Trump’s critics say all he was really doing was embarrassing himself on multiple levels. Before the meeting, Trump said he wanted to make progress on nuclear weapons and the wars in Iran and Ukraine. But he walked away with nothing more than platitudes from Putin and Xi. Even worse, in exchange for some pomp and flattery from China, Trump gave his two autocrat pals plenty of propaganda to use back home, as Anne Applebaum argued in The Atlantic:

The meeting was brief, almost substance-free, and carefully choreographed for the maximum benefit of the Chinese hosts. Its true purpose was not to end any wars — and certainly not to end Russia’s bloody invasion of Ukraine — but to produce propaganda photographs and video clips that each of the three leaders will now use to mask their political failures.

The president’s Asia trip wasn’t just conceptually embarrassing. He also engaged in plenty of Trumpy bumbling, from gushing about his “friend” Putin to falling asleep during a big meeting. Here are some of the lowlights.
He showed up in Asia with a new hair color.
The meeting with Putin and Xi wasn’t Trump’s first stop in Asia. He initially headed to Manila on Tuesday, November 17, for a meeting of Southeast Asian leaders.

Trump was clearly trying to look his best, and it wound up backfiring. He left D.C. with his usual light-blond coif and stepped off the plane with a much darker hair color (which he paired with a goofy flag wave). The shades of brown faded over the next few days, as chronicled by USA Today, and he was mostly back to his usual color by the time he arrived in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
He told Imelda Marcos, “We love you.”
Trump and the former First Lady of the Philippines go way back, as the New York Times explained:

When Imelda Marcos and Donald J. Trump partied in New York in the 1990s, she was the exiled former first lady of the Philippines, the wife of an ousted dictator, and he was a real estate mogul facing multiple bankruptcies.

They met again in Manila on Wednesday in vastly different roles. Mr. Trump, 80, is, of course, the president of the United States. And Ms. Marcos, 97, is the mother of the president of the Philippines, her family ensconced again in Malacañang Palace.

So it makes sense that Trump gave Marcos a warm greeting. But did he have to tell his famously corrupt pal “We love you!” and then let White House communications adviser Margo Martin advertise that fact on social media? Perhaps not.
He took in a performance of “Y.M.C.A.” with Xi.

This is mortifying on two levels. First, the Chinese thought the president of the United States would be flattered by a performance of the Village People’s “Y.M.C.A.” paired with a montage of special moments from his relationship with Xi. Second, they were right. Martin proudly posted video of this moment from the APEC welcome banquet:
He bragged about saving Christmas.

Remember how saying “Merry Christmas!” was outlawed in America until Trump won the 2016 election? No? Well, Trump does, and he thought it was important to tell the assembled dignitaries in the Philippines all about it.
He repeatedly called Putin his “friend.”

Obviously, presidents need to be polite to every foreign leader they meet with. But there’s being cordial, and then there’s Trump spotting Vladimir Putin, chummily teasing “Who is he?,” and then declaring “He’s my friend!”
Later Trump said Xi is his “friend” too, though there was less genuine passion behind it:
Trump announcing that ruthless authoritarian leaders are some of his best buddies didn’t go over well, even on Newsmax:
He fell asleep while Xi was speaking.
Trump once declared that, unlike Joe Biden, “you’ll never see me sleeping in front of a camera.”

That is, arguably, untrue. In his second term, Trump has repeatedly been accused of sleeping on the job. However, the president insists he just likes to rest his “beautiful blue eyes” during meetings so he can “listen intensely.”
Unfortunately for Trump, the rest of the world is not familiar with his preferred terminology for his power-blinking:
To make matters worse, Trump didn’t shut his eyes during a presentation from the leader of, say, Papua New Guinea. He appeared to nod off right as Xi was addressing leaders at the APEC summit:
All in all, Trump didn’t look as powerful as he would have liked during his authoritarian boys’ trip. But hey, at least he didn’t achieve any of his policy goals either!

The preview week of the world’s most prestigious exhibition of contemporary art was an unruly spectacle – charged by political dissent, moments of beauty and works shining brightly through the chaos.
