items.title: Alexandre de Betak Helps Mel Ottenberg Find His Light
items.description: Alexandre de Betak Helps Mel Ottenberg Find His Light
items.author: Mel Ottenberg
paragraphs: Alexandre de Betak Helps Mel Ottenberg Find His Light

Alexandre de Betak knows that the right lighting can change everything. The French artist has spent the last thirty years meticulously demonstrating that fact as the man behind the design of unforgettable runway shows for brands like Dior, Saint Laurent, and Fendi. His work is an interplay of light, shadow, glass, metal, and reflection, transforming every space he takes over into something straight out of a cinematic masterpiece. Earlier this month, de Betak brought this signature expertise to Salon 94 in New York with a show titled TRUSS LIGHT SCULPTURES 01, featuring twelve sculptures based on the trusses and stage lights that are the backbone of all those fashion shows he worked on. Interview Editor-in-Chief Mel Ottenberg stopped by the exhibition where de Betak gave him a personal tour of the show while discussing trial and error, classicism versus punk, and when art becomes fantasy.
TUESDAY 11AM NOVEMBER 10, 2026 NEW YORK CITY
MEL OTTENBERG: A little sound is fine for my heightened experience, but turning it down a bit for the recording is great. Did you design the sound as well?
OTTENBERG: Fabulous. When did you decide to quit your career for this new career?

DE BETAK: To be honest, it just happened. I always thought I was going to do this. I never really felt I needed to sync it so concretely to do it. But the reality is that, yes, I did. Three years ago, I decided to completely leave the fashion show-making world and dedicate myself 100% to doing this, which in a way, is the continuation of the same thing but in a completely different context with a different objective.
OTTENBERG: Wow. Tell me about this story. This is the aluminum? So beautiful.

DE BETAK: There are two series. This one is the aluminum series. It’s made of nine unique pieces inspired by the most obvious and first tools I used when I started doing fashion shows a million years ago—aluminum trusses and stage lights, which no one really uses anymore. Those things were made to light other people’s work and be hidden in order to do so, and they very intentionally and very honestly were the first thing I worked with in my personal artwork. I completely redesigned, rebuilt, and rethought all of those elements. The systems that make the light are custom-designed and concealed so there’s no bulb. It’s just a combination of weird electronic elements that together we can play with and program in similar ways. The goal was to take what normally takes truckloads of very large equipment and many, many people and put them into a very small box that you can artistically, personally control yourself.
OTTENBERG: Very James Bond.
DE BETAK: Well, this one is aluminum. The bronze series is very heavy.
DE BETAK: So the idea was to basically continue with similar tools and ways I’ve always done, but take it to a completely uncompromised context, both commercially and artistically.
OTTENBERG: This is the one that controls this?
DE BETAK: This is the one that controls this one.

DE BETAK: See for example, I go on dancing and dancing is a sound reactive mode. So there are microphones inside of the sculpture and it’s got an evolutive sensibility. And I can change here—that’s warm white to cold white, so you go very warm here to very cold here.
OTTENBERG: Do you prefer warm or cold light?

DE BETAK: This can basically follow the sunlight through the day, the temperature of the sun from very cold in the morning to really warm at night after sunset. I actually like the combination alone, and I like the fact that you can control the temperature of the light to go together with the sun or to go against the sun, whichever way you want. It’s something that’s always obsessed me, to have the perfect temperature of white. It’s very rare. And with this control unit, now you can do it yourself.
OTTENBERG: What’s the technology in these lights? Do you believe in LED lights? Is this old school? What is this?

DE BETAK: It’s basically a mix. It is made of micro LEDs on electronic components that are designed and custom-built in a way that you can control them very specifically, like we were able to before with tungsten light, which you can no longer use.
OTTENBERG: Tungsten light?

DE BETAK: Yeah. Tungsten was what was before LED. And normally with LED, when you buy even a warm white LED, when you dim it, it becomes a bit green and a bit flickery. See, if I’m on glowing, you can go down really, really softly and it doesn’t go green, it doesn’t flicker. You see what I mean?

DE BETAK: It’s a very, very, very sensitive system. Then there’s a breathing mode, which will take a second to go. I put it colder so you see. It’s going to just slowly breathe. Then there is a sparkling mode, which is a little bit inspired by the The Eiffel Tower—on the hour at night it sparkles. Then there is the one that I call the dancing mode, which is basically sound-reactive. But it’s very sensitive. You can whisper to it. You can talk to it. [Coughs] You can cough to it. I have a cold.
OTTENBERG: Me too. I’m so upset about it.
DE BETAK: It’s so annoying.
OTTENBERG: I know. I woke up okay and now I don’t know. My friend that I was with on Saturday has a fever. Everyone is sick in New York.
DE BETAK: Anyways, let’s fight it.
OTTENBERG: Did you become an expert on this through trial and error when you were doing shows, or were you just always good at it?

DE BETAK: I still am trial and error. But in doing the shows, it gave me the means and the resources to experiment. I liked to play with light in particular, and I always felt it was very important to choreograph the synchronization of the light with the sound, music, choreography, and everything else in a very specific way. So I guess it is a combination of extensive trial and error and also extensive use.
OTTENBERG: Decades of both.
OTTENBERG: Are you more aluminum or bronze, personally?

DE BETAK: Let me show you the bronze. I thought I was more aluminum, maybe I am more aluminum as a person, but once we discovered the bronze, it was very touching. I was afraid that it would be too classic for me, and instead I find it almost more vitalistic and punk than the aluminums are because the aluminums are, of course, inspired directly by the original aluminum industrialist elements. But in a way, taking the industrial, ephemeral, and light essence of the original aluminum ones and making it in bronze—the most durable, heavyweight and artistically classic material—makes it extremely elegant, but still very punk in a way that I actually relate to. The combination is cool. It’s really fun.
OTTENBERG: I really like this. Do you have LED light bulbs at home?

DE BETAK: It took me a very long time and I had them special ordered when I decided to actually switch from the old incandescent to LED because I was never happy with them. I do have LED at home now, like we all do, because you can’t find the—
OTTENBERG: I always find the old ones, but I have to learn about the good ones because my supply will run out. There are places in New York that you can get them.
DE BETAK: Yeah, you still can get the very low-wattage ones, but at some point you can’t. Sustainably and ecologically thinking, you have to switch.
OTTENBERG: Oh, wow. They really are incredible.
DE BETAK: It’s really crazy that one.
SPEAKER 1: That’s another one, Ignorance we call it.
OTTENBERG: Yes. But it’s bronze. It’s really good.

DE BETAK: It’s crazy to create these bronze ones—30 molds per unit. We molded every single screw, every string, every part. Literally the screw itself, which functions for the filter, is made out of bronze. The glass is a specially-designed glass that I did to get the perfect diffusion of the light. And everything obviously functions from these lights, but made out of bronze. When I sent the first image of this to the foundry, they were like, “You’re completely mad. It’s going to be impossible. There’s too many pieces.”

DE BETAK: So this is a remote for this one. See, and you can go super low, almost like this. I can go super warm to super cold like this, and then raise really slowly. And then there’s a very slow breath. No, that’s the dancing. Hold on. That’s the breathing, which you can make warmer.
OTTENBERG: They look so good in Salon 94. Where else do you think they would look good?

DE BETAK: Hopefully, in many different settings because, as you saw, downstairs is a more modern, lofty kind of room and it works. And this one is very classic, grand mansion-y, which was where we dreamt of seeing them. And I think that kind of old-world classic is really where they take most of their value.
OTTENBERG: Yeah, I see it. It’s beautiful.
DE BETAK: I find them quite romantic as opposed to what one would have imagined they would be. Let’s see, that’s the sparkling.
DE BETAK: And then, if I go to dancing…See, it’s a very sensitive reaction to the sound. [Stomps feet]
OTTENBERG: I like it. I’m an aluminum guy, but I see the vision. I want a castle.
OTTENBERG: It would look so great. I mean, I want a castle for this. An Upper East Side castle is good too.
DE BETAK: An Upper East Side castle is not bad. Where do you live?
OTTENBERG: Washington Square.
DE BETAK: Have both. You can have the aluminum on Washington Square and then the castle on the Upper East Side.
OTTENBERG: Yes. What you’re doing downstairs is the art in my fantasy. I love art and I love light.
DE BETAK: An illumination of the room and the art.
OTTENBERG: Have you bought lots of lights over the years? Are you always buying a light or are you just making a light?

DE BETAK: I’ve been making a lot and accumulating pieces of old stuff. Some vintage pieces are just remnants of things I had designed and shows I have done. But I don’t know if I buy a lot of lights. At some point I did. There was a time when I had a lot of them, and then I got rid of a lot of things, and now I’m in a more bare environment.
OTTENBERG: Your house looks great. Can I take some pictures of you?
DE BETAK: Yeah, of course.
OTTENBERG: Your stuff looks so good here. It’s so space age, but not retro.

items.title: Sara Boustany and Kristina Bogic Can Keep a Secret
items.description: The Body’s Sara Boustany and Kristina Bogic on Kissing Girls and Keeping Secrets
items.author: Interview
paragraphs: The Body’s Sara Boustany and Kristina Bogic on Kissing Girls and Keeping Secrets

“Everybody start kissing,” Sara Boustany admits to thinking during her first watch of Netflix’s new must-see TV show, The Body. The actress plays Elise Zakaria, a bitch with a heart of gold, in Quinn Shephard’s sapphic, psychological thriller set at a Northeast Catholic high school in the early aughts. The genre-bending series centers around a girls dance troupe that start having strange religious hallucinations following an initiation-mishap. Drugs, Satan, and lesbians—The Body is a coming-of-age story unlike you’ve ever seen. And according to the actresses, the process of making the show also possessed a cult-ish undertone. “Everyone’s getting sick and you’re in sub-40 degrees and they’re like, ’We’re going to put you in this little bikini,’” confesses Kristina Bogic, who plays Anya Butler on the show—the dance team captain and Elise’s other half. Ahead of the show’s release, with Boustany calling from Mexico and Bogic from Australia, the pair braved a 17-hour time difference to discuss slickbacks, dance rehearsals, and magical thinking.—ISABELLA SOCCI
MONDAY 6PM OCTOBER 19, 2026 MEXICO
SARA BOUSTANY: Sorry, I’m in Mexico right now in the middle of nowhere. Are you in Australia?
KRISTINA BOGIC: I’m in Australia now. I went on a little trip.
BOUSTANY: Where was your little trip?
BOGIC: Hamilton Island. It’s in the north of Australia, this little island where you can only drive around on golf buggies.
BOGIC: What are you doing in Mexico?
BOUSTANY: Just for a vacation.
BOGIC: Beautiful. Do you want to talk about our audition experience?
BOUSTANY: I’m down. Everybody had a crazy experience getting the role.
BOGIC: It’s all weirdly a little spiritual as well.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, for sure. You go first.

BOGIC: Okay. I got the original audition, I think a few months before I even got a callback. It was a really long audition process for me. I did the first audition, I did a callback, and then I didn’t hear back for maybe a month or so. I was like, “You know what? I’m going to go to Europe with my best friend.” I was at this tiny, little airport and I got a call from my agent saying, “Hey, you need to get on this callback. It’s with Sara.” And I remember looking Sara up and going, “Oh my god.”
BOGIC: And then we did maybe four—
BOUSTANY: We did three. Was it four? I thought it was three.
BOUSTANY: Maybe your auditions were different.
BOGIC: I did one with Geena [Meszaros] too, who plays Lisbeth.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, I did too. With Anya, it was a long process for me, but I remember it so vividly. Do you?
BOGIC: Yeah, I remember it really well.
BOUSTANY: You had your hair back in a little pony and you were in Italy, right?

BOGIC: Yeah, I was in Italy, in Taormina. They were like, “Can you slick back your hair and wear no makeup for the audition?” Then, I wake up and I’m slicked back. For half of the auditions I was traveling around and it was at 3:00 AM for me because of the different time zones.
BOGIC: I was in the most random hotels. My best friend who traveled with me, she’s like, “I watched a tiny clip of the show. I remember this script so well from how many times I was doing it.”
BOUSTANY: Yeah, my friends as well. I had a couple of my friends audition too.

BOGIC: I actually knew a lot of people that auditioned for this. I remember getting lunch with some of my actor friends in Melbourne and they were all like, “Oh, there’s this open call for The Body.” As soon as I heard about it, I wanted it immediately.
BOUSTANY: Me too. But wait, we’re getting sidetracked.
BOGIC: Let me ask you the proper questions. Can we talk about our rehearsal period and how we all got close? Because it was eight weeks of dance rehearsals.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, there was a really intense week where it was every day, every day, every day. I really think each of us was almost hospitalized at a certain point.

BOGIC: We had Ryan Heffington putting us through boot camp. He was so patient, so graceful and kind when we were all getting to know each other. There was so much energy, but I’m so happy we all had that time because it warmed us up to each other.

BOGIC: I’ve made a point in every interview or conversation I’ve had about the show to say it has never once felt competitive. You’re coming into a group of 12 young girls and it was honestly the most supportive environment.

BOUSTANY: It really was. We just bonded so quickly. I’d never experienced something like that. I just feel so happy and proud to be a part of a group of girls who just love each other. It’s not rare. Women are amazing. But it’s rare in a workplace to be so close.
BOGIC: Yeah. As coworkers, you’re all put together and they’re like, “Okay, now be friends.” And it’s always a little awkward, but we all just clicked.
BOUSTANY: I have a question for you. How did you decompress after a disturbing or challenging scene?
BOGIC: I was going to literally ask you this.
BOUSTANY: Well, you had more of those, so you should answer it.
BOGIC: Honestly, at the beginning, I was very good at shaking off whatever scene I had to do that day. But there were times, I don’t know if you remember, I was in the trenches.
BOUSTANY: What do you mean, do I remember? I was traumatized for you. It was crazy. We were in the freezing cold.

BOGIC: If I’d had one moment of sun throughout the entire six months of filming, it would’ve saved me. But imagine you’re always together. It’s a huge group. It’s a huge crew. Everyone’s getting sick, and you’re in sub-40-degree weather, and they’re like, “We’re going to put you in this little bikini, and you’re going to walk around.”
BOUSTANY: And then also cry and lose your mind.
BOGIC: How to decompress? On the weekend, I would just rot away, but I needed that. I needed time to not speak, to not be touched or anything, and just fade away.
BOUSTANY: Yeah. I don’t think the show would’ve even been what it was if none of us leaned on each other as much.
BOGIC: Yeah. Even when it comes to press stuff, I’m so thankful I get to do it. We’re very lucky. Every time I’m with you guys, I’m like, “I’m safe.”
BOGIC: Okay. I’m going to ask you a question. What was your high school experience like?

BOUSTANY: I truly blocked a lot of it out. I didn’t have a negative experience. Emotions are so heightened when you’re a teenager and your body processes it as some kind of trauma, so it gets stored away.
BOGIC: Everything feels amplified at that age as well. Any experience I had with school was not a good one at all.

BOGIC: I was homeschooled from seventh grade, and then when I got to tenth grade, I went to an art school for three weeks. Imagine those formative years not growing up in a school system. You can go to the bathroom whenever you want. You’re treated like an adult in society because there’s not this hierarchy. When I went back to that, it shook me so much, and I ended up just leaving school. It was the best thing I could have done. If you give teenage girls the chance to just figure out what they want to do and who they want to be, they’re not going to waste that chance. That’s when we have the most excitement for life and innocence about the world. I’m very lucky I had those years to figure out what I wanted to do with my life.

BOUSTANY: Yeah. I also barely went because freshman year was just hell mentally for no reason. So for half of that semester, I was homeschooled. I went back sophomore year, and then I went to Lebanon, and then the revolution happened, and then none of us were going to school for six months. Got back to L.A., COVID hit, no school. I spent senior year at a normal school. I feel like my life just started a couple years ago.
BOGIC: We’re both very lucky we had enough time to figure our shit out.
BOUSTANY: Yeah. My parents were extremely supportive, and I wouldn’t have been able to figure out what I wanted to do without them.
BOGIC: Me too. What was your first impression of me? Tell me everything.

BOUSTANY: At first, you were pretty reserved and I loved it. I had an immediate connection with you. When we first met, we were doing dance stuff. I remember glancing at you and then you would glance at me and then we’d just be like—
BOGIC: I couldn’t believe everyone was real. Imagine walking into a room of 12 of the most beautiful women you’ve ever seen.

BOGIC: When we started filming, Geena and I had a conversation. We were like, “Isn’t Sara so amazing? She’s so amazing. Everything she does.” Whenever I was in a scene with you, I was like, “Girl, I got to fucking bring it.”

BOUSTANY: Oh, that’s so sweet. I love that. We only had one audition scene and I thought our chemistry was so amazing. But I was just curious about how you were going to play Anya because we talked so much about her bad decision making. I was curious about how you were going to bring that warmth to her, and I really felt it. What’s funny is that the only thing we would bicker about on set was Anya and Elise, but now we’re so on the same page about them.

BOGIC: But you know what? That’s such a good sign that we both trusted and believed in our characters so much. You would be able to feel it instantly watching the show if I couldn’t justify one of Anya’s decisions. I had to defend her through everything.

BOUSTANY: We’re in pretty bad shape most of the season. Someone asked me, “What do you think Anya and Elise love about each other?” And I’m like, “We didn’t even have the chance to explore their relationship outside of something happening so abruptly.”

BOGIC: Yeah. You see their dynamic as friends, but I would love to see Anya and Elise have more best friend moments. You get a sense of it in episode one, but once you see a lot of the issues in the show and how they talk, you can tell they’re very comfortable with each other.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, it was the girlness and the gossip of them. I don’t even know what the word is. It’s the conspiring that all girls love to do.
BOGIC: What should we talk about next? Do you have any superstitions? Irrational fears? Psychic experiences? Do you believe in curses? Astrology?

BOUSTANY: It’s more so words having power and what you put out is what you get. I’m going to get real vulnerable right now. When you’re struggling so much with yourself, sometimes you just want to talk about it to the people you care about. But when you tell people something they start focusing on it. So basically, keep what you doubt about yourself to yourself, because what you put out is what people will inevitably feel.

BOGIC: Not putting weight behind words is a big thing, which is basically just what you’re saying. I’m an anxious person in general, and as soon as I tell someone I’m anxious, all of a sudden it’s ten times worse.

BOUSTANY: Yeah, but it needs to be a specific person, because I remember talking to Geena about this and telling her something that was upsetting me. She was just like, “I see you being upset and it makes me feel like you’re human.” I guess it’s kind of superstitious of me to feel that way. I have random ones as well. My OCD comes out in random things, like clenching my teeth for a certain amount of time.

BOGIC: Yeah. This isn’t a superstition. This is weird shit that I do. If I’m eating and I only chew on one side of my mouth, I have to even it out with the other side. It’s a sensory thing. You know what? Say I do an audition and I really want it, I used to manifest and smother it with my hopes and dreams. I’d put all of my energy into it, and then I felt like I wouldn’t get the role because I would suffocate it. As soon as I let them go, they’d come back to me. I’m like, “Okay, I’m very grateful for this,” but I try not to invest so much spiritual energy into it.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, The Body felt that way for me.
BOGIC: I think if I didn’t get The Body, I would’ve dwindled away. I was so obsessed with Anya. I would’ve been heartbroken if I didn’t get her.
BOUSTANY: Oh my god, I would’ve lost my fucking mind.
BOGIC: I can’t even imagine my life without meeting everyone. It’s not even something I can fathom.

BOUSTANY: Me too. Sometimes you feel like these things were bound to happen. Sometimes I’m just like, “I knew that it was going to happen for me,” but it happens and then you’re, like, imposter syndrome to the fucking max. Would you have been friends with the characters in high school?

BOGIC: I feel like Anya would’ve been the girl to be like, “Have you ever made out with girls?” And I would’ve been like, “Girl, okay, I know where this is going.” Or I would’ve shaken her a couple times. [Laughs]
BOUSTANY: I would’ve been friends with Elise for sure, but this bitchy defense mechanism—cut it out. You have a good sense of yourself. You do not need to be doing all that. But it’s funny, I would.

BOGIC: But you know what? I think you thought that about Elise as well. And I think it’s good that you did because you made her so much softer than I ever read her on the page. I think she was always going to be lovable because she’s witty and funny and cheeky. But you gave her such a soft little heart where you’re, like, baby Elise. You just want to hold her.
BOUSTANY: Nobody’s a bitch just because they’re a bitch. It’s always something. Like an unrequited love.
BOGIC: Oh. Well, yes. I have no idea what you’re talking about. [Laughs]
BOUSTANY: I would’ve been friends with Anya.
BOGIC: Me too. I would love to explore her funny, girly side because I didn’t get to explore that as much. I did with Lisbeth a little bit too.
BOGIC: What I love is that although our trope is focused on, there are so many relationships in the show that I really root for. Not always romantically, but platonically.
BOUSTANY: I like everyone to be romantic.
BOGIC: Everyone’s romantic.
BOUSTANY: I’m like, “Everyone, start kissing now.”
BOGIC: The first time we watched it, we were like, “Smash, smash. I want these two together. Everyone has chemistry.”
BOUSTANY: Kind of wish Lisbeth and Anya kissed really quickly.
BOUSTANY: Just really quick, and then nobody ever talked about it ever again.
BOGIC: That would be a Lisbeth thing to do. She’d come up and kiss Anya as a threat.
BOUSTANY: She totally would. I love Lisbeth.
BOGIC: Me too. She’s probably one of my favorite characters.
BOUSTANY: Are you good at keeping secrets?
BOGIC: You are not good at keeping secrets. It eats you up inside.
BOUSTANY: No, I’m not. If I feel guilty about something, I can’t do it. But if it’s a secret that I’m keeping and it doesn’t hurt anybody, my lips are sealed.
BOGIC: I tell everyone everything. Ever since I was little, even people I don’t know very well have told me their deepest, darkest secrets.
BOUSTANY: Me too. I think it’s because we are very vulnerable with people.
BOGIC: True. I don’t remember the last time I lied. You know what? I exaggerate stories.
BOGIC: Not big things, but if it’s something funny, somehow the story gets bigger and bigger each time. But I’m like, “I’m an actor. That’s reasonable.”

BOUSTANY: Yeah, that is reasonable. Everybody’s lied. But I believe in confessing for sure. This is maybe controversial, but if someone tells me something fucked up, I’m like, “Okay, you better tell them before I do.”

BOGIC: Yeah. If I feel guilt for holding a secret, it makes me feel sick. I can’t keep it in. But I’m like Anya in that way where it literally will eat me up inside until I crack, and then I’m like, “Ugh, this is it.” And I just vomit it out.
BOUSTANY: Yeah. It’s weird. I can’t do it.

items.title: Photographer Natalie Curtis on Time, Memory, and Minions
items.description: Photographer Natalie Curtis on Time, Memory, and Minions
items.author: Dora Sahbazovic
paragraphs: Photographer Natalie Curtis on Time, Memory, and Minions

Photographer Natalie Curtis has a knack for transience. Her sentences are pithy and her pictures are taken as if captured in mid-air. The first time I met her, we’d agreed to have a drink by the Gare du Nord before she headed back to London. When she approached me on the cold, crowded terrace, the first thought I had was how she appears to have mastered the realm of time in the way only a true photographer can; I registered dignity, relief, and a shy curiosity. The last-minute hangout ahead of our scheduled interview had been Curtis’s idea, brought out of a desire to ensure I was normal, I gathered. She’s the daughter of Ian Curtis of Joy Division fame, and such an addendum can complicate one’s relationship with vulnerability.

But I don’t care much for biographical facts. I wanted to know how Curtis—whose work incites the same emotional impulse in me as a full-blooded bass line—dreams. Imagination and space are closely connected, and her work is a sublimation of the two rooted in memory, history’s affective peer.

As we glossed over the conspicuous fact that I’d shown up to our conversation with a freshly-bleached head of crunchy 2b hair, we got to talking about logistics the way only two strangers with a talent for never cutting to the chase can. After setting up her new photography show Tower at Galerie Arnaud Lefebvre, Curtis was off to Milan for a work trip. I asked whether she finds it tiring spending so much time on the road.
FRIDAY 1PM NOVEMBER 6, 2026 PARIS
NATALIE CURTIS: It’s alright. Could always be worse.
DORA SAHBAZOVIC: I guess. Could be a gig in Siberia.
CURTIS: Or another town in England.
SAHBAZOVIC: Scary. You also recently had your work shown at the Venice Biennale. How was that?

CURTIS: I had an image in ART-ICON’s Static Cinema exhibition, which took place during the film festival. It was very cool to be a part of something like that. Mostly, since I wasn’t there, I had FOMO. It looked like a great time to be in Venice.
SAHBAZOVIC: You described Tower as an exit project coinciding with you leaving Manchester for good. What has been drawing you back over the years?
CURTIS: I have very good friends in Manchester and it’s close to where I’m from, Cheshire, where my family are. And Manchester’s less expensive than London, though it has gone up in recent years.
SAHBAZOVIC: It feels like much artistic novelty has come out of this not too enormous city. I wonder how something like that occurs, or whether it’s mere chance?
CURTIS: Probably the weather has something to do with it, perhaps people are indoors more. Also, in a non-big city, everything’s less on a plate.
SAHBAZOVIC: When you think of Cheshire, what image comes to mind?
CURTIS: Hills. I really miss seeing the hills.
SAHBAZOVIC: I’m really in awe of the English countryside. It looks so lush. I imagine people still get around on horseback there.
CURTIS: I had a choice once to either save money for driving school or sign up for riding lessons. I still can’t drive.
SAHBAZOVIC: Aw. Was this in childhood?

CURTIS: Oh, this was like ten years ago. [Laughs] I was really passionate about it for a while. The first stable I took classes in though, in the hills, was a children’s riding school. I was the only adult in class.
SAHBAZOVIC: Did they give you a bigger horse?
CURTIS: Not necessarily! We’d always be switching horses. I remember one that was really scared of minions, you know, the small, yellow things.
CURTIS: Yeah, there was an obstacle course with minion cartoon cutouts for obstacles for some reason. And for this horse not to freak out, it was a whole affair of having to move the minions.
SAHBAZOVIC: Sure, happens every day.

CURTIS: There was also one that got demoted from working at the police to this riding gig. He was scared of traffic. Another one just hated bridges. Like he’d come up to a bridge all normal and then just freeze.
SAHBAZOVIC: I love that a horse can be unemployed. Why did you stop riding?
CURTIS: Among other things, there was just a lot of falling involved. There’s a saying one of the children’s moms at the riding school taught me: “Seven falls makes a horse woman.”
SAHBAZOVIC: That’s very strange and beautiful.

CURTIS: I know. Where I’m from in Cheshire, there’s a lot of cows as well—milk cows. You know that’s where the Cheshire cat got its name? They say she grins because she had a lot of cream from the milk cows.
SAHBAZOVIC: Oh, I wondered.

CURTIS: But don’t quote me on that. Anyways, I went to a village school. In the morning, before class, these dairy cows would always be in your way. The cows are crossing the road was the most normal excuse for being late.
SAHBAZOVIC: That’s grand. So, does London feel like home now?

CURTIS: As a person from the northwest, I feel that the southeast should not feel like home, but weirdly it does. When I returned to London, for this my third stint, I was walking through the neighborhood where I lived the first time, in 2010 I think it was, and it felt like I’d never left. As though the subsequent time in Manchester never happened, as though it was just something I dreamt.
SAHBAZOVIC: Do you find you’ve searched out comfort or novelty more as you’ve matured?

CURTIS: I like to be as comfortable as possible! I think novelty is important. But being comfortable helps to get things done. It’s harder to concentrate if you’re physically uncomfortable. When I’m away, I feel so glad that I have my desk at home set up properly, everything in the right place, at the right height, and that I have a mattress I like. Also, if you’re comfortable—physically, in your surroundings, in yourself—there’s a kind of active relaxation. It can happen if I’m taking photos somewhere very familiar, and also I can be doing something, like the washing up, and I’ll get an idea or something I’m working on will make sense. I think routine gives you space to find or see the novelty.
SAHBAZOVIC: You said you were already toying with your grandfather’s camera as a child. How did you get back to it as an adult?

CURTIS: Although sporadic, it never really went away. Then, as an adult, I took the Art Foundation course at my local college and realized photography was a real option and that I could study at art school.
SAHBAZOVIC: What or who did you find inspiration in back then?

CURTIS: Once, I photographed dolls. Mostly photographed my younger brother. I do tend to photograph parts of my life. I was always interested in locations and landscapes. But when I was younger, I couldn’t get my head around how to do what I wanted to do.
SAHBAZOVIC: Why photography?
CURTIS: It’s kind of magical as a medium.
SAHBAZOVIC: You mean the way it works?
CURTIS: Yeah, the science of it.
SAHBAZOVIC: What compels you to take a picture?
CURTIS: It’s a feeling that’s a need.
SAHBAZOVIC: Have you ever felt like getting into cinema as well? You had a part in Control, but that must have been quite an uncommon on-set experience.

CURTIS: Sometimes. Though I think film sets involve too many people for me—amazing people, but it’s just not my kind of thing. Yet I do like to play with moving image. I was an extra on Control, a friend from high school wanted to do it and for me to do it with her, and possibly I should’ve said no! It wasn’t a normal extra experience in that I’d already spent time on set and met everyone. But it was interesting to see different aspects of the filmmaking process in that I went to wardrobe and to hair and make-up—that I really enjoyed, and I guess is maybe special treatment for an extra. However, the actual filming of a riot scene was brutal. It was fun explaining to my dentist how exactly my tooth got chipped.

But when I was a student, with a friend from my photography course and my brother, we had what I think is a more typical extras experience for 24 Hour Party People. We wore our own clothes and most of it was just sitting around waiting in a pub near the set. We didn’t know what to expect and so weren’t prepared, all the other extras had books or work to get on with. My brother curled up and went to sleep. Though at various points actors did pop in, which was ace. During the actual filming—it was a much smaller location than the scene in Control and not a riot—we loved watching the director and cinematographer at work, being in that space is very different to observing during a standard set visit. A dream of a day’s work for a pair of photography students!
SAHBAZOVIC: What did an average night with friends look like in your twenties?

CURTIS: We either watched telly or listened to music, then we went to the pub. After the pub, more telly or music, maybe we played cards. There was a game called Shithead. Often we watched a film, sometimes we’d just drive round the countryside—or not. I remember waiting forever for a badger to move out the road. Everyone smoked and drank loads of tea. I remember laughing a lot. Mid to late-twenties was in Manchester, so I guess I maybe danced more, saw more live music, but it’s not as vivid as the late 90s/early 00s small town days.
SAHBAZOVIC: What’s your favorite photograph of yours?
CURTIS: It changes. As I write, “Union” in the Tower project.
SAHBAZOVIC: Your photographs feel to me as if already being captured from a future moment while being taken. Like an instantaneous, fundamental contortion of time.
CURTIS: I like that. I think maybe that’s what photography is.
SAHBAZOVIC: Talk about melancholy. Which of the four Ancient Greek temperaments do you correspond with best? There’s sanguine, choleric, melancholic, and phlegmatic, I gather.
CURTIS: So I did an online quiz once! The result was something like 75% melancholic, 17% sanguine, and 8% phlegmatic.
SAHBAZOVIC: This is very real. I don’t remember the last time I felt choleric.
CURTIS: I do feel angry sometimes, though maybe anger is too strong a word. Extreme frustration?
SAHBAZOVIC: What’s your relationship with memory?

CURTIS: I suspect that I often take photos in order to process and then not remember. I’m interested in memory in that everyone remembers differently, has their own version. There are facts but the truth varies. I think photographs can be both document and myth—something in between.

SAHBAZOVIC: Now that you mentioned myth, I find that myth-making is one of the most fascinating ways of understanding the modern age. It’s been around forever, but you don’t have to be a god to be the stuff of legend anymore.
CURTIS: Thinking about truth versus myth, I’m glad that people have stopped saying that the camera never lies. I always hated that.
SAHBAZOVIC: Are you at peace with not knowing?
CURTIS: Yes. [a Roma guy playing the accordion really loudly passes by, but not before lingering in front of our table first]
SAHBAZOVIC: What do forties feel like?

CURTIS: Amazing in that I feel very sure of what I’m doing creatively, I know how I want to spend my time and so on, and rubbish all at once. Maybe less pressure because I don’t give a shit, I just want to do what I want to do and have more experience and the confidence that brings. I feel like an adult teenager, actually. It’s like being a teenager, but with knowing things.
SAHBAZOVIC: If your body of work were translated into text, would it largely consist of questions or answers?
CURTIS: Both probably. But short sentences.
SAHBAZOVIC: Yeah. I find a good question is hard to come by.
CURTIS: For me, right now, I am concerned that I don’t give good answers.
SAHBAZOVIC: Who needs those? [Laughs] One more thing: where is beauty?
CURTIS: In good and honest intentions.

items.title: Tinashe Crashes a Plane and Belts Out 'Melatonin' During Hilarious 'GTA VI' Stream
items.description: The whole world has been counting down to Grand Theft Auto VI finally being released, and now that it’s here, people are calling out of work and school to play. One person who wasted no time? Tinashe, who dove straight into the video game for her fans through
items.author: Julyssa Lopez
paragraphs: The whole world has been counting down to Grand Theft Auto VI finally being released, and now that it’s here, people are calling out of work and school to play. One person who wasted no time? Tinashe, who dove straight into the video game for her fans through a hilarious livestream. The singer hopped on X right after midnight, tweeting: “Streaming GTA on twitch lets gooo.”

Once she was locked in, she got to work. The stream captures her cracking fans up by trying to make an epic getaway by flying an airplane and hysterically crashing it into the ground. She also screams her head off as she gets in a shootout but quickly runs out of ammo and has to rely on hand-to-hand combat. “I have no bullets!” she screams. “Holy shit, I’m going to have to beat the fuck out of them myself.”

At one point, during another shootout, she gets so stressed out that she starts singing the bridge of her own hit “Melatonin,” yelping, “Fucking with me, hope you know I’m what you asked for, asked for! Back door, back door!”

Tinashe is a big gamer; in the past, she’s played a lot of Call of Duty: Warzone under the name SniperNashe and streamed it on Twitch and YouTube for gamer fans. She’s also talked about being a fan of Mortal Kombat and Diablo IV. Plus, she’s chronically online — she was all over X earlier this month to clap back at conservatives during the midterms — so it makes sense she’d be celebrating GTA VI‘s big arrival on social media with everyone else.

She wasn’t the only celebrity excited about the video game: After several days of sold-out shows in the U.K., Noah Kahan kicked back after his shows and stayed up wreaking havoc on Vice City while his wife was asleep. F1 champion Lewis Hamilton and actress Millie Bobby Brown also shared how excited they were for the game’s sixth edition.

items.title: The Traitors: New Blood Recap: The Penultimate Peril
items.description: How is this show getting good right at the end? It took you this many episodes to make me feel something other than irritation with Victor? The Traitors loves to use a helicopter and a beaming Alan Cumming to show the triumph of the human spirit, and dammit if
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: How is this show getting good right at the end? It took you this many episodes to make me feel something other than irritation with Victor? The Traitors loves to use a helicopter and a beaming Alan Cumming to show the triumph of the human spirit, and dammit if it doesn’t work on me.

We are down to eight players at the start of this two-part finale: Kriste, Abbey, Katie, Victor, Shane, Wyatt, Clyde, and Jay. Clyde remains very suspicious of Katie and Shane, which is bananas. How is this cast so bad at getting Traitors out, but two of them have been 100 percent right about both their guesses? Victor’s unstoppable personality pushed through Tomica’s and Joe’s eliminations, but can Clyde meet that same level of fruit-based confidence with the remaining players? We’ll see.

Clyde floats Shane’s name to Katie, Abbey, and Jay, which Katie immediately reports to Shane. Their new plan is to get the other players onto Jay. Victor, the zebra from Madagascar, agrees to go after Jay. He is taking his winning streak and running in the completely wrong direction. Meanwhile, with Katie out of the room, Clyde floats her name to Kriste, Jay, and Wyatt. Clyde’s main evidence is that Katie is bad at puzzles. People make “that is a compelling argument” faces because no one knows what the fuck to do anymore.

At the roundtable, Kriste is in a dachshund sweater that’s really radiating mom energy. I didn’t think I needed the insane, Panem Capitol–style fashion we’re trending toward on D-list celebrity Traitors, but I miss it. Not that I wouldn’t buy that sweater. Jay tells the audience that he wants to get Victor out, then states that “if my life is threatened, kitty’s got claws.” Jay, I know sexuality is complicated, but damn. Alan, in a semi-bejeweled lilac suit, sets the stage for their penultimate roundtable and leaves them to it. Shane goes after Jay, which Katie backs him on. The way they talk to him makes me think everyone hates Jay. Is that the case? Katie says that with him, it’s always too little, too late. Ugh, this is why we need more time in these episodes. What have the actual tensions and dynamics been between the cast? We never would have gotten an MJ pants moment with this edit.

Clyde tries to pull focus from the Jay accusations and accuses Katie, then awkwardly laughs and weakly accuses Shane. Clyde! Where’s that fruit confidence?! Victor wants to focus on evidence, and he claims that Jay has voted with the Traitors in past roundtables. I will take his word for it. All I know is that Jay consistently voted for Victor. Jay thinks that Katie and Victor are Traitors. There’s no way that Katie is winning at this point, right? Enough people are suspicious of her that they’re going to be too paranoid to let her survive the sparkle flames at the end.

The voting goes: Abbey (Jay), Clyde says he’s really conflicted but votes (Jay), Wyatt (Jay), Jay (Victor), Shane (Jay), Kriste (Jay), Katie (Jay), Victor (Jay). Jay looks really emotional! Then he walks to the Circle of Truth and does a weird reveal that lands really awkwardly with everyone. It feels like we’re missing a piece of context, but after Jay proclaims, “When I first came in here, I was a Faithful, but now I! Am! A! Faithful.” Wyatt asks, “What the hell was that?” and Alan deems it “a rather different roundtable exit.” Is it because of the misdirect? Or is it because Jay is constantly as dramatic as he can be? Everyone looks awkward and confused.

Before they all disperse for the night, Kriste cries about not being part of a clique and everyone group-hugs her, then Wyatt immediately tells Abbey he still suspects Kriste. Clyde tells the men he is almost 100 percent certain that it’s Katie. Victor stammers in response to this and goes to talk to Katie in the bar. Nothing of substance is said. Everyone goes to bed, and the Traitors meet in the turret.

It’s the last murder! Wyatt and Abbey have shields, so that leaves Victor, Kriste, and Clyde. They’re concerned that murdering Clyde is too obvious, but also, what do they have to lose at this point? Murdering Kriste would maybe put heat on Wyatt, since she’s been saying his name for a while. They briefly consider Victor, and then mutually promise not to rug pull each other in the final eliminations.

The next morning, everyone is really sure that Victor is going to be murdered. Well, guess what, guys, it’s Clyde. Abbey is very disappointed to have lost her buddy, and now is more suspicious of Shane and Katie. But there’s no time for her suspicion, because Alan enters the room in an autumnal ensemble and tells them to get ready for the final mission. Before heading out, Shane tells Wyatt that it could be Victor. “I don’t know, bro,” says our eloquent Wyatt. That’s Wyatt’s one true love, Shane.

The prize pot is at $186,300, and the final mission can add $60,000 to it, getting the players very close to $250,000 if successful. The mission consists of the prize-money gold being in two underground bunkers. The players have to find the bunkers and break into them with dynamite. They’ll split into two teams: Four players will ride in buggies and two will be in a helicopter. The helicopter team has to locate the dynamite, and the ground team has to find the bunkers and identify which should be blown up.

Abbey and Katie immediately volunteer to go in the helicopter. They have one hour to get all this done. They are flown to the dynamite, find the location of the first bunker, and use walkie-talkies to tell the other team where to drive. Abbey is going to deliver the dynamite to them, so she is standing on the helicopter’s landing skids and then has to rappel down 80 feet (no thank you). To decide which bunker, the ground team has to remember whether Joe or Tomica received the most votes at the roundtables. Victor insists it’s Tomica, and he is correct.

For the second and final bunker, the explosives are already set, but the detonator is in the middle of the loch. Katie flies there, also on one of the landing skids, as the ground team races to remember the order in which players were eliminated. They have ten minutes left. Up on the helicopter, Katie is so happy. Alan is so happy. Then, when she starts to rappel down, Katie flips upside down and is just hanging there below a midair helicopter and over a large lake. This is truly a nightmare. Ninety seconds remain. Somehow, she rights herself and slides down, landing in the loch. She gets onto the platform with a minute left and detonates the dynamite. It’s so joyous! It’s so triumphant! “YOU WERE UPSIDE DOWN,” someone yells.

There we have it: the uplifting part one of The Traitors: New Blood finale. They have to raise us so we can be all the more devastated as everyone inevitably betrays each other in part two. Excelsior!

items.title: Southern Charm Recap: Allie Oops
items.description: To paraphrase one of Jacqueline Laurita’s taglines from The Real Housewives of New Jersey, “Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, you better run.” We know that Whitner has been spending lots of time in the gym, so he most likely has his running shoes on a
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: To paraphrase one of Jacqueline Laurita’s taglines from The Real Housewives of New Jersey, “Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, you better run.” We know that Whitner has been spending lots of time in the gym, so he most likely has his running shoes on already, because he’s in danger of fooling us. Why do I feel like this season is setting him up to be West Wilson 2.0? Well, the joke’s on him that he can’t pull a West Wilson because none of the guys on the cast can hold down a woman, and most of the women on the show don’t have any best friends. Instead, he’s just going to fuckboy his way through the hearts of Charleston. I hate to lose an imaginary husband, but it’s not looking great for the heir to Itchy Grass Farm.

Before we can get to all of that, we have to talk about Allie’s confrontation with Austen at the party that kicked off the season. She sits him down and says that Shep told her that Austen called off their romance because he didn’t want to commit. She does not remember it that way. She says she’s the one who ghosted Austen because she didn’t want to insert himself into the throuple of Austen, Salley, and an extraneous E that won’t go away. Austen stutters his way through saying that he never characterized their breakup like that, but even in confessional he says that Allie gave him an off-ramp and he took it because he didn’t want to commit. Sorry, but it doesn’t sound like he had as much of a choice as he’d like to let on. Also, this is all coming from Shep, who is a narrator as reliable as your roommate with the ketamine problem. (“So did you pay the rent or not, Spencer? No, I don’t want to trip balls with you. I would like to not get evicted!”)

The next confrontation is between Salley and Charley, who I didn’t even think was on this show anymore. Is she? Is she just waiting for her demotion to Southern Hospitality with her boyfriend Justin? She asks Salley why they’re not hanging out as much, and Salley says that it’s because Charley only wants to chill with Justin, and even when they do hang, he’s always there with his fine-ass face and his hot-ass body and his gorgeous scraggly facial hair and sexy tattoos just taking up all the attention. Then, right on cue, Justin walks up and says, “Salley, don’t take advantage of Charley.” First of all, he wasn’t there; how did he know that was happening? Second of all, thanks for literally proving the point. God, why is every hot man on this show an absolute nightmare? Is this all men in Charleston? Are the ugly men obnoxious, too? Oh yeah, they are. Remember Thomas? (ZING!)

Salley and Charley ask Justin to leave, and he’s telling them that they like each other and to talk it out, but they can’t while he’s there. Even though they dismiss him, he lingers like the smell of cheese in a broken refrigerator. Salley exits the conversation and tells Madison that Charley said that they always hang out without her and she feels left out. Madison walks right over to Charley and Justin and speaks to Charley and then looks at Justin and says, “Should you leave?” He tucks his head down and trots away, which is exactly why Madison is the only person on this whole cast who knows how to handle a man. Charley then tells Madison she doesn’t feel like anyone reaches out to try to be friends with her, and Madison is like, “Where are your texts? Where is your effort?” I think Charley thinks she has her place on the show solidified thanks to Justin, but I think it’s just the opposite; I think she’s blown her berth on not one but two shows and now she’s scrambling. Madison expertly clears her, and Charley goes crying in the ladies’ room, which, honestly, leave her there. I’m on Team Madison.

After a check-in with Whitney and his mother and then a check-in with Allie and her mother, we get to coffee with Craig and Whitney. Craig is upset that at the reunion Whit called him a narcissist, a word that Craig needs ChatGPT to look up for him because Craig is too busy thinking about himself to learn what a narcissist is. When they sit down, Craig says that he deserves an apology from Whit. For what? For speaking the truth? For saying a thing that was absolutely factual? This is like the sky raining down on us for 40 days and 40 nights because we dared to say it was blue. That Craig can’t even see that maybe he has narcissistic tendencies is crazy. Even ChatGPT says that narcissism is only a problem when it affects your relationships, and Craig makes a face that says, “Well, that is why Paige left me,” so even he knows it’s a problem.

Whit doesn’t apologize for saying it, but he does apologize for instigating a pile-on, but sorry, what he said did not instigate the pile-on; Craig’s narcissistic behavior did. Everyone can’t keep giving Craig a pass because he’s handsome and charming and can sew and has decent style and likes to take care of his home and seems like a nurturing carer for the bees and he’s been working on his fitness and have you seen him with his shirt off and he can’t be that bad … STOP! This is what we all keep doing.

The rest of the episode is spent in Madison’s backyard, where she invites all the girls (feat. Rodrigo) over for a little pool party mostly to show off her new GLP-1 post-baby body that is so good I want to look like that and also maybe sleep with her. I’m a lesbian now, just like Venita. Yes, there are lots of wacky revelations at the party, including that Venita and Salley make out when they’re wasted, and Salley hooked up with a girl in Canada and Venita was so upset that she cried. Wait, wait, wait, wait, wait. Salley has a Canadian girlfriend? Did the dog also eat her homework? Did her parents then take that dog to a nice home upstate? I mean, this is the biggest lie imaginable. But yes, this puts Salley and Venita’s friendship into a whole new perspective. Also, is Venita really bi or fluid or whatever, or is this just a stunt she’s pulling? I am so incredibly confused.

Salley is a little bit mad at Venita because Venita brought Allie to Madison’s party, and we all know that Salley hates Allie because Austen took her out on dates and wouldn’t go out on dates with Salley. But no. That’s not why. Salley says that Allie told Austen that the sexiest thing about him is that he hadn’t slept with Salley yet because everyone else has. How did she learn this? Did Austen tell her? How else would she know? Also, we all know that Austen lies. One of the things he lies about? That he and Salley have never had sex, because come on. You really expect us to believe that? No shade, nothing wrong with it, but these two have had more bangs than a dozen hair salons. Absolutely none of this story is real. Salley may believe it, but the Catholic Jesus does not because he is incapable of telling a lie except to Mormons, whom he has been punking for more than a century now. (Your own planet? Come on. He made that shit up.)

While Salley is talking to Venita about Austen and Allie, she’s saying that there’s no way Austen would lie to her about how their relationship ended, while Madison is on the other side of the pool talking to Allie about how Austen is totally lying about their breakup because that is what he does. If anyone has a Ph.D. in Austen’s shitbaggery, it is Madison LeCroy, so who do you think we’re going to believe?

As everyone is sitting around drinking Modelo with hot sauce in them (grody max), they all start talking about Whit and Allie and how they’re going on a date shortly. Then it comes up that Venita is also into Whit, and they’re all like, “Girl, no, he’s not. Stop it right now.” Yes, Venita. Knock it off. She has already expressed interest, and he has not followed up. This is not a man who is going to make it happen. Do not cook him a branzino; he does not want to pick tiny bones out of his teeth.

Molly and Rod, who are close with Whit, tell Allie that he may have been acting like a ho for the past year since his breakup, but that he’s quite serious about dating her. This is not what Venita wants to hear and not what Salley wants to hear. It’s not that Salley wants Whit; she just wants Allie to be miserable because she is jealous that she walked away from the man that Salley can’t seem to force to love her. (Has she tried an Etsy witch?) Salley keeps saying that Whit is a playboy and is going to break Allie’s heart.

That is when Allie tells us a story that I found a little confusing at first. She says that she and Whit made out and then he went and slept with a good friend of hers. She says that the friend knew Allie was interested in Whit and even told Allie that she should date him, and then slept with the dude. Now, I am not usually one to blame women for men’s bad behavior, but yes, this sounds like a friend that you don’t want to keep around. (Was her name Amanda, by chance?) This would make Whitner look bad, but only if he knew about Allie and Not-Amanda’s relationship before he slept with Not-Amanda. After all, this is Charleston. The pool of young, attractive, eligible people is quite small. There is going to be overlap that may be unintentional. But this girl? No way. She needs to go.

Salley hears this and gets incensed because if it’s true, that means that Whit is pretending like he’s better than Shep, Craig, Austen, and Whitney but doing all the same terrible shit that they’re always doing as well. She’s right on that account, but can Salley be right about anything? We’ve seen her be wrong about so many things: Austen, Craig, getting chickens, that terrible white dress where she can’t raise her arms, letting someone almost drown in her pool, dating Gaston, stealing the E out of her sister’s name and never giving it back. She’s not someone I trust, but as the sun sets on Madison’s poolhouse, as everyone collects their cover-ups and jangles all the empty bottles of Veuve into an already ripping Glad bag, as they call their Ubers and give their forced hugs thinking about their boys and their girls and their dates and their illusions and their loins, she may somehow be right about Whit, and that makes the sun set just a little bit faster.

items.title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: Brad Pitt Hits the Aura Jackpot in a Very Fun Tarantino Hangout Movie That Feels Like QT TV
items.description: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” gives you a highly pleasurable, shaggy heat-of-the-moment buzz. I’m not sure what I was expecting from a sequel to “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” but I dug just about every ambling, low-down minute of this one. (I
items.author: Owen Gleiberman
paragraphs: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” gives you a highly pleasurable, shaggy heat-of-the-moment buzz. I’m not sure what I was expecting from a sequel to “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” but I dug just about every ambling, low-down minute of this one. (I realize that low-down is an ancient phrase, but this is a movie that ends with Boz Scaggs’ “Lowdown” playing over the closing credits. That’s how 1977 it is.)

The film is Quentin Tarantino, who wrote the screenplay, going wherever the day (or night) takes him. And that will do just fine. But it’s also Tarantino honed and manicured, given a polish of precision by the film’s director, David Fincher. As an artist, the hot-blooded, motormouth Tarantino is Dionysian; the rigorously controlled, ice-in-his-veins Fincher is Apollonian. Together, the two merge in a divertingly odd way. “The Further Mis-Adventures” is an enjoyable contradiction — a meticulous hangout movie. It hops from one thing to the next, but it’s disarmingly placid and even-keeled about what it’s doing. In spirit, it’s almost as if someone had slipped the movie half a Quaalude. It’s got no worries, and neither does its hero, Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt), the most sexy-cool aging ex-stuntman you’ll ever see.

“The Further Mis-Adventures” sprawls over one week in Los Angeles in June of ’77 (the specificity has meaning; it’s supposed to be just after “Star Wars” has changed the force of the movie universe), and the tone is less sunlit intense than the 1969 of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” The counterculture has now evaporated, and everyone is stuck in a lackadaisical limbo of diversion, with one foot in the past. That doesn’t mean “The Further Mis-Adventures” is snobbish about the pop-culture era it’s rooted in. The film is brazenly and ever-so-slightly-ironically approving, whether it’s reveling in the throb of disco or the grand orchestral pomp of ELO’s “Tightrope,” smacking its lips at a tacky margarita bar that features mud-wrestling night, or opening with a last-days-of-blaxploitation movie called “Soul Brothers Die Hard!,” in which a couple of mack daddies sit around talking about the libidinous challenge of keeping their stables happy.

There’s a trick that Tarantino and Fincher spring several times here, and that’s to lure us into a piece of entertainment — a movie, a TV show — as if it were actually happening. That’s their tribute to the canny power of this stuff. Yet even as “The Further Mis-Adventures” embraces all this, you can feel a certain what’s-next? affectlessness hanging in the smoggy air. The only one who doesn’t feel it is Cliff, who lives in the eternal present. You might say that Cliff has become something of a loser. His old buddy Rick Dalton, who kept him supplied with stunt-double work, is now history (Rick has moved to Australia), and Cliff, with a slight limp and aching joints, is a man pushing 50, living with his cranky pawn-shop-owner dad (Peter Weller) in Marina del Rey, working odd jobs, driving around in his muscle-car jalopy. Yet in his slightly grizzled way he’s still a dreamboat, not to mention the most comfortable man in his own skin God ever invented.

Bringing Cliff back and expanding him into a more central presence, Brad Pitt hits the aura jackpot. With a Redford mustache and killer grin and golden sweep of honey-blond hair, parading around in gaudy short-sleeve bartender shirts with three or four buttons open, he makes Cliff high on his own supply of flinty good vibes. Cliff takes whatever comes at him, and that’s a life that suits him fine. He’s chivalrous and polite, but that’s connected to how comfortable he is with violence. He has no anxiety about it, and no anxiety about anything else. Pitt takes his own slightly seedy movie-star nobility and turns it up to full irresistible throttle. Even his voice is yummy — the sandy baritone directness of it, with that hint of a SoCal drawl. His Cliff puts everyone at ease, including the audience, but he keeps you guessing because he’s a paradox: a himbo with brains who can read anyone in the room — a sexy cowboy handyman who, if need be, will cut your throat.

The film’s opening episode is an appetizer of violence. It’s Tuesday night, and Cliff is working his shift as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema (the first of the film’s Tarantino Easter-egg in-jokes — there will be more, including a TV commercial for Red Apple cigarettes featuring Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate). The theater is showing “Soul Brothers Die Hard!,” and Cliff talks along with some of the tastier dialogue as he changes reels. But his real job comes after the theater closes. That’s when he has to rendezvous with a scurvy criminal (Karren Karagulian) accompanied by a twink hustler (Corey Fogelmanis), who is out to blackmail one of Cliff’s old director pals, who picked him up on Santa Monica Boulevard. Cliff is supposed to pay them $50,000 for stolen items. Instead, he gets rid of the crook and puts the hustler on a bus back to Ohio. The shock — and joke — of it is that Cliff kills a man as casually as if he were mixing a banana margarita on his bartending night. That’s the Zen of Cliff Booth.

Fincher has referred to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” as “‘Shampoo’ with violence” (an ace description), and that’s to say: It’s all about Cliff drifting around L.A. It isn’t necessarily trying to be a movie story. But the film is fixated on Hollywood, to the point that each new location is identified with an onscreen title that will say (for instance) “Beverly Hills, 4.3 miles west of Hollywood.” And what’s telling about “Cliff Booth” is that it treats Hollywood as the nucleus of the universe, but in its random anecdotal hangout way it’s rooted in the world of television.

Rick moved to Australia because he’s starring in a TV series there called “Dingo Dan.” Those items stolen by the hustler include a best director Oscar statuette, which suggests that that trophy is a relic of a lost age. And the plot of “The Further Mis-Adventures” centers on Cliff getting summoned for a meeting with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a garishly obnoxious star of TV Westerns and combat series. Charlie, who thinks he knows everything, does all his own stunt work (which indicates that he might be a Tarantino tweak of Tom Cruise — though the two characters, aside from being of average height, don’t have much else in common). Charlie, though, needs Cliff for something else: to get him out of an underworld jam. This is, after all, the stuntman who beat up Bruce Lee.

So Cliff meets with Charlie’s agent, the imperially tall and coldly sexy Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki). These two get a flirtation going — one so frosty that in spirit it feels more 2026 than 1977. You can see that there’s a mutual attraction. And you really see it after Cliff confesses his feelings, and their gamesmanship turns weirdly kinky. (The weird part is that the kink stays so casual.) But she’s classy and standoffish, and the most revealing conversation the two have is about the movies.

It’s one of those freewheeling Tarantino digressions (built on what sounds like a scrap from his abandoned script for “The Critic”), in which Karen tells Cliff that she was briefly a film critic who had gotten to know Pauline Kael (who Cliff dismisses because she didn’t like “Butch Cassidy”). Karen, sounding like a corrupt studio executive, says she now thinks of movies strictly as entertainment, and never as art. Cliff asks: Even “The Godfather”? Yes, she says, that’s just a gangster movie with artistic airs. It’s strange that the film never counters this view; it’s almost as if Tarantino agrees with it. Has he gone that far into pulp fetishization? (The author of “Cinema Speculation” is actually a great critic.) Or maybe he’s saying: Now that “Star Wars” has arrived, the movies as we knew them are dead.

I’m going on about this because I think it helps explain the enjoyably random, slightly disjunctive air of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” It’s the first Tarantino film that feels, in its structural DNA, like a glorified television series. At one point, the movie was supposed to be a series, and in spirit that’s kind of what it still is. Call it QT TV. The incidents hook you, but with less consequence than they’d have in a full-blown, let-it-rip Tarantino movie. “The Further Mis-Adventures” looks like a movie (Fincher gives it a stately sheen), and it’s way too violent for television. But the hangout factor, in this case, feels one small step removed from the characters-on-a-TV-series-are-your-family factor.

Driving the action forward are a pair of Filipino hitmen, the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), who are singular in their viciousness; one employs a scary hatchet hammer he calls Esmarelda. Scott Caan does a blustery job of playing Charlie, the blowhard TV star (I enjoyed the scene where he uses a live round of ammunition to put the fear into Timothy Olyphant as a fellow actor playing a Nazi), but given how central the character is, I wish he were less of a putz. I also wish we didn’t have to watch Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II), Charlie’s football-player-turned-actor costar, get not simply beat up but maimed for no good reason. On the other hand, I appreciated the quick reference to Cliff doing porn films, which becomes a punchline to the fact that everyone he meets feels like they’ve seen him before. Speaking of porn, there’s a shoutout/tweak to PTA when “Best of My Love,” the Emotions track that opens “Boogie Nights,” comes on the car radio and Cliff flips the channel.

How is the ultraviolent climax? It’s kind of spectacular. Tarantino doesn’t use it to rewrite history this time, but in a funny way he does a mini version of that. What happens to Cliff in the big fight is so extreme it should have eliminated him from the earth. But it doesn’t. It’s just a scratch. He doesn’t give a fuck, and he’s still there. To put it in QT TV terms: When’s the next episode?

items.title: ‘Gilded Age’ Scores Early Season 5 Renewal at HBO
items.description: “The Gilded Age” has been renewed for Season 5 at HBO, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: “The Gilded Age” has been renewed for Season 5 at HBO, Variety has learned.

The news comes after the period drama has aired just three of its eight episodes for Season 4. This marks the earliest renewal announcement for the show to date, which has continued to grow its audience season to season. Per HBO, Season 4 is averaging 5.9 million U.S. multiplatform viewers per episode to date, with episode three hitting 4.3 million viewers in three days time. The episodic average is up nearly 20% over Season 3, though there are still five more episodes to air.

“Julian Fellowes and the cast of ‘The Gilded Age’ have once again captured the zeitgeist this fall, delivering another captivating, unmissable season, and we love how our growing audience has continued to embrace the series year after year,” said Francesca Orsi, president of HBO Drama Series and Films. “We can’t wait to return to 61st Street, as the Russells, van Rhijns and Kirklands continue to wrestle with the cost of ascent, while we expand the canvas and deepen the operatic stakes for these beloved characters.”

The show’s expansive ensemble cast includes: Carrie Coon, Christine Baranski, Cynthia Nixon, Morgan Spector, Louisa Jacobson, Denée Benton, Taissa Farmiga, Harry Richardson, Blake Ritson, Ben Ahlers, Ashlie Atkinson, Dylan Baker, Kelley Curran, Jordan Donica, Jessica Frances Dukes, Amy Forsyth, Jack Gilpin, Simon Jones, Celia Keenan-Bolger, Ben Lamb, Audra McDonald, Brian Stokes Mitchell, Debra Monk, Hattie Morahan, Donna Murphy, Kristine Nielsen, Kelli O’Hara, Taylor Richardson, Douglas Sills, Erin Wilhelmi, John Douglas Thompson, Taylor Trensch, James Scully, Dennis Haysbert, Maggie Kuntz, Neal Huff, Bonnie Milligan, Jim Gaffigan, Dallas Roberts, Andrew Burnap, Elizabeth Marvel, Adrienne Warren, with Bill Camp and Phylicia Rashad.

“It’s very exciting and deeply satisfying to see audiences fall more in love with ‘The Gilded Age’ every season,” said Erin Underhill, president of series producer Universal Television. “Our remarkable cast, writers – led by Julian Fellowes, and the entire creative team continue to make this world feel both timeless and resonant while keeping us on the edge of our seats season after season. We can’t wait for audiences to see what’s in store for Season 5.”

The official description of Season 4 states, “Bertha Russell (Coon) changed Society at a cost. Now, her family must reckon with the consequences as Agnes van Rhijn (Baranski) seizes an opportunity to regain her position. Meanwhile, Marian (Jacobson) forges a new path for herself, and Peggy (Benton) works to be accepted by her future in-laws. In this new era, you must be careful what you wish for.”

Julian Fellowes is the creator, writer, and executive producer of “The Gilded Age,” with Sonja Warfield also writing and executive producing. Salli Richardson-Whitfield serves as director and executive producer. Additional executive producers are Gareth Neame, David Crockett, Robert Greenblatt, Kate Churchill, Davita Scarlett, and Elaine Aronson. Erica Armstrong Dunbar and Holly Rymon are co-executive producers. The series is co-produced by HBO and Universal Television.

items.title: Brooks Nader Joins ‘Playmates’ Movie at Searchlight (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Brooks Nader is the latest addition to the cast of the upcoming Searchlight movie “Playmates,” Variety has learned exclusively.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Brooks Nader is the latest addition to the cast of the upcoming Searchlight movie “Playmates,” Variety has learned exclusively.

The film is inspired by writer and director Lorraine Nicholson’s childhood experiences at the Playboy Mansion. Nader will appear alongside previously announced cast members Lily-Rose Depp, Bill Pullman, Jessica Biel, Indiana Elle, and Anna Van Patten.

The official logline for “Playmates” states, “Elle (Elle), a thirteen-year-old know-it-all who considers the Playboy Mansion her second home, meets Anna (Depp), one of seven hopefuls vying to be Playmate of the Month. The two form an unlikely friendship and try to help each other get what the other wants most, a magazine cover and a boy.”
Pullman will star as Playboy founder Hugh Hefner, with Biel playing Hefner’s wife. Exact details on Nader’s character are being kept under wraps.

Nader will next be seen in Fox’s reboot of “Baywatch,” which will debut on the broadcast network on Jan. 6. She originally found success as a model, including appearing in the iconic Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue. She also currently stars in the Freeform reality series “Love Thy Nader,” which is prepping a second season, and also appeared in the 33rd season of “Dancing with the Stars.”
She is repped by WME, Dixon Talent, Inc. and by Leigh Fidler, Chief Brand Officer of Nader Sisters Inc.

Searchlight Pictures is the studio behind “Playmates.” As mentioned above, Nicholson will write and direct. Alex Orlovsky and Duncan Montgomery will produce via High Frequency Entertainment, with Depp producing in addition to starring. Searchlight vice president of production Richard Ruiz and creative executive Cornelia Burleigh will oversee the project for the studio. Ruiz and Burleigh report into the Heads of Production and Development, DanTram Nguyen and Katie Goodson-Thomas.

items.title: New ‘Serendipity’ Movie Casts Auli‘i Cravalho (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Auli‘i Cravalho is the latest addition to the new “Serendipity” movie in the works at Amazon MGM Studios and Miramax, Variety has learned exclusively.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Auli‘i Cravalho is the latest addition to the new “Serendipity” movie in the works at Amazon MGM Studios and Miramax, Variety has learned exclusively.

The project is described not as a reboot of the 2001 romantic comedy but rather an update in a modern setting featuring new characters. Cravalho joins previously announced cast members Milo Manheim, Whitney Peak, and Stephen Kalyn. Exact character and plot details are being kept under wraps.

Cravalho is best known for her starring role in the hit Disney animated film “Moana” and its sequel, while she was also an executive producer on the live-action version released in 2026. She has also starred in films like “Zootopia 2,” 2024’s “Mean Girls,” and “Crush.” In TV, she is known for roles in shows like “Rise,” “The Power,” and for voicing Jessica Cruz, a.k.a Green Lantern, in multiple DC animated projects. It was recently reported that she will appear in the series adaptation of “Icebreaker” for Netflix. She was named to Variety’s Power of Young Hollywood Impact Report in 2025.
Cravalho is repped by Gersh, Artists First, and Goodman Genow.

Michael Showalter is attached to direct “Serendipity.” Marc Klein, who wrote the original film, will pen the screenplay and executive produce. Showalter is also a producer alongside Jordana Mollick for Semi-Formal Productions. Simon Fields, who produced the original, is also a producer. Jonathan Glickman, Alexandra Loewy, and Thom Zadra will executive produce for Miramax. Arianna D’Andrea is overseeing the project for Miramax, while Emily Crook is overseeing for Semi-Formal.

The original “Serendipity” starred John Cusack and Kate Beckinsale. In the film, their characters meet one night in New York and decide to leave the chance of meeting again up to fate. They ultimately go searching for each other years later despite being in relationships with other people. The film was a box office success, grossing over $77 million on a reported budget of $28 million.

items.title: Judge Allows Trump to Sue New York Times Reporters Over Tax Fraud Claims
items.description: A judge has allowed President Trump to proceed with a $15 billion suit against the New York Times, finding a plausible claim that its reporters acted recklessly in accusing Trump of tax fraud.
items.author: Gene Maddaus
paragraphs: A judge has allowed President Trump to proceed with a $15 billion suit against the New York Times, finding a plausible claim that its reporters acted recklessly in accusing Trump of tax fraud.

Judge Steven Merryday denied the defendants’ motion to dismiss the lawsuit, holding that the book “Lucky Loser” includes a series of claims about Trump’s business dealings that are potentially defamatory.

Though the book cites tax experts who stated that Trump’s conduct was “highly suspicious” and “smells like a crime,” the judge ruled that was not enough to state outright that Trump had committed tax fraud or tax evasion. Such a clear-cut judgment would require “an explicit opinion from a qualified source after a thorough examination of pertinent facts,” the judge ruled.
Absent such a statement, the judge ruled that the reporters were venturing into risky territory.
“They know that they don’t know, but they are undeterred,” he wrote.

The book, published by Penguin Random House, included the allegation that Trump had obtained the equivalent of $400 million from his father, Fred, “much of it through fraudulent tax evasion schemes.” The book also asserted that Fred Trump had engaged in “likely tax fraud” when he gave his son gifts disguised as loans; and that the arrangement was designed to avoid gift and estate taxes.
In his lawsuit, Trump argued that the statements were false because neither he nor his father had ever been charged with a tax crime.

The New York Times published two articles drawn from the book in 2024. In the ruling, Merryday dismissed the claims pertaining to the first article, which focused on Trump’s relationship with TV producer Mark Burnett and the development of “The Apprentice.”

The judge also tossed statements from the second article that focused on Trump’s school record. But the judge allowed Trump to sue over a statement from that article that authorities had investigated his “ties to the Mafia” and had found “violations of money laundering laws.”
In response, a New York Times spokesperson said the paper was “encouraged” that almost all of the claims against the paper were dismissed.

“We continue to believe the remaining claim in the filing has no legal merit,” the spokesperson said. “We look forward to making this argument as we continue to defend ourselves against this baseless attack on The Times and the rights of the free and independent press in this country.”
The same judge dismissed an earlier version of Trump’s lawsuit last year, finding it overlong and full of colorful but irrelevant detail. Trump’s lawyers refiled a more concise version a month later.
The suit can now proceed to discovery and motions for summary judgment. The defendants in the case are the Times, three of its reporters, and Penguin Random House.
