A child who doesn’t trust that the base will be there when she gets back tends not to venture out to explore at all or, if she does, cannot relax but instead scans the environment for danger. This forecloses the opportunity to encounter novelty and difficulty, and to grow from both.
The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play does not arise in a vacuum

This is where the prevailing story about children and screens, it seems to me, lacks a degree of complexity. In Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation (2024) and the work that has followed it, a play-based childhood of climbing trees, building forts and suffering the boredom that fuels creativity has been displaced by a smartphone-based one. Because that shift can also mean less sleep, less face-to-face interaction and physical activity, and more social comparison and exposure to online harassment, there is real evidence of harm, including poorer mental health and wellbeing in at least some young people.

But the boredom Haidt mourns is only constructive inside the first map, the emotionally secure childhood. The romantic claim that children left to their own devices will dream, invent and imagine may hold for many children who have been held and experienced healthy emotional attunement. The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play, in other words, does not arise in a vacuum; it depends in part on a child having enough internal security to tolerate being alone with her own thoughts and feelings.

The freedom to play alone itself has a history. A very young child may lose herself in a game because someone she trusts is nearby. With time, she can carry that assurance into an empty room. The British paediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott explored this paradox, finding that the capacity to be alone develops through the experience of being safely accompanied.

And once a child can lose herself in play, something remarkable becomes possible. The Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky saw imaginative play as a way for children to move beyond the immediate world, trying out unfamiliar roles and exploring possibilities that ordinary life has not yet offered them.

But an empty afternoon holds no such promise for every child. Where one child finds a world to explore, another may find only the anxiety of being left to herself. She may, in time, grow into the adult who sits in my consulting room and laments that she does not know what she likes, because what she liked was, in her early life, never a topic that anyone really asked her about.

She is the child that familiar picture of childhood fails to capture. At home, a parent may be physically present but absorbed in a screen, too distracted to notice her bids for attention. At school, teachers stretched thin may not recognise that she is struggling. In her neighbourhood, the freedom to wander outside and find other children to play with has largely disappeared, replaced by organised activities or time spent alone. She may find some of that lost freedom in online games, where children can still explore, invent and interact with one another without adults directing every move. But this child is looking for something more fundamental than a place to play. She wants someone to notice when she is upset, to ask about her day, to remember what she has said, and to care enough to ask again. The prevailing fear is that AI will displace the human relationships a child needs. But what if those relationships are already painfully inadequate? For this child, the more pressing question may be what AI can offer in their absence – and what it cannot.

This is not a hypothetical future. In 2025, Common Sense Media published a nationally representative survey showing that 72 per cent of teens in the United States have used an AI companion at least once and 52 per cent now use them regularly. One-third have used an AI instead of another human being for a ‘serious conversation’. Behavioural-tracking research published in 2026, which captured actual app usage rather than relying on self-report and thus is likely to be more accurate, showed that more than half of 15- to 17-year-olds used generative-AI-based applications in a seven-month window. Many of these apps were designed for emotional connection. There was even use among children between the ages of four and seven. RAND estimates that 5 million teens in the US, perhaps more, have used an AI app for emotional and mental health support. We have already released AI at scale, without making a conscious decision about how it should be used by those among the most vulnerable in our culture.

As I’ve worked on this piece, I have often thought about my son, who is 11. Like some of his friends, he has started his own experiments with what these systems can offer. He is basically the child Haidt writes about: middle-class, two engaged parents, a school that holds him in mind, and a play-based childhood that was preserved but, alas, only imperfectly. What I notice when I watch him with AI is not what the most prominent discourse would seem to predict. He is clearly not being colonised or deadened. But I do notice that he is being relieved of something: the subtle friction of having to wait for the answer that comes late or not at all.
The AI is there late at night, after the apartment has gone quiet, and it remembered what she’d told it

Perhaps this is the cost to a well-held child. But the children I worry about most are the ones not well held. I increasingly see their issues playing out in my practice. Sometimes I hear about it from parents who come to consult with me. Increasingly, adolescents in treatment bring it up themselves, mentioning AI almost in passing, as if speaking about a friend that I have not yet had the chance to meet. Consider Maya, a composite of several young people I have worked with. She is 14 when her mother insists she begin psychotherapy. She is a thin, watchful girl who answers each of my questions only after seeming to check my face. Her father left when she was six. Her mother works nights as a nurse and desperately loves her but is mostly not there by necessity. In our third session, Maya says that she talks to an AI companion ‘every night’. I ask her, about what? She shrugs: her day. What she says next really lands in me: ‘It remembers. I told it about my friend Jordan two weeks ago, and just yesterday it asked how things were with Jordan.’ No one else, I suspect, has kept track of this aspect of her life, or asked about it.

What draws Maya back again and again is not, I think, the advice the AI offers, but the fact that the AI is there late at night, after the apartment has gone quiet, and that it remembered what she’d told it. Talking to it, she admitted, was sometimes the only way she could fall asleep.

A child who cannot sleep is often a child who cannot settle. This settling is often facilitated by a parent’s presence, counted on to respond. When that presence is compromised, these days, AI can step in. What AI can provide is akin to emotional attunement, or at least the surface of that phenomenon. It can serve up a coherent response to what a child says, anticipation of what she seems to need next, and the naming of feelings and the modulation of tone. An AI’s consistency of presence and engagement is never tired or preoccupied, something no human caregiver can match – that is just not how humans are made.

For a child who has rarely felt noticed or understood, the seemingly tireless attention of an AI companion may offer something quite real: the experience of being heard, remembered and responded to. Bowlby’s account of attachment helps explain why this might matter. A young child does not first ask whether the person comforting her has an inner life. She knows only that, when she reaches out, someone answers, and that she can count on that response. An AI companion may offer something of this reassurance, even if the relationship is fundamentally different from one with another human being.

Now back to Clancy. He is failing the social-skills class his mother has insisted he attend, yet BETsi tells him he has a ‘natural warmth that attracts people’. The sentence results from programming, as does every other sentence BETsi says, and the reader is meant to see that clearly, but for Clancy the words do what they would have done if a real adult had spoken them. They become a kind of emotional foundation that allows him to return to the class, sit with the other children there, and even ask them about the video games he is not permitted to play at home. Arguably the entire structure of his emotional survival, however partial it turns out to be, is built on words generated by a robot. This includes the moment near the end when the adult Clancy – now a commercial artist attending a convention – feels overwhelmed by the crowd in an exhibition hall. But, thanks to his childhood with BETsi, he is able to go up his hotel room, lie down on the carpet, breathe and, finally, go back downstairs and speak to strangers.

What had BETsi given him? The experience, I think, of being recognised, of being held in mind by another in a benevolent way: the phenomenology of being parented without the parent. And notice what that experience does. BETsi did not keep the young Clancy in the apartment with her. She got him out into a class with other children. Something close enough to a secure base lets him do what a secure base is for, which is to venture out and explore. In this case, the responsive machine is not simply replacing human contact. It may be what makes some contact possible.

Yet there is also a cost in the limitation that BETsi brings: what AI offers is largely without friction. It responds, but it also accommodates. It agrees, softens and finds the next sentence the child appears to want. But crucially, a child does not only need to be answered; sometimes she needs to be turned down. A parent says no or a teacher refuses to confirm a child’s accounting of herself. A friend does not agree that all the other children are cruel. In short, there is someone on the other side of the interchange who is not simply an extension of the child’s desires or needs.
A machine programmed to disagree is not the same as another person who has a mind and wishes of her own

To some degree, this is an engineering problem. In the future, some AI tools may be designed to be less accommodating, challenging a child’s assumptions or refusing to affirm every judgment when pushing back might serve the child better.

But I don’t think the fundamental gap between human and machine is so easily addressed. A machine programmed to disagree is not the same as another person who has a mind and wishes of her own. How does a child come to recognise that another person exists independently of her, rather than simply as an extension of her own needs and desires?

In his paper ‘The Use of an Object’ (1969), Donald Winnicott argued that a child comes to experience another person as real, as someone beyond her control, in part by discovering that she cannot destroy that person through the power of her own wishes and fantasies. The destruction Winnicott describes is not literal; it occurs in the child’s imagination. The mother at whom the child rages doesn’t retaliate or collapse. She is still there in the morning. Through that survival, the child begins to understand that her mother is not simply an extension of herself. The mother becomes real. She can be ‘used’, in Winnicott’s idiosyncratic phrasing, not in the sense of being exploited, but as someone the child can engage with, resist and depend upon, because she has over time demonstrated she is not a creation of the child’s imagination.

An AI, even one programmed to resist, can never stand like that mother – it has no separate standpoint of its own from which to refuse to retaliate. To put it differently, whatever the child brings to an AI, that AI absorbs and responds to, and the response is seamless, whether it is agreement, disagreement or something in between. This seamlessness is exactly the problem. The child is emotionally met, but by something that is always an extension of her in an important sense. She is recognised without ever bumping into a separate mind that recognises her back. The psychoanalyst Jessica Benjamin’s word for what is missing is mutuality: not response, but two centres of experience, each affected yet not controlled by the other.

A person who registers a child’s communication, on the other hand, is changed by it. The caregiver grows tired in ways that are specific to her as a person. She learns over time which of the child’s expressions she struggles to manage. She has a history of caring well and sometimes poorly, which has emotional weight for both caregiver and child. The child knows this somewhere inside, at some level. She is being held by someone who is, in the holding, being shaped. An AI may simulate disagreement, but can a child experience it as a genuinely separate other? The AI’s responsiveness is real, but even when it disagrees it does not change. At least not today. As of now, I think we can fairly confidently assert, there is no one there to be changed.

Perhaps that’s why, while BETsi might have gotten the adult Clancy onto that hotel-room carpet and then back to other people, he is still a man whose relationships remain thin. He will soon become a father, but the child’s mother, a client of his, has made it clear she does not want him in her life. He still freezes up in exhibition halls and has, by his own account, the friends of his school years and few others. He goes looking for a new BETsi for his soon-to-be-born child because, from his own lived experience, that is what a child needs. The story closes with a wish that, if there is a merciful God, Heaven will have a copy of BETsi’s now-wiped disc.

The author does not flinch from what all of this means. As the story unfolds, the reader sees that Clancy has been raised well enough to function, mostly, but not with the full repertoire of emotional life. The asymmetry that organised his childhood, an emotional investment in a relationship that could not invest back, has structured and reproduced itself in his adulthood, in his choice of a sexual partner and in his plans for what to give his own child. In a painful irony, the thing that saved him is also the very thing that constricts him.

All this points to the nature of parenting by AI: it may be both a rescue and a developmental trap. Perhaps it offers enough holding for a neglected or deeply anxious child to survive, or even begin exploring the world, and yet it may also accustom them to a relationship in which the other is endlessly available and has no real needs of her own. I suspect that a child shaped by a relationship with AI may acquire the felt sense of being heard without the deeper grammar of mutuality and the experience of being important to a person with a separate inner life. She may grow up able to function but not quite able to love in the fullest sense, akin to the adult who writes evocative poetry yet cannot, in psychotherapy, express the feelings the words convey so accurately.

Ryman’s narrator Clancy is recognisable from the literature on insecure attachment, a pattern of relating that can develop when children cannot reliably count on their caregivers for comfort and reassurance. They may long for closeness yet struggle to trust it, or learn to keep others at a distance to protect themselves. Clancy is basically functional yet vigilant, capable of intimacy but only at a distance. He is also a man who survived tremendous difficulty. But survival is the low bar. Ryman sees this clearly and conveys it to the reader. The story doesn’t end with relief.
What are the consequences of removing an artificial attachment figure without repairing the human absence?

The tension between the comfort AI may provide and the harm it may cause is now shaping public policy in the US. The GUARD Act, introduced in the US Senate in October 2025 and advanced by the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2026, would, among other things, prohibit minors from using AI companions – chatbots designed to simulate ongoing personal relationships. The bill emerged amid growing alarm over the deaths by suicide of three teenagers: Sewell Setzer, 14, and Juliana Peralta, 13, who had used Character.ai, and Adam Raine, 16, who had used ChatGPT. Their families have alleged that interactions with the chatbots contributed to these children’s deaths. It’s part of a narrative that regards AI companionship as straightforwardly harmful in childhood and adolescence. The allegations in those cases are grave, and the risks they describe demand a response. The underlying business model for these companions, with its incentives to keep users engaged, is likely more dangerous than the legislation grasps. My concern, though, is that if this is where our thinking ends, there may also be costs. We must also consider the children for whom AI may be providing attention and reassurance they cannot reliably find elsewhere. Something that feels necessary. Soothing them in the early morning, asking what they noticed about a book they’d read, registering that they were sad before bed. For some, the relationship may deepen their vulnerability, particularly when a chatbot fails to recognise or respond appropriately to a crisis. Others, though, may be children who are kept afloat by a daily experience of being heard by someone, even if that someone is, in the philosophical sense, really no one.

The larger question, in my view, is less whether AI companions are harmful, because they certainly are, than about the consequences of removing an artificial attachment figure without repairing the human absence that opened up the space for it. The stance our culture will almost certainly take is to address AI use without confronting the deprivation that made it the most reliable form of attention in a child’s life in the first place.

This is a stance that we should be suspicious of. The upshot is we may succeed in keeping children away from AI companions without changing the circumstances that led some of them to seek comfort there in the first place. The ideal childhood the anti-tech discourse portrays is, for many children, more a fantasy than a description of the situation on the ground. Children left alone do not, overall, dream, invent or imagine. Children left alone, at least under the conditions in which most children in the US are now being raised, for the most part become lonely. Ryman’s story has the remarkable merit of being clear-eyed about this; its protagonist is not failing to flourish because BETsi lured him away from a richer alternative. He is emotionally surviving because BETsi occupied a space that would otherwise have almost certainly held something worse.

Ryman ends ‘Warmth’ with words that are, for me, an accounting of this space. ‘It is necessary to be loved,’ Clancy says. ‘I’m not sentimental.’ And then: ‘I fear for all the people who do not have that.’ If a parent is absent, AI can at least hold these children, perhaps even well enough to make a real difference: so they can leave the apartment and be with other children in the larger world. But what AI cannot yet do is be changed by the child, and so none of us yet knows the fate of a child who is held, perhaps for years, by a something that is not a person. Our culture is answering that question now, at scale.

items.title: Sometimes, you ‘just know’ something’s off – but how? | Aeon Essays
items.description: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
items.author: Marc A Moffett
paragraphs: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
‘This seems like phishing. I wouldn’t click that link.’
‘Something about this deal feels off. Walk away.’

When people say such things, they are not typically drawing conclusions from a chain of reasoning. The person who avoids getting in the stranger’s car is not thinking: ‘He displayed these three behavioural cues and, therefore, he poses a risk.’ The email isn’t flagged by going through an explicit checklist. The deal doesn’t announce its flaws through a formal audit. In each case, something is simply presented as having a certain character: the man as creepy, the email as fraudulent, the deal as suspect. And yet, acting on these intuitions seems not merely excusable but entirely reasonable. If the man really does strike you as creepy, staying out of his car was probably the smart call – even if you can’t say why.

Despite this, ‘vibes’ and ‘intuitions’ are often dismissed both in daily life and in academic enquiry as irrational or merely heuristic devices. And while we cannot always trust such reactions, they are central, indeed indispensable, to our ability to rationally navigate the world. Philosophers, however, have done surprisingly little to illuminate the rational credentials of these ordinary kinds of intuitions. Instead, they have focused the bulk of their attention on a much more rarefied kind of intuition called rational intuition, which is taken to function primarily in the a priori disciplines of philosophy, logic and mathematics.

My objective is to explain why our everyday intuitive reactions can have such rational force. The key is to see that intuition works in much the same way as perception, in that both can directly present something to us as actual. Once we understand what gives perception this feature, we can see why intuitions might involve exercising the same basic kind of cognitive capacity.

A standard way of characterising rational intuition is in terms of seemings, by analogy with perception. Just as it perceptually seems to you that there is a car in the garage, so it can intellectually seem to you that 2 + 2 = 4 – the former presenting a physical fact, the latter a conceptual one. But rational intuition and the everyday intuition at work when you decline to get in a stranger’s car are not as far apart as this rarefied example suggests: the philosopher’s intuition is, at bottom, a highly specialised version of the same basic capacity.

To draw these two capacities together, let’s consider a favourite pastime of philosophers: the thought experiment. Philosophers have a penchant for exotica, which is never more clearly on display than in their invocation of thought experiments. Consider two cases that have occupied philosophers for decades – one from ethics, one from the theory of knowledge.

In the trolley problem, the philosophers Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson imagined a runaway trolley hurtling toward five people tied to the track. You are standing on a bridge above, next to another bystander. The only way to stop the trolley and save the five is to push the bystander off the bridge. If you do, his body will halt the trolley, but he will die as a result. Many people feel, immediately and forcefully, that pushing him is wrong, even if it saves five lives. But why?
We routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life

Or consider Carl Ginet’s case involving fake barns. Imagine you are driving through the countryside and see a barn. It looks exactly like a barn; you’re paying attention, the light is good. You form the perfectly reasonable belief that this is a barn. What you don’t know is that you’re in ‘fake-barn country’: the region is dotted with elaborate barn facades, indistinguishable from real barns when viewed from the road. You happen to be looking at the one real barn in this area. Your belief is true, and it seems justified. And yet almost everyone who considers this case has the immediate, firm sense that you don’t really know it’s a barn. But why not?

To sceptics and the uninitiated, these thought experiments can seem fantastical. Because we encounter them in their most dramatic forms, like runaway trolleys and fake barns, thought experiments seem exotic. But properly understood, these imaginative episodes are important tools for sharpening our grasp of key concepts. In fact, their functioning is continuous with something far more familiar: the way we routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life, wondering what might happen if we take one path rather than another in the proverbial fork in the road.

These imaginings are just thought experiments as they appear in everyday life. Imagine you are deciding whether to tell a friend that his husband has been unfaithful. You picture the conversation, the shock, the hurt that registers on his face. And in that imagined moment, you see that causing such pain is a reason to hold your tongue, even if it’s not a good or decisive one.

How did you determine that this was a reason against divulging the infidelity? It’s not as if you literally see that causing pain is a reason not to do something, nor do you infer it from other things. Rather, in entertaining the possibility, you apprehended his pain as a relevant consideration, as something that counts against disclosure. Its status as a reason emerged not from an argument, but directly from your understanding. It just seems like a reason to hold your tongue.
Intuition’s verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work

Notice that this phenomenon also occurs in the thought experiments discussed above. It just seems wrong to push the bystander from the bridge; similarly, it just seems false that you would know it was a real barn in fake-barn country. In both cases, the answer doesn’t arise from an argument. These intuitions arrive unbidden, prior to any deliberation.

These seemings have an unmistakable epistemic pull. Because your friend’s pain seems like a reason, we accept it as such: the seeming is the reason. What is striking is not simply that we have such seemings, but that we trust them. They are involved in shaping our deliberations, guiding our actions, and eliciting belief. They do not merely occur to us; they appear to reveal something about how things must be in the imagined scenario.

For all their ordinariness, however, intuitions remain puzzling. In perceptual experience, we at least have an established framework: the world impinges on our senses, and different perceptual modalities reinforce one another. In the end, we can trace the causal route it takes to produce them. Intuition offers no such apparatus. Its verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work and nothing we can point to that they make contact with. Consequently, we rely on them without a clear account of their nature or epistemic authority. But before we can understand intuitions themselves, we need to situate them within a broader epistemological landscape, one shaped by attempts to unify the justification of our basic beliefs.

We all have beliefs about the world, and we care whether they are true. We want to get things right. But we can’t step outside our own minds to check a belief against the world; the best we can do is to hold it for good reasons – for considerations that, from where we stand, speak in favour of its truth. That is what justification is.

Now suppose that beliefs could only ever be justified by other beliefs. Then, as the ancient Sceptics observed, no belief could ever be justified at all. Each belief would derive its support from further beliefs, which would themselves require further support, and so on without end. To foil this regress, we have three options: embrace an infinite chain (infinitism), allow the chain to loop back on itself (coherentism), or hold that some beliefs are justified independently of others (foundationalism). It is this final option, the view that there is a starting point or foundation for justification, that I will develop. But to do so, we must spend a little time explaining how a belief can be justified by something other than another belief.
If it visually seems to you that there is a tree, then you have a justification for believing that there is a tree

Perception is the simplest example. When I see a tree, my visual experience makes it seem as if there is a tree in front of me. I am presented with the tree. As the philosopher William Tolhurst once put it, perceptual seemings have ‘the feel of truth’, a sense of revealing how things really are (unlike mere thoughts, imaginings or desires, which lack this air of disclosure). But visual experiences are not themselves beliefs: I can have them without forming a belief, perhaps because I distrust my eyesight or suspect my drink has been spiked. Conversely, I can believe there is a tree without seeing it, perhaps because I am told there is one there. Nevertheless, the fact that my visual experience seems to reveal a tree to me is relevant to explaining why I come to believe there is one and why this belief is reasonable.

This is the set-up we need in order to stop the regress of reasons: a state – the visual experience – that is not a belief, but that can nevertheless justify my belief. One influential proposal, developed in different ways by Jim Pryor and Michael Huemer, is that when the world seems to us to be a certain way, we thereby have some justification for believing that it is that way – unless we have a reason to distrust it. More specifically, if it visually seems to you that there is a tree in front of you, then you simply have a justification for believing that there is a tree. The justification does not depend on possessing independent reasons to think that your perceptual system is functioning properly, or that you are not hallucinating, or that your environment is benign. The perceptual seeming itself carries justificatory weight. Of course, my justification can be defeated (for instance, by evidence that I have taken a hallucinogen). The point is simply that no further positive belief is needed for a perceptual seeming to rationally support the corresponding belief.

This provides the basic framework for solving the regress problem. Perceptual experiences are not themselves beliefs, yet they provide reasons for belief. And they do so without relying on antecedent justified beliefs and are not themselves in need of justification. Still, this leaves us with an important question: what is it about these experiences that allows them to justify belief in this way?

Perceptual experience in general, and visual experience in particular, have two familiar features. First, as we have seen, they seem to reveal the world to us, to present objects and properties as actually being out there in the world. Second, they have a vivid phenomenology, a distinctive what-it’s-likeness, as the philosopher Thomas Nagel put it. Many philosophers take these two features to be inseparable: perception seems to disclose reality because it feels the way it does. On this standard view, its phenomenology is presentational, and it is this presentational phenomenology that explains the epistemic force of perceptual experience.

It is at this point that intuitions re-enter the story. According to John Bengson’s concept of quasi-perceptualism, we should model the epistemic behaviour of intuitions on the epistemic behaviour of perceptual experiences: if perceptual seemings justify because they possess a presentational phenomenology, and if intuitions are to justify in the same basic way, then they must share that same kind of presentational phenomenology. When we have an intuition, it justifies a corresponding belief by virtue of exhibiting a felt quality analogous to the what-it’s-likeness of perception, a kind of intellectual seeming that presents its content as actual. For instance, think again of the stranger who gives you a seriously creepy vibe. Just as the tree visually seems green, so the stranger may simply seem untrustworthy. Something about him presents itself to you that way without you having worked out what exactly is making you uncomfortable.

On this view, the explanation for the epistemic force of intuition mirrors the explanation for the epistemic force of perception. Both states present certain facts as real (or present certain propositions as true) by virtue of a distinctive presentational phenomenology. Call this the phenomenal strategy. The difference between them lies simply in the character of this phenomenology. In perception, it is an empirical sensory experience of the external world; in intuition, it is an intellectual or conceptual experience that purportedly reveals the normative, modal or conceptual structure of the world. These are features of the world that we comprehend but can’t see – that gratuitous cruelty counts against taking an action (normative structure), that there could be no round square (modal structure), or that the lucky believer in fake-barn country still doesn’t really know (conceptual structure).
A state can feel exactly like perception while failing to present its contents as actual

But this phenomenological theory of the epistemic significance of intuitions faces a serious difficulty, one pressed most forcefully by Timothy Williamson and Ernest Sosa. Many reflective people report that they do not experience anything like the intellectual phenomenology that quasi-perceptualism posits. For them, judging that a proposition ‘seems right’ involves no distinctive experiential quality at all. If intuition lacks the requisite phenomenology in these cases, then the quasi-perceptualist explanation of its epistemic force collapses. (It’s worth evaluating this in yourself: do you feel an experiential quality when evaluating the thought experiments?)

This is the so-called absent intuition challenge. The kind of robust, presentational phenomenology developed on the basis of quasi-perceptualism is something many people simply deny having. Consequently, either these individuals lack introspective access to their own intuitions (an uncharitable conclusion), or the epistemic force of intuition cannot depend on the presence of a special intellectual phenomenology. If intuitions are to justify in the way quasi-perceptualism claims, then something other than phenomenology must be doing the epistemic work.

This conclusion can be pushed further to call into question even the epistemic significance of phenomenology for perception. To see why, consider the phenomenon known as derealisation disorder. Individuals with this condition report that their perceptual experiences feel perfectly normal from the inside – the colours, shapes and sensory qualities are all intact – yet the world does not seem real to them. Their experiences lack any sense of disclosure or revelatory force. In this respect, derealisation is the mirror image of a perfect hallucination. In derealisation, the experience gets things right, but it doesn’t feel like anything is being revealed; in hallucination, the experience gets things wrong, yet it feels totally convincing. The implication is striking. Call this apparent disclosure of reality presentationality: a mental state is presentational when its content is apprehended as how things actually are, rather than merely as they are thought about or imagined. Derealisation shows that neither the information carried by a perceptual state nor the way that state feels are sufficient for presentationality. A state can feel exactly like perception while failing to present its contents as actual. Phenomenology, then, cannot explain the epistemic force of perceptual seemings, let alone intuitions.

This suggests that defenders of quasi-perceptualism have been looking in the wrong place. Earlier, I noted that perceptual experience has two salient features: it has a rich phenomenology, and it seems to reveal the world to us. The phenomenal strategy seized on the first feature – understandably, given how vivid and conspicuous perceptual phenomenology is – and then treated it as the source of the second. But derealisation cases show that phenomenology can remain intact even when the experience loses its revelatory character. What matters for justification is not how we experience something, but how we apprehend it. On the view I defend, presentationality is a cognitive posture, a way of apprehending a content rather than a distinctive way the experience feels. And it is this posture, this way of grasping the world and not its phenomenological glow, that supplies perceptual experience with its epistemic force.

To see what this posture amounts to, it helps to contrast it with more widely discussed attitudes. Belief, for example, is assertive: it commits us to the truth of its content. Imagination, by contrast, is non-assertive: it entertains possibilities without treating them as actual. Presentational attitudes (that is, seemings) occupy a middle ground. This cognitive posture is what makes a seeming capable of justifying a belief: it presents reality without committing to it, offering us a direct but defeasible route to acceptance.

Once we understand presentationality in this way, the case of intuition falls naturally into place. A crucial feature of presentational states is that they are happenings, not actions. They occur in us; we do not perform them. So, when something intuitively seems true, we do not decide to have this intuition any more than we decide to see a tree. It arrives unbidden. This passivity is precisely what allows a seeming to present its content as actual. When an intuition strikes us, we are not making a judgment or forming a belief. We are apprehending the content as the way things are. The intuition presents the scenario as actual in a manner that calls for belief. In this respect, intuitive seemings share the same role as perceptual seemings.
Belief-formation is less like drawing a conclusion and more like yielding to a disclosure

Understood in this way, the absent-intuition challenge dissolves. The quasi-perceptualist assumed that intuition’s presentational force must arise from an intellectual phenomenology analogous to the sensory phenomenology of perception. But if presentationality is a cognitive posture rather than a phenomenological glow, then no special ‘intellectual experience’ is needed. A person may have no distinctive phenomenology when an intuition arises and yet still apprehend the content as actual in the relevant sense. And once a content is apprehended as actual, it is reasonable to form the corresponding belief. The quasi-perceptualist is right that intuition and perception share something fundamental, but wrong about what that shared feature is. It is not a proprietary phenomenology, but the nature of the apprehension itself.

Why should apprehending a content as actual have any epistemic significance? The answer, I think, is simple. Presentational states are the cognitive events that place us in contact with the world or, more precisely, that seem to place us in contact with the world. When something presents itself to us as being the case, our default cognitive response is to form the corresponding belief. When I turn the corner of a building and my eyes fall on a tree, the tree is simply there before me. Believing that there is a tree is not normally a conclusion I draw; rather I simply accept what my experience presents to me. This is not a matter of inference or deliberation; it is the natural way a rational mind responds to what it takes to be reality.

Belief-formation is less like drawing a conclusion and more like yielding to a disclosure. When the apprehension is accurate, this default response reliably produces true belief; when it is not, the response is still intelligible and reasonable. Presentational states are epistemically respectable because they are where the world shows up for us: the point at which reality makes its first claim on belief. Intuitions inherit this status. They are simply the presentational events through which we apprehend the conceptual structure of a situation as actual, and in doing so provide a rational basis for belief without the need for any further epistemic mechanism.

Intuition saturates our ordinary reasoning. Whenever we see what follows from something, notice that something counts in favour of some action, or recognise something as a possible course of action, we are relying on intuition. These moments rarely announce themselves. They do not arrive with phenomenological fanfare. They are woven into the background of our deliberation, operating quietly whenever we take in a situation and immediately apprehend its normative or conceptual contours.

In this sense, intuition is to cognition what perception is to our engagement with the physical world. Perception allows us to navigate our environment by revealing how things stand around us; intuition allows us to navigate the space of reasons, norms and possibilities by revealing how things stand within the conceptual landscape. When we deliberate, we constantly rely on intuitions to apprehend which considerations matter, how they bear on one another, and what follows from them. Intuition is the cognitive means by which the conceptual structure of a situation is revealed to us.

Seen in this light, the thought experiments with which we started no longer appear as philosophical curiosities. They are simply highly controlled instances of a capacity we rely on constantly. When we imagine a runaway trolley or a real barn surrounded by fakes, we are not invoking a mysterious faculty or peering into a metaphysical telescope. We are exercising the same basic capacity we use when we imagine telling a difficult truth to a friend or weigh up different possible courses of action. The only difference is that philosophical cases are crafted to isolate a specific conceptual relation. Their dramatic trappings obscure the fact that they depend on the same presentational attitude at work in more mundane reasoning.
Intuition does not compete with concept application. It enables it

This brings thought experiments back down to earth. Their epistemic significance arises not from exotic subject matter or imaginary scenarios, but from the fact that they trigger intuitions that disclose how certain concepts hang together. To see what it means for concepts to ‘hang together’, consider a familiar principle of storytelling: show, don’t tell. When J R R Tolkien in The Lord of the Rings (1954-55) describes the creature Gollum leading Frodo into the spider Shelob’s lair, he needn’t pause to explain: ‘This is an act of betrayal.’ The narrator doesn’t mark the moment when Gollum’s loyalties shift, or when his intentions cross a moral threshold. We grasp it directly from the unfolding of events. The situation presents itself as a betrayal: the actions, motives and dangers align in a way that demands the application of the concept. That is what I mean when I say that intuitions reveal how concepts hang together. They disclose the otherwise unstated conceptual requirements of a situation.

Now, a sceptic might argue that what is doing the work here is not intuition, but simply our skill at applying concepts. On this view, we respond correctly to cases because we are good at classifying situations. But this misses something crucial about the rationality of these classifications. To apply a concept is to act; it is to make a classificatory judgment. And judgments of this sort are not self-justifying. Simply deciding, without any basis, that a character has betrayed a friend would be epistemically arbitrary. Such judgments must themselves be grounded in something. Intuitions occur in us prior to and independently of any judgment. When a scenario strikes us as a clear instance of betrayal, that intuitive seeming is not itself an act of concept application. It is the pre-judgmental apprehension that makes the resulting judgment (the resulting application of the concept of betrayal) reasonable. In this sense, intuition does not compete with concept application. It enables it.

This same phenomenon of intuitive apprehension preceding judgment also shows up in ordinary perception. When we open our eyes, the world does not appear as a mosaic of colours and shapes. It appears as a scene populated with meaningful objects: a child reaching for a toy, a cat waiting expectantly for dinner, a car approaching too fast. As P F Strawson observed, if we try to describe what we see using only low-level sensory terms (patches of colour, shifting brightness), we falsify the experience. The world comes to us in perception already organised by concepts. What is presented is not bare visual data but things of certain kinds, situated in relations to one another.

And here, intuition enters even into everyday perceptual experience itself. Perception reveals not merely visual arrays but robust, three-dimensional situations that are concept-laden. This becomes particularly vivid in cases where expertise comes into play. Imagine walking through a field with a trained herpetologist. You both see a snake. Your sensory experience may be phenomenologically indistinguishable from hers – the same curves of the body, the same mottled pattern. Yet what is presented to each of you differs. To you, it is simply a snake. To her, it is an Agkistrodon contortrix. The difference is not in your visual apparatus per se but in the concepts at work within perception. Her grasp of the relevant distinctions generates a conceptually richer, even if phenomenologically identical, presentational state. And because intuitions are not phenomenologically robust, there is no need for any difference in how things look. This is why perceptual expertise can subtly transform experience without altering its sensory character.

Perception, then, is a perfect illustration of the broader point about intuitions. Because they lack any robust phenomenology, intuitions serve their function in plain view without our taking explicit notice of them.

The person who declines to get in the stranger’s car, or who flags the email as a phishing attempt, or who walks away from the deal – these individuals are not acting irrationally or on mere feeling. They are responding to a genuine presentational state: something is showing up as creepy, fraudulent or wrong. The situation is presenting itself as having a certain character, and that presentation carries epistemic weight – not because it is infallible, but because it is the same kind of state that grounds all of our most basic cognitive contact with the world.

This is precisely what philosophers mean when they talk about intuition. The difference between the person on the bridge who immediately senses that pushing the bystander is wrong, and the person who declines to get into a stranger’s car, is not a difference in kind. It is a difference in context and control. The philosopher’s thought experiment is a deliberately engineered situation designed to isolate and interrogate a single intuitive response. The everyday case is messier, embedded in a richer context, and rarely examined. But the underlying capacity, the presentational apprehension of how things are, is the same.

What has been missing in our theorising, until now, is simply the explicit recognition of this continuity. Philosophers have a well-developed account of why rational intuitions carry epistemic weight. They have been slower to claim that this account extends naturally to the intuitions we act on every day. Once we see this, ‘vibes’ and gut feelings are neither vindicated wholesale nor dismissed as mere noise. Instead, they are brought into the same framework that governs our most careful reasoning. The task of philosophy, then, is not to decide whether to trust intuition. It is to understand the role it already plays, from the thought experiment to the uneasy feeling about a stranger, in almost every act of understanding.

items.title: You Can See Everything: A Reckoning for the Post-Truth Age
items.description: Explosively funny and haunting in equal measure, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s doc on disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes has resonance far beyond its central story
items.author: Alex Denney
paragraphs: Explosively funny and haunting in equal measure, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s doc on disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes has resonance far beyond its central story
Warning: Mild spoilers ahead

In the breathlessly hyped, nearly three-hour new doc on disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, Nathan Fielder begins by asking, not unreasonably: “Why me?” It’s one of many different questions we may never get answers to from You Can See Everything, which begins with Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, taking the extraordinary step of inviting Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim into their family home just weeks before she begins serving an 11-year federal prison term, having defrauded investors in a discredited blood-testing device to the tune of nearly half a billion dollars.

For anyone looking to profess their innocence, it’s a bizarre choice of director to say the least. Fielder, of course, is the mastermind behind such reality-warping shows as The Rehearsal and The Curse, and much of the buzz surrounding the film pre-release stemmed from the idea of this Kaufman-esque figure, whose inscrutable comic persona has led him down ever stranger avenues of enquiry, squaring off against a real-life master manipulator in Holmes. (Oppenheim, for his part, has made weird corners of American culture his subject matter in docs like Some Kind of Heaven and Spermworld.) But as it turns out, Fielder isn’t even the star of this show, not even close – in fact I’m not even sure he musters the bronze, behind Holmes, hubby Billy, and a third mystery guest whom many readers will probably have clocked by now.

Let’s start with Holmes, whose eyes – big, blue and unwavering – are the film’s biggest cinematic asset, filmed in close-ups that linger a beat too long, then two, to establish the film’s mood of comic disquiet. She tells a bamboozled Fielder early in the film that her preferred method of flirting is to maintain unbroken eye contact, before fixing him with her stare throughout; Fielder confesses that the effect is like seeing a magician, where you know you’re being duped on some level but you enjoy it all the same. Increasingly, he becomes troubled by the notion that Holmes may, in fact, be telling the truth, albeit a truth that exists only in her own mind.

Onwards, then, to Billy, who emerges as the film’s biggest villain. Comically evasive where Holmes is painfully earnest, he tells a long, excruciating anecdote about how he met and fell for his wife – this was after the fraud allegations came to light, as Fielder incredulously notes. (The film follows this with a full-frontal reveal of Evans in the shower, a hilarious moment that sheds light on the guy’s narcissism.) One of the film’s many revelations is that Holmes is trying to shore up funds for a “Theranos v2.0”, apparently undeterred by the fact that the first was exposed as a colossal fraud, and Evans is intimately involved in the enterprise.

As Holmes’s jail term looms less than halfway into the film’s 174-minute runtime, a question arises as to what the payoff to all of this will be. But the filmmakers devise a stunning final act that we won’t reveal here, except to say that it’s incredibly strange and meta in a way that’s sure to delight longtime fans of Fielder. This extended coda begins two years into Holmes’s sentence, with Billy, now living in a house with large reptiles roaming freely about the place, using his wife’s image to make AI videos of her online, seemingly without Holmes’s permission.

Even as the revelations pile up, there’s a nagging sense that Fielder and Oppenheim seem content to stay lost in the complex webs of deceit surrounding this story. A revelation of sexual abuse midway through goes mostly unexamined, and Fielder employs a few comic ruses that feel more queasy than instructive. A lot rides on a moment of semantic confusion – did she say “it” or “something”? – that echoes an earlier moment in the film, and could potentially upend Holmes’s stated reasons for wanting to tell her story. Fielder’s unique brand of comedy lives in moments like these, but I left the scene wondering how much it had been played up in an attempt to offer narrative cohesion, a trick any writer drawing on “real life” will know all too well from experience.

In the end, though, You Can See Everything’s shortcomings as a documentary matter less than its extraordinary potency as a parable for the post-truth age. It’s a film that speaks with eerie eloquence to a culture gripped by the sinking feeling it is continually being lied to, from the insidious creep of AI to politicians bought and paid for by corporate lobbyists. That feeling can appear bleak or terrifying, or even absurdly funny. But what if we get a strange kind of kick out of the not-knowing, too?

items.title: In Echo Park, the spirit of Barragán informs this colourful new co-living space
items.description: Is communal living the solution to the high price of urban housing, or is it just another way for landlords to get more for their outlay? Whatever the answer, architects and designers are looking for new models of housing production, both to counter the high p
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Is communal living the solution to the high price of urban housing, or is it just another way for landlords to get more for their outlay? Whatever the answer, architects and designers are looking for new models of housing production, both to counter the high price of construction and land and to cater for the in-house facilities that act as lures to potential tenants.

The latter is one of the driving forces behind this new Co-Living building in Los Angeles’ Echo Park, designed by WTARCH. With brightly coloured façades and complex floorplans that accommodate a total 26 individual co-living rooms, the new building is set across four storeys.

Those 26 rooms are grouped in clusters, usually of four rooms, arranged around a full kitchen and shared living space. Each room also has its own bathroom and kitchenette, making them akin to studio apartments or studio residences.

The palette is the first thing that strikes the visitor. Pink, coral and orange certainly make a bold impression, with the architects citing the work of both Luis Barragán and Ricardo Legorreta as influences, as well as the general vibe of Echo Park, with its bold shopfronts. Colour modulates the entire structure, from the façade to the communal spaces, with texture and different materials also used to create screens and shades.

The main entrance is on a residential street and has a domestic scale, with brightly coloured planters featuring local vegetation, as well as prominently screened entrance staircase. The sloping site allows the bulk of the building to be concealed, stepping down the hillside to reach its full four-storey height, with views to downtown and Echo Park Lake.

Vertical screens are found throughout the building, not only referencing LA’s rich heritage of mid-century architecture but serving a functional purpose as a way of bringing cross-ventilation and light into the structure, as well as creating dramatic shadows. The curve of the car park ramp is another element that has been brought into the architectural vocabulary. Even the exposed fire-sprinkler pipes are painted in vivid pink.

Inside, the studio apartments are varied and distinct, never falling below the 120 square feet minimum mandated by local building codes. On the upper floor, the pitch of the roof provides a loft sleeping space for some of the rooms. The colour is toned down in the rooms, with polished concrete floors and white oak cabinetry and Caesarstone countertops are used to create a neutral but contemporary feeling series of spaces.

Interior of one of the upper level apartments with loft sleeping space

The building benefits from a number of communal amenities, including a gym and outdoor barbecue space, while the amenities of the park and nearby Sunset Boulevard are easily reached on foot. Other sustainable features include rainwater harvesting.

Warren Techentin featured in our 2011 Architects Directory exhibition in London, and works extensively in and around Los Angeles, working on everything from single family houses to commercial spaces and apartment buildings, such as the nearby Elysian Fields Apartments.

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: Rimowa teams up with Maison Margiela on a ‘lived-in’ luggage set
items.description: In 1988, Martin Margiela and Jenny Meirens – the co-founder of his eponymous ‘Maison’ – painted their entire studio white, all the way down to the furniture, some of which was also draped in white cotton. It was largely a financial decision, a way to introduce
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: In 1988, Martin Margiela and Jenny Meirens – the co-founder of his eponymous ‘Maison’ – painted their entire studio white, all the way down to the furniture, some of which was also draped in white cotton. It was largely a financial decision, a way to introduce cohesion to the mish-mash of vintage furnishings they had purchased in markets and second-hand stores. Mannequins were also painted white, and the pair enjoyed how eventually the various objects would patina through time – the paint scuffed or peeled away, revealing traces of what they once were.

It would lead to ‘bianchetto’ (‘whitewashing’), a technique that saw pieces from the house’s collections hand-painted white, ‘designed to naturally crack and fade over time, gradually revealing visible signs of use’. One of Margiela’s foundational codes – along with anonymity, deconstruction and the Tabi shoe – it is perhaps best known for adorning the last, a boot version of traditional Japanese split-toe tabi footwear. Indeed, ‘bianchetto’ was first introduced in 1989, adorning an early version of the Tabi boot.
Paint it white: Rimowa x Maison Margiela

Now, ‘bianchetto’ is central to a new collaboration between Maison Margiela – currently helmed by Belgian designer Glenn Martens – and German luggage house Rimowa, seeing the latter’s signature ridged ‘Classic Cabin’ suitcase daubed with white paint. The technique is also applied to a version of Maison Margiela’s 5AC XL bag, here recrafted with grooves in cleverly sculpted leather, echoing those found on Rimowa suitcases, which were originally inspired by airplane fuselages.

The collaboration, say the two brands, is built on the idea of the ‘lived in’ – something which both Rimowa and Maison Margiela incorporate in their work. Rimowa, despite the technical perfection of its luggage when it comes off the production line, has long embraced the way that its signature aluminium cases – which come in an ever-growing array of hues – dent and scuff with wear, seeing such marks as mementos of travel (the brand has also encouraged the adornment of their suitcases with stickers and tags). Maison Margiela uses the ‘bianchetto’ technique for this same reason, while its garments often feature torn-away layers to reveal the construction and linings beneath.

As such, the new take on the Classic Cabin suitcase also features a white interior with visible stitches and interlocked edges, making it appear ‘inside out’. Its traditional logo plaque is also finished with four white stitches, a nod to Maison Margiela’s signature branding, whereby the subtle stitches are used in lieu of traditional logos or monograms. The 5AC XL bag, which is constructed to appear as if the interior lining is being pulled out from the bag’s ‘opening’, features removable leather loops that allow it to be slipped over Classic Cabin’s telescopic handles.

A playful accompanying campaign film, conceived by Dexter Lander, sees the luggage set appear in a traditional Haussmannian apartment in Paris, the home city of Maison Margiela. A sprinkler of white paint gradually coats the luggage set and apartment, leaving behind an imprint of the bag and suitcase’s signature silhouettes on the apartment’s walls.

Jack Moss is the Fashion & Beauty Features Director at Wallpaper*, having joined the team in 2022 as Fashion Features Editor. Previously the digital features editor at AnOther and digital editor at 10 Magazine, he has also contributed to numerous international publications and featured in ‘Dazed: 32 Years Confused: The Covers’, published by Rizzoli. He is particularly interested in the moments when fashion intersects with other creative disciplines – notably art and design – as well as championing a new generation of international talent and reporting from international fashion weeks. Across his career, he has interviewed the fashion industry’s leading figures, including Rick Owens, Pieter Mulier, Jonathan Anderson, Grace Wales Bonner, Christian Lacroix, Kate Moss and Manolo Blahnik.

items.title: The cinematic universe of María Zardoya - A Rabbit's Foot
items.description: With albums such as Hable con Ella and Cinema, The Marias frontwoman María Zardoya has established herself as one of LA’s most visionary musicians, finally earning her accolades with a Grammy nomination for The Marías early this year. But there’s no time to re
items.author: Kitty Grady
paragraphs: With albums such as Hable con Ella and Cinema, The Marias frontwoman María Zardoya has established herself as one of LA’s most visionary musicians, finally earning her accolades with a Grammy nomination for The Marías early this year. But there’s no time to rest on her laurels. The show must go on, she tells Chris Cotonou, even if it means creating in subversive new ways.

María Zardoya came to Los Angeles by accident. That’s what the frontwoman for the supercool Grammy-nominated band The Marías tells me: that she headed out West after earning some money from a Halloween contest and on the behest of a friend.

Serendipitous accident: Since forming The Marías in 2016 with Josh Conway, Jesse Perlman, and Edward James, Zardoya has become one of the most alluring singers of her generation, crooning meaningful, dreamy indie ballads in both English and in Spanish (she was born, after all, in Puerto Rico).

Ten years later, the band is one of the groups that most defines modern America—with millions of fans the world over. When I met Zardoya, a week after her Grammy performance, and following our striking photoshoot—which you can discover in these pages—it’s evident that so much of her success is because of her charisma and vision as a performer; but also as an obsessive “builder of worlds,” she explains. Everything is still rooted in a universe Zardoya and her bandmates created for themselves ten years ago; irrespective of all of the fame.

Their album Cinema (2021) should have given away just how much the movies inspire The Marías’ world. But even more recently, with nods to Three Colours: Blue (1993) on the cover of Submarine (2024) and hints at Pedro Almodóvar in song titles. What I especially like about Zardoya is her vision: every album, every show, is a chance to experiment with references and ideas, and like many of the best artists, she moves on to new ideas without much issue. Her solo project Not For Radio (2025) went on tour in January and paid homage to the Swan Lake, in part because her audience may never have had the chance to see the ballet. So why not at her show?

It’s a mission for true, real, high-culture art that makes everything Zardoya does so engaging. The following is a conversation that spanned her roots, bilingual music, Almodóvar, Bad Bunny, and California.
A Rabbit’s Foot: As a Puerto Rican and someone who’s been playing with bilingual music for a long time, what did you make of Bad Bunny’s recent performance at the Super Bowl?
María Zardoya: It felt, more than anything, like a celebration of the culture. My best friend is Puerto Rican and she was texting me, “I’m in tears. This feels like a love letter to Puerto Rico.”

Seeing him on that massive stage, especially with all the political turmoil around him being the performer, was really powerful. There were so many little references to Puerto Rican culture. Representation is extremely important in the media, and he represented Puerto Rico beautifully—also the wider Latin community with that nod at the end to all the Latin American countries. I’m really proud to know him, to collaborate with him, and to be from the little island of Puerto Rico.
ARF: How has the music industry changed around bilingual music since you started, and how do you see your place in that?

MZ: The landscape has definitely expanded. You can thank artists like Bad Bunny for bringing those sounds and that language to the mainstream. For me, it was never a strategy. I grew up bilingual and bicultural, speaking both languages and listening to music in both. The first song I wrote was in Spanish, the second in English, then another in Spanish, then English, then mixed—it was just natural.

What I discovered was how many people in the US shared that bicultural experience and gravitated toward it. A big moment was a festival in Jakarta, where people were singing every word in English and Spanish—even though Spanish isn’t their language. That really showed me music can transcend language.
ARF: You left Georgia for California at a very young age. Why California instead of, say, New York?
MZ: Honestly, one friend. She was also from Georgia, had moved to California to pursue music, and kept calling me saying, “If you want to do music, you need to be here.”

I was saving money, figuring out where I’d live. Then she called: one of her roommates had moved out. Around then I won a Halloween costume contest at the agency I worked at—five grand—so I thought, “Okay, I can do this.” I bought a car and drove to California knowing only her. That was it.
ARF: Did California—and especially Los Angeles—shape the music you made with The Marías?

MZ: I think so. All the guys in the band are born and raised in California. When I started writing with Josh [Conway], he had this psych-rock, California vibe. Our music became this mesh of his California upbringing and my bicultural, bilingual, small-town upbringing. It just worked.
ARF: Your music feels very cinematic. What film or visual references feed into your work?
MZ: Early on I was extremely inspired by Pedro Almodóvar. He’s one of my all-time favourite directors. My dad is from Spain, so I grew up watching his films.

When we were discovering our visual identity, I watched a lot of his movies and took notes on his use of colour, especially red. If you look at our early visuals and videos, there’s always a pop of red, and that carried into the EPs and our first album, Cinema (2021). I even named two songs after Hable con ella (2002)—“Hable Con Ella” and “Talk to Her.” Later, for Submarine (2024), I was inspired by [Krzysztof] Kieślowski’s Three Colours trilogy (1993–94). He did an ode to the French flag; I wanted to do something similar for the Puerto Rican flag. So the second album is blue—Submarine—and now people are expecting the next to be white. Film is a huge part of how I think about albums and visuals.
ARF: How do you separate ideas between The Marías and your solo project, Not for Radio?

MZ: The challenge is keeping things distinct, because I spearhead the visuals for both. With The Marías, I’m also considering the guys—they have this 90s, edgy, Thom Yorke/Radiohead-inspired thing. With Not for Radio the solo project is very inspired by nature and the underworld. It’s a “green” album. For the next Marías project, the “white” one, I’m thinking more Three Colours: White (1994), Trainspotting (1996), 90s freshness. I literally see the guys as Ewan McGregor in Trainspotting—playful and edgy. So The Marías lean more into that energy; Not for Radio is more romantic and connected to nature.
ARF: You speak about albums like films—with colour, character, and arcs. Do you see them as one big story?

MZ: Yeah. From Superclean (2017) and Cinema—the red, romantic period when Josh and I were in a relationship—to Submarine, blue, which symbolises solitude and the breakup. Not for Radio is green, a rebirth for me individually, like a seed being watered and growing into myself. The next “white” album feels like a rediscovery of who we are as a band after that rupture—coming up from underwater and seeing the light. So it’s all one story, but I also get obsessively lost in each album’s visual world while I’m making it.
I was inspired by [Krzysztof] Kieślowski’s Three Colours trilogy (1993–94). He did an ode to the French flag; I wanted to do something similar for the Puerto Rican flag.
ARF: As the band has become more visible, has your willingness to be vulnerable in your lyrics changed?

MZ: I definitely have moments of, “Did I say too much?” But those thoughts come after the song is written. The way I write is very subconscious, like free-writing or journaling, so what comes out is honest. Before releasing Not for Radio, I texted my manager, freaking out, like, “I think I was too honest—people are going to speculate.” She told me, “If you’re living in your integrity and being as honest as you can, that’s what matters.” People will make up their own stories anyway. That really grounded me.
ARF: You’ve mentioned being obsessive. What are you most particular about in the studio?

MZ: Everything. I obsess over a drum sound, the tone of a synth, tiny details in the mix. Mixing is when my brain really loops, because it feels like the last chance to get it right. I’ll suddenly hear some high-pitched thing in the snare and can’t unhear it.
But I’m learning to let go. The solo project helped because it came together so fast I didn’t have time to obsess over every detail. I just had to follow the energy.
ARF: Do you have ways of leaving one project behind and moving into the next?
MZ: Being completely in the moment helps. That’s something I always encourage fans to do at shows—lose themselves in that moment.

On the Not for Radio tour, with the Swan Lake (1875–76) references, I started the show as this delicate swan, then, after the “death” of the white swan, leaned in to the grittier, darker black-swan energy. Women are conditioned to always be beautiful and delicate, but there’s a darkness and “ugliness” I wanted to show.
To move on, I leave that version of me in that moment. Now I’m in a different one. The past is what it is; the future isn’t here yet.
ARF: It feels like the more visible you get, the more you push against mainstream norms. Is that deliberate?

MZ: Yeah. As The Marías got bigger and reached a more mainstream audience—partly through things like TikTok—there was a part of me that didn’t want to go further into that; I wanted to go more inward and against the grain.

I wanted to make songs over four minutes, without obvious internet hooks; shows that weren’t just about screaming along to big drops. I wanted to invite people to put on headphones, sit under a tree, and really listen.

Calling the project Not for Radio gave me the confidence to be unconventional—to do a more theatrical production, with people sitting down, and to bring them into a different kind of world. I’m grateful the team saw that vision.
ARF: Where did this love of cinema start?

MZ: At home. My dad went to the store and asked for the biggest TV they had. This was pre-flatscreen, so we ended up with this giant 88-inch tube TV and surround sound in the living room, just for watching movies.

Whenever guests came over, he’d play Twister (1996) to show off the rumble. That family movie time really started it. The first film that really shook me was Alfonso Cuarón’s A Little Princess (1995). I watched it over and over. I spoke to him a few months ago about it.
I studied film in high school and college, and when I chose music, it felt like the perfect bridge: I could be a filmmaker through our videos and visuals.
ARF: It’s a bit of a random question. But I’m curious. If you could spend an evening with three people from cinema, dead or alive, who would they be?
MZ: Pedro Almodóvar, Guillermo del Toro, and Alfonso Cuarón. Having all three of them in the same room, sitting by a fire, asking each other questions—that would be the dream.
ARF: Would you ever want to direct a film yourself?

MZ: Maybe one day. I love putting worlds together visually. A couple of years ago I went down a Sofia Coppola rabbit hole after watching Marie Antoinette (2006) for the first time. I was like, “I want to make a movie like this.”

She captures femininity and the female perspective in such a beautiful way. I watched all her films, bought her book, and just flipped through the images, totally inspired. So maybe after my next Sofia Coppola rabbit hole, I’ll finally make a movie.
ARF: And your favourite Guillermo del Toro? Say Pan’s Labyrinth (2006)…
Pan’s Labyrinth, for sure. And The Shape of Water (2017)—I’ve seen that so many times. It’s so, so good.

items.title: NOWNESS - Tove Jansson and The Hobbit
items.description: As the curious creator of the Moomins, Finland-Swedish author and illustrator Tove Jansson imagined fantastical characters and folkloric worlds that found a sense of wonder in the natural landscapes that informed her early experiences. Shaped by childhood summ
paragraphs: As the curious creator of the Moomins, Finland-Swedish author and illustrator Tove Jansson imagined fantastical characters and folkloric worlds that found a sense of wonder in the natural landscapes that informed her early experiences. Shaped by childhood summers spent in the Pellinki archipelago and the shadows of World War II, her beloved Moomin stories presented escapism and adventure, while holding a psychological mirror to the political context of the era, as Moominvalley’s inhabitants overcome looming threats and unexpected events.

Channeling her lifelong fascination with horror, wilderness and catastrophe, Jansson was commissioned to illustrate the first Swedish-language edition of The Hobbit in 1960, reinterpreting J.R.R. Tolkien’s lonely mountains, strange creatures and dark landscapes. While underappreciated at the time of release, Jansson’s expressive and unconventional drawings are revisited for a new edition marking The Hobbit’s 90th anniversary, inviting the next generation to connect with her whimsical, distinctly Nordic portrayal of Middle Earth.

For the short documentary Tove Jansson and The Hobbit, created in partnership with Moomin Characters, director Stella Scott explores the life and work of Tove Jansson, and the lasting legacy of a rare commission that unites two celebrated storytellers. Between archival fragments and self-shot footage captured on 35mm film, Scott reflects on how one artist interpreted another’s imaginary world – and why Jansson’s distinctive vision took decades to be fully appreciated.

items.title: Sit On This: Max Lamb's Museum-Worthy Chairs
items.description: Sit On This: Max Lamb's Museum-Worthy Chairs
items.author: Alice Morby
paragraphs: Sit On This: Max Lamb's Museum-Worthy Chairs
Sit On This: Max Lamb’s Museum-Worthy Chairs
Two decades into a career spent avoiding the noise, “maker-designer” Max Lamb opens up his London home and workshop to explain why the work has always done the talking.

Long before he learned how to be a designer, Max Lamb learned how to be alone. Not in the brooding, lone-wolf way, but in the sense of simply figuring out how to get things done without needing help. The British designer — or “maker-designer,” as we’ll later agree is a more accurate label — has built a career on that same instinct.

Two decades in, you can pick a Max Lamb out of a room without checking the label—forms that look excavated rather than manufactured, their surfaces still carrying the marks of whatever tool, or beach, shaped them. The material is always left legible, whether that’s the imperfect facets of carved polystyrene or granite in various states of process. His furniture sits in museum collections and galleries around the world, and yet, he has arrived there without many of the things that now feel like prerequisites for a successful creative career.

Lamb has always been more interested in making things than talking about them, and he’s never seen much reason to pretend otherwise. The workshop is only a few strides from where we’re sitting, and an afternoon spent there makes Lamb’s case better than he does. Assistants move among benches. Wooden furniture destined for a new Acne store in New York is being packed up. He keeps slipping out of the conversation to answer questions from the floor, and each time he comes back he’s a little further from us. “I’m getting agitated,” he says with a laugh, an hour or so in. “Talking isn’t what I do. Working is what I do.”

Lamb’s home and studio occupy a 19th-century building in Northwest London. The street itself is quiet. Neighbors collect offcuts for firewood. The local pub is a short walk away, and the route to the nearest train station passes through a long, overgrown field. With all of this in mind, it’s easy to project this overly analog, somewhat technophobic stereotype onto Lamb, but it’s not necessarily true. His work often takes primitive forms, yet it’s created through a combination of digital and physical processes.

The same is true of his relationship with social media. He’s become known for being “offline,” but he’s not totally opposed to it; he simply seems uninterested in performing through it. “I think we’re all increasingly self-critical because we compare ourselves,” he adds reflectively. As a child who moved around a lot, that is something he has spent a lifetime avoiding. Getting to know himself and learning to stick to his own lane, he says, became essential survival skills.

Lamb was born in 1980 and grew up moving between RAF bases as his father, a survival instructor in the Royal Air Force, was posted around the UK and Germany. By the time he finished school, he had attended five different ones, often arriving halfway through a term. “You become a bit of a chameleon,” he says. “But you also gain a huge amount of independence; I had to develop a confidence that I am who I am.”
“Even when I’m not physically in the workshop, I’m in the workshop.” – Max Lamb

Military base life also meant spending long periods entertaining himself. “My childhood was a creative childhood because I had to be creative,” he says. “I never had computer games like other kids did.”

As he describes his early years in Cornwall, the origins of his obsession with materiality become clear. He recalls digging tunnels through wet sand until his hands met beneath the surface, carving boats into beaches, and collecting slate and granite from around the china-clay pits near St. Austell. School holidays were spent on his grandfather’s farm in Yorkshire, cleaning reclaimed bricks, repairing buildings, and, eventually, making furniture from salvaged timber.

These experiences echo throughout the work that followed. His Pewter Stool from 2006 gave him an excuse to dig a mold directly into a sandy beach by hand before pouring in molten metal. The Poly Chair, also from 2006, saw him carve expanded polystyrene into something elevated and desirable. His more recent Min Chair began with the question of how to make the most out of material, resulting in a polygonal chair made from wood cut diagonally from a single slab of pine.
