Sai then fills in what Daisy doesn’t know: that on her shopping trip with Hailey last episode, she asked Hailey all the questions she had and told her that things didn’t add up. Sai did talking shit the right way. You say it behind that person’s back, and then, when you get a chance, you say it to their face. Daisy never did that. She just talked shit and only brought it up to Hailey when she wanted to incriminate someone else, namely Sai. Daisy is totally in the wrong here and is expecting everyone in the group to look bad so she could look better. Who’s going to make that bargain? It’s like intentionally looking for the goat behind door No. 3 on Let’s Make a Deal. The problem is that what Sai did was real; what Sai did was being a good friend. Daisy thinks what she did was real because she’s exposing everyone, but her ulterior motive is to make herself look better, so even her realness is fake. The more we see of Daisy, the more it seems like she wants everyone to like her, and when they don’t, she throws a temper tantrum and tries to make everyone else look worse by throwing popcorn ceiling at them.

Sai can’t spend too much time on Daisy, though, because she’s fully fighting with Carole. Devyn, doing only one thing whereas Lindsay does four, reads Carole’s Substack post about meeting an onion recently and how she didn’t like peeling back the layers. We’ve heard this already in her confessionals, and now the whole world gets to hear it, even though they don’t know it’s about Sai. I get where Carole is coming from, and I agree that when Sai questioned Carole on the Epstein files, she was much more accusatory than “just asking questions,” as she said she was. She was talking to Carole like she had already committed a crime, and if I were Carole, that would make me have my guard up with Sai. But writing a whole Substack about it? I don’t know. Is that overkill? It’s sure adding a lot to the show, which I clearly love.

I also like that Sai brings it up and shows that she’s not afraid of Carole and is going to make her confront these things in the group. Everyone here is doing their job, and everyone is a little bit right and a little bit wrong, which is a great place for Housewives to be. Sai does take it back to a dark place, though, when she asks, “Did you write it or was it ChatGPT?” Oh no. Not Hashtag Bookgate all over again. I thought we fully exorcised the ghost of Carole’s ghostwriter; we don’t need it coming back to haunt us again. It is a great bit when Carole then analyzes Sai’s own Substack to show that it’s 85 percent written by AI. That’s where it’s all going, all of us, all of this. We’re all going to lose our jobs to the robots eventually, whether we like it or not. But maybe not the Housewives. AI couldn’t act as irrationally as Daisy, trying to say she’s trying to help Sai’s relationships with the women while also trying to dismantle them. It couldn’t compose a toast as awkward as Pavit’s, a Substack as metaphoric as Carole’s, a joke as bad as Erika’s, a dress as terrible as Sai’s with the metallic spoiler across the boobs, a personality as nice-nasty as Erin’s, and certainly not a mystery wrapped in plastic surgery and hair dye like Daisy’s. She’s confounding, and just like when we look at her, any AI analyzing Daisy, or any of the women, really, would be met with a fervent “Does not compute. Does not compute.”

items.title: Below Deck Recap: Power Hungry
items.description: Well, the good news is that Moe isn’t quitting. After some encouragement from his co-workers and a strong charter performance to redeem his last, he feels more like himself again. His daughter’s screech of excitement when he tells her they’re going on a trip t
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Well, the good news is that Moe isn’t quitting. After some encouragement from his co-workers and a strong charter performance to redeem his last, he feels more like himself again. His daughter’s screech of excitement when he tells her they’re going on a trip to Tokyo is another incentive for him to see the season through. The bad news is that Matt got what he wanted — by the end of this week’s episode, Kerry has promoted him to bosun and demoted Alex to lead deckhand. And if the preview at the end of the episode is any indication, Matt’s new position of power will embolden him to terrorize the boat even more than he already is.

On the morning of the second day of the charter, Matt wakes up in a combative attitude, contradicting every instruction given to him by the bosun. In the aftermath of their conversation about Matt’s ugly behavior on the crew night out, Matt’s negativity gets worse. Finding himself alone with the captain in the crew mess, Matt doesn’t miss the opportunity to say that “some people” on deck are “getting complacent.” Yet Matt himself whines about his tasks all day long. His feet hurt, he’s tired, he’s hungry. It’s true that Alex has relied too heavily on Matt, but I also see how, by deliberately not pulling his weight, Matt is aiming to illustrate his point about the team’s dysfunction. As usual with Matt, his reasons are not entirely wrong, but his methods are horrible.

Besides, it’s not like Kerry is blind to Matt’s efforts. In a confessional, he says that he thinks Matt would make a more assertive leader, but would his brashness lead to efficiency or simply more drama? Kerry, I think you know the answer to that question. Unfortunately, though, rooting for Alex is as emotionally taxing as rooting for the Red Sox. You want them to win so bad. You are confident they have it in them — they used to be great, the best, even! But they just keep breaking your heart. In the evening, Alex asks James and Matt to put some of the inflatables away, but leave the Jet Ski out. Matt knows that’s a bad call — anyone who has seen even just one episode of this franchise knows it’s a bad call to leave the Jet Ski out — but, because he wants to see Alex hang himself with his own rope, he doesn’t say anything; to James, he explains that he doesn’t want to “deal with” it.

Kerry catches up with James and Matt later, while the guests are enjoying a kind of random fireworks display. He is surprised to see them still in their blues. Matt explains they were putting away the inflatables and that Alex instructed them to leave the Jet Ski out. Annoyed, Kerry tells them that the inverse should have been done: They should have left out the inflatables, in case the guests wanted to use them before leaving, and bring in the Jet Ski, which could be stolen or sink in the night. Matt stomps over to Alex and Sen to relay the directions, and takes the opportunity to point out that the Jet Ski hasn’t been flushed. He continues to huff and puff all night, complaining about picking up Alex’s slack. Switching anchor watch shifts with James, he notes that James should have a list of nighttime tasks, and in the morning, he finds that the laz is too messy.

It’s finally too much for Matt. He goes straight to Kerry to air his frustrations, saying that he’s always cleaning up after a messy boat, and that Alex “rolls out of bed” in the morning and doesn’t brush his teeth. Um, okay. Kerry promises to “investigate,” though there doesn’t seem to be much to find out. As Sen tells Rainbeau, the vibes on deck are off (which is the reason why she and Alex keep their flirtationship limited to nights out). A chaotic docking later that afternoon is the last straw for the captain. So far, Alex’s competent dockings have made up for his lackluster charter performances, but heading into a marina busy with jellyfish-harvesting boats and a strong tide, he fumbles. The hooks set aside for the fenders are the wrong size, which Kaylee and Rosa — enlisted to help with the fenders — find out as they need to secure them. Sen scrambles to find the right ones, running past Kerry’s wingstation while he’s docking and creating confusion and distraction. Sen and James radio for help, but Alex looks on and lets them figure it out. His passivity aggravates Kerry.

They manage to dock the boat without further complications, but Kerry concludes that “this program is not supporting Alex’s style” in a generous assessment of the “It’s not you, it’s me” variety. After the tip meeting, he calls Alex to the wheelhouse and says he has “lost faith in [him]” as a bosun, but still wants him to be part of the team. So, he effects the swap: Alex will now be lead deckhand, and Matt will rise to bosun. Matt is ecstatic that his plan worked, but Kerry warns him to keep his ego in check. This pointless instruction reminded me of those Instagram videos when a parent puts a bowl of candy in front of a kid, tells them not to touch it, and leaves the room to see if the kid obeys. Of course Matt is going to reach into the bowl, eat all the candy, and blame his sibling for it. This switcheroo reeks of production interference to me. I don’t know how common this kind of maneuver is in the yachting industry, but it seems toxic to demote someone, promote his rival, and then let them have it out for the rest of the season. It’s a drama machine!

Production must be happy, because the interior department is also starting to come apart at the seams, not that Fraser seems very concerned. I’m worried about Rainbeau. Her fake English accent, Elizabeth Holmes–style staring and nodding, and soft whispering tone are pointing to something more serious than just acting for the camera going on. Last season, her first in the franchise, Rainbeau was automatically sympathetic: She was a hard worker and a good team player going up against Solène, a slacker with a mean streak. Now, as part of a team of capable stews, she seems to be at a loss as to how to find her place in the cast, and she is alienating herself from the other girls. As promised, Fraser sends Rainbeau to do the beach picnic with Kaylee on the second day of the charter. Under Rainbeau’s iron fist, they manage well (although, again, they set up the picnic table facing the ocean with the guests sitting next to each other, an awkward dining arrangement that really bothers me), and Rainbeau only snaps at Kaylee once.

Kaylee is usually positive, but Rainbeau’s uptight nature is starting to wear on her. She shares with Rosa that Rainbeau was short with her on the beach, and the next morning, when Rainbeau asks her to take the guests’ coffee orders in front of Fraser, Kaylee — who had already taken the orders — thinks Rainbeau is trying to make her look bad. Rosa, who has never liked Rainbeau, doesn’t appreciate Rainbeau’s tone when she tells her not to unpack the beach picnic bag. (“This is my bar stuff.”) To make matters worse, as they’re setting the decorations for the final night’s “celebration of love” theme, Rainbeau rhymes “violets are blue” with “Rosa is the third stew” and allegedly doesn’t get why Rosa doesn’t like the ditty. Rainbeau vents to her boyfriend on FaceTime that the other girls think she’s trying to “steal their men.” Her boyfriend isn’t worried and tells her to focus on work, which is not bad advice. But if the girls are peeved that Rainbeau is too flirty with the deckies, they are also responding to the fact that she seems closed off to exchange and friendship.

Even Madison and Paris, the bratty teens onboard, think Rainbeau hates them. Madison and Paris wreak havoc this week — I loved every second of it. First, they can’t decide whether or not they want to go to the beach picnic. Every time they’re about to decide, one of them goes wait wait wait and brings them back to square one. Just as Fraser is about to lose his mind, they decide to go because James is going. In a confessional, James says that the girls are not his “cup of tea” because they are “in different generations,” and he will “keep [his] head down” and “be a good boy,” which is a weird way of saying, “They are teenagers.” The girls love flirting with the deckhands, though, and later Matt says to Kaylee that if it seems “weird” that the girls are all over him, he’s also “just doing [his] job.” Again, weird way to say, “They are teenagers.” At least Kaylee doesn’t kid herself that Matt isn’t loving the attention.

At dinner, Madison and Paris want chicken instead of fish, though their preference sheets didn’t specify that they don’t like fish. Moe worries that the rest of the entrees will get cold while he whips up the chicken, but he manages to send everything out warm (Kerry, who is sitting with the guests, reassures him later). But even after the chicken, the girls are still hungry. They push each other to ask Rainbeau for more food until one of them finally asks for more “mashed potato” (they’re actually eating mashed parsnips). Rainbeau tells them that their giggling is making her “confused.” At this moment, she is like an alien who has never seen a teenager before. It’s painful to watch — it would be so easy to connect with the girls by offering to ask the chef to throw some chicken nuggets in the oven. And Moe gets it — he has a teenager; he knows how they are. He sends up additional bowls of risotto and mash, and the girls settle down.

The guests leave happy with their experience — they tip $35,444, which comes out to $2,954 each — and at no point do they complain about the food. Moe starts off the charter worried that he isn’t “good enough,” so it’s a huge boost to perform so well. Throughout, Fraser checks in on the chef. He asks Moe to say something right away if he feels like he’ll quit, because he doesn’t want to be left in a chef-less position; but he also emphasizes that he wants Moe to stay. In time, Moe gets his Moe-Jo back, and on the final day of the charter, he wakes up feeling rested and refreshed and makes heart-shaped pancakes for breakfast. Thank God.

Speaking of hearts: Reason, or at least some semblance of it, seems to have dawned in the interior department. Kaylee tells Rosa that though she likes Matt, she can sense that she should protect herself, so she plans to keep a wall up. Rosa, for her part, gives a masterclass in self-respect rarely seen in this franchise. James pulls her aside to clarify that he wants to “keep it chilled” and not go any deeper than “one night of fun,” so she says okay and moves on. She knows her worth, and she won’t let this ruin her life, or even her day. Later, she says that she’s hoping to save up her tip money for a house, so she can secure some stability for herself. If every woman on Below Deck had this much healthy self-esteem, we would never have to deal with the likes of Matt. For his part, James seems to have an eye on Fraser — they’ve been quite flirty lately.

That’s it for this week’s episode, but I’d be remiss not to mention the news that João Franco has been arrested in Turkey for being involved in a bar fight that left a teenager dead. That’s two arrests for assault in the Below Deck universe just in the past few months. It’s about time Bravo started rethinking its casting process.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Potomac Recap: Water Under the Bridge
items.description: In a recent Substack essay, reality TV commentator Kate Casey laments the Housewives universe’s gradual shift from an intimate, often surprisingly illuminating portrait of women’s lives to an elaborate workplace drama where cast members spend more time negotia
items.author: Shamira Ibrahim
paragraphs: In a recent Substack essay, reality TV commentator Kate Casey laments the Housewives universe’s gradual shift from an intimate, often surprisingly illuminating portrait of women’s lives to an elaborate workplace drama where cast members spend more time negotiating filming rules than revealing anything substantive about themselves. While the early seasons gave us women whose complicated lives and stories provided the context for their conflicts, today, we’re often introduced to new Housewives through grievances that require an encyclopedic knowledge of the Bravo universe to understand. Potomac certainly met that argument this week, as Courtney learns that joining The Real Housewives of Potomac means forfeiting the right to decide which parts of your behavior are fair game for public discussion, because not only are the cameras always watching, the women (chiefly Ashley) are always collecting evidence.

We pick up where we left off, with Ashley and Courtney enjoying a night out at a Rehoboth bar that appears to have approximately four patrons. Courtney is dancing with the enthusiasm of someone headlining a sold-out nightclub, occasionally sneaking tequila shots as though she’s a teenager trying to evade the chaperones at prom. Given that she’s spent the season emphasizing her religious calling and carefully maintained public image, I’m beginning to wonder whether Courtney understands how reality television works or genuinely believes the cameras stop recording whenever she finds their presence inconvenient.

The next morning, Chanel Ayan makes her obligatory appearance as the international gossip correspondent of the Housewives Cinematic Universe. Listen — I’ve had the good fortune of witnessing Ayan’s social prowess firsthand during an afternoon at the Baccarat Hotel, and her particular brand of East African auntie interrogation remains unmatched. But Ayan’s real contribution isn’t her nosiness about Karen’s alcoholism; it’s the revelation that Wendy’s Glamour Bulgaria cover may have been a paid placement.

For anyone unfamiliar with the more obscure corners of international fashion publishing, certain foreign editions and magazine-adjacent platforms have developed reputations for offering promotional covers or editorial packages for a fee (Harper’s Vietnam is notorious for this, for example). It’s an open secret in some publicity circles, although the details vary considerably by publication, and Gizelle wastes no time declaring that Wendy should be avoiding any no-glitz glam in preparation for their trial. Usually, Wendy evades being held to the fire for these shameless stunts of self-promotion — but with Chanel offering the explanation from the fashion world and Monique revealing that she received a similar promotional offer in 2025 for $10,000, it’s clear that the women are ready to chip away at Wendy’s air of superiority by revealing that she resorts to the same tactics as everyone else.

While Wendy is reaching into her savings to get a Queen’s treatment in Bulgaria, Stacey is in New York enjoying her Vulture Masterminds cover shoot, an accomplishment that seems to have left several of the women more irritated than this weekend’s delays at JFK. The contrast between Stacey’s actual editorial opportunity and Wendy’s allegedly purchased cover is too delicious for Gizelle to resist, although Stacey’s professional visibility is becoming a problem for her in its own right. But Gizelle has another investment in mind: securing Tia’s allegiance against Stacey.

For Gizelle, the issue is simple. Stacey’s growing prominence threatens her ability to dictate the group’s hierarchy, and drawing Tia back into her orbit helps consolidate her position, so she works with Ashley to use her real estate search as a pretense to bring Tia back into her web. In her plea, Gizelle insists that while she may be messy, she isn’t responsible for the bad behavior of other women’s husbands — and technically, she’s correct. But the problem is that her gossip rarely focuses on holding the men accountable. Instead, it’s the wives who are forced to endure her scrutiny, judgment, and public humiliation. Gizelle, of all people, should understand the indignity of being made to wear your husband’s scarlet letter. Yet once again, Gizelle insists that it is Stacey who maliciously exposed the allegations about Robert’s dating profiles, conveniently overlooking that the inciting fight was because Gizelle herself had discussed the situation on her podcast after promising to stop.

Despite Gizelle’s motivations being painfully obvious, Tia, astonishingly, seems willing to accept this revisionist history, even entertaining the possibility that she owes Stacey an apology for how their relationship has deteriorated. While Tia may simply be recognizing where her bread is buttered in this group, her reasoning not only defies logic to me; it really reveals where her insecurities lie in her personal dynamics: beneath the stiff upper lip and British affectations, Tia seems increasingly inclined to accept whichever interpretation of events allows her to avoid a difficult confrontation. We see it in her relationship with her mother, in her decision to postpone reckoning with the deeper problems in her marriage, and now in her willingness to adopt Gizelle’s narrative rather than examine the contradictions.

Back at the house, Wendy and Courtney are shucking oysters when Courtney offers an increasingly implausible account of her night out that was fully caught on camera. According to her, the shots she was drinking were mostly water, which is kind of like when I say the jalapeño smashburger I order once a week is for my “protein gains.”

Listen, if Courtney genuinely doesn’t want to consume alcohol, there are approximately eight thousand mocktails she could order without drawing attention to herself. Nobody is forcing her to drink tequila. What seems to be troubling her is not the alcohol itself, though, but the possibility that her behavior might complicate the image she’s attempting to maintain. There’s nothing inherently contradictory about being a minister by day and a hot girl by night, but Courtney seems unwilling to acknowledge that the two versions of herself might coexist, at least on camera.

At brunch, Ashley eventually confronts Courtney about drinking Don Julio 1942, and Courtney continues insisting that she was mostly consuming water. Nobody particularly cares that she had a few drinks, but the extreme reaction she has to acknowledging it is immediately concerning. She bursts into tears and retreats to the bathroom, where the women attempt to calm her down and offer practical advice to help her navigate confrontational scenes together. Karen and Robyn start by offering some practical advice at the lunch table: Don’t do anything in front of these women (particularly Ashley) that you aren’t prepared to discuss publicly. But Courtney seems unable to recognize the warning for what it is. (Karen, understandably exhausted by the endless equivocation about alcohol, excuses herself with Tia.)

It’s almost shocking how clueless Courtney seems to be at playing the game of Housewives, despite all of her bluster. She needs Robyn to explain to her why Stacy is still frosty with her, while she continues to insist that her exchange with Stacey over event-planning services was perfectly innocent. Robyn points out that conflicts have to be addressed on-camera if they’re ever going to be resolved. Yes, it’s an absurd principle when applied to ordinary human relationships, but a perfectly sensible one within the Bravo workplace; if you don’t have the conversation while production is rolling, it might as well not have happened. Despite having a relatively muted presence on the show so far, Courtney is already on her back foot, all over a bottle of liquor and an empty dance floor.

Back at the house, Monique attempts to offer Courtney another lesson in Housewives survival: Own what you said and did before the group has an opportunity to turn your denial into an extended prosecution. It’s sensible advice, but Courtney responds by veering into an emotional explanation about the scrutiny her family has endured in matters of faith, medicine, and spirituality (and while she declined to mention their names, I am sure the true crime detectives of Reddit will dig up her family tree by week’s end). Frustrated at the women’s reasonable questions to her distress, she starts sobbing again, seemingly overwhelmed by a combination of personal pressures, including her fertility struggles, that the rest of the cast is unaware of; the women look rightfully bewildered and alarmed but offer comfort anyway.

Courtney’s erratic behavior has become immediately exasperating for the women; at least Angel waited until the trip to Nevis to start acting out. She’s an insufferable mix of both confrontational and extraordinarily sensitive, which will always be a volatile combination in a television universe built around managing high-stress interpersonal conflict. Whether she can reconcile those impulses will determine how long she survives in Potomac, but so far, the odds are not in her favor.

The episode concludes with a beachside bonfire, where the women assemble in an absurd collection of fur coats and blankets, carefully positioning themselves to prevent their expensive hair extensions from catching fire. As the women continue to manufacture luxury under circumstances that are actively hostile to the concept, the conversation eventually turns toward Wendy’s legal troubles, as Gizelle and Tia begin floating the theory that Eddie may bear greater responsibility for the alleged financial misconduct. Wendy remains conspicuously quiet, explaining that she cannot discuss the matter while legal proceedings are ongoing; even if she wanted to be visibly frustrated by the conversation, she would have no right to after the third-degree she gave Tia and her husband.

Wendy has already discussed enough of the situation on-camera to make her sudden commitment to discretion feel rather selective. It’s an uncomfortable middle ground, allowing her to benefit from a potentially exculpatory narrative while maintaining that she cannot comment, but she appears willing to let the other women speculate about Eddie’s culpability without either endorsing or challenging their theories as Tia fans the flames on her behalf. The Real Housewives may have become a show about the mechanics of being a Housewife, but the women of Potomac are also reminding us why those mechanics exist in the first place: everybody wants to control the story.
Next week, Wendy and Eddie have their court date, and Stacey and Courtney finally confront one another over the allegations surrounding Stacey’s religious background. See you all then!

• Gizelle and Karen are play-fighting like two elderly siblings who have spent decades competing for their parents’ attention. It’s a genuinely delightful moment, and a reminder that these women can be funny together when they aren’t attempting to destroy one another’s reputations.

• I’ve also developed a lay theory that Karen’s entertainment value is inversely proportional to the condition of her wig. The worse the hair looks, the better the personality that shows up. It’s not a perfect science, but the evidence is mounting.

• I wholeheartedly endorse Gizelle complaining about having to wait for everyone else before eating. There are few indignities greater than watching your dinner grow cold because someone insists on maintaining the fiction that a group of adults can coordinate their appetites.
• Karen referring to Ashley’s rose gift as a “wee-wee suction cup” nearly ended me.
• The older I get, the more I relate to Karen’s obscenely early cut-off time. Last night I went to bed at 9 p.m., and it was glorious.
• It’s great to see Robyn and Karen getting along again; the levity in their scenes is offering a lightness and balance that we haven’t seen on the show in what feels like several seasons.

• Uncle Lump sitting quietly in the corner, sipping his drink and laughing at all the lunchtime chaos, is precisely the type of peanut gallery commentator I would want to be if I were invited to a scene.

• Ashley stating that people who abruptly change their stories are dangerous was a statement so spectacularly lacking in self-awareness that I nearly fell out of my chair. It is a fair observation to make about Courtney, but talk about a pot meeting a kettle.

• The conversation on Stacey’s history with the Jehovah’s Witnesses is such an unforced error, especially since the women seem determined to frame it as some sort of scandal. Trying to pretend that you are in a position to take issue with extreme religious sects is, honestly, laughable to me on a network that has spent years accommodating whatever it is Mary Cosby is subjecting the white girls of Salt Lake City to. More importantly, if Stacey did leave a restrictive religious community, that empathy, not gossip.

items.title: The 100 Greatest Movie Stars of All Time
items.description: We all know a movie star when we see one. But how can you tell which stars shine the brightest? Measuring the greatness of a movie star can be like catching lightning in a bottle. It’s a process that requires chemistry and finesse, as well as a search for the
items.author: Owen Gleiberman; Guy Lodge; Daniel D'Addario; Alison Herman; Aramide Tinubu
paragraphs: We all know a movie star when we see one. But how can you tell which stars shine the brightest? Measuring the greatness of a movie star can be like catching lightning in a bottle. It’s a process that requires chemistry and finesse, as well as a search for the perfect mix — that fusion of artistry and popularity, history and currency that adds up to the incandescent ideal of stardom. Not every movie star is a great actor; not every great actor is a movie star. Many of the choices on our list reflect that. Yet there’s a magic zone where talent and luminescence fuse. And there’s another overlap that might be even more important: the one between the way these people pop onscreen and the way they dance in our dreams. To choose the 100 Greatest Movie Stars, we had to use our heads, our hearts, our guts, our fantasy lives. We were looking for the stars who magnetize us, the ones who awe and overpower us and make us swoon. The ones we wish we were, and the ones who inspire the ultimate movie-star thought: “That’s who I am.”

- Henry Fonda His signature film was, by its very narrative design, an encapsulation of his virtues as a performer: In a room of 12 angry men, you could count on him to be the calmer, quieter one, a bastion of sense and reason. Upstanding integrity may not be the sexiest thing to be known for as a movie star, but Fonda was never stodgy with it. It’s fitting that Abraham Lincoln was one of his breakout roles, but it’s the urgently striving all-American masculinity of his Tom Joad in “The Grapes of Wrath” that really defined the Fonda aura, at least until his stubbornly humane Juror #8 came along. And the occasional, disorienting effect of his playing against type — bewildered doofus in “The Lady Eve,” ruthless villain in “Once Upon a Time in the West” — proved the strength of that type in the first place. — G.L. MUST SEE: “12 Angry Men”

- Sylvester Stallone In half a century of stardom, Sylvester Stallone has had just two roles that connected with audiences on the mythological level from which movie stardom is sculpted. But that turned out to be just enough. The first role was, of course, Rocky Balboa, who Stallone played with hooded eyes and a voice of muffled molasses and a groggy valor that came to life. The beauty of “Rocky” is that it connected the glory of Frank Capra to the grittiness of the New Hollywood. And what made it work was the shabby majesty of Stallone’s presence, the way he believed in the character — the way he made Rocky, in his tattered dreams, an echo of us all. The second role was John Rambo, a character who critics loved in his first movie and hated in his second. Yet if “Rambo: First Blood Part II” had problematic politics, Stallone’s smoldering fury — combined with an action flair so rooted in endurance it was nearly sadomasochistic — made the character into a galvanizingly stylized pop hero. Consider “Rocky” and “Rambo” the yin and yang of a star with old movies in his (first) blood. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Rocky”

- Zendaya You probably think that we think she became a movie star in “Dune.” Nope. It was well before that. She’s scintillating in the “Dune” films, where her stoic warrior Chani does a dance of fury around Paul Atreides’ shifting sympathies. But the Zendaya moment that gave us that first star tingle came in a musical that never got the love or respect it deserved: “The Greatest Showman.” As she sings “Rewrite the Stars,” hanging from a hoop trapeze, her face lights up with the pleasure of knowing that a forbidden love might be stronger than prejudice. And at that moment, her joy becomes ours. Zendaya took a leap into the acting stratosphere in “Challengers,” as a tennis champ who becomes the vertex angle — now seductive, now demanding, now who’s she going to choose? — of an isosceles love triangle. She smoldered onscreen, and in “The Drama” she shored up that smolder as a vibrant bride with the darkest of secrets. Keep watching her; she’s rewriting stardom. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Challengers”

- Alain Delon Delon was, at his peak, almost too beautiful to be a functioning movie star: unapproachably, almost icily perfect, with a flinty gaze that either conveyed tortured depths or no soul whatsoever. Yet his beauty was never merely decorative — he was fortunate to be at his most ravishing in a testy, challenging era of European cinema that knew what to do with difficult beauty. Rather than playing straightforward heroes or objects of desire, he was happy to be the statuesque psycho: a lethally yearning Tom Ripley in “Purple Noon,” a hit man whose unnerving silence is a loaded weapon in “Le Samouraï.” Even when the men he played were slightly less tortured, his unlined, fine-cut face was an ideal vessel for the ambiguities that were the stock-in-trade of filmmakers like Visconti and Antonioni. He could make action of stillness, and a character trait of mystique. — G.L. MUST SEE: “Le Samouraï”

- Eddie Murphy From the start, he’s led with his delirious effrontery. It’s there in his great characters from “Saturday Night Live” (Buckwheat, Mr. Robinson), to the point that he was practically a movie star then. When he took the literal leap in “48 Hrs.,” he became a movie star the moment you saw him singing “Roxanne” with his Walkman on. From then on for Eddie Murphy, it was “Party All the Time.” Yet from his scene-stealing role as Donkey in the “Shrek” films to the serious acclaim he earned for “Dreamgirls,” Murphy made it impossible for the entertainment industry to define him as just one thing. In the ’80s, he was the Hollywood comedy star, triumphantly irreverent in “Beverly Hills Cop” and “Coming to America,” winning the capital to make his own films his way, with all-Black casts. And starting with “The Nutty Professor,” those casts would often include Murphy in half a dozen roles, a seeming stunt that he elevated into uproarious artistry, with one guiding rule: In an Eddie Murphy movie, the more of him the better. — A.T. MUST SEE: “The Nutty Professor”

- Philip Seymour Hoffman It might not be as iconic as “You talkin’ to me?” or “I coulda been a contender,” but the scene that made Philip Seymour Hoffman a movie star is every bit as potent and defining. It comes in the first half of “Boogie Nights,” when Scotty J., the awkward, closeted boom operator, sits in his car after making a failed pass and says, “I’m a fuckin’ idiot!” over and over again, letting you touch the nerve of his self-hatred — and cuing you to the fact that every person watching this movie has known that feeling. That’s movie-star poetry, and Hoffman brought it to every role. He was a virtuoso chameleon who could play pathologically shy (“Happiness”) or blissfully arrogant (“The Talented Mr. Ripley”). He could be a sap (“Before the Devil Knows You’re Dead”), a manipulator (“The Master”) or a tragic head case (“Owning Mahowny”). Or he could be every one of those things at once (“Capote”). — O.G. MUST SEE: “Capote”

- Emma Stone In “La La Land,” the movie that solidified her place as one of the stars of our time, Emma Stone plays a struggling actress who becomes a movie star. A common enough scenario to encounter at the movies. Only in this case, you feel the chemical evolution: how Stone’s Mia starts as a pragmatic striver, only to look like she’s failed until she sings “Audition (The Fools Who Dream),” at which point her very being is suffused with stardom. Stone never looked back from that incandescent moment. In a career of dizzying and daring choices, she can play vintage heroic (“Battle of the Sexes”), saintly or scheming or both at once (“The Favourite”), a cawing lascivious Frankenstein monster (“Poor Things”), a ruthless corporate sociopath you start to root for (“Bugonia”), or she can turn a kids’ movie into a thrilling ride for adults (“Cruella”). Here’s to the ones — like Emma Stone — who dream. — O.G. MUST SEE: “La La Land”

- Joaquin Phoenix Remember “I’m Still Here,” Casey Affleck’s 2010 mockumentary in which Joaquin Phoenix played “Joaquin Phoenix,” the very picture of a self-congratulatory tortured actor, seemingly blowing up his career to pursue rapping instead? It was the kind of dumb stunt that could indeed have tanked a lesser talent; for Phoenix, coming at what turned out to be only the halfway mark of a consistently adventurous, exploratory career, the film seems both a blip and a telling reflection of what a reluctant and system-averse star he is. Phoenix has made a career of being a misfit — whether playing Johnny Cash in his pomp or the addled seeker of “The Master” — though his most defining outcast role, as the grimmest, most unwell incarnation of DC’s Joker yet put onscreen, became an Oscar-winning, billion-dollar-grossing pop icon. Such are his contradictions. — G.L. MUST SEE: “Joker”

- Shah Rukh Khan Now in his sixties, Bollywood cinema titan Shah Rukh Khan has held Indian audiences in thrall through more than 90 films across four decades — showing daunting staying power in one of the world’s most restlessly churning film industries. His secret? An unabashed flair for peacocking showmanship and drama writ large, allied to a self-aware comic intelligence, a combination that served him through multiple phases of stardom. He broke out in 1993 as a rakish villain in “Baazigar” and “Darr,” before his megawatt charisma and leonine good looks vaulted him to romantic-lead status, putting audiences on full swoon alert in the likes of “Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge” and the global hit “Devdas.” Restless diversions into comedy and character acting have followed; recently, he’s made himself over as a venerable action star. Named “King Khan” by local fans, he remains comfortable in his throne. — G.L. MUST SEE: “Devdas”

- Kristen Stewart Movie-star energy tends to burst outward. But Kristen Stewart has a different energy — doleful and pensive, in a way that recalls the young Jane Fonda, who also brandished a fraught inward gaze. In movies like “Adventureland,” Stewart established herself as a new kind of actor, with a captivating too-cool-for-school millennial glamour. But then the “Twilight” films elevated her into a teen idol, even though the franchise came with a special challenge: She was tasked with carrying Bella Swan’s tormented romantic doubts through half a dozen movies, and she brought it off, finding endless variation in her push-pull attraction to Robert Pattinson’s vampire bad boy. And when the series ended, Stewart sprung herself into adult roles, notably channeling Princess Diana in a performance of rippling depths in “Spencer,” acting with a fervor that continues to display her onscreen paradox: the movie star hiding under the reluctant movie star. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Spencer”

- Lauren Bacall Bacall was just 19 when she made her indelible screen debut in “To Have and Have Not,” projecting a self-possessed sexuality far beyond her years — and thus bridging the age gap with her 44-year-old leading man (and soon-to-be husband), Humphrey Bogart. (It was, shall we say, a different time.) “You know how to whistle, don’t you? You just put your lips together and blow,” she famously said — absurd innuendo that, in her delivery, sounded coolly in command. She was a woman in control at all stages of her career, whether as the smoky, precocious femme fatale of the Bogey-and-Bacall years or as the more imperious grande dame that she shifted into in middle age and beyond. Her senior years yielded some of her best, most challenging work in art films like Jonathan Glazer’s “Birth” and Lars von Trier’s “Dogville,” but she could just as easily wield her brittle authority to imposing effect in instant coffee commercials. — G.L. MUST SEE: “To Have and Have Not”

- Nicolas Cage You might say there are two Nicolas Cages. As one of the most compelling actors of his generation, he has a hangdog sincerity he wore on his sleeve from his first hit, “Valley Girl,” through his crowd-pleasing turns in “Moonstruck” and “Raising Arizona” and on to the film in which he gives his greatest performance: the funny, tragic, delicately baroque drama of love and alcohol, “Leaving Las Vegas.” But then there’s the other Nicolas Cage — the self-consciously over-the-top stylized junk-movie clown, who first appeared, full on, in “Vampire’s Kiss” and “Con Air,” and who went on to carve out an identity as the Man of 1,000 Paycheck Gigs. In our view, both versions of Cage are integral to the singularity of his stardom. Few actors hold the camera the way he does — but in his dozens of bad movies, he never phoned in his flamboyance. He made the degradation of his stardom the point, in a way that only a quintessential star could do. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Leaving Las Vegas”

- Lillian Gish At a time when the stars of silent cinema were largely stage-schooled, Gish was perhaps the first intrinsically cinematic Great Actor of the era, her vast expressive range and quivering physicality both minimized and magnified for the camera, relative to the theatrical gestures of many of her peers. Her pioneering innovations are inseparably braided with those of filmmaker D.W. Griffith, whose epic experiments were frequently anchored by her extraordinary, ecstatic, anguished features. The ugly presence of “The Birth of a Nation” in their joint filmography can’t be ignored, but it shouldn’t cancel out the technical and thespian achievements of “Intolerance” or “Broken Blossoms,” with its haunting “closet scene,” a master class in confined emotional torment. Sound didn’t end Gish’s career — eventually delivering her an Oscar nod for “Duel in the Sun” and an all-time classic in “The Night of the Hunter” — but hers remains a legacy defined by silence. — G.L. MUST SEE: “Broken Blossoms”

- Whoopi Goldberg She melted our hearts as Celie, the heroine of “The Color Purple,” who emerges from a life of deprivation and abuse with a soul intact enough to lunge for freedom and joy. But that defining performance in Steven Spielberg’s 1985 film was just the tip of the iceberg of Goldberg’s movie-star mojo. She spent the next few years lurching around in ill-defined action comedies, but then, in what turned out to be one of the genius casting coups of the ’90s, she showed up as Oda Mae Brown, the huckster psychic in “Ghost” who only thinks she’s a charlatan. Outrageously brash and uproariously full of fury, she seems to be channeling Groucho Marx, Richard Pryor and Medea. And from that moment on she went Full Goldberg, hiding out in a convent and dressing down her fellow nuns in the delectably irreverent “Sister Act” and hunting down a Hollywood killer in Robert Altman’s “The Player.” What makes her not just a funny but enchanted presence is the way she elevates flippant forthrightness into a kind of delirious cathartic truth-telling. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Ghost”

- Timothée Chalamet At 30, Chalamet is one of the youngest stars on this list, yet his career already feels storied enough to justify his inclusion. The bright, beseeching teenager of “Interstellar” and “Call Me by Your Name” grew into a fresh-faced but confident matinee idol in the likes of “Dune” and “Little Women.” Yet as Chalamet heads into his 30s, the more intriguingly perverse instincts of a character actor seem to be guiding his choices: Playing men as disparate as Willy Wonka and Bob Dylan, he seems drawn to their mystery and peculiarity. His recent turn in “Marty Supreme” represented a boldly big swing: an agitated, eccentric inhabitation of a genuine asshole that he carried to a $192 million gross. No one else of his generation can lead such a vast audience to a character so hard to love, and that courage and clout bodes well for his next chapter. — G.L. MUST SEE: “Marty Supreme”

- Burt Reynolds Imagine that Marlon Brando had a country-boy cousin who was less interested in Method acting than in his own advanced methods for charming the ladies. That would be Burt Reynolds. At times, he can be a hell of an actor, notably in “Deliverance,” where he faces down his hillbilly adversaries with a cutthroat resolve that smolders. Yet what made Reynolds just about the biggest movie star of the 1970s was his mixture of macho bluster and teasing self-mockery. He was perhaps the first hunk of Hollywood beefcake who refused to take himself seriously (a quality he honed on the late-night talk-show circuit) — and that lends his performances in everything from “The Longest Yard” to the chicken-fried drive-in juggernaut of “Smokey and the Bandit” a quality of insolent swagger marked by his irresistible wink at his own magnetism. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Smokey and the Bandit”

- Kate Winslet Winslet fought hard for the lead role in “Titanic,” but today it’s difficult to imagine any other actress having taken Rose DeWitt Bukater’s spot on the ship of dreams. Rose, an heiress fallen on hard times who insists on pursuing love over security, etched into box office history what Winslet does as well as anyone: She shows us a woman who understands the rules of society and then attempts, fiercely, to claw through the veneer of propriety. Whether Winslet, onscreen, is blowing up her marriage (“Little Children”) or her career (“Steve Jobs”) or her entire existence (“Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind”), she seems always to be making decisions utterly in the moment — and surprising even herself. Little wonder that with “Titanic,” Winslet became the onscreen avatar for untold millions of teen girls. Perhaps no other actress might have so perfectly merged earthy realism with, just a millimeter beneath, a dreamer’s sense of possibility. — D.D. MUST SEE: “Titanic”

- Robert Pattinson No one becomes a movie star without trying to. But after fashioning himself into the moody pinup heartthrob of a generation in the “Twilight” films, Robert Pattinson made a radical left turn. He’d become a star, but he almost seemed to leave stardom at the altar when he took on a series of edgelord roles in defiantly niche art films (“Good Time,” “The Childhood of a Leader,” “The Lost City of Z”), spending the better part of a decade doing the character-actor-in-a-leading-man’s-body thing. We don’t mean to make light of it; he was honing his chops, showing the world the kind of star he wanted to be. And when he was cast in “The Batman,” the best of both worlds finally came together: Behind the gruff voice, Pattinson created a Batman who was more complexly dynamic and riveting than any who had come before him. As his daring performances in “Primetime” and “The Drama” attest, he’s a new kind of movie star: hushed and saturnine, plugged into the dark side of his time. Will that be reflected in his upcoming role as James Bond? We’re betting that Pattinson leaves us as shaken as we are stirred. — O.G. MUST SEE: “The Batman”

- Morgan Freeman It’s no accident that he became the voice of God. Though if you chart his career path, that was hardly his destiny. In the midst of a thriving New York theater career, Freeman became a regular on the ’70s children’s TV series “The Electric Company.” But he didn’t explode into the spotlight until he was nearly 50, when he starred in “Street Smart” (1987), giving the most authentic performance as a wily, vicious street operator that the movies had ever seen. As he quickly proved, though, he could play deep-grained benevolence as complexly as he did ferocity. He became a humanistic everyman, as embodied by his memorable performance in “The Shawshank Redemption.” For this immense orator, the leap to voicing the Almighty came all too naturally, since that voice emerged from his inner quality — a higher wisdom that envelops you in its warmth. — A.T. MUST SEE: “The Shawshank Redemption”

- Liv Ullmann The actresses in Ingmar Bergman’s films weren’t just accomplished artists. Like Bergman himself, they were groundbreakers, expressing sides of women’s experience that had never been seen onscreen before, and doing it with a lacerating intimacy that took on an almost confessional quality. But even within that gallery of acting genius, Ullmann stands apart. In “Persona,” the movie that introduced her to the world, she gave a nearly silent performance as a theater actor so traumatized she had decided to stop speaking. Yet Ullmann spoke volumes with her face — the gaze that could be furious or beatific or full of fear. And as she became Bergman’s most complex and impassioned surrogate, what you saw in her was the charisma of unbridled expression, culminating in her virtuosic performance in “Scenes From a Marriage,” which she turned into nothing less than “A Doll’s House” for the postwar age. What’s a movie star? Someone who makes the truth shine as brightly as Liv Ullmann did. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Scenes from a Marriage”

- Sean Penn You knew he was a movie star the moment he charmed the world into a collective giggle fit in “Fast Times at Ridgemont High,” playing the stoner surf dude Jeff Spicoli with a blitzed bravado that made every line sound like a stupido catchphrase. But even in that lighthearted career launch, he was sneakily authentic. And that became Penn’s calling card — that whatever the role, he was going to whittle it down to the bone of reality. From the moment he played a juvenile con in “Bad Boys,” you knew you were seeing the next-generation De Niro, and he knew it too. That’s why he was drawn, compulsively, to playing criminals, losers, lowlifes, renegades and ugly-mustache freaks. Yet in every case, he found the character’s underlying humanity. And that’s his glory as a star: the way he will always go to that place other actors won’t, daring to excavate the hidden reality of a lost soul. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Dead Man Walking”

- Divine The shaved head that’s like an angry egg, topped by a wave of synthetic hair. The giant dagger eyebrows and mouth that curls into an evil leer. The body that makes her look like Jayne Mansfield crossed with Godzilla. It would be hard to think of an image in movie history as magnetic, scary, hilarious and flat-out insane as Divine in “Pink Flamingos.” In that 1972 midnight classic, she plays “the filthiest person alive,” who is also a homicidal demon-clown maniac with the personality of the Wicked Witch of the West on PCP. It’s a performance that’s pure drag Dada, but as Divine proved in every movie she made with director John Waters (the von Sternberg to her deranged Dietrich), she was no one-trick pony. Whether playing a psycho rebel (“Female Trouble”) or a fuddy-duddy mom (“Hairspray”), Divine owned the screen with a delirious punked-out effervescence unlike any star who came before or after. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Pink Flamingos”

- Gregory Peck He’ll always be Atticus Finch because of how large he made that character loom in the American imagination. It all started, of course, with Harper Lee’s great novel, but in the 1962 film adaptation of “To Kill a Mockingbird,” Peck turned Atticus into such an intractable yet homespun figure of relatable valor that it’s almost as if he was playing Abe Lincoln. The performance earned him an Oscar while spotlighting America’s racial discord and racial criminality at a time when the issue of race was starting to rip the country apart. Peck tended to play thoughtful and rather reserved characters, notably opposite Audrey Hepburn in “Roman Holiday,” but that made him the perfect actor to step into Alfred Hitchcock’s psychologically twisted “Spellbound,” which seemed to be stress-testing the limits of his charmed rationality. — A.T. MUST SEE: “To Kill a Mockingbird”

- Ryan Gosling It’s easy to forget that Gosling began his career on Disney Channel’s “All New Mickey Mouse Club” in the ’90s — before becoming one of the rare child stars to rise above the chaos of the industry to become an acclaimed actor in his own right. While the hit tearjerker “The Notebook” catapulted Gosling to superstardom in 2004, it was his performance as a drug-addicted teacher in “Half Nelson” two years later that showed his range and landed him the first of three Oscar nominations. A millennial dreamboat with a singing voice to match, he has thrived in everything from indies like “Lars and the Real Girl” to genre blockbusters like “Project Hail Mary” to the glittery showbiz epiphany that was “La La Land,” playing everyone from Neil Armstrong to, well, just Ken. — A.T. MUST SEE: “Drive”

- Burt Lancaster Few stars have hit the jackpot with their film debut in quite the way Lancaster did: with a leading role in a hell of a movie — Robert Siodmak’s icily hardboiled 1946 noir “The Killers” — that also just happened to encapsulate his whole deal as an actor. As an ex-boxer embroiled in an underworld scheme, ultimately undone by obsessive love, Lancaster’s character is a bruiser with a soul. It’s a tender-tough archetype that served the actor well in such films as “The Birdman of Alcatraz,” “Atlantic City” and, of course, “From Here to Eternity.” The enduring cultural memory of the latter is of him rolling around in the surf with Deborah Kerr, his brawny physique made barely decent with a tight swimsuit, but that scene rather obscures the portrait he etched in the film of military alpha masculinity with a stout liberal conscience. In Lancaster, Hollywood got itself a man who could do both. — G.L. MUST SEE: “From Here to Eternity”

- Pam Grier The action star was a phenomenon that rose up in the 1970s, and it took years for the concept of the “female action star” to seem anything more than a counterintuitive anomaly. But that shouldn’t have been the case, since the female action star was born, full-blown and electrifying, in the person of Pam Grier. She was fast and furious and decades ahead of her time, but she came up in the world of blaxploitation films, which were highly successful and influential movies that were marginalized as an “underground” happening. The reality, however, is that they were cultural bombshells, and Grier was nothing less than a revolutionary movie star. In the raw funk revenge thriller “Coffy,” she’s sly-eyed and insolent, proudly sexual, rivetingly spontaneous in her violence (she wields a sawed-off shotgun like James Bond in an Afro), with a ruthlessness that feels rooted in experience. This was a whole new kind of star: a badass with soul. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Coffy”

- Robert Downey Jr. Even in the ’80s, when he was just an overgrown kid, Robert Downey Jr. never stopped talking. As the title lothario of “The Pick-up Artist,” or the spiraling druggie of “Less Than Zero,” he talked circles around his co-stars, cajoling, hustling, pleading, bargaining. For a while, that was Downey’s comic eccentricity (it’s telling that when he finally made an awards-bait movie, he had to put a cork in it to play Charlie Chaplin). But in “Natural Born Killers,” where he gave a brilliant performance as the hell-bent tabloid-TV chatterbox Wayne Gale, it finally began to look as though Downey’s motormouth might be the stuff of movie stardom. And in “Iron Man,” something fantastically ironic happened. He was starring in a comic book movie — a genre that tends to swallow up stars, even when the movies are hits. But Downey’s Tony Stark gave the new superhero culture just the buzzy, chewy center it needed. He humanized this most corporate of genres … and in a funny way, it humanized him. — O.G. MUST SEE: “Iron Man”

- Barbara Stanwyck The hottest tickets at the most recent edition of Il Cinema Ritrovato, the classic film festival in Bologna, Italy, were for the Stanwyck retrospective. That 20-something cinephiles were queueing in rush lines even for relative obscurities like “Ladies of Leisure” and “Night Nurse” was a testament to the enduring modernity of Stanwyck as a star. Exuding cool, controlled reserve in romantic comedy and film noir alike, with a distinctively husky tone and a pragmatic, forthright demeanor that tolerated only the bare minimum of studio glamour, she was an independent woman decades ahead of a feminist revolution that, as a staunch Hollywood Republican, she likely wouldn’t have had much time for anyway. That slightly forbidding no-bullshit attitude gave her the air of a character actor in a leading lady’s body, as spiritually aligned with the likes of Cagney and Bogart as any of her female peers. — G.L. MUST SEE: “Double Indemnity”

- Nicole Kidman Back in 2017, when Film Twitter was a happier place, I launched the Kidman World Cup: a bracket tournament of polls to determine Kidman’s best performance that went semi-viral, with Barry Jenkins and Melanie Lynskey among those lobbying for their picks. “To Die For” wound up beating “Birth” by a hair, but what the exercise mainly proved was that there’s little consensus on the best version of Kidman: the old-school multiplex goddess (“Moulin Rouge!”); the art-house boundary pusher (“Dogville”); the raw, turbulent emoter (“The Hours”); the untouchable ice queen (“Stoker”); or the anything-goes adventurer (“The Paperboy”). And all that was before she shored up her queenly reputation not just with typically gutsy, wide-ranging performances in the likes of “Babygirl” and “Destroyer,” but as the official spokeswoman for cinema itself in her immediately iconic AMC spots. Heartbreak does indeed feel good when Kidman is the breaker, or the broken. — G.L. MUST SEE: “Moulin Rouge!”

- Matt Damon It was Matt Damon’s fate to be a golden boy who came along just at the moment when the world was starting to look askance at golden boys. But it’s the measure of his stardom that he took that twist of karma and owned it. Having used his brain to melt our hearts with “Good Will Hunting,” Damon took the most daring of left turns, portraying the murderous protagonist of “The Talented Mr. Ripley” as a silky but vulnerable psychopath, haunted by what he can’t have. His great performance in that film was no one-shot. It opened the door to the real Matt Damon — a golden boy who never shined brighter than when he was showing us his dark side. He turned the “Bourne” films into riveting downbeat action psychodramas, and he was brilliantly duplicitous in “The Good Shepherd.” Yet he

items.title: Skydance to Fold Paramount TV Studios Into Warner Bros. TV Under Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell
items.description: Skydance is officially combining Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios, two of its key TV production units, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Skydance is officially combining Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios, two of its key TV production units, Variety has learned.

The new combined entity will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios, with Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell serving as presidents. They will report into George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV. Cheeks made the announcement Wednesday morning in an internal memo to staff, which can be read in full below.

Dungey and Thunell will also oversee BET Studios and Warner Bros. International Television Production, while it was previously announced that Dungey also now serves as chair of Skydance Global Cable Media, which combines the cable network portfolios of Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount.
The merger of the two studios will be completed in early 2027.

Meanwhile, CBS Studios will continue to operate as a standalone entity under David Stapf, also reporting to Cheeks. CBS Studios International, Skydance Sports Entertainment and See It Now Studios will operate under the CBS Studios umbrella.

“Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine, uniting extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level,” Cheeks said. “With Channing and Matt at the helm, we have two exceptional leaders who understand what it takes to empower creative talent, foster bold ideas and deliver programming that resonates with audiences everywhere. Alongside CBS Studios, led by the incomparable David Stapf, Warner Bros. Television Studios gives us two world-class studios, with the breadth, depth and creative ambition to deliver for Skydance platforms and third-party partners across the industry.”

It had previously been speculated that PTVS would be merged back into CBS Studios as it had been before. But the move to combine PTVS into one of the other studio units is not surprising. WBTV is a major powerhouse, with its current slate across a number of networks and streamers including shows like “The Pitt,” “Ted Lasso,” “Shrinking,” “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage,” “Abbott Elementary,” and the upcoming “Harry Potter” HBO series.

“Matt has extraordinary creative instincts, and a deep understanding of great storytelling,” Dungey said. “I couldn’t ask for a better partner as we bring these storied studios together. “We have a unique opportunity to create something truly special for our creative partners and audiences around the world. I’m very excited to begin this new chapter.”

Paramount Television Studios currently produces or co-produces shows such as “Reacher” at Prime Video and Taylor Sheridan’s Paramount+ shows, including “Landman,” “Tulsa King,” “Dutton Ranch” and more. However, PTVS has been shut down and revived multiple times under various names, with Skydance only bringing the division back in its current form in 2025 upon the completion of the Skydance-Paramount merger.

“Channing is one of the most accomplished and respected executives in our industry, with an extraordinary track record of building successful businesses, developing enduring partnerships and delivering some of television’s most acclaimed programming,” Thunell said. “Ever since our time together at Netflix, I’ve hoped we’d have the opportunity to work together again, and I’m thrilled that day has finally come. We’re bringing an unmatched roster of talent under one roof, building on the remarkable legacies of two storied studios. The possibilities ahead are extraordinary, and I couldn’t be more excited to partner with Channing to champion the ambitions of our creative talent and bring exceptional stories to audiences around the world.”

CBS Studios, meanwhile, continues to produce a long string of hit shows under Stapf and his team. The studio still has the CBS cornerstone “NCIS” on the air in its 24th season, with the franchise currently encompassing the prequel “NCIS: Origins” and “NCIS: New York.” CBS Studios also co-produces “Criminal Minds,” which aired for 15 seasons on CBS and was revived for an additional five at Paramount+.

The studio also has shows like the “FBI” franchise, the hit comedy “Ghosts,” “Elsbeth,” the “Fire Country” franchise, and “Little House on the Prairie” at Netflix. Meanwhile, consistent hitmakers Robert and Michelle King, who have called CBS Studios home for more than two decades, just launched to legal drama “Cupertino” on CBS via CBS Studios.

This marks the latest moves under the combined Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery under David Ellision. In addition to the previously announced cable networks reorganization, it was reported earlier this week that Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein have set their leadership team.
INTERNAL MEMO FROM GEORGE CHEEKS,
Co-Chair & Chief Content Officer, Skydance TV

Today, I’m sharing an important next step for how our television studios will serve the creative community. We are combining the Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios into one studio, which will operate as Warner Bros. Television Studios, beginning in early 2027. Until then, both studios will continue to operate independently.

This move aligns our leadership, resources and creative focus for two studios with considerable success producing for streaming, as well as broadcast. By bringing these teams together, we can build on their strengths and create an even stronger home for great talent and great storytelling.

Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell will be Presidents of Warner Bros. Television Studios, jointly leading the combined studio and reporting to me, with oversight of its creative departments and an expansive and growing portfolio of scripted and unscripted programming. They are exceptional creative leaders who understand how to support talent, champion bold ideas and build strong partnerships across our industry. Channing and Matt will also oversee BET Studios and Warner Bros. International Television Production studios around the world.

David Stapf continues in his role as President of CBS Studios, reporting to me, building on the studio’s strength as one of the industry’s leading global studios. Home to many of the Network’s biggest franchises and hits, David and his team remain a critical supplier to our broadcast business while continuing to grow their streaming footprint. CBS Studios International, Skydance Sports Entertainment and See It Now Studios will operate under the CBS Studios umbrella.

Collectively, Warner Bros. Television Studios and CBS Studios present two powerful creative engines with extraordinary talent, award-winning programming, hit franchises and the global scale to serve Skydance platforms and third-party partners across the industry. Add to that, CBS Entertainment, led by Amy Reisenbach, and the Global Cable Media team under Channing, Skydance TV is a creative force in entertainment across scripted, unscripted and live events.

Channing, Matt and David will be connecting with teams in the coming weeks to talk more about the new structure. We know there will be questions about what this means for individual teams. HR will share more information as plans are finalized.

I’m excited about what we’re building. We have extraordinary creative talent, an unmatched portfolio and tremendous opportunity ahead. Bringing these teams together gives us an even stronger foundation to support storytellers, champion great ideas and bring exceptional television to audiences around the world.

items.title: Elon Musk Has Invested in Skydance, David Ellison Confirms: ‘To Have Him as a Shareholder Is an Honor’
items.description: David Ellison, chairman and CEO of Skydance, confirmed that tech mogul Elon Musk has invested in the company, formed through the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: David Ellison, chairman and CEO of Skydance, confirmed that tech mogul Elon Musk has invested in the company, formed through the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.

Musk, the world’s richest person, invested about $1 billion in Skydance post-merger, CNBC and Semafor reported last month. Ellison, speaking Wednesday at the New York Times’ 2026 DealBook Summit at Manhattan’s Jazz at Lincoln Center, acknowledged that Musk has become a part-owner of Skydance but he did not confirm the investment amount.

The New York Times’ Andrew Ross Sorkin asked Ellison about the reports that Musk invested a billion dollars into Skydance, “and I think some people wanted to know whether this is the beginning of something bigger with [SpaceX-owned] Starlink long-term, or is a one-off as a given his relationship with your father,” Oracle founder and billionaire Larry Ellison.

Ellison responded, “So look, I have so much admiration and respect for Elon. I mean, I don’t know if you saw recently, but literally watching, you know, [SpaceX’s] Starship, it’s a marvel…. I mean, he is both the [Nikola] Tesla and [Thomas] Edison… He is, from my perspective, the greatest entrepreneur of our time, and he doesn’t invest in a lot of companies.”

Ellison continued, “So to have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege. And if there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future… [which] is the appropriate opportunity in the future, we’d be thrilled to do so. But there’s nothing [right now].”

Sorkin asked Ellison whether he is still planning to put Alex Gibney’s documentary “Musk” — which prompted a legal threat from the tech titan against the filmmaker — on HBO. (“Musk” has been pegged to begin streaming on HBO Max in the first quarter of 2027.) Ellison responded, “Of course.”

Ellison’s Paramount Skydance closed its $111 billion megamerger with Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6, with major backing from his father. The company, one of the biggest media and entertainment conglomerates in the industry, has around $80 billion in net debt and is expected to lay off thousands of employees as part of achieving $6 billion in annualized savings by 2029.

Asked by Sorkin how he was able to “convince” his father to back the Paramount-WBD deal to the tune of $40 billion, Ellison said, “Look, one of the things I think people have to understand, and I want to dispel what might be a myth, is my father is an incredible partner.”

Larry Ellison, his son said, “demands an incredible performance, an incredible result as a result of this investment.” David added that he speaks with his dad on average four times per week. “We are building a company to create long-term shareholder value. That’s what my father is motivated by. That’s what all of our investors are motivated by.”
Sorkin asked about Larry Ellison’s ties to President Donald Trump, who has called the tech exec “a friend of mine, big supporter of mine” and said of the Ellisons, “They’re terrific people.”
“What are your politics?” Sorkin queried, and asked Ellison if he voted for Trump.

“I’ve actually never disclosed that,” Ellison said about whether he voted for Trump. “I voted both sides of the aisle basically my entire life. I’m not a partisan.” He said “we’ve been fortunate enough to be able to work closely with this administration, but also, when we started the Paramount deal, that was under the Biden administration… and you know, our hope is to be able to work with whoever the next president is as well.”

Asked about a report that Trump pushed for Paramount to greenlight “Rush Hour 4,” Ellison said the project did not originate at Trump’s behest. According to Ellison, Paramount Pictures co-president Josh Greenstein (now co-chair of Skydance Motion Picture Group) “walked into my office” and that was the “first conversation we had about ‘Rush Hour 4.'”

“I’m not going to go into addressing every single basically made-up story,” Ellison said. “But what I also think is really important is when it comes to the news, and I’ve said this publicly multiple times, we believe in editorial independence that will never change. Period.”

Does Skydance plan to merge CNN and CBS News? “Right now, we are incredibly happy operating them basically within status quo,” said Ellison. “There might be some news sharing in the future, but for right now we’re happy to operate them as they are.”

Sorkin noted that Bari Weiss, whom Ellison appointed head of editorial at CBS News, has shaken up “60 Minutes,” referencing the exit of staffers including Scott Pelley. “When you saw all this happen, when Scott Pelley quits, when you see all this, what are you thinking to yourself?” asked Sorkin. “So again, one, we are really proud of the work that basically all of our journalists are basically doing across both news organizations. And again, I think you got to step back and talk about where everything currently sits” in terms of a decline in trust in the news media, Ellison said. “When you look at what our goal for news is, and we’re one year into this journey, it is to make sure that we can rebuild trust back to at least where it was previously, if not even higher… That is our mission today. That is our mission tomorrow. That will be our mission five years from now.”

Ellison reiterated that the new Skydance anticipates $6 billion in “synergies” within three years. The company expects to generate $10 billion in free cash flow by 2030 to help it lower it its debt load — while “investing more in content than any of our peers.” Skydance, on a pro-forma basis (Paramount and Warner Bros.) spent over $30 billion on content; for comparison, Disney has forecast cash content spending of $26 billion in fiscal 2027. “The scale of this company I do not think is fully appreciated,” he said.

Skydance has committed to making at least 30 movies next year under its settlement with 12 state attorneys general. “I spent the last 16 years of my life on the filmmaking side of this business. I have I have lived on set. I’ve slept on Hans Zimmer’s couch. I’ve been in editorial rooms for 20 hours nonstop,” Ellison said. “I do understand the creative process of this business, and the goal has to be in any film that you make is how do you reach the broadest possible audience for that particular story, and there is no one-size-fits-all approach.”

Asked whether Ellison would release Tom Cruise’s “Digger,” a flop from Warner Bros. that has been tracking to lose $245 million at the box office, the Skydance CEO didn’t directly answer the question. He said, “I’m glad you bring that up. I’ve made eight movies with Tom. Look, I think he’s one of the seminal artists of our time. We’re literally working on a sequel to ‘Days of Thunder’ right now, and then we want to try to roll right into ‘Top Gun’ after that.”

On the topic of AI, Ellison said industry needs to focus on what artificial intelligence “is going to do across our business and what it is capable of today.” AI is “going to be one of the most significant creative unlocks in modern history,” he said. “Like going back to the early days of Pixar, the lesson was always be wrong as fast as possible… We’re going to be living in a world where you can make the movie not 10 times but 20 times before it actually gets put out.”

Also during the session, Ellison spoke about his lobbying for a federal film incentive, starting in October 2025, “to basically bring film production back to the United States of America.” He said the most interaction he’s had with Trump on the issue was through late Sen. Lindsey Graham.

“When you look at who this incentive helps, the misnomer out there is like you’re giving Tom Cruise a tax break,” Ellison said. “That’s not true. Tom Cruise [and] the biggest talent in the world are going to get paid whatever they get paid, no matter where they shoot in the world. It is the union workers, it is the makeup artist, it is the craftsmen, it is the set builders that fundamentally are being subsidized. You are creating jobs, you are helping small businesses.”

Earlier in the conversation, Ellison shared details of his childhood, which he said “is a big part of what kind of you know kind of brought me here today.” Raised by his mother, they had a movie collection “that was like 3,000” VHS tapes. “Sunday was the one day when we could kind of do whatever you wanted. And me and Megan would be like, ‘Let’s watch all five ‘Rocky’ movies, or ‘Let’s watch the Star Wars trilogy,’ and so it really was kind of that foundational kind of love in childhood where I’m very passionate about what we get to do every day.”

“I fell in love with movies when I was a 2-year-old kid. You know, I was raised by a single mother, by my mom. You know, my parents got divorced when I was 3, and I really started building my relationship with my father when I was 13 years old.” David said he saw his father “once a year, every other year” but that the two “couldn’t be closer now.”

In his final question, Sorkin mischievously asked Ellison which family-dynasty drama that Skydance now owns — “Succession,” “Yellowstone,” “Billions” or “The Godfather” — best represents his own family.

Ellison responded with a smile, “The answer is I actually love all of those stories. I really do.” About family dynamics, he said, “one of the things that I am really grateful for is, despite the last name, my family was able to shield a very large part of my childhood from all of that…. and I want to give the same to my kids. You know, I want them to have a grounded life. I don’t want them to be focused on what dad’s doing at work.”

The Ellison family — with the multibillion-dollar backing of Larry Ellison — holds the largest equity stake in Skydance. RedBird Capital Partners, led by managing partner Gerry Cardinale, invested $4 billion into Skydance, and philanthropist and investor Laurene Powell Jobs, founder and president of Emerson Collective, has invested $250 million.

Equity investors in the Paramount-WBD merger also included the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. The Ellisons and investment firm RedBird Capital Partners together are the sole holders of Paramount Class A common stock, including 100% of the combined company’s voting shares.

items.title: Mark Ruffalo, Tilda Swinton, Michael Moore, Barry Jenkins and More Rally to the Defense of Iranian Filmmaker Jafar Panahi
items.description: The heads of Venice and Berlin film festivals as well as actors such as Mark Ruffalo and Tilda Swinton, and directors like Michael Moore, Barry Jenkins and Alex Gibney are among a host of prominent film players who have rallied to the defense of Iranian filmma
items.author: Leo Barraclough
paragraphs: The heads of Venice and Berlin film festivals as well as actors such as Mark Ruffalo and Tilda Swinton, and directors like Michael Moore, Barry Jenkins and Alex Gibney are among a host of prominent film players who have rallied to the defense of Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi.

A statement shared with Variety, so far signed by 200 individuals or institutions, states that they are “deeply concerned” by reports of the new prison sentence of five years and one month issued by the Tehran Revolutionary Court against Panahi, as well as the confiscation of his assets, the freezing of his bank accounts, a two-year travel ban and a two-year social media ban.

It notes that in December, Iran issued a sentence against Panahi of one year in prison and a two-year ban on leaving the country. It adds that in March, Panahi “courageously decided to return to Iran, aware of the risks but having always spoken of his deep love for his country, and for his desire to stay and work there.”

The statement, which was instigated by the International Coalition for Filmmakers at Risk in collaboration with a group of filmmaker in the U.S. and Europe, follows a similar letter of protest published by Cannes on Tuesday that said the festival “condemns the judicial persecution of Jafar Panahi and calls for the lifting of all restrictions that prevent him from traveling, creating and expressing himself freely.”

Other filmmakers to add their names to the latest statement of protest include Kleber Mendonça Filho, Laura Poitras, Rithy Panh, Lucrecia Martel, Liz Garbus, Asif Kapadia, Jacques Audiard, Olivier Assayas, Roger Ross Williams, Catherine Breillat, Dominik Moll and Abigail Disney, as well as actor-writer-director Arthur Harari.

As well as Alberto Barbera at Venice and Tricia Tuttle at Berlinale, other festival chiefs to sign the statement include Locarno’s Giona Nazzaro, Rotterdam’s Vanja Kaludjercic, New York’s Dennis Lim, Telluride’s Julie Huntsinger, Karlovy Vary’s Karel Och and IDFA’s Isabel Arrate Fernandez.
