The two of them had standout roles in the movie, and we’re dying for them to get some more screen time together. “He is an enigma himself,” Debicki told Variety about Pattinson’s Bond casting. “He’s beautiful, and he’s funny and he’s smart. I think he’s perfect. I’m so thrilled.” — Jordan Moreau

- Idris Elba Having spent so many years being tipped by the media for the 007 job — and then being asked about Bond in every interview — it feels only right that Idris Elba be given a juicy bad guy role to play. But this is no consolation prize for the Brit, who has excelled in intimidating, scene-commanding villainy on more than one occasion, including as the brooding and calculating Stringer Bell in his “The Wire” breakout, the ruthless mercenary leading a group of child soldiers in “Beasts of No Nation,” the genuine action movie baddie in “Hobbs & Shaw” and, er, the master criminal feline Macavity in “Cats.” OK, fine. — Alex Ritman

- Colin Farrell Colin Farrell has already gone toe-to-toe with Pattinson, buried under prosthetics as Oz Cobb in “The Batman.” The Oscar nominee from “The Banshees of Inisherin” has played a hit man with a conscience in films like “In Bruges” and an assassin as Bullseye in “Daredevil.” Now let’s picture that Irish charm curdling into something far more dangerous, like an arms baron who’s a blast to watch even as he’s trying to kill Bond. Do it. — Clayton Davis

- Michael Fassbender Fassbender spent years playing an empathetic villain in Fox’s “X-Men” series as a young Magneto. Now, he’s played a suave spy in last year’s surprise sleeper hit “Black Bag,” a cold assassin in David Fincher’s 2023 thriller “The Killer” and a CIA officer in “The Agency” on Paramount+. He certainly fits the bill to star in a Bond movie, perhaps as a double-crossing 00 spy who faces off against Pattinson. –Jordan Moreau

- Rebecca Ferguson Rebecca Ferguson has shown she can keep up with Tom Cruise’s Ethan Hunt in the “Mission: Impossible” franchise, so it could be time for her to face off against cinema’s other iconic man of mystery. Outside of her three “Mission” films, she recently took on internal affairs as a high-level situation room officer in Kathryn Bigelow’s “House of Dynamite.” Ferguson is probably best known for her leading role in Apple TV’s “Silo” as Juliette Nichols, a mechanic-turned-post-apocalyptic liberator. It also helps she’s in Denis’ orbit already with the “Dune” franchise. She’s already a pro at unraveling a conspiracy, so she is sure to be an expert at weaving one together in the face of Bond. — Jack Dunn

- Walton Goggins Walton Goggins is already one of Amazon’s most valuable assets, starring in Prime Video’s post-apocalyptic drama “Fallout” as a 200-year-old zombie cowboy. Of course, Goggins made Boyd Crowder, the silver-tongued soul of FX’s crime drama “Justified,” one of his most memorable creations. Plus, he nearly stole the show on HBO’s anthology series “The White Lotus” as the haunted Rick. Some of the best Bond villains are a little unhinged and completely charming, and Goggins brings both. –Clayton Davis

- Jake Gyllenhaal Villeneuve and Gyllenhaal have already worked together on “Prisoners” back in 2013, and they’re long overdue for a reunion. Gyllenhaal has played a wide variety of unsettling bad guys in recent years, like a grimy journalist in “Nightcrawler,” a theatrical Mysterio in “Spider-Man” and a smooth-talking criminal in “Ambulance.” He’s also bulked up and trained in UFC fighting for two “Road House” movies. His Bond villain could mix all of these past roles into one and be a true chameleon. — Jordan Moreau

- Tom Hiddleston Isn’t it safe to say that AMC’s “The Night Manager” was pretty much Tom Hiddleston’s 007 audition tape? He reprised his role as former British intelligence operative Jonathan Pine earlier this year in the second season streaming on Prime Video. However, the tuxedo never came, so maybe being another scene-stealing bad boy can get him into the fold. As Loki in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Hiddleston proved audiences will adore a villain even while he betrays everyone. Maybe casting him as a disgraced MI6 golden boy, or an agent who was supposed to get the number but then didn’t, will let him spend the whole movie proving he actually deserved it. — Clayton Davis

- Angelina Jolie Angelina Jolie has already shared the screen with one 007 when Daniel Craig played her rival in “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider” (2001). What if she took a shot at the next one? The Oscar winner of “Girl, Interrupted” has played both sides of the spy game in films like “Salt” and “Mr. & Mrs. Smith.” She also gave Disney one of its most iconic villains in the live-action format with “Maleficent.” Let her bring a menacing rage to the MI6 team and watch what happens. –Clayton Davis

- Daniel Kaluuya Daniel Kaluuya is reuniting with his “Judas and the Black Messiah” director, Shaka King, on a new Amazon MGM movie, “The Parlay,” so technically he’s already in the family, right? For anyone who saw Steve McQueen’s “Widows,” they’ll remember how terrifying the Oscar winner can be as he played the enforcer Jatemme and delivered one of the most chilling henchmen of the past decade. Let’s not forget “Black Panther,” where he played W’Kabi, the trusted friend who betrays his king. Once thrown out as a worthy contender to play Bond, this Londoner, with his knack for exuding menace, would have MI6 very worried. — Clayton Davis

- Barry Keoghan Barry Keoghan has already said that, rather than Bond, he’d prefer to play the villain. Still, he’s certainly got the credentials to prove it. From a sinister teen who embarks on a campaign of revenge in “The Killing of a Sacred Deer” to a swaggering, volatile gangster in “Calm with Horses” to the murderous manipulator of “Saltburn,” the Irishman has shown he could be 007’s perfect, cherubic master of menace. And then there’s that deleted scene in “The Batman” as the Joker opposite Pattinson. Time for a proper face-off between the two. — Alex Ritman

- Cillian Murphy From Nolan to Villeneuve, Murphy could follow Robert Pattinson from one major director to another. Murphy hit the lotto with his “Oppenheimer” Oscar win, and playing a Bond villain could be his second wave. We know he’s up to the challenge after seeing him as J. Robert Oppenheimer, the Scarecrow in “Batman Begins” and Tommy Shelby in “Peaky Blinders.” Aside from a cameo in “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” Netflix’s “Peaky Blinders” movie and a return in “A Quiet Place 3,” Murphy’s slate has been too quiet since “Oppenheimer” and a Bond movie would be the perfect big-screen welcome back. — Jordan Moreau

- Brad Pitt Upon learning that Pattinson would be Bond, Pitt pitched himself to play the villain at his “Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” premiere. Pitt has produced “Mickey 17” and “The Lost City of Z,” both of which starred Pattinson, so the two already have a connection. “I love what he’s been doing. I love his choices. I think he’s the real deal. That’s good. A good call, I like it,” Pitt said, then threw his hat in the ring to play the bad guy. “I’d like to do that. My man Javier [Bardem] did it so well. It’s tall shoes, but I’d take that on.” –Jordan Moreau

- Jesse Plemons Nobody in Hollywood makes politeness more terrifying than Jesse Plemons. He was Todd, the soft-spoken killer of AMC’s crime series “Breaking Bad.” In Alex Garland’s “Civil War,” he turned one question, “What kind of American are you?“ into one of the frightening scenes of the year, in a one-scene wonder, no less. A Bond villain who never raises his voice and never apologizes before he pulls the trigger. That’s what exactly Plemons does best. The Oscar nominee of “The Power of the Dog,” who won Best Actor at Cannes for “Kinds of Kindness,” is playing Plutarch Heavensbee in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” this year, a role originated by the late Philip Seymour Hoffman. And famously, also played a villain in “Mission: Impossible III” (2006). Let’s continue the trajectory. — Clayton Davis

- Florence Pugh Florence Pugh may be on many fans’ lists as a potential Bond girl (and so did Variety), but it seems the Brit — who stars alongside Robert Pattinson in “Dune: Part Three” — would rather go a different route. Speaking at Elle’s Women in Hollywood event shortly after 007 was cast, she said she’d messaged Villeneuve to say: “Congratulations on finding your Bond, nice catch. Any villains the size of a 5ft 4in female?” While Pugh’s roles haven’t yet seen her dip into full-scale global terrorism, as Cathy in the recent “East of Eden” adaptation, she has shown she could certainly explore her darker side. — Alex Ritman

- Bill Skarsgård With his shape-shifting ability to transform into a menacing clown or a cadaverous vampire, Bill Skarsgård can become just about any villain the Bond creative team imagines. Skarsgård’s roles in “It,” “Nosferatu,” “Barbarian,” and “The Crow” are just a few of the horror-tinged roles he’s inhabited, suggesting his take on a Bond villain could lean more toward the grotesquely menacing side. The Swedish actor even appeared with Robert Pattinson, a fellow famous vampire, in the Netflix movie “The Devil All the Time,” though they didn’t share any scenes. –Pat Saperstein

- Kristen Stewart As soon as Pattinson’s name was floated as 007, hordes of Twihards were immediately fan-casting Stewart to give the Bond universe a “Twilight” crossover. But instead of playing a Bond Girl, Stewart would be a much more entertaining choice as a villain. Please, Amazon MGM, make this ultimate Bella Swan and Edward Cullen fan fiction come true. Better yet, cast Taylor Lautner as a henchman to Stewart’s Bond villain. — Jordan Moreau

- Tilda Swinton A great James Bond villain is known for their striking, singular presence – and who better to provide that presence than Tilda Swinton? Her otherworldly, androgynous persona has been put to good use by everyone from the Avengers to Wes Anderson, Bong Joon Ho and the Coen brothers, and she could easily switch on the evil vibes as a Bond villain. Swinton hasn’t worked with Robert Pattinson yet, but Pattinson is a big admirer of her performance in 2008’s “Julia.” “I think that’s one of the great performances, and it’s kind of criminally underseen,” he told Rotten Tomatoes. –Pat Saperstein

- Fernanda Torres In “I’m Still Here,” Fernanda Torres played Eunice Paiva, a woman standing up to a military dictatorship and the role earned her a Golden Globe statue and an Oscar nomination for best actress. While on the awards circuit, the Brazilian star knew exactly what she wanted to do with her next big venture: play a Bond villain. “I would love to be the secretary of a James Bond villain,” she said on the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast. “And just say, ‘He will be waiting for you in the next room, Mr. Bond.’ That’s it. That’s my dream. Just this line. That’s all I want to do.” Imagine Torres as the power behind the throne: a Rio de Janeiro media baroness who smiles for the cameras while quietly buying off half the government? Give her what she wants! — Clayton Davis

items.title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Sets First-Ever Live Finale for Season 35
items.description: For the first time in “Dancing With the Stars” history, the ballroom competition show will air its finale live.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: For the first time in “Dancing With the Stars” history, the ballroom competition show will air its finale live.

The three-hour finale will air on Nov. 24 from 8:00-11:00 p.m. ET, 7:00-10:00 p.m. CT, 6:00-9:00 p.m. MT and 5:00-8:00 p.m. PT on ABC and Disney+. The finale will re-air from 8:00-11:00 p.m. PT and stream the next day on Hulu.

Currently in its 35th season, six celebrities remain in the competition heading into Tuesday night’s semi-finals: Tatyana Ali, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins, Harry Shum Jr. and Connor Wood. The following week, the remaining couples will compete for the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, performing three routines each: a Judges’ Choice Dance, the return of the Instant Dance Challenge and a Freestyle.

The season’s September premiere reached a strong 6.7 million viewers, a 24% increase from the performance of the Season 34 premiere. The episode also marked the series’ best opener in six years, since Season 29 launched with 8.1 million viewers in 2020.
And the audience is still watching along. “Dancing with the Stars” hit a season high with 6.91 million same-day viewers during last week’s Grammy Night.

Season 35 cast members also included now-eliminated celebrities Jenna Dewan, Jackson Olson, Julia Stiles, Ciara Miller, Conner Leavitt, Guillermo Rodriguez, Taylor Hanson, Tyler Cameron, Sarah Jane Nader and Giada De Laurentiis. The reigning champions are Robert Irwin and pro Whitney Carson, who took home the Mirrorball Trophy in Season 34.
“Dancing with the Stars” is produced in front of a live audience by BBC Studios Los Angeles Productions.

items.title: Netflix Eyes Return to Cannes After 10 Years as Festival Lobbies for Joel Coen’s ‘Jack of Spades,’ Starring Josh O’Connor
items.description: The ice appears to be thawing between Netflix and Cannes.
items.author: Alex Ritman; Elsa Keslassy
paragraphs: The ice appears to be thawing between Netflix and Cannes.

The streamer, which hasn’t debuted a film at the festival in almost a decade due to France’s strict rules around theatrical releases, is eyeing a return to the south of France in 2027, Variety has learned. Ted Sarandos suggested as much earlier this year, when he told Variety he hoped to “do something special” for Cannes’ 80th edition.
Now it turns out that Cannes boss Thierry Frémaux has also been making a push to bring Joel Coen’s “Jack of Spades” to the festival for more than a year, sources say. Netflix declined to comment.

The American gothic mystery, starring Josh O’Connor, Patsy Ferran, Frances McDormand, Lesley Manville and Damian Lewis, was at one point expected to be ready for this year’s Cannes, then Venice, but is now on track for next May. Coen also has a strong relationship with Frémaux, who honored him alongside his brother Ethan at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival.
But there’s a catch. Netflix recently acquired “Jack of Spades,” complicating plans for what would otherwise have been a natural Cannes contender.

Under the festival’s rules, all films competing for the Palme d’Or must receive a theatrical release in France. That would trigger the country’s strict windowing regulations, forcing Netflix to wait 15 months before making the film available to French subscribers — something the streamer isn’t prepared to do. And while Cannes would very much like to have Netflix back, it isn’t willing to bend its rules to make that happen.

That means the only way for Netflix to return to Cannes with “Jack of Spades” would be out of competition, which has been a deal-breaker for Sarandos. Sources say Frémaux has been trying to convince Netflix and Sarandos that an out-of-competition premiere can be just as prestigious as a competition slot, pointing to the recent examples of Martin Scorsese’s Apple-backed “Killers of the Flower Moon” and Tom Cruise’s “Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning,” both of which made a major splash on the Croisette without competing for the Palme d’Or.

But recent changes could help smooth the path towards a Netflix comeback on the Croisette. The streamer’s newly-appointed chief content officer Peter Rice is a longtime friend of Cannes who has known Frémaux since his days at Searchlight. His arrival could help bring the two sides closer after years of tensions over theatrical releases.

Netflix may also have good reason to seek a return to Cannes. After losing a few big-name filmmakers, the streamer could be looking to ramp up its prestige profile. While it has increasingly turned to Venice to launch major awards contenders, including Guillermo del Toro’s “Frankenstein” and Noah Baumbach’s “Jay Kelly,” Cannes remains the world’s biggest film festival and arguably the most powerful platform for launching auteur-driven movies.

Netflix knows that better than most. Despite not bringing its own movies to the festival in 10 years, it has snapped up several on the ground there. In 2024, it bought Jacques Audiard’s “Emilia Pérez” which went on earn 13 Oscar nominations and win two Oscars, including best actress for Zoe Saldana. This year, it acquired “La Bola Negra,” now its main hope for awards season — with many tipping it for best picture.

“Jack of Spades” would seem a perfect fit for the festival, where Joel Coen is one of its favorite auteurs. Alongside his brother Ethan, the director has brought films including “Barton Fink,” which won the Palme d’Or and best director awards, “No Country for Old Men” and “Inside Llewyn Davis.”

Netflix hasn’t taken a film to Cannes since 2017, when it premiered both Bong Joon-ho’s “Okja” and Noah Baumbach’s “The Meyerowitz Stories.” It sparked an outcry from French exhibitors, prompting the festival to change its rules the following year to require competition films to receive theatrical releases in France.

The streamer has, however, softened its stance on theatrical releases considerably. “La Bola Negra” is in the middle of a 46-day theatrical rollout, the longest Netflix has given any of its films to date. Next year, “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” will have an exclusive theatrical run, as will Taika Waititi’s animated take on Roald Dahl, “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory.”

items.title: Disney+ and Hulu App Merger Slated to Be Complete in December
items.description: Disney‘s years-long effort to unify the Disney+ and Hulu apps is “nearly complete,” Mouse House execs said, as the company looks to concentrate its streaming firepower on the Disney+ platform.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Disney‘s years-long effort to unify the Disney+ and Hulu apps is “nearly complete,” Mouse House execs said, as the company looks to concentrate its streaming firepower on the Disney+ platform.
The company made the announcement in reporting earnings for the September 2026 quarter.

Beginning this December, Disney+ and Hulu bundle subscribers “will have a fully unified experience on Disney+, including live TV and select premium add-ons, creating a more seamless way to discover and engage with the breadth of content across our brands and franchises,” CEO Josh D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston said in their quarterly letter to shareholders. “We believe our continued focus on product and technology will yield further benefits in engagement and churn over time.”

Also in December, Disney expects to begin introducing creator content on Disney+ through its recent agreement with TikTok. The TikTok content rollout will be “strategically aligned” to the lead-up to Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday” theatrical premiere on Dec. 18, according to the Disney execs.
“We are also adding more vertical video, live sports and podcasts to the [Disney+] platform, while continuing to explore other emerging content genres,” D’Amaro and Johnston said.

Disney’s integration of Hulu and Disney+ kicked off in 2023 under then-CEO Bob Iger, two years before the company closed its deal with Comcast to buy out NBCUniversal‘s one-third stake in Hulu in June 2025.
Disney has not announced a sunset date for the Hulu app, and as of now Hulu stand-alone subscriptions in the U.S. continue to be available.

This September, Disney announced another round of streaming price hikes, its fourth rate increases in as many years. The pricing strategy is aimed at pushing consumers toward bundles: The Disney+/Hulu Premium bundle increased two dollars, from $19.99 to $21.99/month, which is nearly half what it costs if you purchase them separately, while the ad-supported Disney+/Hulu bundle remained unchanged at $12.99/month (just 50 cents more than each of the services purchased individually).

According to Disney’s D’Amaro and Johnston, ESPN “plays an important role in the overall Disney portfolio by contributing live and on-demand offerings to Disney+, lifting engagement and supporting revenue growth, and encouraging users to upgrade to the Disney+, Hulu, ESPN bundle.”

This fall, Disney increased the volume of sports content we offer Disney+ subscribers without the need for an ESPN subscription. That has included the simulcast of “College GameDay” on Disney+ and adding more live college football games and select NFL games, which kicked off with Dallas Cowboys vs. Philadelphia Eagles on Oct. 26. Following the expansion of ESPN content into Europe and select Asia-Pacific markets this year, ESPN now reaches consumers through Disney+ in about 100 markets.

items.title: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: A Worthier Prequel to the Dystopian Battle Royale, Powered by Joseph Zada’s Star-Making Turn
items.description: The sixth movie in the $3.3 billion Hunger Games franchise contends, like many series entries before it, with a somewhat jarring tonal discordancy between the glitzy spectacle and grotesque political satire of the Capitol and the emotionally loaded brutality o
items.author: David Rooney
paragraphs: The sixth movie in the $3.3 billion Hunger Games franchise contends, like many series entries before it, with a somewhat jarring tonal discordancy between the glitzy spectacle and grotesque political satire of the Capitol and the emotionally loaded brutality of the Arena, where children and teens from each of the 12 districts of Panem are forced to fight for their lives until only one is standing. But Sunrise on the Reaping overcomes that imbalance because the horror of the survival battle and the sorrow of the losses sustained are rendered with as much scalding pathos as suspense and excitement.

Francis Lawrence, who has directed all but the first of the features adapted from Suzanne Collins’ hugely popular YA novels, knows what he’s doing. But the surprise asset here is Australian actor Joseph Zada in a breakout performance as 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, the rebellious victor of the 50th Hunger Games.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Cast: Joseph Zada, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Ben Wang, Billy Porter, Molly McCann, Iona Bell, Lili Taylor, Percy Daggs IV, Iris Apatow, Edvyn Ryding, Jhaleil Swaby, Laura Marcus, Scot Greenan
Director: Francis Lawrence
Screenwriters: Billy Ray, Michael Lesslie, based on the novel by Suzanne Collins
Rated PG-13, 2 hours 43 minutes

Played as an adult by Woody Harrelson in the first four films, Haymitch was subsequently forced to serve as a mentor to contestants every year but remained furtively on the side of the resistance. Zada (seen recently as Cal on Netflix’s East of Eden) doesn’t have much physical resemblance to Harrelson, but the voice is convincingly that of the Haymitch we know, coming into manhood with firm convictions born out of injustice and providing a resonant link to the earlier films.

Invested with tenacity, kindness and heartrending vulnerability by Zada, Haymitch provides a much more poignant and involving origin story than that of Coriolanus Snow in the lumbering first prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. The autocratic Capitol leader would go on to consolidate his power by using the televised Games to keep the Panem population scared and under control.

Set 40 years after Songbirds and Snakes and 24 years before the first Hunger Games movie, Sunrise on the Reaping opens on Haymitch’s 16th birthday, which coincides with the second Quarter Quell, when the names of “tributes” from each district are drawn to enter the Arena. Being a special edition that happens just once every 25 years, the traditional choice of one male and one female has been doubled to two of each.

Haymitch initially is not among the four selected tributes for District 12, the grimly industrial coal mining sector where everyone appears to be living on or below the poverty line. But when one of the chosen boys tries to make a run for it and is shot by the Stormtrooper-like “Peacekeepers,” Haymitch is drawn into a skirmish and dropped into the vacant slot as punishment.

The showbiz cynicism of the operation is illustrated by Plutarch Heavensbee — Jesse Plemons in the role previously played by Philip Seymour Hoffman as an older man, following his promotion to Head Gamekeeper. Designated by the Capitol to oversee the nationwide broadcast, Plutarch dashes about giving camera directions and insisting on do-overs to maximize the drama of tributes being painfully separated from their loved ones and ushered off to almost certain death. As in the propaganda films of most dictatorial regimes, the heavily edited televised content removes all signs of messy rebellion and anti-Capitol sentiment.

The separation is especially wrenching for Haymitch from his widowed mother and adoring younger brother, but equally or perhaps even more so from his girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), who tends geese on her father’s farm. (She’s a descendant of Lucy Gray Baird, the winner of the 10th Hunger Games, played by Rachel Zegler in Songbirds and Snakes.)

The sobriety of the farewells, however, is undercut by the unrestrained caricatures of some high-ranking Capitol officials. Every time the movie lurches into high-camp excess it lessens the emotional weight. The most intrusive example is Glenn Close, exploring new frontiers for over-the-top as Drusilla Sickle, her contemptuous cruelty fueled by her indignation over being assigned to chaperone the District 12 tributes, whom she regards as grimy subhumans.

Wheeled out onstage like Hannibal Lecter to draw the lottery, Drusilla is trussed up in what looks like a leather bumblebee costume, with a red Aunt Gladys wig topped by a raven fascinator, crazy-lady makeup and a mouthful of prosthetic dentures that even Tilda Swinton might balk at. All the better to chomp on the scenery. Shrieking like a pantomime dame, Close goes full Norma Desmond and then flips to Joan Crawford mode, losing her shit with a riding crop (see 1955’s Queen Bee) when she’s sassed by Haymitch’s smart-mouthed fellow tribute Maysilee (Mckenna Grace), a shopkeeper’s daughter.

Even higher on the shrill scale is Drusilla’s husband, Capitol stylist Magno Stift (Billy Porter), sashaying around in extravagant finery with tiny live golden snakes as earrings. He declines to dress the District 12 unfortunates, sharing his lunatic wife’s opinion that they are not fit for couture. Mercifully, Magno is not around for long, making way for the familiar figure of Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning, amusingly playing a younger version of the character originated onscreen by Elizabeth Banks). The future chaperone briskly takes charge of 12’s tributes, giving their outfits an elegant upgrade before the opening ceremony chariot parade.

While Fanning gives Effie a shot of humanity beneath her giddy glam manner, the same cannot be said of Kieran Culkin as preening TV broadcast host Caesar Flickerman. “Look alive, children, while you still can!” he tells the tributes in a bit of gallows humor that might have been funny had he not been so obnoxiously glib. Where Stanley Tucci offset Caesar’s callous showmanship with mischievous charisma in the first films, Culkin just plays sarcastic mockery. His Caesar is a charmless creep.

While the sinister combination of razzle-dazzle and fascist barbarity has always been essential to the Hunger Games world, it’s a relief here when the Capitol monsters take a backseat to the young people whose lives hang in the balance. From the very beginning, we see what a beloved figure Haymitch is in the village, how pure is the love he shares with Lenore and how tender and reassuring he is with the youngest of the district’s tributes, Louella (Molly McCann).

They make a pact to be allies, extending also to Maysilee and fourth District 12 tribute Wyatt (Ben Wang), even if his sideline as an oddsmaker on the Games earns him some initial distrust. But when tragedy strikes early on during the chariot parade, Haymitch stares down Coriolanus Snow, his eyes expressing fury, disgust and defiance. While that uneasy moment will be cut for the broadcast, it was witnessed by the public at the opening ceremony, an embarassment to Snow that puts a target on Haymitch’s back.

Played as a youth by Tom Blyth in Songbirds and Snakes and by Donald Sutherland as an older man in the original Hunger Games quadrilogy, Snow here has the soft-spoken menace and steely authority of Ralph Fiennes. His intelligence is unquestionable but he’s also paranoid and gullible about his consigliere Plutarch and given to fits of petulant rage.

The certainty that Snow will ensure he dies an agonizing death in the Arena makes Haymitch rethink his alliances, telling the other District 12 tributes that it’s not safe to be around him. But he does enter cautiously into a pact with Ampert (Percy Daggs IV) from District 3, who informs him that other districts are open to collaboration in order to prevail over the elite contestants from Districts 1 and 2. Known as Career tributes, these are the most frequent victors in the Games, due to their wealth, privilege and extensive combat and weaponry training.

Ampert was entered into the games by Snow in retaliation for the attempt to sabotage Capitol communications by the boy’s father, Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), now forced to serve as a mentor but still secretly plotting. The mentors specifically assigned to District 12 are past victors Wiress (Maya Hawke) and Mags (Lili Taylor); neither actor is given a lot to do but they are a welcome presence — warm, supportive and candid with the tributes.

Lawrence and screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie have relatively little time and breathing room to give the more ruthless Arena opponents much character definition. But two District 1 Careers are memorably lethal — Silka (Laura Marcus) with her double-headed axes and muscle-bound Panache (Jhaleil Swaby) with his ferocious anger and strength.

The nail-biting Arena action is vicious and bloody, sustaining high stakes as Haymitch attempts to break the Capitol’s brain hub, which sends in “mutts” — genetically modified animals, from electrified butterflies to killer squirrels and birds — to overwhelm the tributes earmarked for death.

Zada is the beating heart of the film, mutinous but neither cocky nor fearless, and he has stirring scenes with Ampert and Maysilee. The hair from one of Britney Spears’ blonde bangs periods is a distraction, but Grace is fiery in the latter role — gutsy, determined and a loyal friend to Haymitch once their allegiance is cemented. She’s also handy with a poisoned blow dart. Iona Bell as a young substitute tribute drugged into compliance by the Capitol also has touching moments.
Other cast standouts are Peak, lovely as Haymitch’s sweetheart; and the always dependable Plemons, who deftly navigates Plutarch’s double duty as a Capitol official playing for the other side.

Bolstered by DP Jo Willems’ muscular camerawork, James Newton Howard’s soaring score and Uli Hanisch’s imaginative production design, Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies. There’s even a brief appearance by baby Katniss Everdeen to complete the circle. It’s impossible not to feel sympathy when young people are being sacrificed in horrific ways for the ritualistic entertainment of the masses and the power-flexing of a pitiless overlord. A moving coda set many years later re-introduces familiar faces that will add to the satisfaction for longtime franchise fans.

items.title: Disney Expects to Increase Annual Content Spend to $26 Billion Next Year
items.description: The Walt Disney Co. isn’t slowing down when it comes to spending major cash on original content.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: The Walt Disney Co. isn’t slowing down when it comes to spending major cash on original content.

The company disclosed Tuesday in its quarterly earnings report that it expects to spend $26 billion on content in fiscal 2027 (which started this quarter), up 9 percent from the $24 billion or so it spent in fiscal 2026.
Disney says that the increase in spending is being driven by increased investment in international programming, growing sports rights costs, and the timing of feature film production spend.

Disney has been pursuing more international programming as it seeks to grow its streaming business abroad, while sports rights like the NBA and NFL continue to rise like clockwork every year. Film production, meanwhile, can be lumpy, with some years with a lot of physical production and other years with less.

For comparison, the newly-formed Skydance is telling Hollywood that it is committing to spend some $30 billion annually on content, inclusive of sports, films and TV, while Netflix is spending $20 billion on content this year. Comcast is in the $25 billion range.

KPMG, in an analysis released last week, noted how more and more professional content spend is being sent toward creators and live sports, a trend that is true for Disney, which has been adding creator content to Disney+, and which continues to bulk up ESPN.
But Disney is also cutting costs, revealing plans to generate $3 billion in run-rate synergies by 2029… with the savings largely being plowed into more content and experiences.

items.title: In ‘The Matriarch,’ Germany’s First Film With an All-Vietnamese Lead Cast, Human Trafficking Thriller Meets Family Drama
items.description: Kim, 17, lives with her emotionally distant mother and younger brother near Germany’s Baltic coast. Their home has a secret space behind a family shrine where strangers come and go. The strangers are Vietnamese migrants. But the mother is not hiding them out o
items.author: Georg Szalai
paragraphs: Kim, 17, lives with her emotionally distant mother and younger brother near Germany’s Baltic coast. Their home has a secret space behind a family shrine where strangers come and go. The strangers are Vietnamese migrants. But the mother is not hiding them out of the goodness of her heart. She is The Matriarch (Die Matriarchin), and she runs an illegal trafficking operation that brings Vietnamese migrants to Europe.

The sensitive Kim knows that money can’t buy her mother’s love and recognition. But when an associate of her mother defects to launch a rival operation, the young woman looks to seize the opportunity to prove herself to her mother while navigating her first romance. Can Kim earn the matriarch’s respect while staying true to her own moral compass?

The Matriarch is the second feature from writer-director Alison Kuhn. And it is the first German film with an all-Vietnamese lead cast. Thriller meets coming-of-age drama in a movie that explores migration, human trafficking, family dynamics and inherited expectations. The movie premieres in the main competition of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

“I’ve always felt the urge to tell a story set within the German-Vietnamese community I was born into and to explore the complex, often unspoken, dynamics of mother-daughter relationships within it,” says Kuhn. “Through extensive conversations with members of the diasporic community in Berlin, I encountered recurring emotional patterns: intergenerational tensions, inherited trauma and, to my surprise, the persistent presence of human trafficking – a subject that remains largely unnoticed by the wider German public.”
The ensemble cast features newcomer Lissy-Marie Nguyen as Kim, Tuyen Do (Shadow and Bone, Enola Holmes) as her mother, Viet Pham, Trang Le Hong, Viet Long Hoang and Marlon Minh-Hai Leyck.

Written and directed by Kuhn, The Matriarch was produced by Martin Lehwald and Philipp Goeser for Schiwago Film, with Paula Klossner and Stephan Buske of Tidewater Pictures as co-producers. The movie received support from ZDF – Das Kleine Fernsehspiel, MV Filmförderung, Medienboard Berlin-Brandenburg and Nordmedia. The director of photography is Jan Mayntz, with Christian Zipfel as editor. Pluto Film is handling sales. Watch the trailer for The Matriarch here.

Kuhn has been a director on the series Druck, Watch Me and Shadow Leaks, which reached the Netflix Top 10 in Germany. Her 2025 feature debut Holy Meat, about a village’s amateur production of the Passion of Christ that spirals into a blasphemous rave, premiered at Filmfest Munich and won the jury prize at Cinequest in California.

Ahead of the Tallinn world premiere of The Matriarch, Kuhn talked to THR about the research she did for the movie, combining genre filmmaking with family drama and her hopes for more opportunities for Vietnamese creatives in Germany and beyond.

What’s different for the creative between directing series and films is that she also writes her features. “They are stories that have been accompanying me for years, and it was the same in this case,” she tells THR. Actually, several years ago, Christian Cloos, the commissioning editor of ZDF – Das Kleine Fernsehspiel, asked her if there was any story she wanted to tell. “Well, there is this story about Vietnamese families because half of my family is Vietnamese, and the other half is German,” Kuhn recalls telling him. She started sharing ideas and stories from her own family.

“But it became too private,” she tells THR. “The film was not a thriller back then. It was more a classical social drama, and then I realized I had to find an abstraction. I had to find another perspective.”

That led her to talk to and about Vietnamese people in Germany, “and I collected stories, I collected issues that they had, and I started noticing patterns there. There were recurring themes that concerned them. It was a lot about family tensions, intergenerational tensions, responsibility, being pushed into certain roles and sacrificing being close to family members in order to help them grow.”

And there was one key figure that kept being mentioned. “Especially the role of mothers, Vietnamese mothers, was something that came up again and again, and so I started creating this character,” Kuhn shares. “Another thing that came up in these intense research interviews was the aspect of human trafficking, which is very present in Germany, in Berlin especially. So, I got the idea that I could translate what I wanted to say about mother-daughter relationships into this suspenseful thriller, crime genre without losing the heart of the story. At the heart of it, the film is a mother-daughter story, but it had another guise, or clothing, around it.”

Audiences outside of Berlin and Germany will find themselves caring about the characters in The Matriarch, and the filmmaker says going deep and local helps with that. “The more specific you get as a filmmaker, the more you can tell stories about the larger issues of life,” she explains. “The emotions underneath all these conflicts that might be culture-related are really universal, and everyone knows them. Everyone wants to be loved by their parents and wants to be appreciated and wants to find their own way. So there are a lot of things there that people from diasporic communities can relate to in particular, but that everyone else also really [understands].”

The human trafficking side of the story in The Matriarch contains some language that will surprise, maybe even shock, audiences. For example, when someone discusses the idea of opening a “flower shop,” which turns out to be code for something much more sinister.

“I always love intense research,” Kuhn tells THR. “Before I shoot or write a fictional piece, it’s so important for me to know what the actual situation is in order to sort out which parts you need to represent in a realistic, documentary kind of way, and in which parts you can be a little bit more free. In this case, I talked to a lot of investigative journalists and also to the German federal police. They granted me cool insights. I really wanted to understand the structures of these networks and all these operational things. So, for example, flowers, as you mentioned, is a code word for prostitutes. There are a lot of code words that I found very interesting.”

But she also took creative license and freedom to enhance the story. “There are fantastic little elements in the film, such as the altar in the living room, which is also the door to a secret room,” the filmmaker notes. “This is not something I found in my research. It’s based on rooms where these people have to sleep, often under very poor conditions, but there’s not this mystery door.”

Now, how about the cast and how it breaks new ground? “Yes, we actually are the first German feature film with an all-Vietnamese lead cast,” Kuhn says with pride. “It’s about time because there is so much talent there that has gone unseen and that has had to put up with small roles – one-liners or very stereotypical roles in German movies and series. So it was so cool to have this ensemble, and they all were so appreciative of getting the chance to play parts that have more facets and are more than just one thing on the surface.”

That said, it was a “hard” casting process “because there are not that many Vietnamese actors and actresses, especially over the age of 45, I would say,” Kuhn explains. “There are basically no trained actors and actresses here because of structural and also racist reasons. They did not have the chance to go to acting school and stuff like this. So we had a worldwide casting, especially for the role of the mother and found Tuyen Do, who is based in London.”

How did she find young Lissy-Marie Nguyen? “She didn’t have any acting experience,” which you wouldn’t believe once you see the film, the director says. “We found her through her high school. A few years ago, I shot a youth series at a Berlin high school, and they have a huge Vietnamese population there. So our casting director, Stephanie Meile, who is great, wrote to a lot of schools with a lot of Vietnamese families, and we had an open audition process, and she just came in like a force of nature. She has this raw talent. I’m so proud of her because after our shoot, she has continued acting.”

Kuhn hopes that The Matriarch can help open more doors for Vietnamese talent. “I have high hopes that people in the industry finally see these talented people,” she tells THR. “I hope it will not be the last German film with an all-Vietnamese cast. And I think it’s so important to tell different stories from different perspectives. When you talk about movies about human trafficking, there are some in Germany, but most of them are told from an investigator’s perspective, and they look down on the people in these networks. But to me, it was very important to tell a story from the perspective of the people involved and show what dramatic situations have pushed them into that place.”

That social and political context is often chilling. “You see in some scenes with the mother that, for her, it also has roots going back to the GDR, where contract workers from Vietnam came over and were discriminated against by the state,” the writer-director notes. “And they were not allowed to interact with the German community, have children with German people, or learn the language. And after the Wall came down, they were just left alone and had no way to earn money to support their families. Of course, some of these trafficking networks grew out of that.”

Kuhn didn’t run into any opposition or backlash when she pitched The Matriarch as a genre experience. “But I think there’s also a want here of having more female-driven thrillers because there aren’t that many,” she tells THR. “I looked up a while ago what percentage of thrillers are directed by women, and it was really shockingly low. It seems like this genre has been reserved for men. Also, badass characters have been reserved for men. So, it was very important to me to create this character of the mother who’s powerful and really sets the tone.”

And that comes not only through force but something also through silence or lower-key but effective actions. “Showing another way of being a leading figure was important because I was asking myself what makes the difference between a female and a male leader of such a network,” Kuhn says. “It was very interesting to dive into that. She’s not the one with the muscles. She has her people who do that for her. But she has maybe another way of making deals. And she might have another way of putting emotional pressure on people. So that’s very interesting about a female boss and often unseen.”

items.title: Anne Hathaway Welcomes Third Child With Husband Adam Shulman
items.description: After a busy 2026, Anne Hathaway has ended the year with a new addition to her family.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: After a busy 2026, Anne Hathaway has ended the year with a new addition to her family.

The Oscar winner has welcomed her third child with her husband, Adam Shulman, according to photos shared by TMZ on Tuesday. The actress was spotted in public in New York City for the first time since giving birth, with her newborn baby strapped to her in a front-facing carrier.
The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to her rep for more details.

Hathaway revealed her pregnancy in June, showing off her baby bump in a video posted on Instagram. She added in the caption, “x Baby, I’m yours x,” as the song ”Baby I’m Yours” by Barbara Lewis played over the video.

The following month, the actress made an appearance on Late Night With Seth Meyers, where she admitted she and Shulman were “shocked” to be expecting again. “It’s amazing. I mean, we knew what we were doing,” Hathaway quipped to host Seth Meyers at the time. “But we were so shocked it worked … we were just so shocked it went this way. So we’re calling this one our buzzer-beater.”
The birth of Hathaway’s third baby makes her and Shulman now a family of five. The pair, who married in 2012, already have two sons, Jonathan, 10, and Jack, 6.

This year has been notably jam-packed for the actress, as she had five films hitting theaters, including Mother Mary, The Devil Wears Prada 2, The Odyssey, The End of Oak Street and Verity. And with all those projects came their respective global press tours.

Once her final film of the year, Verity, was released in October, Hathaway quipped that she planned to “vanish into a plume of smoke” and take some much-needed personal time away from the spotlight to be with her family.
“There’s been more than enough of me for quite some time,” she previously said on CBS Mornings. “And I’ve been really, really happy, but I think it’s time to leave the party.”

items.title: Chris Rock on Directing an A24 Movie and ‘Crying Like a Bitch’ in Therapy
items.description: Chris Rock enters a room a bit diffidently, like he’s feeling out what’s inside, making quiet observations about the world around him that sometimes tip over into jokes and sometimes don’t. Because today we’re meeting on the 24th floor of the World Trade Cente
items.author: Zach Baron; Richard Burbridge
paragraphs: Chris Rock enters a room a bit diffidently, like he’s feeling out what’s inside, making quiet observations about the world around him that sometimes tip over into jokes and sometimes don’t. Because today we’re meeting on the 24th floor of the World Trade Center, I will not repeat the jokes. He looks around at the setup for the interview, which is being filmed: lights and cameras and microphones everywhere. “I just shot a movie with, like, three people,” he says. “It was much lower-budget than this.”

That movie is Misty Green, Rock’s fourth feature as a director. It’s about an actress named Misty, played by Rosalind Eleazar, who has talent and who has had success but who cannot quite get out of her own way. Rock identifies and he doesn’t. “I like to say there’s a part of me that’s been every character in the movie,” he says—including Misty’s best friend, played by Anna Kendrick, who is mostly there to crack jokes and report on her own unsatisfying romantic life. The film is a portrait of Hollywood that is dystopian but not cliché; Misty goes through hell, much of it of her own making, but her talent never dims. It has a lived, almost casual quality that belies Rock’s grasp of his craft: At 61, he hasn’t lost his eye for the telling, damning detail or hypocrisy, but there is also a warmth here, a genuine love for his characters. With Misty Green, you can feel both Rock’s lifetime of experience making things for audiences, and also something new—and more finely observed emerging.

Misty Green is part of a growing tradition in Rock’s work, including the previous film he directed, 2014’s Top Five, about the highs and lows of show business—something Rock has also chronicled, in exacting autobiographical detail, in his past two comedy specials: 2018’s Tamborine (which is about, among other things, Rock’s divorce) and 2023’s Selective Outrage (about, among other things, his encounter with Will Smith at the 2022 Academy Awards ceremony).

Rock has been at times the most famous man in all of comedy. His 1996 special Bring the Pain was a cultural phenomenon on a level few humans will ever experience. But as a director, he has increasingly been drawn to smaller ’70s-style character studies of people making an earnest attempt just to figure out themselves and their demons. “I’d love to make Man on Fire or something,” he says. “It’s not really my thing. I make a tailored suit. My suits are made by hand, by one guy. And it’s okay.”
This interview has been condensed and edited; watch this cover story—an episode of GQ’s One More Question—above or on YouTube, and listen on Spotify or Apple Podcasts.
Chris Rock: No, no. We’re going to be good. I think.
“How’d you get started?” “Were you funny in school?” Stuff like that. Whatever. I get it. You guys have a job. I’m not Harry Styles. Sometimes it requires a reintroduction.

I mean, it’s a thing you worry about every day. Am I still funny? Well—you don’t worry about being funny. You worry about being professionally funny. On a world-class level. I always had a joke: If I ever did a talk show, I’d do a morning show. I wouldn’t do a late-night show. Because I would only have to be funnier than Al Roker. You know what I mean? Al’s lovely, but I think I could take him in a joke-off.
You guys have a job, and the job is to get clickbait and things you can turn into controversy, and what’s the headline that has nothing to do with the actual article.

I mean, it’s your job, though. You might have better intentions, and I appreciate your interest. But a lot of what I read, it’s like: “Oh okay.” People want to talk about your personal life. I get it. We’re in a gossipy culture. We live in a world where Andy Cohen is Norman Lear and Ryan Murphy is Steven Spielberg. That is the world we live in. So people want gossip. We’re righteous people that follow nine commandments. And the one commandment we don’t follow is Thou shall not spread false witness. We are all about spreading false witness now. That is the world we live in. And that’s what journalism, or at least entertainment journalism, has become. Not that everything’s false, but it is definitely amplified to create sides, no matter what the issue is. How’s that? How am I doing?
Misty Green, in theaters now.

Some of it is I got divorced. Nobody has a successful divorce, so that takes time. Then once it’s done, okay, you’re not sitting on the money you had before, so now you got to really make some money. So you go on tour, or two tours. So there was a lot of stand-up. There was a lot of getting my life together. You got a pandemic, you got a bunch of nonsense going on there.
I was not a great husband. I watched a lot of porn. I don’t watch porn anymore. I haven’t watched porn in five, six years.

It’s not anything I’m proud of, but it’s something I had to go through. It’s like you watch a Marvel movie, and the guy, he has to test his powers. You know what I mean? Every Marvel movie, man or woman, they have to test their powers. They’re assholes. They get these powers and they’re assholes, and they’re racing trains and they’re lifting up ocean liners and they try to go to the sun, then they crash down because they realize they’re not God. And then they start helping people. I tested my powers. I definitely realized I wasn’t God or anywhere near him, and I was severely humbled, as I should have been.

It’s basically Bring the Pain to Kill the Messenger. That’s one guy. Tamborine’s the beginning of a new guy. And that guy’s in fucking pain in Tamborine. That guy is damn near—Tamborine’s like the blues, man. Where Selective Outrage is like—there’s some pain in that one. Well, there’s a lot of pain in that one, but Tamborine is like: What have I become? [Starts singing Johnny Cash’s cover of Nine Inch Nails’ “Hurt.”] Goes away, in the end. I’m Johnny Cash with Rick Rubin, singing about my empire of dirt. That’s Tamborine. Tamborine is the fucking blues.
Yeah. I’m not one for a hint. You got to tell me exactly what the fuck you want. You have to tell me exactly what the fuck you mean.

A friend just kind of blurted it one day. You ever have somebody say something and you’re like, “Okay, let me get this looked into”? And it’s before Tamborine, but around that time. So I’m already quitting porn. You know what I mean? I’m already in a place where, “Okay, what the fuck’s wrong with me?” And I got a cognitive assessment test. And it’s like eight hours of testing to basically see—it’s the kind of thing you would get if you were bipolar or something. So it’s a lot of testing, and that’s what they came up with.

It made me realize how insensitive a lot of my behavior was throughout the years. Because it’s weird. I’ve got a friend who always says, this is a side joke, but he says, “When a schizophrenic sees a famous person, they go, ‘Ha, see? Told you!’ ” Mental illness and celebrity—it’s a weird combination there, because you think people are reacting a certain way because of celebrity. Because it’s this weird thing that you can’t quantify. So I used to just blame everything on celebrity. It’s like, “Oh, we’re not connecting because I had a chronic unique-ism.” I thought I was so fucking unique.

But also, okay, what are the symptoms? Black-and-white thinking. It’s an advantageous thing to have if you’re a comedian, black and white. Catastrophizing, great. You know what I mean? When you see one of those specials—okay, the average comedian, or even above average, probably does 40 shows before they record a special. And maybe they did 20 club things before this, so that’s 60 times onstage. My average special, I’ve gone onstage over 250 times. So I’m working it. It looks like I’m just, “Oh my God, he’s got this great insight.” But it’s like, “Yo man, I’m grinding this stuff.” Also, I have a hard time picking up on social cues, but I have a weirdly accurate ear. I can pick up on things in my ear. Sometimes I can pick up on a cue, but I can’t decipher it. I don’t know what just happened for a week, and I’m like, “Oh, that’s what she meant. Oh, that’s what he was trying to say.” It’s like my mind is working on the case. It just can’t solve it at that moment. Does that make sense?

Well, yeah. We do have this thing where everybody’s like—they brag about their therapy. Put it this way, my personal life wasn’t what I wanted it to be. And I’ll leave it at that. And that’s my relationship with everybody. So yeah, I went in there crying like a bitch. Like: What the fuck is going on?

You never come out. It’s an ongoing thing. You know what I mean? You’re always an alcoholic. So it’s a combination of therapy and what I have, NVLD, nonverbal learning disorder. So I have a person that helps me with that, and I have another therapist. I mean, it’s okay.
I mean, it’s not like a threat or anything. I’m just saying it’s okay. Whatever happened happened. Everybody saw it. I don’t really like talking about it. By the way—any awards show.

Yeah. Something happened. It wasn’t cool. And I would like to move on. I would like to—I had a nice career before it, and I know there’s a part of that that’s going to follow me the rest of my life. I got jokes. I got scripts. I got movie scripts. I got TV shows. I’m writing a book. I’m doing shit. I have a plethora of art I’m trying to get out, and that’s what I want you to pay attention to, not some crazy night.

I don’t get a lot of stuff. I honestly don’t. I mean, I probably get more offers as a director, to tell you the truth, than as an actor. It’s weird. When you’re really famous, it works for you and it works against you. So you got name recognition, but you also have people thinking they know what you can do and thinking that there’s a ceiling on your talent. So you got to fight that. The hardest thing you can do in show business is change perception. Reinvention is the hardest thing. So it’s kind of relatively easy to get famous, in the sense that it’s twice as hard to become a new person that is already famous. You know what I mean? The John Travolta that was on Welcome Back, Kotter, that was probably easy compared to the guy that did Pulp Fiction. Like: Wow, I got to change everybody’s perception about who I am. I don’t get a lot of offers, but it’s okay.
They don’t really make comedies anymore. Not like they used to. I don’t want to be [cast in the role of] the judge. Plus, I’m at this weird place. People are like, “How old is he?”

I’m older than Morgan Freeman was in Shawshank. I’m older than Danny Glover was in Lethal Weapon. You know what I mean? So it’s like: “Is he the guy, or is he like Michael Douglas in Ant-Man?” Like: You go get him, Antie.

Hey, I’ll do it. I’ll shine Michael B. Jordan’s guns. “All right. They’re ready. They’re ready.” I don’t give a fuck. If that’s where I am now, you got to make these adjustments. I’m just trying to stay in the league, man. So I don’t get 25 shots anymore. Now I’m just boxing out. I’m playing good defense. Come in off the bench.

Oh, I totally identify. I mean, I like to say there’s a part of me that’s been every character in the movie. So I’m her, I’m the agent, I’m my character. I’m Anna Kendrick, even. I’m everybody in there. And yeah, Misty’s going through what I just said. It is hard when people actually think they know who you are to give you another chance, to think you’re worthy of another chance. And she doesn’t make it easy for herself. You know what I mean?

I mean, not to that extent. But here’s the thing about self-destructive behavior. Can you be nice while you’re doing it? Some addicts are better than others. I’ve never been that guy. I’ve never been poison on a set. I would even say, and I say this about most actors, 40, 50 percent of your work’s going to be from friends, from people just going, “Hey, you know who’s really cool to hang out with? Chris.” You know what I mean?

I’ve been in that audition. And then Kadeem Hardison walked in the room. You’re like, Kadeem! When I write a Hollywood thing—and I’m not trying to diss anybody—I’ve actually worked jobs. Most of my friends that work in show business have never worked a fucking real job. And if they worked a real job, they were working their way through college, knowing good and well they weren’t going to be there [forever]. So they never really thought the job was going to be their life. So when I write Hollywood, I’m still writing the guy that worked at Red Lobster. I’m writing the guy that loaded trucks at the Daily News. These are jobs that I had. It’s not a Hollywood thing. It’s an everywhere thing.
Why’d I cast myself? I don’t know. I guess I could have given it to somebody. I did think about it. It’s just like, “Eh, it’s not that time yet.”

You know what? It was like a quick on-set thing, basically, so I’m not the same guy in Top Five. A lot of directors, a lot of Black directors, have this hat uniform. They have a hat, and the hat’s got the name on it. So it’s Spike. It was the Hughes brothers. It was Matty Rich. There’s this uniform in being a Black director sometimes. It’s my homage to Robert Townsend and Reggie Hudlin and Malcolm Lee, and all these guys.

I mean, a little. I had a brother who struggled with alcohol, yes. It’s a lot of other people I’ve met. We just have so much mental illness now. And there’s something about—it’s weird. When you’re the sibling of somebody like that, or even my brother, your friends, everybody around you, only sees the drunk person, only sees the manic schizophrenic person, but you always see the person you grew up with. You still remember this brother that was like your best friend, and you don’t give that up. No matter what behavior you see, you’re just holding on [to] all the hope in the world that you can get that brother back. And that’s what Misty goes through. A lot of people are like, “Well, just leave him.” It’s like, “Nah, man. You didn’t know him like I knew him.”
I know some dead people. I know a lot of dead people. How old are you?

I’ll give you about 12 years, 15 years. You start losing the people that just don’t eat right. Just as simple as that. It’s not even the addicts who start going. And it’s not even that they OD; it’s just at some point your body can’t fight this fight anymore. So [in your] 50s, you start losing people. You start losing people to natural causes sometimes. It’s crazy.

There’s a weird statistic I read a long time ago. Of the 45 presidents, like 35 of them lost a father or a parent early in life. It makes you grow up. It’ll make you or break you. So yeah, it sobered me up somewhat. My father died in ’88; ’90, I’m on SNL. You know what I mean? So it’s like, Get serious, figure it out. It’s time to figure it out.
I was successful, I guess. But you got to also remember, at that time, all of us were in the shadow of Eddie Murphy. That’s what success was.

How do I explain it? I bought a house a year and a half, maybe two years before, bought a carriage house in Brooklyn, and I couldn’t afford it. And so I just had to get onstage a lot, and I had to work every gig. You ever read the Gladwell book? The Beatles basically just did more shows than everybody. So it was the Beatles, the Kinks, all these other bands. And the Beatles had the worst boss. The Beatles just did way more shows than everybody. We try to make it into this mythical thing. It’s kind of the same thing, man. I bought a house, and I had to fucking get onstage. Two things happened. I had to get onstage to pay for this house, but I also, privately anyway, I had quit show business in a sense.

I had given up because I’d done CB4, I’d done New Jack City, I’d been on SNL, and I was like, “Okay, I’m going to just be a comedian.” Not that there was any shame to it, but my goal was to be George Wallace. George Wallace is a great comedian, and I love George Wallace because all he did was stand-up and he had a real schedule in his life. Most comedians have no schedule, right? George Wallace works from here to here. He goes on vacation these months of the year. I kind of, in the back of my mind, always wanted a family, always wanted kids. So that was my goal. I do this special, and it’s hard to even explain. The world went crazy.

Here’s a funny story. I got Bring the Pain. I have a VHS of Bring the Pain. I left my agent, and I left my manager, but I have Bring the Pain. Now nobody knows what it is. It’s very similar to Dre and Snoop walking around with The Chronic, trying to get a deal. And by the way, it’s around the same time. So I go to this agent. I’m not going to say his name, whatever. He’s made up with me since. I still got a little ego, and I’m like, “Hey, I’d like you to be my agent.” I give him the Bring the Pain tape. He watches it. He says, “It’s okay.” He goes, and I quote, “I got too many Black guys.” He said, “I got too many Black guys.” Whatever. Cut to two months later, Bring the Pain airs and it’s like this big thing. I’m on Oprah, I’m on 60 Minutes, and that agent calls me back, “Hey. I’ll handle you for 5 percent.”
I thought about it, but then I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t do it. I got too many Black guys. A guy actually said that to me.

Bigger & Blacker is bigger than Bring the Pain. It’s like, what if Bad sold more than Thriller? I got a nice body of work. I’m fine with Head of State, I’m fine with I Think I Love My Wife, [which are] the two films before Top Five, but I think I could have been more serious about directing. That’s the only thing I would say. I never let my ego mess up my stand-up. Every special, I put a ton of work into. Kill the Messenger, I remember Mike Nichols calling me and he said, “I like it, but you got onstage too much. It’s like: You worked it too much. And I can see at points you’re a little robotic. You don’t need to work it that hard.” But yeah, I was learning a lot of things on the fly. I didn’t know anything about money. Lorne Michaels said to me a long time ago, “Everybody loses their first money. But if you’re talented, you’ll make more.” I knew nothing about just the dynamics of fame and how it affected the people around you and all that stuff. It was a lot.

No, I’m not doing it for money. I mean, I’ll make money off of it, but the thing with Misty Green, what I realized when I did Top Five, it’s like: This is my lane as a filmmaker. I’d love to make Man on Fire or something. I would love to make fill-in-the-blank big-budget movie and have this big-budget Rush Hour–esque idea. Those guys are really good at that. It’s not really my thing. I make a tailored suit. My suits are made by hand, by one guy. And it’s okay. A little movie is what I should probably be doing, and it’s where my interest is. And some of those other movies I did was kind of me trying to get famous.

Robert De Niro’s like 84. He’s got a little baby. He’s my man. He’s got literally a two-year-old or something. I mean, I never plan too much ahead. I’m just trying to get as much work done as possible. Having kids that are grown, it seems like I got a little more time on my hands. So hopefully that results in more work. I’m probably going to direct more. I don’t know how much [more] stand-up I’m going to do.

I got like six, seven specials, man. That’s a lot. So I don’t know. I’m not announcing anything or anything, but if I do it, I want to do it right. In sports, especially in football, they always talk about separation. “Can he get separation?” You know what I mean? “Yeah, he’s fast, but is he fast enough? Can he get separation?” And that’s the way I feel, like, as far as stand-up. As long as I can get separation, I’ll do it. Yeah, I’m going to write. That’s basically what it boils down to. Wake up, write. That’s it. Just write, write, write, write, write. Get it all out. ✦
Photography by Richard Burbridge
Production by Kendal Steensen and Felix Cadieu for NEIGHBORS
A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 issue of GQ with the title “Chris Rock’s ‘Small Movie’ Is a Really Big Deal.”

items.title: The OG 'Thomas Crown Affair' Is an Essential Menswear Movie. How Will the Reboot Stack Up?
items.description: Between a stacked roster of Hollywood icons in their prime (Newman, Poitier, Redford) and a cadre of auteur directors on the come-up (Kubrick, Peckinpah, Coppola), the late 1960s produced some of the 20th century’s most stylish movies. Right up there with the
items.author: Jeremy Freed
paragraphs: Between a stacked roster of Hollywood icons in their prime (Newman, Poitier, Redford) and a cadre of auteur directors on the come-up (Kubrick, Peckinpah, Coppola), the late 1960s produced some of the 20th century’s most stylish movies. Right up there with the best of them is The Thomas Crown Affair, a 1968 caper film directed by Norman Jewison and starring Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway. Fast-forward a few days and the same could be said about the 1999 remake starring Bond-era Pierce Brosnan, which is worth watching for the suits alone.

Now, in other news of a formerly Brosnan-led, menswear-centric franchise being rebooted: Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan is the producer, director, and star of a third riff on The Thomas Crown Affair, as he announced at CinemaCon back in April. Judging by the first trailer that dropped last week, the film aims to uphold the sartorial reputation of its forebears.

Hitting theaters in March 2027, Jordan’s The Thomas Crown Affair remake follows the same premise as the 1968 and 1999 versions: a wealthy playboy businessman plots art heists for fun while being pursued by a sexy insurance investigator, played in this iteration by potential future Wonder Woman Adria Arjona. There’s crime, there’s glamour, there’s sexual tension—but most of all, in the spirit of the Thomas Crowns before him, there appears to be plenty of high-octane menswear. The movie’s style credit is bolstered by Ruth E. Carter, the two-time Oscar-winning costume designer of the Black Panther movies, who also dressed Jordan for his Oscar-winning turn in Sinners.

But how will MBJ’s high-fashion Thomas Crown land? In the trailer, he can be seen wearing a stiff gray shirt with a matching tie and trousers by Bottega Veneta. The shirt, marked by the luxury brand’s signature triangle pocket detail, had an odd fit: taut around the torso yet puffy around the biceps. Here’s hoping we’ll see some sharper tailoring in the next preview.

Still, to understand Thomas Crown’s legacy as one of the best-dressed guys in film, and why the forthcoming reboot will likely be a smorgasbord of big-time menswear, it’s worth looking back at what made the original such a gem of classic American style. Beyond Jewison’s use of Mondrian-esque split-screen and a very cool soundtrack by French composer Michel Legrand, McQueen’s wardrobe is a perfect embodiment of late 1960s cool, and a how-to for anyone looking to capture it.

Equal parts finely tailored and adventurous, Crown is the ultimate man’s man: He closes million-dollar deals by day, but also flies planes, plays polo, and does donuts on the beach in a juiced-up dune buggy. Likewise, his wardrobe is split between incredible tailoring and a supremely dialed-in lineup of casual pieces. Crown’s suits are a primer on old-school Savile Row: structured, traditional, and precisely tailored, and his shirts, ties, and pocket squares are equally on point. Crown’s double-Albert style watch chain (attached to a Patek Philippe pocket watch, naturally) is a decidedly advanced swerve, but his Cartier Tank Cintrée looks as good in 2026 as it did in 1968 (or 1928, for that matter).

Off-duty Crown’s casual looks include a parade of hall-of-fame menswear pieces like the Baracuta G9 Harrington jacket (classic navy blue with a red tartan lining), brown suede desert boots, and Persol aviators he wears while piloting his glider (gliders—also extremely cool). Club rules be damned, he plays golf in a non-regulation long-sleeved tee, whacks polo balls in an outfit straight out of a Ralph Lauren campaign, and later dons an Aran sweater for a romantic evening clambake at his beach house. It’s often said that Steve McQueen could look good in anything, and that might be true, but the clothes in this movie hit hard enough to make anyone look several orders of magnitude cooler.

Set to the funky bars of Fela Kuti’s “Gentleman,” the trailer for Jordan’s forthcoming Thomas Crown Affair offers several tantalizing tidbits of what’s in store, including a Ferrari F40, several razor-sharp tuxes, and a glimpse at a watch that’s almost certainly a vintage Piaget. That monochrome Bottega look aside, between Jordan’s leading man chops and Carter’s knack for high-concept menswear, we’re assuredly in good hands.

items.title: The Best Celebrity Watches From the GQ Men of the Year Red Carpet 2026
